meta.title: TrustLab Smart Report — Parameter Interpretation Database

TLP-001.name: Haemoglobin
TLP-001.meas: The amount of haemoglobin, the iron-containing protein inside red cells that carries oxygen from your lungs to every tissue.
TLP-001.sig: The single most-used test for anaemia, which affects roughly half of Indian women and a quarter of men. Low haemoglobin quietly limits energy, concentration and exercise capacity long before it causes obvious symptoms.
TLP-001.ind: Low haemoglobin points to iron, B12 or folate deficiency, blood loss (heavy periods, gut bleeding), chronic illness, kidney disease or a haemoglobin disorder such as thalassaemia trait. High values suggest dehydration, smoking, living at altitude, sleep apnoea or, rarely, polycythaemia.

fy.lo: Your haemoglobin is well below the healthy range, which means your blood is carrying noticeably less oxygen than it should. Iron deficiency from diet, heavy periods or slow gut bleeding is the usual reason; B12 deficiency and chronic illness are others. Please see your doctor soon so the cause can be found and corrected rather than just treated.
fy.blo: Your haemoglobin is slightly below the healthy range, which counts as mild anaemia. In India this is most often iron deficiency, sometimes B12 or folate deficiency or a thalassaemia trait. Look at the MCV and ferritin on this report, add iron-rich foods, and discuss with your doctor whether a short course of supplements is appropriate.
fy.n: Your haemoglobin is in the healthy range, so your blood is carrying oxygen efficiently and anaemia is unlikely right now. Keep it there with a diet that includes iron-rich foods, vitamin C alongside them, and adequate B12 if you are vegetarian. Recheck as part of your routine annual health screen.
fy.hi: Your haemoglobin is above the usual range, which thickens the blood slightly. Dehydration on the day of the test, smoking, sleep apnoea or living at altitude are the common explanations; a bone-marrow condition called polycythaemia is rare. Retest well hydrated, and if it stays high your doctor may check oxygen levels and a hormone called erythropoietin.

TLP-001.notes: Pregnancy: WHO defines anaemia as < 11.0 g/dL (< 10.5 in the second trimester). Children 6–59 months: < 11.0; 5–11 years: < 11.5; 12–14 years: < 12.0. Smokers and people living above 1,000 m run naturally higher values.
TLP-001.src: WHO 2011 haemoglobin thresholds; ICMR; Dacie & Lewis Practical Haematology 12e
TLP-001.retest: If low, recheck 4–8 weeks after starting treatment to confirm response; if unexplained high, repeat after adequate hydration and abstaining from smoking.

TLP-002.name: PCV / Haematocrit
TLP-002.meas: The percentage of your blood volume that is made up of red blood cells.
TLP-002.sig: Haematocrit tracks haemoglobin closely and is the value clinicians use to judge how concentrated or diluted the blood is. It is the parameter most sensitive to hydration status on the day of the test.
TLP-002.ind: A low haematocrit indicates anaemia from nutritional deficiency, blood loss, chronic disease or over-hydration. A high haematocrit points to dehydration, smoking, chronic lung disease, sleep apnoea, testosterone use or polycythaemia vera.

fy.lo: The red-cell fraction of your blood is clearly reduced, which almost always goes hand in hand with a low haemoglobin. Iron or B12 shortage, bleeding and long-standing illness are the common causes. Read this alongside your haemoglobin and red-cell indices, and let your doctor guide further tests to find the cause.
fy.blo: Your haematocrit is a little below the healthy range. This is often an early sign of iron deficiency or simply being well hydrated when the sample was drawn. Check whether your haemoglobin and ferritin agree, focus on iron-rich foods, and recheck in a few weeks if the picture is unclear.
fy.n: Your red cells make up a healthy share of your blood, confirming there is no anaemia and no excessive thickening. Staying well hydrated and eating a balanced diet keeps this stable. No action is needed beyond routine screening.
fy.hi: Your blood is more concentrated than usual. Most often this is dehydration, smoking or heavy exercise before the test; less commonly it reflects low oxygen from lung or sleep problems, testosterone therapy or a marrow disorder. Repeat the test well hydrated, and if still high your doctor may look further.

TLP-002.notes: Newborns run 45–65 %; values fall through infancy and reach adult ranges in adolescence. Pregnancy lowers haematocrit by dilution (typically 33–38 %).
TLP-002.src: Dacie & Lewis Practical Haematology 12e; CLSI EP28-A3c adult intervals
TLP-002.retest: Repeat with haemoglobin after 4–8 weeks of treatment, or after rehydration if the value was unexpectedly high.

TLP-003.name: RBC Count
TLP-003.meas: The number of red blood cells in a microlitre of blood.
TLP-003.sig: Read together with haemoglobin and MCV, the red-cell count separates the two big causes of small red cells: iron deficiency (count falls) and thalassaemia trait (count stays high). That distinction changes treatment completely.
TLP-003.ind: A low count accompanies most anaemias, blood loss and marrow suppression. A high count occurs in thalassaemia trait, dehydration, smoking, hypoxia and polycythaemia vera.

fy.lo: You have fewer red cells than expected, which usually reflects anaemia from iron, B12 or folate shortage, blood loss or a chronic condition. The pattern of your haemoglobin, MCV and ferritin will point to the cause. Your doctor may suggest a nutritional work-up or, if unexplained, further blood tests.
fy.n: Your red cell numbers are where they should be, which supports healthy marrow production and a normal lifespan for your red cells. Adequate protein, iron and B vitamins keep production steady. No action needed beyond your regular check-up.
fy.hi: You have more red cells than typical. If your MCV is low, this pattern is classic for thalassaemia trait, a harmless inherited variant common in India that is often mistaken for iron deficiency. Otherwise dehydration, smoking or low oxygen are likely. Your doctor may order haemoglobin electrophoresis or a repeat count.

TLP-003.notes: Newborns 4.0–6.6; values dip in infancy then rise to adult levels by adolescence. Pregnancy lowers the count slightly by dilution.
TLP-003.src: Dacie & Lewis Practical Haematology 12e; CLSI EP28-A3c
TLP-003.retest: Recheck with a full CBC and, where thalassaemia trait is suspected, add HPLC haemoglobin analysis.

TLP-004.name: MCV
TLP-004.alias: Mean corpuscular volume, Mean cell volume
TLP-004.meas: The average volume of a single red blood cell.
TLP-004.sig: Red-cell size is the first branch point in working out why someone is anaemic: small cells suggest iron deficiency or thalassaemia, large cells suggest B12 or folate deficiency, alcohol or thyroid problems. It often shifts before haemoglobin does.
TLP-004.ind: Low MCV (microcytosis) indicates iron deficiency, thalassaemia trait or anaemia of chronic disease. High MCV (macrocytosis) indicates B12 or folate deficiency, alcohol excess, liver disease, hypothyroidism, some medicines or a raised reticulocyte count.

fy.lo: Your red cells are smaller than average. In India the two common reasons are iron deficiency and thalassaemia trait; a normal or high red-cell count with a low MCV favours the trait. Check your ferritin, and if iron is normal ask your doctor about a haemoglobin HPLC test before taking iron tablets.
fy.n: Your red cells are a normal size, which makes both iron deficiency and B12/folate deficiency less likely as causes of any tiredness. A mixed deficiency can occasionally hide behind a normal MCV, so the RDW and ferritin are worth a glance. Nothing more is needed here.
fy.hi: Your red cells are larger than usual. Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency is the most frequent cause, especially on a vegetarian diet; alcohol, thyroid underactivity, liver disease and certain medicines are others. Your doctor will likely check B12, folate and thyroid levels and review any regular medication.

TLP-004.notes: Children have lower MCVs (about 70–86 fL from 6 months to 6 years); newborns are higher (95–120 fL). A modest rise is normal in later pregnancy.
TLP-004.src: Dacie & Lewis Practical Haematology 12e; CLSI EP28-A3c
TLP-004.retest: Repeat 2–3 months after treating a deficiency; MCV normalises slowly because red cells live about 120 days.

TLP-005.name: MCH
TLP-005.alias: Mean corpuscular haemoglobin, Mean cell haemoglobin
TLP-005.meas: The average weight of haemoglobin contained in one red blood cell.
TLP-005.sig: MCH moves in step with MCV and tells you whether each red cell is adequately filled with haemoglobin. A low MCH is one of the earliest laboratory clues to iron-restricted red-cell production.
TLP-005.ind: Low MCH indicates iron deficiency, thalassaemia trait or chronic inflammation limiting iron supply. High MCH accompanies macrocytosis from B12 or folate deficiency, alcohol or liver disease.

fy.lo: Each of your red cells is carrying less haemoglobin than it should, which is the hallmark of iron-limited blood production. Poor iron intake, heavy periods or blood loss are the usual reasons; thalassaemia trait can look identical. Ask your doctor to check ferritin before starting iron so the right cause is treated.
fy.n: Each of your red cells holds a healthy amount of haemoglobin, so iron supply to the bone marrow is currently adequate. This is a good sign even if your total haemoglobin is slightly off. Maintain iron-rich foods and routine screening.
fy.hi: Your red cells are larger and carry more haemoglobin than usual, which follows the same pattern as a raised MCV. B12 or folate shortage, alcohol or liver and thyroid problems are typical causes. This finding is best read with the MCV; your doctor may test B12 and folate.

TLP-005.notes: Children aged 6 months to 6 years have lower values (about 23–29 pg). MCH is derived from haemoglobin and red-cell count, so it is unaffected by mild sample storage changes that raise MCV.
TLP-005.src: Dacie & Lewis Practical Haematology 12e; CLSI EP28-A3c
TLP-005.retest: Recheck with a CBC 2–3 months after correcting a deficiency.

TLP-006.name: MCHC
TLP-006.meas: How concentrated the haemoglobin is inside your red cells, expressed as grams per decilitre of packed red cells.
TLP-006.sig: MCHC falls only when iron restriction is fairly established, so it is a specific marker of hypochromic anaemia. A genuinely raised MCHC is uncommon and points to abnormally shaped red cells, making it a useful smear trigger.
TLP-006.ind: Low MCHC indicates iron deficiency anaemia or thalassaemia. High MCHC suggests hereditary spherocytosis, autoimmune haemolysis or a sample artefact such as lipaemia or cold agglutinins.

fy.lo: The haemoglobin inside your red cells is diluted, giving them a pale, 'hypochromic' appearance. This usually means iron deficiency has been present for a while, or reflects thalassaemia trait. Your ferritin and smear will help distinguish the two; your doctor can then advise on iron replacement or further testing.
fy.n: Your red cells are normally filled with haemoglobin, which argues against significant iron deficiency and against the cell-shape disorders that raise this value. This is a reassuring finding that needs no follow-up on its own.
fy.hi: A raised MCHC is unusual and often turns out to be a sample effect, such as high blood fats or cold-reacting antibodies. When genuine, it suggests rounded red cells, as in hereditary spherocytosis, or immune haemolysis. The lab typically reviews the smear; your doctor may repeat the test or add a haemolysis screen.

TLP-006.notes: MCHC is a calculated index (Hb ÷ Hct); it is relatively stable across age groups. Values above 37 g/dL are rarely physiological and warrant sample review.
TLP-006.src: Dacie & Lewis Practical Haematology 12e; CLSI EP28-A3c
TLP-006.retest: If high, repeat on a fresh, warmed sample with smear review; if low, recheck after iron therapy.

TLP-007.name: RDW
TLP-007.meas: How much your red blood cells vary in size from one another.
TLP-007.sig: A rising RDW is often the earliest sign that iron or vitamin stores are running short, appearing before haemoglobin drops. It also helps separate iron deficiency (RDW high) from thalassaemia trait (RDW usually normal).
TLP-007.ind: A high RDW indicates a mixed population of cells from iron, B12 or folate deficiency, recent transfusion, recovering marrow or haemolysis. A low RDW has no clinical significance.

fy.n: Your red cells are a uniform size, which means your marrow is producing them steadily from adequate iron and vitamin supplies. Together with a normal MCV, this makes an early nutritional deficiency unlikely. Nothing needs to be done.
fy.bhi: Your red cells vary in size slightly more than usual. This can be the first hint of a developing iron or B12/folate shortage, or simply recovery after a recent illness or blood donation. Check ferritin and B12 if you feel tired, and repeat the CBC in about three months.
fy.hi: Your red cells vary markedly in size, meaning a mixture of old and new, small and large cells is circulating. This most often reflects iron deficiency, sometimes combined with B12 or folate deficiency, or a marrow recovering from illness. Your doctor may order iron studies and vitamin levels to pinpoint the cause.

TLP-007.notes: Reference limits differ slightly between analysers; the upper limit ranges from 14.0 to 15.0 % depending on platform. Newborns run higher (up to 17 %).
TLP-007.src: Dacie & Lewis Practical Haematology 12e; analyser-derived CLSI intervals
TLP-007.retest: Repeat after 8–12 weeks of correcting a deficiency; RDW normalises once the older, abnormal cells have been replaced.

TLP-008.name: WBC Total
TLP-008.meas: The total number of white blood cells, your infection-fighting cells, in a microlitre of blood.
TLP-008.sig: White cells rise within hours of infection, injury or stress and fall when the marrow is suppressed. A total count outside range is a prompt to look at the individual cell types below it, which carry the real diagnostic information.
TLP-008.ind: A high count suggests bacterial infection, inflammation, steroid use, smoking, stress or, when very high, a blood cancer such as leukaemia. A low count points to viral infection, vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, autoimmune disease, some medicines, chemotherapy or a benign ethnic variant.

fy.lo: Your white cell count is clearly low, which can leave you more open to infection. A recent viral illness, certain medicines (including some for thyroid, epilepsy or pain), B12 deficiency or autoimmune conditions are common causes. Please see your doctor promptly, particularly if you have fever, mouth ulcers or repeated infections.
fy.blo: Your white cell count is just under the usual range. Many healthy people, especially of South Asian or African ancestry, naturally sit here, and a recent viral infection can also cause a temporary dip. If your neutrophil count is adequate and you feel well, simply repeat the test in a few weeks.
fy.n: Your white cell count is within the healthy range, indicating no active infection or inflammation that the marrow is responding to. Good sleep, not smoking and managing stress help keep it stable. No follow-up is required.
fy.bhi: Your white cell count is mildly raised. This is commonly seen with a current or recent infection, smoking, physical stress, pregnancy or steroid tablets. Look at which cell type is raised in the differential. If you are otherwise well, a repeat count in two to four weeks usually settles the question.
fy.hi: Your white cell count is substantially raised, most often because your body is fighting a significant infection or inflammation, or because of steroid medication. Very high counts occasionally indicate a bone marrow disorder. Your doctor should review this together with the differential and smear, and may repeat it once any infection has resolved.

TLP-008.notes: Children have higher counts (up to 15,000–17,000 in infants, 5,000–13,000 in pre-school years). Pregnancy raises the count to 6,000–16,000, and labour higher still. Benign ethnic neutropenia can give totals of 3,000–4,000 in healthy adults.
TLP-008.src: Dacie & Lewis Practical Haematology 12e; CLSI EP28-A3c
TLP-008.retest: Repeat 2–4 weeks after an infection has cleared, or sooner if the count is very low or very high with symptoms.

TLP-009.name: Neutrophils %
TLP-009.meas: The share of your white blood cells that are neutrophils, the first responders against bacterial infection.
TLP-009.sig: Neutrophils dominate the white cell count and surge in bacterial infection, tissue injury and stress. The percentage is a screening figure; the absolute neutrophil count is the number that actually governs infection risk.
TLP-009.ind: A high percentage indicates bacterial infection, inflammation, steroids, smoking, stress or heavy exercise. A low percentage typically indicates a viral infection, drug effect, B12 deficiency or a relative rise in lymphocytes.

fy.lo: Neutrophils make up a smaller share of your white cells than usual. This often means a viral infection has temporarily shifted the balance toward lymphocytes, or that a medicine or vitamin shortage is affecting neutrophil production. Check the absolute neutrophil count; if that is low too, your doctor should review it.
fy.n: Neutrophils make up a healthy proportion of your white cells, which is what we expect when there is no active bacterial infection or unusual stress on the body. No action is required.
fy.hi: Neutrophils make up a larger share of your white cells than usual, the typical response to a bacterial infection, an injury, physical or emotional stress, smoking or steroid tablets. If you have symptoms of infection, see your doctor; otherwise repeating the count once you are well usually shows it has settled.

TLP-009.notes: In children under about 5 years lymphocytes normally outnumber neutrophils, so lower neutrophil percentages (30–50 %) are expected. The percentage must always be interpreted with the absolute count.
TLP-009.retest: Repeat with a CBC 2–4 weeks after recovery from any infection.

TLP-010.name: Lymphocytes %
TLP-010.meas: The share of your white blood cells that are lymphocytes, the cells that fight viruses and make antibodies.
TLP-010.sig: Lymphocytes rise in viral infections and some chronic conditions, and fall with steroids, acute stress or HIV. Because it is a percentage, a shift here is often a mirror image of what the neutrophils are doing.
TLP-010.ind: A high percentage indicates viral infections (including dengue, mononucleosis, hepatitis), tuberculosis, thyroid overactivity or, if persistent and high, a lymphoid disorder. A low percentage indicates steroid use, acute infection or stress, HIV, malnutrition or immunosuppressive therapy.

fy.lo: Lymphocytes form a smaller share of your white cells than usual. Most often this is simply because neutrophils have risen during an infection or stress, but steroid medicines and some immune conditions can also lower it. Look at the absolute lymphocyte count; if that is low as well, discuss it with your doctor.
fy.n: Lymphocytes make up an appropriate proportion of your white cells, consistent with a balanced immune system that is not currently responding to a viral illness. No follow-up is needed.
fy.hi: Lymphocytes form a larger share of your white cells than usual, which is the expected pattern during and after a viral infection such as a cold, flu or dengue. Persistent elevation can occur with tuberculosis or thyroid problems and, rarely, a lymphocyte disorder. If it remains high on a repeat test, your doctor may examine the smear.

TLP-010.notes: Children under about 5 years normally have lymphocyte percentages of 40–70 %, so adult limits do not apply to them.
TLP-010.retest: Repeat 3–4 weeks after a viral illness if the percentage was high.

TLP-011.name: Monocytes %
TLP-011.meas: The share of your white blood cells that are monocytes, which clear debris and fight chronic infections.
TLP-011.sig: Monocytes rise in slow-burning infections such as tuberculosis, in chronic inflammation and during recovery from acute infection. A persistently high monocyte fraction is a recognised marker of long-term inflammatory load.
TLP-011.ind: A high percentage indicates tuberculosis, chronic bacterial or parasitic infection, autoimmune disease, recovery from infection or, rarely, a chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia. A low percentage is rarely significant on its own.

fy.n: Monocytes make up a normal share of your white cells, which suggests there is no long-standing infection or chronic inflammation demanding extra clean-up cells. No action needed.
fy.hi: Monocytes form a larger share of your white cells than usual. This commonly happens while recovering from an infection, with chronic infections like tuberculosis, or with autoimmune conditions. If the absolute monocyte count is also raised on a repeat sample in a few weeks, your doctor may look for a chronic source of inflammation.

TLP-011.notes: Neonates have transiently higher monocyte fractions. Percentages should be read with the absolute monocyte count.
TLP-011.retest: If raised, repeat CBC in 4–6 weeks once any acute infection has settled.

TLP-012.name: Eosinophils%
TLP-012.meas: The share of your white blood cells that are eosinophils, which respond to allergies and parasitic worms.
TLP-012.sig: In India a raised eosinophil fraction is most often caused by intestinal worms or allergic airway disease, both readily treatable. It is a cheap, useful pointer that frequently explains a chronic cough, wheeze or itch.
TLP-012.ind: A high percentage indicates allergy (asthma, rhinitis, eczema), parasitic infestation, drug reactions, skin disease or, when very high and persistent, hypereosinophilic syndromes. A low percentage has no clinical significance.

fy.n: Your eosinophils are in the normal proportion, which makes an active allergic reaction or a parasitic infection unlikely as a cause for any current symptoms. No follow-up is needed.
fy.bhi: Your eosinophils are a little higher than usual. Seasonal allergies, mild asthma, eczema or an intestinal worm infection are the usual reasons, and some medicines can do the same. If you have itching, wheeze or gut symptoms, mention it to your doctor; a stool test or deworming is often all that is required.
fy.hi: Your eosinophils are clearly raised, which points strongly to allergy, a parasitic infection or a reaction to a medicine. Persistently very high levels can occasionally affect the heart or lungs, so this deserves attention. Your doctor may check the absolute count, a stool examination and, if needed, IgE levels.

TLP-012.notes: Eosinophil percentages show a morning-low, evening-high daily rhythm. Interpret with the absolute eosinophil count.
TLP-012.retest: Repeat 4–6 weeks after treating allergy or parasitic infection to confirm the count has fallen.

TLP-013.name: Basophils%
TLP-013.meas: The share of your white blood cells that are basophils, the rarest white cell type, which releases histamine in allergic reactions.
TLP-013.sig: Basophils are normally so scarce that any sustained rise is worth noticing. Persistently raised basophils are a classic early clue to chronic myeloid leukaemia and other myeloproliferative disorders.
TLP-013.ind: A high percentage indicates chronic myeloid leukaemia or other myeloproliferative disease, hypothyroidism, allergic reactions, ulcerative colitis or chickenpox. A low percentage is not clinically significant.

fy.n: Your basophils are at the expected trace level, which is normal for almost everyone and shows no sign of the allergic or marrow-related processes that raise them. There is nothing here to act on beyond routine screening.
fy.hi: Your basophils are higher than the usual trace level. Allergic conditions, an underactive thyroid or inflammatory bowel disease can cause a mild rise, and a single raised value is often a counting artefact. Because a sustained rise can signal a bone marrow disorder, the lab reviews the smear and your doctor may repeat the count in a few weeks.

TLP-013.notes: Automated counts of basophils are imprecise at low numbers; a raised value is usually confirmed on a manual differential.
TLP-013.retest: If raised, repeat CBC with manual differential in 4 weeks.

TLP-014.name: Platelet Count
TLP-014.meas: The number of platelets, the small cell fragments that plug damaged blood vessels and start clotting.
TLP-014.sig: Platelets are the frontline of bleeding control; a fall is the key laboratory sign in dengue and a range of drug and immune conditions. Marked highs are also important, as they raise clotting risk and can signal a marrow disorder.
TLP-014.ind: A low count indicates dengue and other viral infections, immune thrombocytopenia, liver disease with enlarged spleen, B12 deficiency, medicines (including heparin, some antibiotics), pregnancy, or marrow disease. A high count indicates iron deficiency, infection, inflammation, post-surgery states or essential thrombocythaemia.

fy.lo: Your platelet count is significantly low, which can cause easy bruising, gum or nose bleeding and, at very low levels, more serious bleeding. Viral infections such as dengue, immune reactions, liver disease and certain medicines are common causes. Please contact your doctor today, and seek urgent care if you notice bleeding, a rash of tiny red spots or severe headache.
fy.blo: Your platelet count is a little below the usual range. A recent viral illness, mild immune effects, alcohol, some medicines or pregnancy often account for this, and clumping in the sample tube can falsely lower the count. Avoid unnecessary painkillers like aspirin or ibuprofen, and repeat the test in one to two weeks.
fy.n: Your platelet count is healthy, which means your blood can clot normally and there is no sign of marrow suppression or excess platelet production. No action needed.
fy.bhi: Your platelet count is modestly raised. This is most often a 'reactive' response to iron deficiency, infection, inflammation or recent surgery, and it settles once the trigger resolves. Check your ferritin and CRP on this report. A repeat count in four to six weeks usually confirms it has returned to normal.
fy.hi: Your platelet count is well above the normal range. Reactive causes such as severe iron deficiency, chronic inflammation, infection or spleen removal are still the most likely, but a persistently high count can indicate essential thrombocythaemia, a marrow condition that raises clotting risk. Your doctor should review this and may order iron studies, inflammatory markers and a smear.

TLP-014.notes: Some individuals have EDTA-induced platelet clumping giving a falsely low count; a citrate sample corrects this. Pregnancy lowers platelets modestly (gestational thrombocytopenia, usually > 1,00,000). Displayed in Indian lakh notation.
TLP-014.src: Dacie & Lewis Practical Haematology 12e; ASH ITP guideline 2019; WHO dengue guidelines
TLP-014.retest: If low, repeat within 1–2 weeks (daily in suspected dengue); if high, repeat after 4–6 weeks once any infection or iron deficiency is treated.

TLP-015.name: MPV
TLP-015.meas: The average size of your platelets.
TLP-015.sig: Young platelets are larger, so MPV tells you whether a low platelet count is due to rapid destruction (marrow compensating, MPV high) or reduced production (MPV normal or low). Larger platelets are also more active and have been linked to cardiovascular risk.
TLP-015.ind: A high MPV indicates increased platelet turnover, as in immune thrombocytopenia, dengue recovery, myeloproliferative disorders, hyperthyroidism or diabetes. A low MPV indicates reduced production from marrow suppression, aplastic anaemia, chemotherapy or inherited platelet disorders.

fy.lo: Your platelets are smaller than average, suggesting the marrow is releasing fewer fresh, large platelets. If your platelet count is also low, this can point to reduced production, as with some medicines, a viral effect on the marrow or a vitamin deficiency. On its own it is rarely important; your doctor will interpret it with the platelet count.
fy.n: Your platelets are a normal size, which suggests balanced production and turnover in the bone marrow with no excess of young, oversized platelets. Read with a normal platelet count this is fully reassuring, and nothing needs to be done.
fy.hi: Your platelets are larger than average, which usually means your marrow is releasing young platelets quickly, for example while recovering from a viral illness or in immune-related platelet loss. Large, more active platelets have also been associated with diabetes and heart disease risk. This is best read alongside your platelet count; no action is needed if that is normal.

TLP-015.notes: MPV rises with EDTA storage time (up to 30 % over several hours), so results depend on how quickly the sample was processed. Reference limits vary by analyser (roughly 7–12 fL).
TLP-015.src: Dacie & Lewis Practical Haematology 12e; analyser-derived CLSI intervals
TLP-015.retest: Only worth repeating alongside an abnormal platelet count.

TLP-016.name: Peripheral Smear
TLP-016.alias: Blood film, PBS, Peripheral blood picture
TLP-016.meas: A pathologist's microscope description of the size, shape and colour of your red cells, white cells and platelets.
TLP-016.sig: Analysers count cells; the smear looks at them. It confirms or corrects machine flags, detects malaria parasites, abnormal or immature cells and cell-shape changes that no automated index can capture.
TLP-016.ind: Microcytic hypochromic cells suggest iron deficiency or thalassaemia; macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils suggest B12/folate deficiency; spherocytes or fragmented cells suggest haemolysis; blasts or atypical cells suggest leukaemia or infection; parasites indicate malaria or filaria; platelet clumps explain a falsely low count.

rng.n: Normal picture (Normocytic normochromic; WBC and platelets adequate)

fy.n: Under the microscope your red cells are of normal size and colour, your white cells look mature and appropriately distributed, and your platelets are adequate with no clumping. This confirms the automated counts and rules out visible parasites or abnormal cells. No follow-up is needed.
fy.hi: The pathologist has noted a feature outside the usual picture; the report text describes exactly what was seen. Common findings are small pale cells (iron deficiency or thalassaemia trait), large cells (B12/folate shortage), platelet clumps that falsely lower the count, or reactive white cells after infection. Rarely, immature cells or parasites need prompt review. Discuss the comment with your doctor.

TLP-016.notes: Smear morphology in children and newborns differs (more lymphocytes, occasional nucleated red cells in neonates). Findings are qualitative and observer-dependent; significant findings are cross-checked by a second reviewer.
TLP-016.src: Dacie & Lewis Practical Haematology 12e; ICSH guidelines for blood film review
TLP-016.retest: Repeat only if the pathologist recommends it or the CBC changes.

any.label: Normocytic normochromic; WBC and platelets adequate

TLP-017.name: Absolute Neutrophils
TLP-017.meas: The actual number of neutrophils in a microlitre of blood, calculated from the total white count and the neutrophil percentage.
TLP-017.sig: This is the number that determines your real-world risk of bacterial infection, not the percentage. Below about 1,000 the risk climbs steeply, and below 500 even minor infections can become serious.
TLP-017.ind: A low count indicates viral infection, drug-induced marrow suppression, B12 or folate deficiency, autoimmune disease, hypersplenism or benign ethnic neutropenia. A high count indicates bacterial infection, inflammation, steroids, smoking, stress, or a myeloproliferative disorder.

fy.lo: Your neutrophil count is low enough to meaningfully weaken your defence against bacterial infection. Medicines, a recent viral illness, vitamin deficiency or an immune condition are the usual reasons. Contact your doctor promptly, and treat any fever above 38 °C as needing same-day medical attention until the cause is clear.
fy.blo: Your neutrophil count is mildly reduced. Many healthy people of South Asian ancestry naturally sit in this zone (benign ethnic neutropenia) and a passing viral infection is another common cause. If you are well and have no recurrent infections, a repeat count in four to six weeks is usually all that is needed.
fy.n: Your neutrophil count is in the healthy range, so your first-line defence against bacterial infection is intact. There is no sign of marrow suppression or of an active bacterial process. Nothing further is needed.
fy.hi: Your neutrophil count is raised, which is your body's standard response to a bacterial infection, an injury, surgery or acute stress; smoking and steroid tablets also push it up. If you have symptoms of infection, see your doctor. Otherwise a repeat once you are well should show it back in range; if it stays high, further review is sensible.

TLP-017.notes: Benign ethnic neutropenia: counts of 1,000–1,500 are normal for some healthy individuals of Indian, African and Middle Eastern descent. Infants and young children have lower neutrophil counts (about 1,000–8,500). Pregnancy raises the count.
TLP-017.src: Dacie & Lewis Practical Haematology 12e; BSH neutropenia guidance
TLP-017.retest: Repeat in 4–6 weeks if mildly low and asymptomatic; within days if < 1,000 or if fever develops.

TLP-018.name: Absolute Lymphocytes
TLP-018.meas: The actual number of lymphocytes in a microlitre of blood.
TLP-018.sig: A persistently low absolute lymphocyte count is an important, often overlooked marker of impaired immunity, seen in HIV, malnutrition, steroid use and severe illness. A persistently high count is the main screening flag for chronic lymphocytic leukaemia in older adults.
TLP-018.ind: A low count indicates HIV infection, steroid or immunosuppressive treatment, acute severe infection or sepsis, malnutrition, autoimmune disease or radiotherapy. A high count indicates viral infections, tuberculosis, pertussis, or a lymphoproliferative disorder such as CLL.

fy.lo: You have fewer lymphocytes than expected, which can reduce your ability to fight viral infections. A recent severe infection, steroid medicines, poor nutrition or an immune condition are common causes, and a single low reading after illness often recovers on its own. If it persists on a repeat test, your doctor may consider an HIV test and immune review.
fy.n: Your lymphocyte count is in the normal range, which indicates a healthy immune reserve with no sign of the excessive rise seen in some blood disorders. No action is required.
fy.hi: You have more lymphocytes than usual. A recent or current viral infection is by far the most common explanation, and the count returns to normal within weeks. If it remains high on a repeat test, especially if you are over 50, your doctor may ask for smear review or a flow cytometry test to confirm the cells are normal.

TLP-018.notes: Children have much higher lymphocyte counts (up to 10,000 in infants, 2,000–8,000 in pre-school years); adult limits apply from about 12 years. Smoking modestly raises the count.
TLP-018.src: Dacie & Lewis Practical Haematology 12e; iwCLL 2018 (lymphocytosis threshold)
TLP-018.retest: Repeat in 4–6 weeks after an infection; sooner with smear review if very high or with enlarged glands.

TLP-019.name: Absolute Monocytes
TLP-019.meas: The actual number of monocytes in a microlitre of blood.
TLP-019.sig: A raised absolute monocyte count that persists for more than three months is one of the defining criteria for chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia, and more commonly flags tuberculosis or chronic inflammatory disease. The absolute figure is more reliable than the percentage.
TLP-019.ind: A high count indicates tuberculosis, endocarditis, chronic infections, inflammatory bowel disease, autoimmune disorders, recovery from neutropenia or a myelomonocytic disorder. A low count is uncommon and rarely significant, except in hairy cell leukaemia or severe marrow failure.

fy.n: Your monocyte count is within the expected range, which suggests there is no chronic infection or long-running inflammation calling for extra clean-up cells. No follow-up is needed.
fy.bhi: Your monocyte count is slightly raised. This frequently reflects recovery from a recent infection, ongoing mild inflammation or smoking. It usually settles by itself; a repeat count in about six weeks will confirm whether it has.
fy.hi: Your monocyte count is clearly raised. Chronic infections such as tuberculosis, gut or joint inflammation and some autoimmune conditions are the usual reasons; a persistent rise over several months occasionally indicates a marrow disorder. Your doctor may review your symptoms, order a chest X-ray or inflammatory markers, and repeat the count in a few weeks.

TLP-019.notes: Neonates have higher monocyte counts. Persistent monocytosis > 1,000/µL for > 3 months warrants haematology review (WHO 2022 CMML criteria).
TLP-019.src: Dacie & Lewis Practical Haematology 12e; WHO 2022 classification (CMML threshold)
TLP-019.retest: Repeat in 6 weeks if raised; if persistently > 1,000/µL, haematology referral.

TLP-020.name: Absolute Eosinophils
TLP-020.meas: The actual number of eosinophils in a microlitre of blood.
TLP-020.sig: The absolute eosinophil count is the standard way to grade eosinophilia and decide how hard to look for a cause. Above 1,500 that persists, the cells themselves can damage the heart, lungs and nerves, so this threshold matters.
TLP-020.ind: A raised count indicates allergic disease (asthma, rhinitis, atopic eczema), parasitic worm infection, drug hypersensitivity, adrenal insufficiency, skin disorders or, when persistent and high, hypereosinophilic syndrome or eosinophilic leukaemia. A low count is not clinically significant.

fy.n: Your eosinophil count is in the normal range, which makes an active allergic reaction or worm infection an unlikely explanation for any symptoms you may have. Nothing to act on.
fy.bhi: Your eosinophil count is moderately raised. Allergic rhinitis, asthma, eczema, an intestinal worm infection or a new medicine are the usual causes. A stool test for parasites and a review of your allergy symptoms are sensible first steps; many doctors will simply treat for worms and recheck in six weeks.
fy.hi: Your eosinophil count is markedly raised. Parasitic infections (including filaria and strongyloides), severe allergy and drug reactions are the most likely causes, but a count this high that persists needs proper evaluation because eosinophils can injure organs. Please see your doctor; they may arrange stool tests, IgE, a chest X-ray and a repeat count.

TLP-020.notes: Counts follow a daily rhythm (lowest in the morning, highest late evening) and fall with steroid therapy. Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia should be considered in India with counts > 3,000 and cough.
TLP-020.src: Dacie & Lewis Practical Haematology 12e; ICOG-Eo 2012 consensus; WHO 2022
TLP-020.retest: Repeat 4–6 weeks after treatment of allergy or parasites; sooner with organ symptoms.

TLP-021.name: Absolute Basophils
TLP-021.meas: The actual number of basophils in a microlitre of blood.
TLP-021.sig: Basophils are normally very few, so an absolute count that stays above the limit is meaningful. It is one of the earliest laboratory features of chronic myeloid leukaemia, where basophils rise before symptoms appear.
TLP-021.ind: A raised count indicates chronic myeloid leukaemia or other myeloproliferative neoplasms, hypothyroidism, allergic or drug reactions, ulcerative colitis or viral infections such as chickenpox. A low count is not clinically significant.

fy.n: Your basophil count is at the normal trace level, as expected in healthy people, with no hint of the sustained rise seen in allergic states or marrow disorders. No follow-up is required beyond your routine check-up.
fy.hi: Your basophil count is above the usual trace level. A mild rise can come from allergies, an underactive thyroid or bowel inflammation, and analyser counting at such low numbers is imprecise. Because a persistent rise can be an early sign of a marrow disorder, the lab confirms it on the smear and your doctor may repeat the test.

TLP-021.notes: Automated basophil counts have poor precision below 200/µL; confirmation by manual 200-cell differential is standard before acting.
TLP-021.src: Dacie & Lewis Practical Haematology 12e; WHO 2022 classification
TLP-021.retest: If raised, repeat CBC with manual differential in 4 weeks.

TLP-022.name: Reticulocyte Count
TLP-022.meas: The percentage of red cells that are reticulocytes, the young cells released from the marrow in the last one to two days.
TLP-022.sig: This is the direct read-out of how hard your bone marrow is working. In anaemia it separates under-production (low retics: nutritional deficiency, marrow suppression) from over-destruction or bleeding (high retics), and it is the earliest sign that iron or B12 treatment is working.
TLP-022.ind: A low count in anaemia indicates iron, B12 or folate deficiency, kidney disease, marrow suppression by drugs or aplastic anaemia. A high count indicates haemolysis (including dapsone- or G6PD-related), recent blood loss or a marrow response to treatment.

fy.lo: Your marrow is releasing fewer new red cells than expected. If you are anaemic, this suggests the problem is under-production, typically from iron, B12 or folate shortage, kidney disease or a medicine affecting the marrow. Your doctor will match this with your ferritin and vitamin levels to decide what to replace.
fy.n: Your marrow is producing red cells at a normal, steady rate. If you are not anaemic this is entirely reassuring; if you are, it hints the marrow is not fully compensating and a nutritional cause should be checked. No separate action is needed for this result.
fy.hi: Your marrow is producing red cells faster than usual, which means it is replacing cells being lost or destroyed. Recovery after bleeding, a response to iron or B12 treatment, or ongoing haemolysis (red-cell breakdown, for example from dapsone or a G6PD deficiency) are the common reasons. Your doctor may check bilirubin and LDH to look for haemolysis.

TLP-022.notes: Newborns have counts of 2–6 % in the first week. In significant anaemia the percentage overstates production; the corrected reticulocyte count or absolute count (25,000–75,000/µL) should be used. Dapsone therapy monitoring uses this test to detect haemolysis.
TLP-022.src: Dacie & Lewis Practical Haematology 12e; ICSH reticulocyte guidelines
TLP-022.retest: Recheck 7–10 days after starting iron or B12 therapy to confirm response; monthly on dapsone or other haemolysis-prone drugs.

TLP-023.name: Ferritin
TLP-023.meas: The protein that stores iron in your body; the blood level mirrors your total iron reserves.
TLP-023.sig: Ferritin is the best single test for iron deficiency, dropping well before haemoglobin does. It is also an inflammation marker, so a normal or high value does not exclude deficiency when the body is inflamed or the liver is fatty.
TLP-023.ind: Low ferritin is diagnostic of iron deficiency from poor intake, heavy periods, pregnancy demands or gut blood loss. High ferritin indicates inflammation, infection, fatty liver or alcohol-related liver injury, metabolic syndrome, iron overload (haemochromatosis, repeated transfusion) or, when very high, haemophagocytic syndromes and some cancers.

fy.lo: Your iron stores are depleted; this is iron deficiency even if your haemoglobin is still normal. Low dietary iron, heavy periods, pregnancy or slow gut blood loss are the usual reasons, and tiredness, hair fall and poor stamina are common. Your doctor can advise iron replacement and, especially in men or after menopause, may look for a source of bleeding.
fy.blo: Your iron stores are on the low side. This zone often precedes true deficiency, particularly in menstruating women, vegetarians, regular blood donors and endurance athletes. Increase iron-rich foods with a source of vitamin C, limit tea or coffee with meals, and discuss with your doctor whether a short supplement course is sensible. Recheck in three months.
fy.n: Your iron stores are adequate, which means your body has a healthy reserve to make haemoglobin and support energy and immunity. A balanced diet maintains this. If you have inflammation or fatty liver, ferritin can read falsely normal, so an unexpectedly low MCV still deserves a look at iron saturation.
fy.bhi: Your ferritin is at or slightly above the upper limit. In most people this reflects inflammation, a recent infection, fatty liver, alcohol or metabolic syndrome rather than genuine iron overload. Check your CRP, liver enzymes and iron saturation on this report. If saturation is normal, a repeat in three months after addressing lifestyle factors is usually all that is needed.
fy.hi: Your ferritin is substantially raised. Common causes include ongoing inflammation or infection, liver disease, heavy alcohol use and metabolic syndrome; true iron overload from haemochromatosis is less common but important to exclude, especially if iron saturation is also high. Your doctor may repeat the test with iron saturation, liver tests and CRP, and consider genetic testing if overload is suspected.

TLP-023.notes: WHO 2020: ferritin < 15 ng/mL indicates depleted stores in adults, < 12 in children under 5; in the presence of inflammation (CRP > 5) a cut-off of < 70 is used. Pregnancy: < 30 indicates deficiency. Post-menopausal women may use male limits. Ferritin > 1,000 warrants urgent evaluation.
TLP-023.src: WHO 2020 ferritin guideline; BSH iron deficiency guideline 2021; Endocrine/AASLD haemochromatosis guidance
TLP-023.retest: Recheck 3 months after starting iron; if raised, repeat with CRP and iron saturation after 6–12 weeks.

TLP-024.name: Serum Iron
TLP-024.meas: The amount of iron currently travelling in your blood bound to its carrier protein, transferrin.
TLP-024.sig: Serum iron swings by up to 30 % through the day and drops within hours of a meal, infection or menstruation, so on its own it is an unreliable measure of iron status. Its value lies in the saturation calculation and in detecting iron overload.
TLP-024.ind: Low serum iron indicates iron deficiency or the iron-sequestration of chronic inflammation and infection. High serum iron indicates haemochromatosis, recent iron tablets or injections, haemolysis, liver disease, or repeated transfusions.

fy.lo: The iron circulating in your blood is low. This is consistent with iron deficiency, but a temporary drop also happens with any infection or inflammation and after a meal. Read it with ferritin and iron saturation: if those are low too, iron replacement is likely; if ferritin is normal or high, inflammation is the more likely explanation.
fy.n: The iron circulating in your blood is in the normal range, supporting adequate iron delivery to the marrow. Because serum iron varies so much through the day, this figure should always be read with ferritin and saturation; if those are normal too, your iron status is healthy.
fy.hi: The iron circulating in your blood is higher than usual. Taking an iron supplement in the last day or two is the most common reason, followed by liver disease and red cell breakdown; if iron saturation is also high, inherited iron overload should be considered. Stop supplements for a week and repeat as a fasting morning sample before drawing conclusions.

TLP-024.notes: Best drawn fasting in the morning; values are 20–30 % lower in the afternoon. Avoid iron supplements for 24 hours before testing. Children have lower values (about 50–120 µg/dL); women run slightly lower than men.
TLP-024.src: Tietz Textbook of Clinical Chemistry; BSH iron deficiency guideline 2021
TLP-024.retest: Repeat as a morning fasting sample off iron supplements if the result was unexpected.

TLP-025.name: TIBC
TLP-025.alias: Total iron binding capacity, Transferrin capacity
TLP-025.meas: The maximum amount of iron your blood proteins (mainly transferrin) could carry, which reflects how much transferrin your liver is making.
TLP-025.sig: The liver makes more transferrin when iron is scarce and less when it is plentiful or when inflammation is present. A high TIBC therefore helps confirm true iron deficiency, and a low TIBC points toward inflammation or overload instead.
TLP-025.ind: High TIBC indicates iron deficiency, pregnancy or oestrogen therapy. Low TIBC indicates anaemia of chronic disease, inflammation, liver disease, malnutrition, nephrotic syndrome or iron overload.

fy.lo: Your blood's iron-carrying capacity is reduced, meaning your liver is making less transferrin. This is typical of chronic inflammation or infection, liver disease or poor protein nutrition, and it also occurs in iron overload. It usually means a low haemoglobin is not simple iron deficiency; your doctor will look at ferritin and CRP to sort this out.
fy.n: Your blood's iron-carrying capacity is normal, which indicates healthy transferrin production and argues against both marked iron deficiency and significant inflammation. No action is needed for this result.
fy.hi: Your blood's iron-carrying capacity is raised, which is what the body does when iron is in short supply: it makes more carrier protein to grab whatever iron is available. Together with a low ferritin this confirms iron deficiency. Pregnancy and oral contraceptives also raise TIBC. Your doctor may recommend iron replacement and, in some cases, a search for blood loss.

TLP-025.notes: TIBC rises in pregnancy and with oestrogen-containing contraceptives independent of iron status. Reference limits vary modestly by method (240–450 µg/dL).
TLP-025.src: Tietz Textbook of Clinical Chemistry; BSH iron deficiency guideline 2021
TLP-025.retest: Repeat with full iron studies 3 months after iron treatment.

TLP-026.name: Iron Saturation
TLP-026.dn: Transferrin saturation (% of carrier filled with iron)
TLP-026.meas: The percentage of your iron-carrying protein that is actually loaded with iron, calculated as serum iron divided by TIBC.
TLP-026.sig: Saturation is the most useful indicator of iron available for red-cell production and the standard screening test for iron overload. A saturation above 45 % is the accepted trigger for haemochromatosis testing.
TLP-026.ind: Low saturation indicates iron deficiency or functional iron restriction from inflammation and chronic kidney disease. High saturation indicates hereditary haemochromatosis, recent iron therapy, haemolysis, liver disease, ineffective red-cell production or transfusion overload.

fy.lo: Only a small fraction of your iron-carrier protein is loaded with iron, meaning the marrow is not getting enough to make red cells efficiently. Iron deficiency is the usual cause; in people with kidney disease or chronic inflammation it can occur even when ferritin looks normal. Your doctor may suggest iron replacement and look into why iron is short.
fy.blo: Your iron saturation is a little below the healthy range, suggesting iron supply is just keeping up. This is common in menstruating women, vegetarians and endurance athletes, and a low-iron day or a mild infection can also do it. Improve dietary iron, check your ferritin, and repeat fasting in the morning in about three months.
fy.n: Your iron saturation is in the healthy range, so iron is being delivered to the marrow efficiently and there is no sign of iron overload. Combined with a normal ferritin this confirms good iron balance. Keep up a varied diet; nothing else is needed.
fy.bhi: Your iron saturation is above the usual limit. Recent iron tablets or a non-fasting afternoon sample can push it up, but a fasting value in this range is the standard trigger to consider inherited iron overload, especially if ferritin is also raised. Repeat as a fasting morning sample off supplements; if still high, your doctor may order HFE gene testing.
fy.hi: Your iron saturation is markedly raised, which most often reflects recent iron supplements or injections, liver disease, or excess iron absorption from haemochromatosis. Persistent high saturation lets iron build up in the liver, heart and joints, so it should not be ignored. Your doctor will repeat it fasting and, if confirmed, arrange ferritin, liver tests and genetic testing.

TLP-026.notes: Calculated from a morning fasting sample for best accuracy. Some guidelines use a lower overload threshold for women (> 45 %) than men (> 50 %). Pregnancy and oral contraceptives lower saturation by raising TIBC.
TLP-026.src: AASLD 2011 / EASL 2022 haemochromatosis guidelines; BSH iron deficiency guideline 2021
TLP-026.retest: Repeat fasting in the morning, off iron supplements for a week, if the result was unexpectedly high or low.

TLP-027.name: UIBC
TLP-027.meas: The spare capacity of your blood's iron-carrier protein, that is, how much more iron transferrin could still bind.
TLP-027.sig: UIBC is the mirror image of saturation: it rises when iron is scarce and falls when iron is abundant or transferrin is low. It is calculated as TIBC minus serum iron and serves mainly as a cross-check on the rest of the iron panel.
TLP-027.ind: High UIBC indicates iron deficiency (lots of empty carrier capacity) or pregnancy. Low UIBC indicates iron overload, recent iron therapy, or reduced transferrin from inflammation, liver disease or malnutrition.

fy.lo: There is little spare room on your iron-carrier protein, which happens either because it is already well loaded with iron (recent supplements, iron overload) or because you are making less carrier protein during inflammation or liver disease. This finding should be read with your saturation and ferritin, which tell the two situations apart; your doctor will interpret them together.
fy.n: The spare iron-carrying capacity in your blood is normal, indicating a healthy balance between iron supply and its transport protein. No action is required for this result.
fy.hi: A large share of your iron-carrier protein is empty, which is typical when iron is in short supply and the body has increased carrier protein to capture more. Alongside a low ferritin, this supports iron deficiency. Pregnancy also raises it. Your doctor may recommend improving iron intake or a supplement course and rechecking in three months.

TLP-027.notes: Derived value (TIBC minus serum iron); its reference limits depend on the method and vary between laboratories (roughly 110–400 µg/dL). Rises in pregnancy and with oestrogen therapy.
TLP-027.src: Tietz Textbook of Clinical Chemistry; laboratory method-derived intervals
TLP-027.retest: Repeat with the full iron panel 3 months after treatment.

TLP-028.name: Prothrombin Time
TLP-028.meas: The number of seconds your plasma takes to clot after a tissue-factor trigger, testing the liver-made clotting factors II, V, VII and X and fibrinogen.
TLP-028.sig: PT is the most sensitive routine test of liver synthetic function and the basis for monitoring warfarin. A prolonged PT before surgery or a procedure flags a bleeding risk that can usually be corrected in advance.
TLP-028.ind: A prolonged PT indicates warfarin or related anticoagulants, vitamin K deficiency (poor diet, antibiotics, malabsorption, obstructive jaundice), liver disease, disseminated intravascular coagulation, or an inherited factor deficiency. A short PT has no clinical significance.

fy.n: Your blood clots within the normal time, which shows your liver is producing adequate clotting factors and your vitamin K status is fine. If you are not on blood thinners this needs no follow-up, and it is reassuring before any planned procedure.
fy.bhi: Your clotting time is slightly longer than usual. If you take warfarin this may be expected. Otherwise mild vitamin K shortage after a course of antibiotics or a poor diet, early liver strain or a sampling issue (underfilled tube) are common reasons. Repeat the test, and mention any planned surgery or unusual bruising to your doctor.
fy.hi: Your clotting time is clearly prolonged, which means your blood takes longer to form a clot and you may bruise or bleed more easily. Anticoagulant medicines, liver disease, vitamin K deficiency or, rarely, an inherited factor problem are the usual reasons. See your doctor promptly, especially before any procedure or dental work, and avoid aspirin-type painkillers until reviewed.

TLP-028.notes: The reference interval is reagent- and instrument-specific; compare with the control value quoted on the report. Newborns have longer PT in the first week. Tube must be filled correctly (9:1 blood-to-citrate) for a valid result.
TLP-028.src: CLSI H21-A5; BSH guideline on investigation of bleeding disorders 2014
TLP-028.retest: Repeat if the tube was underfilled or the result unexpected; on warfarin, monitor via INR as your doctor directs.

TLP-029.name: INR
TLP-029.meas: Your prothrombin time expressed as a standardised ratio so that results are comparable between laboratories worldwide.
TLP-029.sig: INR is the universal language for warfarin dosing: too low and clots are not prevented, too high and bleeding risk rises sharply. In people not on warfarin it is a key part of liver disease scoring and pre-procedure bleeding assessment.
TLP-029.ind: A raised INR indicates warfarin therapy (target usually 2.0–3.0), vitamin K deficiency, liver disease, DIC or factor deficiency. Values below 0.8 are not clinically meaningful.

fy.n: Your INR is in the normal range for someone not taking warfarin, confirming normal clotting-factor production by the liver and adequate vitamin K. If you are on warfarin, a value here is below the usual protective target and you should let your prescribing doctor know.
fy.bhi: Your INR is slightly above the normal range. If you are not on warfarin this is usually mild vitamin K shortage, recent antibiotics, early liver strain or a sample-handling issue. If you take warfarin, a value here is below the common therapeutic target. Either way, share it with your doctor and repeat the test.
fy.hi: Your INR is raised. For someone on warfarin, values of 2 to 3 are usually the intended target, and only readings above that need dose review. If you are not on an anticoagulant, this level suggests liver disease, significant vitamin K deficiency or a clotting factor problem and needs prompt medical review, particularly before surgery or if you notice bleeding.

TLP-029.notes: Therapeutic targets on warfarin: 2.0–3.0 for most indications, 2.5–3.5 for mechanical mitral valves; these bands apply to patients NOT on anticoagulants. INR is not validated for monitoring newer anticoagulants (DOACs).
TLP-029.src: WHO INR standardisation; BSH oral anticoagulation guideline 2011; CLSI H21-A5
TLP-029.retest: Not on warfarin: repeat if unexpectedly raised. On warfarin: monitor at the interval your doctor sets, typically every 4–12 weeks when stable.

TLP-030.name: PT Ratio
TLP-030.dn: PT ratio (your clotting time vs. control)
TLP-030.meas: Your prothrombin time divided by the laboratory's normal control time for the same reagent.
TLP-030.sig: The PT ratio removes day-to-day reagent variation by comparing you with a normal control run alongside. It is the raw ratio from which INR is derived and is easier to read at a glance: 1.0 means you clot exactly like the control.
TLP-030.ind: A raised ratio indicates anticoagulant therapy, liver disease, vitamin K deficiency, DIC or inherited factor deficiency. A ratio below 0.8 has no clinical significance.

fy.n: Your clotting time matches the laboratory's normal control closely, which confirms healthy clotting-factor production and no significant effect from medicines or liver problems. No follow-up is required.
fy.bhi: You are clotting a little more slowly than the normal control. Mild vitamin K shortage, a recent course of antibiotics, early liver strain or a partly filled tube are the usual reasons, and warfarin will do this if you take it. A repeat test, ideally alongside INR and liver tests, will clarify.
fy.hi: You are clotting noticeably more slowly than the normal control, which raises your tendency to bruise or bleed. Anticoagulant medicines, liver disease or vitamin K deficiency are the most likely reasons. Your doctor should review this before any procedure; if you are not on blood thinners, liver tests and a vitamin K trial may be considered.

TLP-030.notes: Ratio depends on the reagent's sensitivity, so it is not transferable between laboratories; INR is used for cross-lab comparison and warfarin monitoring.
TLP-030.retest: Repeat with INR if unexpectedly raised or before an elective procedure.

TLP-031.name: Fibrinogen
TLP-031.meas: The level of fibrinogen, the liver-made protein that is converted into the fibrin mesh of a blood clot.
TLP-031.sig: Fibrinogen is both a clotting factor and an acute-phase protein: it falls dangerously in consumptive states such as DIC and obstetric haemorrhage, and rises with inflammation, where a chronically high level independently predicts heart attack and stroke.
TLP-031.ind: Low fibrinogen indicates DIC, severe liver disease, massive bleeding, thrombolytic therapy, snake envenomation or an inherited deficiency. High fibrinogen indicates acute or chronic inflammation, infection, pregnancy, smoking, obesity, diabetes, cancer and increased cardiovascular risk.

fy.lo: Your fibrinogen is low, which means your blood has less of the raw material needed to build a firm clot, so bleeding can be harder to stop. Severe liver disease, a consumptive clotting process during serious illness, or a rare inherited deficiency are the main causes. Please see your doctor promptly, particularly if you have bleeding, bruising, or are pregnant.
fy.blo: Your fibrinogen is just below the usual range. Mild liver dysfunction, a recent large bleed, some medicines or simply the lower end of your natural variation can explain this. If you have no bleeding symptoms, a repeat test in a few weeks alongside liver function tests is a sensible check.
fy.n: Your fibrinogen is in the healthy range, which means you have enough clot-forming protein for normal healing and there is no sign of the excess seen with ongoing inflammation. Not smoking and keeping weight and blood sugar under control help keep it there.
fy.hi: Your fibrinogen is raised. As an acute-phase protein it climbs with any infection, injury or inflammation, and in pregnancy; if it stays high once you are well, it points to ongoing low-grade inflammation linked to smoking, excess weight or diabetes and to higher heart risk. Address those factors and recheck in about three months, ideally with hsCRP.

TLP-031.notes: Pregnancy raises fibrinogen physiologically to 400–600 mg/dL by the third trimester; obstetric values below 200 are a warning sign. Newborns have lower values. Clauss method assumed; PT-derived fibrinogen reads higher.
TLP-031.src: CLSI H30-A2; BSH DIC guideline 2009; AHA inflammatory-marker statement
TLP-031.retest: Repeat 6–12 weeks after an acute illness if high; urgently with a full coagulation screen if low with bleeding.

TLP-032.name: APTT
TLP-032.alias: Activated partial thromboplastin time, PTT, KCCT
TLP-032.meas: The seconds your plasma takes to clot after a contact activator, testing the intrinsic-pathway factors VIII, IX, XI, XII and the common pathway.
TLP-032.sig: APTT is the screening test for haemophilia and von Willebrand disease and the standard way to monitor heparin. Paradoxically, a prolonged APTT can also signal lupus anticoagulant, an antibody that causes clots and miscarriage rather than bleeding.
TLP-032.ind: A prolonged APTT indicates heparin, haemophilia A or B, von Willebrand disease, factor XI or XII deficiency, lupus anticoagulant / antiphospholipid antibodies, liver disease or DIC. A short APTT has no established clinical significance.

fy.n: Your intrinsic clotting pathway works within the normal time, which makes haemophilia, von Willebrand disease and a lupus anticoagulant unlikely. This is a reassuring pre-procedure or fertility-work-up result and needs no follow-up.
fy.bhi: Your clotting time on this test is slightly longer than usual. A partly filled or slow-to-process tube, mild liver dysfunction or a mild factor deficiency are common reasons, and heparin prolongs it if you receive any. In fertility work-ups a mild prolongation can hint at a lupus anticoagulant. Repeat the test; if still prolonged, a mixing study follows.
fy.hi: Your intrinsic clotting time is clearly prolonged. If you are on heparin this may be intended. Otherwise it can indicate an inherited bleeding disorder, liver disease or an antiphospholipid antibody (lupus anticoagulant), which is linked to clotting and pregnancy complications rather than bleeding. Please see your doctor; mixing studies and specific tests will identify the cause before any procedure.

TLP-032.notes: Reference interval is reagent-specific (typically 25–38 s); compare with the quoted control. Newborns have longer APTTs. Pregnancy shortens APTT slightly; oral contraceptives and high factor VIII (inflammation) can mask a mild abnormality.
TLP-032.src: CLSI H47-A2; BSH guideline on investigation of bleeding disorders 2014; ISTH lupus anticoagulant guidance 2020
TLP-032.retest: Repeat on a correctly filled, promptly processed sample; if confirmed prolonged, proceed to mixing studies.

TLP-033.name: APTT Ratio
TLP-033.meas: Your APTT divided by the laboratory's normal control APTT for the same reagent batch.
TLP-033.sig: Expressing APTT as a ratio corrects for reagent-to-reagent variation and is the format used for heparin dose adjustment. A ratio of 1.0 means you clot exactly like the healthy control.
TLP-033.ind: A raised ratio indicates heparin, factor VIII/IX/XI/XII deficiency, von Willebrand disease, lupus anticoagulant, liver disease or DIC. A ratio below 0.8 has no established significance.

fy.n: Your clotting time on this pathway matches the normal control, which confirms there is no significant factor deficiency or interfering antibody. Nothing further is needed.
fy.bhi: You are clotting a little more slowly than the control on this pathway. Sample handling, mild liver strain, a mild factor deficiency or a weak lupus anticoagulant can all cause this; heparin will too if you are receiving it. A repeat sample, and a mixing study if it persists, will sort out the reason.
fy.hi: You are clotting noticeably more slowly than the control on this pathway. Unless you are on heparin, this needs investigation for an inherited bleeding disorder, liver disease or an antiphospholipid antibody, which matters especially before surgery or in pregnancy planning. Your doctor will arrange the follow-up tests.

TLP-033.notes: Ratio is reagent-dependent and not transferable between labs. Therapeutic unfractionated heparin typically targets a ratio of 1.5–2.5; these bands apply to patients not on heparin.
TLP-033.retest: Repeat with APTT and, if prolonged, a mixing study.

TLP-034.name: Creatine Kinase (CK)
TLP-034.alias: CK, CPK, Creatine phosphokinase, Total CK
TLP-034.meas: An enzyme that leaks from muscle fibres into the blood when they are stressed or damaged.
TLP-034.sig: CK is the most sensitive blood test for muscle injury, from over-training and statin side-effects to inflammatory muscle disease and rhabdomyolysis. Values above five times normal signal enough muscle breakdown to threaten the kidneys.
TLP-034.ind: A raised CK indicates strenuous exercise, intramuscular injection, statin or fibrate myopathy, muscular dystrophy, dermatomyositis or polymyositis, hypothyroidism, seizures, trauma or rhabdomyolysis; heart-muscle injury raises the CK-MB fraction. A low CK is of no clinical concern and simply reflects low muscle mass or inactivity.

fy.n: Your CK is within the normal range, which shows no significant muscle breakdown at the moment. This is reassuring if you take a statin, train hard or have muscle aches, and confirms recovery from any recent heavy exercise. No follow-up is needed.
fy.bhi: Your CK is raised but under five times the upper limit. Hard exercise in the previous three days, an intramuscular injection or a minor injury are the most common reasons, followed by statin side-effects and an underactive thyroid. Rest from heavy training for a week and repeat; if it stays up, your doctor will review your medicines and thyroid.
fy.hi: Your CK is markedly raised, indicating substantial muscle breakdown. Extreme exertion, a crush injury, a seizure, certain medicines or an inflammatory muscle disease can do this, and at this level the released muscle proteins can strain the kidneys. Contact your doctor today, drink plenty of fluids, and report any dark urine or severe muscle pain urgently.

TLP-034.notes: IFCC 37 °C method. Individuals with greater muscle mass, people of African ancestry and athletes have higher baselines; a persistently raised CK in a well person may be normal for them. Avoid vigorous exercise and IM injections for 72 hours before testing. Newborns have transiently high CK.
TLP-034.src: IFCC reference intervals (Tietz); ACC/AHA statin myopathy guidance 2018; EFNS paucisymptomatic hyperCKaemia guideline
TLP-034.retest: Repeat after 5–7 days of rest from strenuous activity; if statin-related, your doctor will decide on a pause and recheck.

TLP-035.name: LDH
TLP-035.meas: An enzyme present in almost every cell of the body that is released into the blood when cells are damaged or destroyed.
TLP-035.sig: LDH is a non-specific but sensitive signal that cells somewhere are breaking down, whether red cells (haemolysis), muscle, liver or tumour tissue. It is a standard marker for monitoring dermatomyositis activity, haemolysis, dengue severity and lymphoma.
TLP-035.ind: A raised LDH indicates haemolysis, muscle injury or inflammatory myopathy, liver damage, heart attack, lung injury or pneumonia, dengue and other severe infections, megaloblastic anaemia, or cancers such as lymphoma and germ-cell tumours. A low LDH is not clinically significant.

fy.n: Your LDH is in the normal range, indicating no significant ongoing cell damage from muscle, liver, blood or other tissues. For anyone being monitored for muscle inflammation or red-cell breakdown, a normal value suggests the condition is quiet. No follow-up is needed.
fy.bhi: Your LDH is mildly raised. Very often this is a sample effect, since red cells breaking during collection release LDH, or the after-effect of strenuous exercise. Genuine mild rises occur with muscle strain, liver irritation, recent infection or mild red-cell breakdown. Repeat on a carefully drawn sample; if it stays up, your doctor will check CK and liver tests.
fy.hi: Your LDH is clearly raised, which means cells somewhere in the body are being damaged faster than normal. Red-cell breakdown, an inflammatory muscle disease, liver or lung injury, a severe infection such as dengue, or occasionally a lymphoma can cause this. Because it is not specific, your doctor will match it with CK, liver tests and your symptoms.

TLP-035.notes: Method-dependent (IFCC 37 °C, lactate-to-pyruvate); some laboratories quote 120–246 U/L. Children and adolescents run higher (up to about 350 U/L). Haemolysed samples give falsely high results and should be redrawn.
TLP-035.src: IFCC reference intervals (Tietz Textbook of Clinical Chemistry)
TLP-035.retest: Repeat on a non-haemolysed sample; in dermatomyositis or haemolysis, recheck at the interval your doctor sets for disease monitoring.

TLP-036.name: Blood Group
TLP-036.meas: Which of the four ABO types (A, B, AB or O) your red cells carry, determined by the sugar antigens on their surface.
TLP-036.sig: Knowing your ABO group is essential for safe transfusion and for pregnancy, where a mismatch between mother and baby can occasionally cause newborn jaundice. TrustLab confirms the result by both forward and reverse grouping.
TLP-036.ind: All four groups are normal variants and none is a disease. An ABO discrepancy (forward and reverse results disagreeing) can arise from a weak subgroup, recent transfusion, very young or elderly age, low antibody levels, or an underlying blood disorder and requires reference-lab resolution before any transfusion.

rng.n: A / B / AB / O (A, B, AB or O (all normal))

fy.n: Your ABO group has been determined and confirmed by two methods. Every group is normal and there is nothing to treat; it simply tells the blood bank which blood you can safely receive. Note it in your records and share it with your obstetrician when planning a pregnancy, as ABO differences between mother and baby occasionally cause mild newborn jaundice.
fy.hi: Your forward and reverse grouping did not fully agree, or a rare subgroup was detected, so your ABO type could not be assigned with full confidence. This is usually a laboratory puzzle rather than an illness: weak antigens, a recent transfusion or low natural antibodies are typical causes. The lab will arrange reference testing; meanwhile tell hospitals it is unconfirmed.

TLP-036.notes: Reverse grouping is unreliable under 4–6 months of age because infants have not yet made their own anti-A/anti-B; neonatal grouping relies on the forward test alone. In India group O and B are the most common.
TLP-036.src: AABB Technical Manual 21e; DGHS / Drugs and Cosmetics Rules (Indian blood bank standards)
TLP-036.retest: A confirmed ABO group does not change; retest only if a discrepancy was flagged or for blood-bank protocol on a new sample.

any.label: A, B, AB or O (all normal)

TLP-037.name: Rh Typing
TLP-037.alias: Rh factor, RhD typing, D antigen
TLP-037.meas: Whether your red cells carry the Rh (D) antigen, reported as Rh positive or Rh negative.
TLP-037.sig: Rh status matters most in pregnancy: an Rh-negative mother carrying an Rh-positive baby can form antibodies that harm a future baby, which is entirely preventable with anti-D injections. It also governs safe transfusion matching.
TLP-037.ind: Rh positive and Rh negative are both normal inherited types. Rh negative carries planning implications for pregnancy and transfusion; a weak or partial D result means the antigen is present in reduced or altered form and the blood bank must decide how to classify you.

rng.bhi: Negative (Rh (D) negative – plan for pregnancy / transfusion)
rng.hi: Weak D / variant (Weak D / partial D (variant))

fy.n: You are Rh positive, like roughly 95 % of people in India. This carries no health implications and no special precautions in pregnancy or transfusion related to the D antigen. Simply keep a record of your group alongside your ABO type.
fy.bhi: You are Rh negative, a normal inherited type found in about one in twenty Indians. It is not a condition, but it needs planning: in pregnancy your obstetrician will arrange antibody screening and anti-D injections around 28 weeks, after delivery and after any bleeding, which protects future babies. For transfusion you should receive Rh-negative blood.
fy.hi: Your red cells carry the D antigen in a weak or altered form, an uncommon variant. The blood bank may perform genotyping to decide whether to treat you as Rh positive or negative; until then you will usually be managed as Rh negative for transfusion and anti-D prophylaxis. It is a classification matter, not a disease.

TLP-037.notes: Rh-negative prevalence in India is about 5 %, lower than in European populations. In pregnancy, Rh-negative women require an antibody screen at booking and 28 weeks and anti-D prophylaxis per FOGSI/RCOG guidance. Partner's Rh type is useful in fertility and pre-wedding screening.
TLP-037.src: AABB Technical Manual 21e; FOGSI / RCOG anti-D guidance; ACOG Practice Bulletin 181
TLP-037.retest: Rh type does not change; retest only if a weak D result needs confirmation or for blood-bank protocol on a new sample.

any.label: Rh (D) negative – plan for pregnancy / transfusion

TLP-038.name: Indirect Coombs Test (Antibody Screen)
TLP-038.alias: ICT, Indirect antiglobulin test, IAT, Red cell antibody screen
TLP-038.meas: Whether your blood contains antibodies against red-cell antigens you do not have yourself, which could attack a baby's or donor's red cells.
TLP-038.sig: In pregnancy this test detects antibodies (most importantly anti-D, but also anti-c, anti-Kell and others) that can cross the placenta and destroy the baby's red cells. Finding them early lets the pregnancy be monitored and treated before harm occurs.
TLP-038.ind: A positive screen indicates a clinically significant red-cell alloantibody from a previous pregnancy or transfusion, passive anti-D from a recent injection, or occasionally a cold or autoantibody. A negative screen means no such antibodies are detectable at present.

fy.n: No antibodies against red-cell antigens were found in your blood, which means there is no current risk of them affecting a baby's red cells or complicating a transfusion. If you are Rh negative and pregnant, the screen is repeated at around 28 weeks before your anti-D injection. Nothing else is needed now.
fy.hi: An antibody against a red-cell antigen was detected. If you recently had an anti-D injection this is often just that passive antibody and is harmless. A true antibody, usually from a previous pregnancy or transfusion, needs identification and its level tracked through pregnancy so the baby can be monitored and treated if necessary. Your obstetrician will guide the next steps.

TLP-038.notes: In pregnancy an antibody screen is recommended at booking and again at 28 weeks for all women, regardless of Rh type. Passive anti-D from prophylaxis can give a weak positive for up to 8–12 weeks after injection. A positive screen leads to antibody identification and titration.
TLP-038.src: AABB Technical Manual 21e; BSH guideline for blood grouping and antibody testing in pregnancy 2016; FOGSI
TLP-038.retest: Repeat at 28 weeks in every pregnancy; if positive, titres every 2–4 weeks as directed by your obstetrician.

TLP-039.name: D-Dimer
TLP-039.meas: A fragment released when a blood clot is dissolved by the body, indicating recent clot formation and breakdown.
TLP-039.sig: A normal D-dimer reliably rules out deep-vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism in people at low or moderate risk, avoiding scans. A raised value does not confirm a clot but signals that clotting and clot-breakdown are active, as in sepsis, severe dengue, COVID-19 or DIC.
TLP-039.ind: A raised D-dimer indicates venous thromboembolism, DIC, severe infection or sepsis, dengue, COVID-19, recent surgery or trauma, pregnancy, cancer, liver or kidney disease, or advancing age. A low result has no clinical significance.

fy.n: Your D-dimer is in the normal range, which makes a recent significant blood clot in the legs or lungs very unlikely and shows no evidence of the widespread clotting seen in severe infections. No further action is needed for this result.
fy.bhi: Your D-dimer is mildly raised. This is common with any infection or fever, after surgery or injury, in pregnancy, and simply with age; it does not by itself mean you have a clot. If you have a swollen painful leg, chest pain or breathlessness, see a doctor the same day. Otherwise it is usually rechecked once the illness settles.
fy.hi: Your D-dimer is substantially raised, which indicates active clot formation and breakdown somewhere in the body. With fever this often reflects the severity of the infection (as in dengue or sepsis), but a clot in the leg or lung must be considered, particularly with leg swelling, chest pain or breathlessness. Please contact your doctor today; imaging may be needed.

TLP-039.notes: Cut-off is assay-specific; 500 ng/mL FEU is the conventional threshold (equivalent to 250 ng/mL DDU).
