Age-adjusted cut-off (age × 10 ng/mL FEU) is validated for people over 50 to reduce false positives. D-dimer rises physiologically through pregnancy, so the standard cut-off does not apply after the first trimester.
TLP-039.src: ACCP / ASH 2018 VTE diagnosis guidelines; ADJUST-PE (age-adjusted cut-off); ISTH DIC scoring
TLP-039.retest: Repeat 2–4 weeks after an acute illness resolves; urgent imaging rather than repeat testing if symptoms suggest a clot.

TLP-040.name: Factor V Leiden mutation (PCR)
TLP-040.profile: ADD-ON · THROMBOPHILIA WORK-UP (on VTE history only)
TLP-040.meas: Whether you carry one or two copies of the Factor V Leiden variant, which makes clotting factor V resistant to being switched off by protein C.
TLP-040.sig: Factor V Leiden is the most common inherited clotting tendency in people of European descent but is rare in India. It raises the lifetime risk of vein clots and is tested after unexplained thrombosis or, selectively, in recurrent pregnancy loss.
TLP-040.ind: A heterozygous result (one copy) roughly triples to quintuples the risk of venous thrombosis, especially with oral contraceptives, pregnancy, surgery or immobility. A homozygous result (two copies) raises it substantially more. A negative result excludes this particular variant but not other causes of thrombophilia.

fy.n: You do not carry the Factor V Leiden variant, which removes the most common inherited clotting tendency from consideration. This does not rule out all clotting risks, so the rest of your thrombophilia panel and your personal and family history still matter. No action is needed on this result.
fy.bhi: You carry one copy of the Factor V Leiden variant, which modestly increases your tendency to form vein clots, particularly during pregnancy, after surgery, with long immobility or on oestrogen-containing contraceptives. Many carriers never have a clot. Share this with your doctor and obstetrician so preventive measures can be planned when your risk is temporarily higher.
fy.hi: You carry two copies of the Factor V Leiden variant, which raises your risk of vein clots considerably more than a single copy. A clot is not inevitable, but pregnancy, surgery, long travel and hormonal contraception need careful planning with a haematologist or obstetrician, who may recommend preventive anticoagulation at those times. First-degree relatives may also wish to be tested.

TLP-040.notes: A genetic result does not change over time and need never be repeated. Prevalence in Indian populations is under 1 %, so testing is reserved for those with a personal or strong family history of venous thrombosis. Guidelines (ASH 2023, RCOG) do not support routine thrombophilia testing for recurrent miscarriage alone; results should be interpreted with a specialist.
TLP-040.src: ASH 2023 thrombophilia testing guideline; ACMG; RCOG Green-top 17
TLP-040.retest: No repeat needed; a genetic result is permanent.

TLP-041.name: Prothrombin G20210A mutation (PCR)
TLP-041.profile: ADD-ON · THROMBOPHILIA WORK-UP (on VTE history only)
TLP-041.meas: Whether you carry one or two copies of the prothrombin G20210A variant, which causes your body to make about 30 % more prothrombin (clotting factor II) than usual.
TLP-041.sig: This is the second most common inherited clotting tendency in European populations and is very uncommon in India. Carriers have a two- to three-fold increase in vein clot risk, which combines with Factor V Leiden, pregnancy and hormones.
TLP-041.ind: A heterozygous result indicates a mild inherited tendency to venous thrombosis; a homozygous result or combination with Factor V Leiden indicates a higher risk. A negative result excludes this variant only.

fy.n: You do not carry the prothrombin G20210A variant. Together with a negative Factor V Leiden result this excludes the two most common inherited clotting variants, though other causes of thrombosis remain possible. There is nothing to do about this result.
fy.bhi: You carry one copy of the prothrombin G20210A variant, which makes your blood slightly more prone to vein clots, especially in pregnancy, after operations, during long immobility or with oestrogen contraception. Most carriers stay well. Let your doctor and obstetrician know so preventive steps, such as compression stockings or short-term blood thinners after surgery or delivery, can be considered.
fy.hi: You carry two copies of the prothrombin G20210A variant, or it has been found in combination with another clotting variant, which places you at a clearly higher risk of vein clots than the general population. A haematologist should advise on when preventive anticoagulation is warranted, particularly around pregnancy and surgery, and close relatives may benefit from testing.

TLP-041.notes: A permanent genetic result. Prevalence in South Asian populations is well under 1 %. Current guidelines do not recommend testing for recurrent pregnancy loss without a personal or family history of venous thromboembolism; results are best discussed with a haematologist.
TLP-041.src: ASH 2023 thrombophilia testing guideline; ACMG; RCOG Green-top 17
TLP-041.retest: No repeat needed; a genetic result is permanent.

TLP-042.name: Protein C activity
TLP-042.profile: ADD-ON · THROMBOPHILIA WORK-UP (on VTE history only)
TLP-042.meas: How well your protein C works, expressed as a percentage of normal; protein C is a vitamin K-dependent protein that switches off clotting factors V and VIII.
TLP-042.sig: Protein C deficiency is a recognised inherited cause of vein clots and, when severe, of a skin-necrosis reaction to warfarin. Because it is made by the liver and depends on vitamin K, the test must be timed away from warfarin, liver illness and acute clots.
TLP-042.ind: Low activity indicates inherited protein C deficiency, warfarin or vitamin K deficiency, liver disease, DIC, acute thrombosis or sepsis. Raised activity has no clinical significance.

fy.lo: Your protein C activity is reduced, which weakens one of the body's natural brakes on clotting. Before calling this an inherited deficiency, warfarin, vitamin K shortage, liver problems, a recent clot or serious infection must be excluded, as they all lower it temporarily. Your doctor will repeat the test off anticoagulants and, if confirmed, refer you to a haematologist.
fy.blo: Your protein C activity is just under the usual range. This is often a temporary effect of illness, a recent clot, anticoagulant medicine or low vitamin K rather than a true deficiency. A repeat test in a few weeks, when you are well and off warfarin, will show whether it persists; if so, assessment with a haematologist is sensible.
fy.n: Your protein C works normally, so this natural anticoagulant is not the reason for any clotting or pregnancy problem being investigated. No further testing of protein C is needed unless your doctor advises otherwise.

TLP-042.notes: Do not test during warfarin therapy (falsely low), within 4–6 weeks of an acute clot, in pregnancy, or during acute illness. Newborns have physiologically low levels (about 20–40 %), reaching adult levels by adolescence. Reference interval typically 70–140 %; method-dependent.
TLP-042.src: BSH thrombophilia testing guideline 2022; ASH 2023; ISTH SSC recommendations
TLP-042.retest: Confirm any low result on a second sample at least 4–6 weeks later, off warfarin and away from acute illness or pregnancy.

TLP-043.name: Protein S activity (free)
TLP-043.profile: ADD-ON · THROMBOPHILIA WORK-UP (on VTE history only)
TLP-043.meas: How well your free protein S works, expressed as a percentage of normal; protein S helps protein C switch off clotting.
TLP-043.sig: Inherited protein S deficiency is among the more common thrombophilias found in Indian patients with vein clots. It is also the thrombophilia test most easily thrown off by everyday factors: pregnancy, the pill, warfarin and inflammation all lower it.
TLP-043.ind: Low activity indicates inherited protein S deficiency, pregnancy or oestrogen therapy, warfarin, vitamin K deficiency, liver disease, DIC, acute thrombosis, nephrotic syndrome or HIV. Raised activity has no clinical significance.

fy.lo: Your protein S activity is reduced, which lowers your natural protection against vein clots. Pregnancy, the pill or hormone therapy, warfarin, liver disease, a recent clot or inflammation all reduce protein S temporarily, so this must be confirmed at a better time before an inherited deficiency is diagnosed. If persistently low, a haematology review will plan for pregnancy or surgery.
fy.blo: Your protein S activity is a little below the usual range. Women naturally run lower, and oestrogen contraception, early pregnancy, a recent illness or anticoagulants push it down further, so a mild dip like this is frequently not an inherited problem. Repeat in a few weeks off hormones and away from illness; if still low, a specialist can advise.
fy.n: Your protein S activity is normal, indicating this natural anticoagulant is not contributing to any clotting or pregnancy-loss concern being investigated. No further testing of protein S is needed.

TLP-043.notes: Women have lower reference limits than men; levels fall further with oestrogen contraception and progressively through pregnancy (to 30–50 % in the third trimester), when testing is not recommended. Do not test on warfarin or within 4–6 weeks of an acute clot. Newborn levels are physiologically low. Method-dependent interval.
TLP-043.src: BSH thrombophilia testing guideline 2022; ASH 2023; ISTH SSC recommendations
TLP-043.retest: Confirm a low result on a second sample 4–6 weeks later, off hormones and warfarin and outside pregnancy.

TLP-044.name: Antithrombin III activity
TLP-044.alias: AT III, Antithrombin activity, Heparin cofactor
TLP-044.profile: ADD-ON · THROMBOPHILIA WORK-UP (on VTE history only)
TLP-044.meas: How well your antithrombin works, expressed as a percentage of normal; antithrombin is the main protein that neutralises thrombin and is what heparin acts through.
TLP-044.sig: Antithrombin deficiency is the least common but most potent inherited thrombophilia, carrying a high lifetime risk of vein clots and reducing the effect of heparin. A confirmed deficiency changes how pregnancy, surgery and anticoagulation are managed.
TLP-044.ind: Low activity indicates inherited antithrombin deficiency, acute thrombosis, heparin therapy, liver disease, nephrotic syndrome, DIC, sepsis, pre-eclampsia or L-asparaginase treatment. Raised activity has no clinical significance.

fy.lo: Your antithrombin activity is reduced, which meaningfully weakens the body's main defence against unwanted clotting. A recent clot, heparin treatment, liver or kidney disease and serious infection can lower it temporarily, so confirmation on a repeat sample is essential. If an inherited deficiency is confirmed, a haematologist will plan preventive treatment around pregnancy and surgery.
fy.blo: Your antithrombin activity is slightly below the usual range. Heparin, a recent clot, liver strain, protein loss through the kidneys or an acute illness commonly cause a mild, temporary dip. Repeat the test once you are well and off heparin; if it remains low, a specialist assessment is advisable, as even mild inherited deficiency carries a meaningful clot risk.
fy.n: Your antithrombin activity is normal, which rules out the most potent of the inherited clotting tendencies and means heparin would work as expected if ever needed. No further testing of antithrombin is required.

TLP-044.notes: Do not test during heparin therapy or within 4–6 weeks of an acute thrombosis. Pregnancy lowers antithrombin modestly; pre-eclampsia lowers it markedly. Newborns have 40–60 % of adult activity, normalising by 6 months. Warfarin can raise levels slightly. Method-dependent interval, typically 80–120 %.
TLP-044.src: BSH thrombophilia testing guideline 2022; ASH 2023; ISTH SSC recommendations
TLP-044.retest: Confirm any low result on a second sample at least 4–6 weeks later, off heparin and away from acute illness.

TLP-045.name: MTHFR C677T polymorphism
TLP-045.profile: ADD-ON · THROMBOPHILIA WORK-UP (on VTE history only)
TLP-045.meas: Which version of the MTHFR gene you carry at position 677; the T variant slows the enzyme that processes folate and can raise homocysteine when folate intake is low.
TLP-045.sig: This variant is extremely common (about a third of Indians carry at least one copy) and by itself is not a thrombophilia. Its only practical relevance is that TT carriers with low folate may have raised homocysteine, which is easily corrected with diet or supplements.
TLP-045.ind: The TT genotype indicates a roughly 60–70 % reduction in enzyme activity and a tendency to higher homocysteine if folate is insufficient; CT indicates a mild reduction of little consequence. Neither genotype is an established cause of venous thrombosis or recurrent pregnancy loss, and major guidelines advise against testing it for those purposes.

fy.n: You carry the common (CC) version of the MTHFR gene, so your folate-processing enzyme works at full capacity. This has no bearing on clotting risk either way and needs no action; a normal folate intake through diet or standard pregnancy supplements is all that is recommended.
fy.bhi: You carry one copy of the MTHFR C677T variant, as do around a third of people. The enzyme works slightly less efficiently, but this has no proven effect on clotting, miscarriage or pregnancy outcome. No treatment is needed beyond the usual folate-containing supplements advised for anyone planning pregnancy; your doctor may check homocysteine if there are other reasons to.
fy.hi: You carry two copies of the MTHFR C677T variant. The enzyme works at reduced capacity, which can push homocysteine up when folate intake is low, but current evidence does not link this genotype to clots or recurrent miscarriage on its own. Ensure adequate folate through diet and a standard supplement, and ask your doctor to check homocysteine.

TLP-045.notes: A permanent genetic result. ACMG (2013), ACOG and the ASH 2023 thrombophilia guideline recommend against MTHFR testing in thrombophilia, recurrent pregnancy loss or IVF evaluations; homocysteine measurement is the clinically useful test if hyperhomocysteinaemia is suspected. TT prevalence in India is roughly 5–10 %.
TLP-045.src: ACMG Practice Guideline 2013 (MTHFR); ASH 2023; ACOG Practice Bulletin 197
TLP-045.retest: No repeat needed; a genetic result is permanent. Check fasting homocysteine if the TT genotype is found.

TLP-046.name: MTHFR A1298C polymorphism
TLP-046.profile: ADD-ON · THROMBOPHILIA WORK-UP (on VTE history only)
TLP-046.meas: Which version of the MTHFR gene you carry at position 1298; the C variant mildly reduces enzyme activity.
TLP-046.sig: The A1298C variant is even less consequential than C677T: on its own it does not raise homocysteine and has no established link to clotting or pregnancy loss. It is reported mainly so that combined heterozygosity with C677T can be identified.
TLP-046.ind: The CC genotype indicates a mild reduction in enzyme activity without a homocysteine effect in most people; AC indicates a negligible change. Combined heterozygosity (A1298C plus C677T) behaves roughly like C677T TT and may modestly raise homocysteine if folate is low. It is not a thrombophilia.

fy.n: You carry the common (AA) version of the MTHFR gene at this position, so there is no reduction in enzyme activity from this site. It has no effect on your clotting risk or pregnancy outlook, and no action is required.
fy.bhi: You carry one copy of the MTHFR A1298C variant, which is very common and causes only a trivial change in enzyme activity. It does not increase clotting or miscarriage risk. If you also carry a C677T copy, the two together can slightly raise homocysteine when folate is low, so a standard folate supplement and a homocysteine check are enough.
fy.hi: You carry two copies of the MTHFR A1298C variant. Even in this form the enzyme retains most of its activity, homocysteine is usually normal, and there is no proven link to clots or pregnancy loss. Adequate folate through diet and a routine supplement is all that is recommended; your doctor may check homocysteine for completeness.

TLP-046.notes: A permanent genetic result. ACMG, ACOG and ASH advise against MTHFR genotyping for thrombophilia or recurrent pregnancy loss evaluation; a homocysteine level is the useful test where relevant. Results should be interpreted together with C677T.
TLP-046.src: ACMG Practice Guideline 2013 (MTHFR); ASH 2023; ACOG Practice Bulletin 197
TLP-046.retest: No repeat needed; a genetic result is permanent.

TLP-047.name: Aldolase
TLP-047.meas: An enzyme involved in sugar metabolism inside muscle fibres that leaks into the blood when muscle is damaged.
TLP-047.sig: Aldolase is a second muscle enzyme that can be raised in dermatomyositis and other inflammatory muscle diseases even when CK is normal, particularly when the disease affects the connective tissue around muscle fibres. It is used alongside CK to detect and monitor myositis.
TLP-047.ind: A raised aldolase indicates dermatomyositis or polymyositis, muscular dystrophy, rhabdomyolysis, strenuous exercise, hepatitis or liver injury, haemolytic anaemia, heart attack or some cancers. A low aldolase is not clinically significant.

fy.n: Your aldolase is in the normal range, which, together with a normal CK, indicates no significant muscle inflammation or breakdown at present. In someone being monitored for dermatomyositis this suggests muscle involvement is quiet. No follow-up is required for this result.
fy.bhi: Your aldolase is mildly raised. Hard exercise in the previous few days, a minor muscle injury, liver irritation or red-cell breakdown can all account for this. If you have a rash, muscle weakness or difficulty climbing stairs, tell your doctor, as early inflammatory muscle disease can show a modest rise before CK moves. Otherwise rest and repeat in two weeks.
fy.hi: Your aldolase is clearly raised, which points to active muscle damage or, less commonly, liver injury or red-cell breakdown. Combined with muscle weakness or a skin rash this supports inflammatory myositis such as dermatomyositis; combined with recent extreme exertion it suggests exercise-induced breakdown. Your doctor will interpret it alongside CK and liver tests and may refer you to a rheumatologist.

TLP-047.notes: Method-dependent; adult intervals are typically 1.2–7.6 U/L at 37 °C, with children running higher (up to about 15 U/L under 16 years). Avoid vigorous exercise for 72 hours and IM injections before testing; haemolysed samples read falsely high.
TLP-047.src: Tietz Textbook of Clinical Chemistry; ACR/EULAR 2017 myositis classification criteria
TLP-047.retest: Repeat after 1–2 weeks of rest if mildly raised; in myositis, monitor with CK at the interval set by your rheumatologist.

TLP-048.name: Fasting Blood Sugar
TLP-048.meas: The amount of glucose in your blood after at least 8 hours without food or calorie-containing drinks.
TLP-048.sig: A snapshot of how well your body controls sugar when no food is coming in. It is the first-line screening test for pre-diabetes and diabetes and reflects how your liver and insulin are working overnight.
TLP-048.ind: High values point to impaired fasting glucose or diabetes, and can also follow steroid use, acute illness, stress or an inadequate fast. Low values suggest excess diabetes medication, prolonged fasting, alcohol, liver disease or, rarely, an insulin-producing tumour.

fy.lo: Your fasting sugar is below the usual range. This can happen after an unusually long fast, heavy alcohol the night before, or with sugar-lowering medicines. If you felt shaky, sweaty or light-headed, or you take diabetes medication, please discuss it with your doctor soon.
fy.n: Your fasting sugar is in the healthy range, which means your body is handling glucose well overnight. Keep it here with regular meals, limited refined carbohydrates and sugary drinks, daily physical activity and a healthy weight. Repeat with your routine annual check-up.
fy.bhi: Your fasting sugar sits in the pre-diabetic zone, sometimes called impaired fasting glucose. It usually reflects early insulin resistance linked to weight, inactivity or family history. This stage is very often reversible with diet, exercise and weight loss; your doctor may confirm it with HbA1c and repeat testing.
fy.hi: Your fasting sugar is in the range used to define diabetes. A single reading is not a diagnosis; your doctor will usually confirm with a repeat fasting test or HbA1c. Please book a consultation soon, as early treatment and lifestyle change protect your heart, kidneys, eyes and nerves.

TLP-048.notes: Requires a true 8–12 hour fast; water only. Pregnancy uses stricter cut-offs (fasting ≥ 92 mg/dL is abnormal on an OGTT). Fluoride tube prevents glycolysis; delayed separation in plain tubes falsely lowers results.
TLP-048.retest: If borderline or high, repeat on a separate day with HbA1c to confirm; if normal, recheck yearly (every 3 years if no risk factors).

TLP-049.name: HbA1c
TLP-049.meas: The percentage of haemoglobin in your red cells that has sugar attached, reflecting average blood glucose over roughly the past 3 months.
TLP-049.sig: Averages your blood sugar over the past ~90 days. Unlike a one-time reading, it cannot be 'gamed' by fasting the night before, and it is the value doctors use to diagnose and monitor diabetes.
TLP-049.ind: Higher values indicate pre-diabetes or diabetes, or poor control in a known diabetic. Values can be falsely high or low with anaemia, recent transfusion, haemolysis, kidney failure or haemoglobin variants, so they are read alongside glucose.

fy.n: Your 3-month sugar average is in the healthy range, confirming that your day-to-day glucose has stayed well controlled. Maintain it with balanced meals, regular movement and a healthy weight. If you have a family history of diabetes, an annual recheck is a sensible habit.
fy.bhi: Your average sugar sits in the pre-diabetic band. Without intervention the 5-year conversion risk to type-2 diabetes is meaningful; with structured lifestyle change (weight loss of 5–7%, 150 minutes of activity a week, fewer refined carbohydrates) it drops sharply. Your doctor may recheck in 3–6 months.
fy.hi: Your 3-month average is in the diabetic range. If you are not known to have diabetes, your doctor will confirm with a repeat test or fasting glucose and discuss treatment. If you already have diabetes, this suggests control needs tightening; a review of diet, activity and medicines is worthwhile.

TLP-049.notes: For people with established diabetes, the usual treatment target is < 7%, individualised by age and comorbidity. Unreliable in haemolytic anaemia, recent blood loss or transfusion, pregnancy (second and third trimester), and some haemoglobin variants (HbS, HbE, HbD are common in India).
TLP-049.src: ADA Standards of Care 2024; NGSP-certified method
TLP-049.retest: Every 3 months while diabetes is being brought under control; every 6 months once stable; yearly if pre-diabetic.

TLP-050.name: Fasting Insulin
TLP-050.meas: The level of insulin, the hormone that moves sugar into your cells, circulating in your blood after an overnight fast.
TLP-050.sig: Shows how hard your pancreas is working to keep fasting sugar normal. A high insulin level with a normal glucose is the earliest laboratory sign of insulin resistance, often years before sugar itself rises.
TLP-050.ind: High fasting insulin suggests insulin resistance linked to central obesity, PCOS, fatty liver or metabolic syndrome, and rarely an insulin-secreting tumour. Low insulin with high sugar suggests failing beta-cells, as in long-standing type-2 or type-1 diabetes.

fy.lo: Your fasting insulin is very low. In someone with normal sugar this is usually of no concern, particularly if you are lean and active. If your glucose is high at the same time, it suggests your pancreas is not producing enough insulin, and your doctor may want to look at C-peptide and antibody tests.
fy.n: Your fasting insulin is in the healthy range, suggesting your body responds to insulin efficiently and your pancreas is not under strain. Keep it that way with regular exercise (muscle is your biggest sugar consumer), limited sugary and processed food and a healthy waistline.
fy.bhi: Your fasting insulin is at the upper end of normal, an early hint that your cells are becoming a little resistant to insulin. It commonly goes with weight around the middle, inactivity, poor sleep or PCOS. Strength training, a lower-refined-carbohydrate diet and modest weight loss usually bring it down.
fy.hi: Your fasting insulin is raised, which is consistent with insulin resistance: your pancreas is over-producing to keep sugar normal. This is a strong, reversible warning sign for type-2 diabetes and fatty liver. Discuss with your doctor, who may check HOMA-IR, lipids and liver tests and guide a structured lifestyle plan.

TLP-050.notes: Must be a true 8–12 hour fast; insulin rises sharply after any food. Not interpretable in people taking insulin injections. Method-dependent; values above ~15 µIU/mL are considered elevated in many Indian studies.
TLP-050.src: Endocrine Society / ADA; CLSI adult reference interval
TLP-050.retest: Recheck in 3–6 months after lifestyle change, together with fasting glucose for HOMA-IR.

TLP-051.name: HOMA-IR
TLP-051.alias: Homeostatic Model Assessment of Insulin Resistance, Insulin resistance index
TLP-051.meas: A calculated index combining fasting glucose and fasting insulin to estimate how resistant your body is to insulin.
TLP-051.sig: Puts a number on insulin resistance, the root process behind type-2 diabetes, fatty liver, PCOS and much heart disease. It flags trouble while glucose alone still looks normal.
TLP-051.ind: A high HOMA-IR indicates insulin resistance driven by excess body fat, inactivity, sleep loss, steroids or PCOS. A very low value simply reflects high insulin sensitivity or very low insulin output; it is not a disease marker on its own.

fy.n: Your insulin resistance index is in the healthy range, meaning your cells respond well to insulin and your metabolism is in good shape. Regular activity, adequate sleep and avoiding weight gain around the waist are the best ways to keep it there.
fy.bhi: Your index shows early insulin resistance: sugar is still normal, but your body is working harder to keep it so. It typically follows weight gain, inactivity or PCOS. This is the ideal stage to act; consistent exercise and dietary change often normalise it within months.
fy.hi: Your index indicates established insulin resistance, a key driver of pre-diabetes, fatty liver and cardiovascular risk. It is very much reversible. Please review with your doctor, who may check HbA1c, lipids and liver tests and guide a structured programme of weight management and exercise.

TLP-051.notes: Formula: fasting insulin (µIU/mL) × fasting glucose (mg/dL) / 405. Cut-offs vary by population; Indian studies suggest values above ~2.0–2.5 indicate insulin resistance. Not valid in people taking insulin or with very high fasting glucose (> 200 mg/dL).
TLP-051.src: Matthews et al. 1985; Indian population studies (ICMR-INDIAB)
TLP-051.retest: Repeat after 3–6 months of lifestyle change to track improvement.

TLP-052.name: C-Peptide
TLP-052.meas: A fragment released in equal amounts with your body's own insulin, so it reflects how much insulin your pancreas is making.
TLP-052.sig: Tells whether your pancreas is still producing insulin, unaffected by injected insulin. It helps distinguish type-1 from type-2 diabetes and guides whether tablets can still work.
TLP-052.ind: High values indicate insulin resistance with over-production, kidney disease (reduced clearance) or rarely an insulinoma. Low values indicate reduced beta-cell function, as in type-1 diabetes, advanced type-2 diabetes or after pancreatic damage.

fy.lo: Your C-peptide is low, meaning your pancreas is producing less insulin than usual. In someone with high sugar this suggests type-1 diabetes or advanced type-2 disease that may need insulin; in someone with normal sugar it may just reflect a long fast. Your doctor will interpret it alongside glucose and antibody tests.
fy.n: Your C-peptide is in the normal range, confirming your pancreas is producing insulin at a healthy rate. Together with a normal glucose this is reassuring. Maintain it with an active lifestyle and a diet low in refined sugar.
fy.bhi: Your C-peptide is at the upper end of normal, suggesting your pancreas is producing a little extra insulin, an early sign of insulin resistance. This usually accompanies weight gain or inactivity and responds well to exercise and dietary change. Your doctor may check HOMA-IR to confirm.
fy.hi: Your C-peptide is raised, which is consistent with insulin resistance where the pancreas over-produces to compensate, or with reduced clearance in kidney disease. In a type-2 diabetic it means tablets that improve insulin sensitivity are likely to help. Please discuss the result with your doctor.

TLP-052.notes: Fasting value; rises 3–5-fold after meals. Falsely high in chronic kidney disease because C-peptide is cleared by the kidneys. Method-dependent; some labs report in nmol/L (multiply ng/mL by 0.331).
TLP-052.src: ADA / Endocrine Society; CLSI adult reference interval
TLP-052.retest: Repeat when diabetes type is uncertain or before changing from tablets to insulin; a stimulated (post-meal) value may be requested.

TLP-053.name: Total Cholesterol
TLP-053.meas: The total amount of cholesterol carried in all lipoprotein particles in your blood, both the harmful (LDL, VLDL) and protective (HDL) kinds.
TLP-053.sig: A broad measure of the fat load in your bloodstream and one of the oldest predictors of heart attack and stroke. It is most useful when read with its components, LDL and HDL.
TLP-053.ind: High values reflect a diet rich in saturated fat, genetics (familial hypercholesterolaemia), hypothyroidism, kidney disease, diabetes or cholestatic liver disease. Low values may occur with malnutrition, hyperthyroidism, chronic liver disease, malabsorption or serious illness.

fy.lo: Your total cholesterol is unusually low. This is often harmless, particularly in slim, active people or those on cholesterol-lowering medicines. Occasionally it points to an overactive thyroid, poor absorption, liver disease or undernutrition, so your doctor may check these if you have symptoms such as weight loss.
fy.n: Your total cholesterol is in the desirable range, which lowers your long-term risk of heart attack and stroke. Look at the LDL and HDL breakdown too, since the balance matters. Keep it here with a diet rich in vegetables, whole grains and nuts, limited fried and processed food, and regular exercise.
fy.bhi: Your total cholesterol is borderline high. On its own this is a modest risk, but combined with high LDL, low HDL, smoking, diabetes or high blood pressure it adds up. Reducing saturated fat, losing excess weight and exercising typically lowers it by 10–15%. Recheck in 3–6 months and discuss with your doctor.
fy.hi: Your total cholesterol is high, which is consistent with a significantly raised risk of heart disease over time. Diet plays a part, but genetics and thyroid function can contribute too. Please review with your doctor, who will look at your overall risk and may discuss treatment alongside diet and exercise.

TLP-053.notes: Fasting is no longer essential for total and HDL cholesterol. Rises 20–40% in the third trimester of pregnancy. Lipid Association of India recommends TC < 200 mg/dL for the general population and lower targets in high-risk individuals.
TLP-053.src: NCEP ATP-III; Lipid Association of India 2020
TLP-053.retest: Every 4–6 years if desirable and low risk; yearly if borderline or on treatment; 6–12 weeks after starting therapy.

TLP-054.name: HDL Cholesterol
TLP-054.meas: The cholesterol carried by high-density lipoprotein particles, which transport excess cholesterol away from artery walls back to the liver.
TLP-054.sig: The protective fraction of cholesterol: higher levels are linked with lower rates of heart attack and stroke. Low HDL is particularly common in South Asians and is a core feature of metabolic syndrome.
TLP-054.ind: Low HDL is associated with insulin resistance, obesity, smoking, inactivity, high triglycerides, type-2 diabetes and certain drugs (anabolic steroids, beta-blockers). Very high HDL is usually genetic or linked to regular exercise and moderate alcohol; extremely high values are not necessarily more protective.

fy.lo: Your good cholesterol is lower than recommended, which weakens your natural protection against artery blockage. It commonly goes with being overweight, inactive, smoking or having high triglycerides. Aerobic exercise, quitting smoking, healthy fats like nuts and fish, and weight loss all raise HDL. Discuss your overall risk with your doctor.
fy.n: Your good cholesterol is in the acceptable range, giving you a reasonable level of protection against artery disease. Regular brisk exercise, not smoking and a diet with healthy unsaturated fats can nudge it higher still. Read it alongside your LDL and triglycerides for the full picture.
fy.hi: Your good cholesterol is in the optimal range, which counts as a protective factor against heart disease. This often reflects an active lifestyle or favourable genes. Keep doing what you are doing; note that extremely high values are not necessarily extra protective, so continue to watch LDL and triglycerides.

TLP-054.notes: For HDL the 'high' band is favourable, not a warning. Cut-offs for low HDL differ by sex (< 40 mg/dL men, < 50 mg/dL women). Fasting not required.
TLP-054.src: NCEP ATP-III; Lipid Association of India 2020
TLP-054.retest: With each lipid profile; recheck 3–6 months after exercise and smoking-cessation efforts.

TLP-055.name: LDL Cholesterol
TLP-055.meas: The cholesterol carried by low-density lipoprotein particles, the type that deposits in artery walls and forms plaque.
TLP-055.sig: The single most important lipid target: every reduction in LDL translates into fewer heart attacks and strokes. Statins and diet changes are judged by how far they bring this number down.
TLP-055.ind: High LDL results from saturated and trans fat intake, familial hypercholesterolaemia, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, cholestasis or diabetes. Low LDL is seen with lipid-lowering therapy, hyperthyroidism, malnutrition, chronic illness or rare genetic conditions, and is generally not harmful.

fy.lo: Your bad cholesterol is very low. If you take a statin or similar medicine this shows it is working well, and low LDL is not harmful to the heart. If you are not on treatment, it may reflect an overactive thyroid, poor absorption or illness, which your doctor can review if you have other symptoms.
fy.n: Your bad cholesterol is in the optimal-to-near-optimal range for a healthy adult, which keeps plaque build-up in your arteries to a minimum. If you already have diabetes or heart disease your doctor may want it lower still. Maintain it with less saturated fat, more fibre and regular exercise.
fy.bhi: Your bad cholesterol is borderline high, meaning plaque can accumulate faster than ideal, especially if you also smoke, have diabetes or high blood pressure. Cutting fried foods, ghee, butter and red meat, adding oats, nuts and legumes, and exercising usually brings it down. Recheck in 3–6 months.
fy.hi: Your bad cholesterol is high, which is consistent with a materially increased risk of heart attack and stroke over the coming years. Diet helps, but at this level genetics often play a role and your doctor may discuss cholesterol-lowering treatment alongside lifestyle change. Please book a review.

TLP-055.notes: Calculated by the Friedewald equation (TC − HDL − TG/5) and unreliable when triglycerides exceed 400 mg/dL or in non-fasting samples with high TG; direct LDL is used then. Targets are individualised: < 100 mg/dL for high-risk, < 70 mg/dL for very-high-risk (established heart disease or diabetes with organ damage), < 50 mg/dL for extreme risk per LAI.
TLP-055.src: NCEP ATP-III; ACC/AHA 2018; Lipid Association of India 2020
TLP-055.retest: 6–12 weeks after starting or changing treatment; then every 6–12 months.

TLP-056.name: Triglycerides
TLP-056.meas: The main form in which your body stores and transports fat from food and from the liver.
TLP-056.sig: High triglycerides go hand in hand with insulin resistance, fatty liver and low HDL, the classic South Asian pattern that raises heart risk. Very high levels can also trigger acute pancreatitis.
TLP-056.ind: Raised by refined carbohydrates and sugar, alcohol, obesity, uncontrolled diabetes, hypothyroidism, kidney disease, certain drugs (steroids, oestrogens, retinoids) and familial hypertriglyceridaemia. Low values are seen with malnutrition, malabsorption or hyperthyroidism and are rarely a concern.

fy.n: Your triglycerides are in the normal range, suggesting your body is handling dietary fat and sugar well. Limiting sweets, refined rice and flour, sugary drinks and alcohol, and staying active will keep them here. Low values are not a concern.
fy.bhi: Your triglycerides are borderline high. This is most often driven by refined carbohydrates, sugar, alcohol and extra weight around the middle, and is an early marker of insulin resistance. Triglycerides respond quickly to diet: cutting sugar and alcohol and adding exercise can normalise them within weeks. Recheck in 3 months.
fy.hi: Your triglycerides are high, which is consistent with insulin resistance and raises your risk of heart disease and fatty liver; very high levels can inflame the pancreas. Check that the sample was fasting. Reduce sugar, refined carbohydrates and alcohol, and please discuss with your doctor, who may check glucose, thyroid and liver tests.

TLP-056.notes: A 9–12 hour fast is required; non-fasting samples run higher. Values ≥ 500 mg/dL carry a risk of acute pancreatitis and need prompt attention. Rises physiologically in the third trimester of pregnancy.
TLP-056.src: NCEP ATP-III; AHA 2011 scientific statement; Lipid Association of India 2020
TLP-056.retest: If borderline or high, repeat after a strict 12-hour fast and 3 months of dietary change.

TLP-057.name: VLDL
TLP-057.meas: An estimate of the cholesterol carried in very-low-density lipoprotein particles, the triglyceride-rich particles made by the liver.
TLP-057.sig: VLDL is the liver's fat-export vehicle and a precursor of LDL; a high value is another face of high triglycerides and contributes directly to plaque. It is calculated as triglycerides divided by five.
TLP-057.ind: High VLDL mirrors high triglycerides: excess sugar and refined carbohydrates, alcohol, obesity, diabetes, hypothyroidism and kidney disease. Low VLDL simply reflects low triglycerides and is not clinically significant.

fy.n: Your VLDL cholesterol is in the normal range, which means your liver is not exporting excess fat into the bloodstream. It moves together with triglycerides, so the same habits, limited sugar, refined grains and alcohol plus regular activity, keep both in check.
fy.bhi: Your VLDL is borderline high, reflecting a modest excess of triglyceride-rich particles from the liver. This is usually driven by dietary sugar, refined carbohydrates, alcohol or weight gain. Because VLDL tracks triglycerides, the dietary changes that lower triglycerides will bring this down too. Recheck in 3 months.
fy.hi: Your VLDL is high, which goes hand in hand with raised triglycerides and adds to the plaque-forming particles in your arteries. It is consistent with insulin resistance or a high-sugar, high-alcohol intake. Please discuss with your doctor, who may check glucose, liver and thyroid function alongside a diet and exercise plan.

TLP-057.notes: Calculated as triglycerides / 5 (mg/dL); invalid when triglycerides exceed 400 mg/dL. Requires a fasting sample.
TLP-057.retest: Recheck with the lipid profile after 3 months of dietary change.

TLP-058.name: TC / HDL Ratio
TLP-058.alias: Cholesterol ratio, Castelli risk index I, TC:HDL
TLP-058.meas: Your total cholesterol divided by your good (HDL) cholesterol, showing the balance between total fat load and its protective fraction.
TLP-058.sig: A single number that captures the interaction between harmful and protective cholesterol; it predicts heart risk better than total cholesterol alone, especially when HDL is low as is common in India.
TLP-058.ind: A high ratio results from raised total or LDL cholesterol, a low HDL, or both, and signals accelerated atherosclerosis. A low ratio reflects a favourable balance with high HDL or low total cholesterol.

fy.n: Your cholesterol ratio is in the optimal range, meaning you have a healthy balance between total cholesterol and its protective HDL fraction. This is one of the better predictors of long-term heart health. Keep it here with regular exercise, not smoking and a diet low in saturated fat.
fy.bhi: Your cholesterol ratio is in the moderate-risk zone, which typically reflects either a rising total cholesterol or a good-cholesterol level that is too low. Aerobic exercise raises HDL while cutting saturated fat lowers total cholesterol, so both ends of the ratio can be improved. Recheck in 3–6 months.
fy.hi: Your cholesterol ratio is in the high-risk range, which is consistent with an unfavourable balance of cholesterol that speeds up plaque build-up in your arteries. This deserves a discussion with your doctor about your overall cardiovascular risk and whether treatment is needed alongside diet and exercise.

TLP-058.notes: Ratio below 3.5 is optimal; above 5 is high risk. Interpret alongside the individual LDL and HDL values; the ratio can look acceptable with a very high HDL despite an elevated LDL.
TLP-058.src: Castelli / Framingham Heart Study; NCEP ATP-III

TLP-059.name: LDL/HDL Ratio
TLP-059.meas: Your bad (LDL) cholesterol divided by your good (HDL) cholesterol.
TLP-059.sig: Directly compares the cholesterol that builds plaque with the cholesterol that clears it; a higher ratio means the balance is tilted towards artery damage.
TLP-059.ind: A high ratio reflects raised LDL, low HDL or both, and is associated with metabolic syndrome, diabetes and higher coronary risk. A low ratio indicates a protective lipid balance.

fy.n: Your LDL-to-HDL ratio is optimal, meaning your protective cholesterol comfortably balances the plaque-forming kind. This favourable pattern lowers your risk of heart disease. Continue with regular activity, healthy fats such as nuts and fish, and avoiding smoking.
fy.bhi: Your LDL-to-HDL ratio is moderately raised, suggesting the balance is tipping towards artery-clogging cholesterol. This usually results from a diet high in saturated fat combined with too little exercise to raise HDL. Both are correctable; aim for 30 minutes of brisk activity most days and recheck in 3–6 months.
fy.hi: Your LDL-to-HDL ratio is in the high-risk range, which is consistent with a lipid pattern that promotes plaque build-up. Please discuss with your doctor, who will weigh this with your blood pressure, sugar and family history and may recommend treatment along with diet and exercise.

TLP-059.notes: Ratio below 2.5 is optimal; 3.5 or above is high risk. Depends on calculated LDL, so unreliable if triglycerides exceed 400 mg/dL.
TLP-059.src: Castelli / Framingham Heart Study; NCEP ATP-III

TLP-060.name: HDL/LDL Ratio
TLP-060.meas: Your good (HDL) cholesterol divided by your bad (LDL) cholesterol; the inverse of the LDL/HDL ratio.
TLP-060.sig: Expresses the same lipid balance the other way round, so that a higher number is better: more protective cholesterol relative to the plaque-forming kind.
TLP-060.ind: A low ratio means HDL is low relative to LDL, the pattern seen in insulin resistance, obesity, smoking and diets high in saturated fat. A high ratio reflects strong HDL protection or a well-controlled LDL.

fy.lo: Your HDL-to-LDL ratio is low, meaning protective cholesterol is outweighed by the plaque-forming kind. This pattern is common with extra weight, inactivity, smoking or a diet rich in fried and fatty food, and it raises heart risk. Please review with your doctor, who will consider your overall risk and may discuss treatment alongside lifestyle change.
fy.blo: Your HDL-to-LDL ratio is moderately low, which suggests the balance between good and bad cholesterol could be better. Raising HDL through aerobic exercise and quitting smoking, and lowering LDL by cutting saturated fat, will each improve the ratio. Recheck in 3–6 months.
fy.n: Your HDL-to-LDL ratio is in the optimal range, meaning you have plenty of protective cholesterol relative to the harmful kind. This is a favourable sign for your heart. Keep it up with regular activity, healthy unsaturated fats and not smoking.

TLP-060.notes: For this ratio a higher value is better; 0.40 or above is desirable, below 0.29 (equivalent to LDL/HDL above 3.5) is high risk. Depends on calculated LDL.
TLP-060.src: Derived from Castelli / Framingham cut-offs; NCEP ATP-III

TLP-061.name: Non HDL
TLP-061.meas: All the cholesterol carried in plaque-forming particles (LDL, VLDL, IDL and lipoprotein(a)) combined, calculated as total cholesterol minus HDL.
TLP-061.sig: Captures every artery-damaging cholesterol particle in one number and, unlike LDL, stays accurate when triglycerides are high or the sample is not fasting. Many guidelines now treat it as a co-primary target with LDL.
TLP-061.ind: High non-HDL cholesterol indicates an excess of atherogenic particles, typically from high LDL, high triglycerides or both, as in diabetes, metabolic syndrome, hypothyroidism or familial lipid disorders. Low values are seen with lipid-lowering treatment or low overall cholesterol and are not harmful.

fy.n: Your non-HDL cholesterol is in the desirable range, meaning the total amount of plaque-forming cholesterol in your blood is low. This is one of the most reliable single indicators of lipid-related heart risk. Keep it here with a Mediterranean-style diet and regular exercise.
fy.bhi: Your non-HDL cholesterol is borderline high, indicating a modest excess of artery-damaging particles, often from a combination of raised LDL and triglycerides. Reducing saturated fat and sugar, losing excess weight and staying active usually bring it down. Recheck in 3–6 months; your doctor may set a lower target if you have diabetes.
fy.hi: Your non-HDL cholesterol is high, which is consistent with a large burden of plaque-forming particles and a raised risk of heart attack and stroke. This warrants a discussion with your doctor about your overall risk and whether cholesterol-lowering treatment is appropriate alongside diet and exercise.

TLP-061.notes: Non-HDL targets are 30 mg/dL above the LDL target: < 130 mg/dL for high-risk, < 100 mg/dL for very-high-risk individuals. Valid on non-fasting samples.
TLP-061.src: NCEP ATP-III; ESC/EAS 2019; Lipid Association of India 2020
TLP-061.retest: With each lipid profile; 6–12 weeks after starting treatment.

TLP-062.name: Apolipoprotein B
TLP-062.meas: The main protein on every plaque-forming lipoprotein particle (LDL, VLDL, IDL, Lp(a)); since each particle carries one ApoB, it counts the number of harmful particles.
TLP-062.sig: Counts atherogenic particles rather than the cholesterol inside them, which is what actually damages arteries. It is especially useful when LDL looks normal but triglycerides are high, a common Indian pattern with many small, dense LDL particles.
TLP-062.ind: High ApoB indicates a high number of atherogenic particles, seen in familial hypercholesterolaemia, diabetes, metabolic syndrome, hypothyroidism and nephrotic syndrome. Low values reflect effective lipid-lowering treatment, or rarely a genetic condition such as hypobetalipoproteinaemia.

fy.n: Your ApoB is in the optimal range, meaning the number of artery-damaging particles in your blood is low. This is a reassuring marker even if other lipids are borderline. Maintain it with a diet low in saturated fat and refined carbohydrates and regular exercise.
fy.bhi: Your ApoB is borderline high, suggesting more plaque-forming particles than ideal even if your LDL reads acceptably. This pattern often accompanies high triglycerides, extra weight or early insulin resistance. Dietary change, weight loss and exercise lower ApoB; your doctor may set a tighter target if you have other risk factors.
fy.hi: Your ApoB is high, which is consistent with a large number of atherogenic particles and a raised risk of heart attack and stroke, sometimes hidden behind a normal-looking LDL. Please review with your doctor, who will assess your overall risk and may discuss lipid-lowering treatment alongside lifestyle measures.

TLP-062.notes: Targets are risk-based: < 80 mg/dL for high-risk and < 65 mg/dL for very-high-risk individuals (ESC/EAS). Fasting not required. Immunoturbidimetric method.
TLP-062.src: ESC/EAS 2019; ACC/AHA 2018; Lipid Association of India 2020
TLP-062.retest: 6–12 weeks after starting or changing treatment; yearly thereafter.

TLP-063.name: Lipoprotein(a)
TLP-063.meas: A genetically determined LDL-like particle with an extra protein (apolipoprotein(a)) that promotes both plaque and clotting.
TLP-063.sig: An inherited risk factor for heart attack, stroke and aortic valve narrowing that is largely independent of diet and statins. South Asians tend to have higher levels than Europeans; one measurement in a lifetime usually tells the story.
TLP-063.ind: High Lp(a) is almost entirely genetic and identifies people at increased cardiovascular risk who need aggressive control of their other risk factors; it also rises with kidney disease and hypothyroidism. Low values carry no adverse meaning.

fy.n: Your Lp(a) is in the normal range, meaning you do not carry this inherited addition to heart risk. Because Lp(a) is set by your genes and changes little over life, it rarely needs repeating. Your other lipids and blood pressure remain the levers you control.
fy.bhi: Your Lp(a) is moderately raised. This is inherited rather than caused by diet, and adds a modest extra layer of heart risk. It cannot be lowered much by lifestyle, but the response is to keep LDL, blood pressure, sugar and smoking under especially tight control. Your doctor may suggest testing close relatives.
fy.hi: Your Lp(a) is high, an inherited trait that meaningfully increases lifetime risk of heart attack, stroke and aortic valve disease. Diet does not change it, but the risk it adds can be offset by keeping LDL and other risk factors very low. Please discuss with your doctor; family members may benefit from testing too.

TLP-063.notes: Units vary: mg/dL and nmol/L are not directly interchangeable (roughly 1 mg/dL ≈ 2–2.5 nmol/L); ≥ 50 mg/dL (≈ 125 nmol/L) is the accepted high-risk cut-off. Rises in kidney disease, hypothyroidism, menopause and acute inflammation. Immunoassay method matters; isoform-insensitive assays preferred.
TLP-063.src: ESC/EAS 2019 & 2022 consensus; Lipid Association of India 2020
TLP-063.retest: Usually once in a lifetime; repeat only if kidney or thyroid disease develops, or to monitor a specific Lp(a)-lowering therapy.

TLP-064.name: hsCRP
TLP-064.meas: Tiny amounts of C-reactive protein, a liver-made inflammation protein, detected with a highly sensitive assay.
TLP-064.sig: Low-grade inflammation inside artery walls drives plaque rupture; hs-CRP picks up this quiet inflammation and adds to cholesterol-based risk estimates. It is not the same as a standard CRP used for infection.
TLP-064.ind: Higher values indicate greater cardiovascular risk from vascular inflammation, but also rise with obesity, smoking, diabetes, gum disease, sleep apnoea and any recent infection or injury. Low values indicate minimal inflammatory burden.

fy.n: Your hs-CRP is in the low-risk band, suggesting little inflammation in your blood vessels. This is a favourable sign that complements a healthy cholesterol profile. Keep inflammation low by staying active, sleeping well, avoiding smoking and looking after your teeth and gums.
fy.bhi: Your hs-CRP is in the average-risk band, indicating some low-grade inflammation. Extra weight, smoking, poor sleep, gum disease or a recent minor illness are common causes. Weight loss and regular exercise reduce hs-CRP noticeably. Your doctor may repeat it in a few weeks to confirm it is not a passing infection.
fy.hi: Your hs-CRP is in the high-risk band. If you have had any infection, injury or dental problem in the past fortnight, the value may simply reflect that and should be repeated. If persistently raised, it suggests vascular inflammation that adds to your heart risk, and your doctor may want to look at your overall risk profile more closely.

TLP-064.notes: Values above 10 mg/L usually reflect acute infection or inflammation rather than cardiovascular risk and should be repeated after 2–3 weeks. Rises in pregnancy, with oral contraceptives and hormone therapy. Average of two readings 2 weeks apart gives the most reliable estimate.
TLP-064.retest: Repeat after 2–3 weeks if raised or if recently unwell; the average of two readings is used for risk assessment.

TLP-065.name: Total Bilirubin
TLP-065.meas: The total amount of bilirubin, the yellow pigment produced when old red blood cells are broken down and processed by the liver.
TLP-065.sig: The pigment that turns skin and eyes yellow in jaundice. It rises when red cells break down too fast, when the liver cannot process the pigment, or when bile flow is blocked, so it is a core marker of liver and bile duct health.
TLP-065.ind: High values point to hepatitis, cirrhosis, bile duct obstruction (gallstones, tumours), haemolysis, or the harmless inherited condition Gilbert's syndrome. Low bilirubin has no clinical significance and may even be mildly protective.

fy.n: Your total bilirubin is in the normal range, confirming that your liver is clearing pigment efficiently and your red cells are not breaking down faster than usual. A low value is not a concern. Support your liver by limiting alcohol and avoiding unnecessary medicines and unregulated supplements.
fy.bhi: Your bilirubin is mildly raised. In an otherwise healthy person with normal liver enzymes, this is most commonly Gilbert's syndrome, a harmless inherited trait that shows up more after fasting, dehydration or illness. Your doctor will check the direct/indirect split and liver enzymes; if those are normal, no treatment is needed.
fy.hi: Your bilirubin is high enough that yellowing of the eyes may be visible. This is consistent with liver inflammation, a blocked bile duct or rapid red-cell breakdown, particularly if you have dark urine, pale stools, itching or abdominal pain. Please see your doctor promptly; the direct/indirect split and an ultrasound usually clarify the cause.

TLP-065.notes: Newborns have physiologically high bilirubin that is interpreted with age-specific charts. Fasting for over 24 hours raises bilirubin, especially in Gilbert's syndrome. Sample must be protected from light. Some labs use an upper limit of 1.0 mg/dL.
TLP-065.src: CLSI adult reference interval; Tietz Textbook of Clinical Chemistry
TLP-065.retest: If mildly raised with normal enzymes, repeat after a normal meal (non-fasting) with direct and indirect fractions.

TLP-066.name: Direct Bilirubin
TLP-066.meas: The water-soluble fraction of bilirubin that the liver has already processed (conjugated) and made ready for excretion in bile.
TLP-066.sig: A rise in the direct fraction tells you the liver has processed the pigment but cannot get rid of it, pointing to bile-flow obstruction or liver-cell damage rather than red-cell breakdown.
TLP-066.ind: High direct bilirubin indicates cholestasis or hepatocellular injury: gallstones or tumours blocking the bile duct, hepatitis, cirrhosis, drug-induced liver injury, or rare inherited conditions (Dubin-Johnson, Rotor). A low value has no significance.

fy.n: Your direct bilirubin is in the normal range, showing that bile is flowing freely from the liver into the gut and that liver cells are excreting pigment normally. If total bilirubin is raised but this fraction is normal, the cause is usually a harmless one such as Gilbert's syndrome.
fy.bhi: Your direct bilirubin is mildly raised, which suggests a slight slowing of bile flow or minor liver-cell stress. Recent medication, alcohol, a viral illness or early gallstone disease are common reasons. Your doctor will compare it with your liver enzymes and may repeat the test or arrange an ultrasound.
fy.hi: Your direct bilirubin is high, which is consistent with a blockage of bile flow (for example gallstones) or damage to liver cells from hepatitis, drugs or alcohol. Dark urine and pale stools often accompany this. Please see your doctor promptly; an ultrasound and full liver panel are usually the next steps.

TLP-066.notes: Direct fraction should normally be less than 20–30% of total bilirubin. Some labs use an upper limit of 0.2 mg/dL. In newborn jaundice, a direct fraction above 1 mg/dL is always significant and needs urgent evaluation.
TLP-066.src: CLSI adult reference interval; Tietz Textbook of Clinical Chemistry
TLP-066.retest: Repeat with full liver function tests and ultrasound if raised.

TLP-067.name: Indirect Bilirubin
TLP-067.meas: The fat-soluble fraction of bilirubin that has not yet been processed by the liver, calculated as total minus direct bilirubin.
TLP-067.sig: Rises when red cells are breaking down faster than the liver can keep up, or when the liver's processing enzyme is sluggish as in Gilbert's syndrome. It points away from bile-duct blockage and towards blood or enzyme causes.
TLP-067.ind: High indirect bilirubin suggests haemolysis (thalassaemia, G6PD deficiency, autoimmune haemolysis), ineffective red-cell production (B12 or folate deficiency), reabsorption of a large bruise or haematoma, or Gilbert's syndrome. Low values have no significance.

fy.n: Your indirect bilirubin is in the normal range, which indicates that your red blood cells are living out their normal lifespan and your liver is processing pigment at a healthy pace. Nothing further is needed.
fy.bhi: Your indirect bilirubin is mildly raised. With normal liver enzymes and a normal blood count, the most common explanation is Gilbert's syndrome, a harmless inherited trait affecting around 5–10% of people that becomes noticeable after fasting or illness. Your doctor may repeat the test after a normal meal to confirm.
fy.hi: Your indirect bilirubin is high, which suggests either accelerated red-cell breakdown (as in thalassaemia trait, G6PD deficiency or autoimmune haemolysis) or a marked Gilbert's pattern. Your doctor may check a blood count, reticulocytes and haemolysis markers to tell these apart. Please arrange a review, particularly if you feel tired or look pale.

TLP-067.notes: Calculated value; accuracy depends on the direct bilirubin method. Common in India because of the high prevalence of thalassaemia trait and G6PD deficiency. Newborn values are interpreted with age-in-hours charts.
TLP-067.src: CLSI adult reference interval; Tietz Textbook of Clinical Chemistry
TLP-067.retest: If raised, repeat non-fasting with a complete blood count and reticulocyte count.

TLP-068.name: SGOT / AST
TLP-068.meas: An enzyme found in liver cells and also in heart, skeletal muscle, kidney and red cells, released into the blood when these cells are injured.
TLP-068.sig: A marker of cell injury that is most often read as a liver test but also rises with muscle damage after hard exercise. Its ratio to ALT helps tell alcohol-related and advanced liver disease from simple fatty liver.
TLP-068.ind: High AST indicates liver injury from fatty liver, viral hepatitis, alcohol, medicines or cirrhosis, but also muscle injury, strenuous exercise, heart attack or haemolysis. Low values have no clinical significance (occasionally seen with vitamin B6 deficiency or dialysis).

fy.n: Your AST is in the normal range, suggesting no significant ongoing injury to liver or muscle cells. A low value is not a concern. Keep your liver healthy with moderate alcohol intake, a healthy weight and caution with unregulated herbal or bodybuilding supplements.
fy.bhi: Your AST is mildly raised, up to about twice the upper limit. Common causes are fatty liver, alcohol, recent intense exercise or muscle strain, and certain medicines. If ALT is also up, the liver is the likely source. Avoid alcohol and heavy workouts for a few days and repeat in 2–4 weeks; your doctor may add an ultrasound.
fy.hi: Your AST is significantly raised, which is consistent with active liver inflammation (viral hepatitis, alcohol, drug reaction) or marked muscle injury. Please see your doctor soon, particularly if you have jaundice, abdominal pain, dark urine or muscle pain. A repeat test with CK, hepatitis screen and ultrasound will help locate the cause.

TLP-068.notes: Upper limits vary by lab and method (typically 35–40 U/L). Rises for several days after intense exercise or intramuscular injections. Haemolysed samples give falsely high values. Slightly higher in men than women.
TLP-068.src: CLSI adult reference interval; AASLD / ACG guidelines
TLP-068.retest: Repeat in 2–4 weeks after avoiding alcohol, heavy exercise and unnecessary medicines; sooner if symptomatic.

TLP-069.name: SGPT / ALT
TLP-069.meas: An enzyme concentrated almost entirely in liver cells and released into the blood when they are inflamed or damaged.
TLP-069.sig: The most liver-specific of the routine enzymes and the earliest signal of fatty liver, which affects roughly one in three urban Indian adults. Even mild persistent elevation deserves attention.
TLP-069.ind: High ALT points to fatty liver (NAFLD/MASLD), viral hepatitis B or C, alcohol, medicines (statins, anti-TB drugs, paracetamol excess, herbal remedies), autoimmune hepatitis or coeliac disease. Low values have no clinical significance.

fy.n: Your ALT is in the normal range, a good sign that your liver cells are not inflamed. Because fatty liver is so common, keeping ALT here means maintaining a healthy weight, limiting alcohol and sugary drinks, and being careful with over-the-counter and herbal products.
fy.bhi: Your ALT is mildly raised. The most frequent cause in otherwise well adults is fat in the liver linked to weight, diabetes or high triglycerides; alcohol, recent medicines and viral infections are other possibilities. Weight loss of 5–10% can normalise it. Repeat in 4–8 weeks; your doctor may arrange an ultrasound and hepatitis B and C tests.
fy.hi: Your ALT is well above normal, which is consistent with active liver inflammation from a virus, alcohol, a medicine or supplement, or advanced fatty liver. Please see your doctor soon, especially if you have jaundice, nausea or right-sided abdominal pain. Stop alcohol and non-essential medicines until you are reviewed.

TLP-069.notes: Some guidelines propose lower 'healthy' upper limits (about 30 U/L men, 19–25 U/L women); the lab reference interval is used here. Slightly higher in men. Persistent elevation for over 6 months qualifies as chronic and warrants full evaluation.
TLP-069.src: CLSI adult reference interval; ACG 2017 guideline on abnormal liver chemistries
TLP-069.retest: Repeat in 4–8 weeks if mildly raised; promptly with a hepatitis screen if high or symptomatic.

TLP-070.name: AST/ALT Ratio
TLP-070.meas: The AST value divided by the ALT value, showing which of the two liver enzymes is predominantly raised.
TLP-070.sig: The pattern of enzyme rise hints at the cause of liver injury: ALT-dominant (ratio below 1) suggests fatty liver or viral hepatitis, whereas AST-dominant (ratio above 2) suggests alcohol-related disease or established scarring.
TLP-070.ind: A ratio above 2 is characteristic of alcoholic liver disease and also seen in cirrhosis from any cause, muscle injury and haemolysis. A ratio below 1 is typical of fatty liver and acute viral hepatitis. The ratio is only meaningful when at least one enzyme is raised.

fy.n: Your AST/ALT ratio is below 1, the usual pattern in healthy people. If your enzymes are raised, this pattern is most consistent with fat in the liver or a viral cause rather than alcohol or scarring. If both enzymes are normal the ratio needs no interpretation.
fy.bhi: Your AST/ALT ratio is between 1 and 2. When enzymes are normal this has no significance. When they are raised, this in-between pattern can be seen in progressing fatty liver, some medicines, or early scarring, and your doctor may look at fibrosis scores or an elastography scan to clarify.
fy.hi: Your AST is more than twice your ALT. If the enzymes are raised, this pattern is consistent with alcohol-related liver injury, established scarring (cirrhosis), or a muscle rather than liver source. Please discuss with your doctor, who may ask about alcohol intake, check GGT and CK, and consider a liver scan.

TLP-070.notes: Interpret only when AST or ALT is above the reference range; in people with normal enzymes the ratio is frequently above 1 and has no meaning. Muscle injury and haemolysis raise AST and inflate the ratio.
TLP-070.src: De Ritis 1957; ACG 2017 guideline on abnormal liver chemistries
TLP-070.retest: Recalculated whenever liver enzymes are repeated.

TLP-071.name: Alkaline Phosphatase
TLP-071.meas: An enzyme produced mainly by the bile ducts of the liver and by bone-forming cells, with smaller amounts from the intestine and placenta.
TLP-071.sig: Rises when bile flow is obstructed or when bone is being actively remodelled, so it bridges liver and bone health. Reading it with GGT tells you which organ is responsible.
TLP-071.ind: High ALP indicates bile duct obstruction or cholestasis (gallstones, drugs, primary biliary cholangitis), infiltrative liver disease, or bone conditions such as vitamin D deficiency (osteomalacia), Paget's disease, fractures and bone metastases; it rises normally in growing children and late pregnancy. Low ALP suggests zinc or magnesium deficiency, hypothyroidism, malnutrition or the rare inherited hypophosphatasia.

fy.lo: Your ALP is below the usual range. This is uncommon and often harmless, but it can reflect low zinc or magnesium, an underactive thyroid, poor nutrition or, very rarely, an inherited bone enzyme deficiency. Your doctor may check thyroid function and minerals if you have bone pain or dental problems.
fy.n: Your ALP is in the normal range, which suggests your bile ducts are draining freely and bone turnover is at a healthy adult level. Adequate vitamin D and calcium, plus weight-bearing exercise, support both bone and this result.
fy.bhi: Your ALP is mildly raised. The commonest explanations are vitamin D deficiency affecting bone, a recent fracture, gallstones or medicines; it is also normal in pregnancy and in adolescents. Your doctor will look at GGT (raised means liver source) and vitamin D to decide between bone and liver causes. Repeat in 4–6 weeks.
fy.hi: Your ALP is substantially raised, which is consistent with blocked bile flow, an infiltrative liver problem or active bone disease. Itching, jaundice or bone pain would help point to the source. Please see your doctor, who may check GGT, vitamin D, calcium and arrange an ultrasound or bone imaging as needed.

TLP-071.notes: Children and adolescents have 2–3 times adult values because of bone growth. Rises to 2–3 times normal in the third trimester of pregnancy (placental ALP). Blood group O and B individuals show a post-meal intestinal rise, so fasting is preferred. Reference intervals vary by method (IFCC 40–129 U/L is used here).
TLP-071.src: IFCC / CLSI adult reference interval; ACG 2017 guideline
TLP-071.retest: If raised, repeat fasting with GGT and vitamin D to identify liver versus bone origin.

TLP-072.name: GGT
TLP-072.meas: An enzyme in the cells lining the bile ducts that rises with bile-flow problems and is very sensitive to alcohol and many medicines.
TLP-072.sig: The most sensitive routine marker of alcohol effect and drug-induced liver stress, and the test that confirms a raised ALP comes from the liver rather than bone. Also an independent marker of fatty liver and metabolic risk.
TLP-072.ind: High GGT indicates alcohol intake, fatty liver, cholestasis or bile duct obstruction, enzyme-inducing drugs (anti-epileptics, rifampicin), obesity, diabetes or heart failure. Low values are of no clinical concern.

fy.n: Your GGT is in the normal range, suggesting your bile ducts are healthy and that alcohol, medicines and body fat are not stressing your liver. It also makes a liver cause unlikely if your ALP is raised. Keep it here with alcohol in moderation and a healthy weight.
fy.bhi: Your GGT is mildly raised. Regular alcohol, even at 'social' levels, is the commonest cause; fatty liver, obesity, diabetes and medicines such as anti-epileptics or statins are others. GGT falls within 2–4 weeks of stopping alcohol, so a repeat after an alcohol-free month is a useful test in itself. Discuss with your doctor if it stays up.
fy.hi: Your GGT is substantially raised, which is consistent with significant alcohol effect, blocked bile flow or drug-related liver stress, particularly if ALP or bilirubin are also up. Please see your doctor, who will review your alcohol intake and medicines and may arrange an ultrasound. Cutting out alcohol completely is the most important first step.

TLP-072.notes: Reference intervals vary by method; men run higher than women. Rises with obesity and age. Enzyme-inducing drugs and oral contraceptives affect values. Falls with a half-life of about 2–3 weeks after stopping alcohol.
TLP-072.src: IFCC / CLSI adult reference interval; ACG 2017 guideline
TLP-072.retest: Repeat after 4 weeks without alcohol; if still raised, evaluate for fatty liver or bile duct disease.

TLP-073.name: Total Protein
TLP-073.meas: The combined amount of all proteins in your blood serum, chiefly albumin and globulins.
TLP-073.sig: A broad indicator of nutrition, liver synthetic function, kidney protein loss and immune activity. Its two halves, albumin and globulin, are more informative than the total alone.
TLP-073.ind: High total protein usually reflects dehydration or increased globulins from chronic infection, chronic liver disease, autoimmune disease or a plasma-cell disorder such as myeloma. Low values indicate poor nutrition, malabsorption, liver failure, kidney protein loss (nephrotic syndrome), severe burns or over-hydration.

fy.lo: Your total protein is low, which suggests either reduced production (poor dietary intake, malabsorption or liver disease) or increased loss through the kidneys or gut. Ensure adequate protein in your diet, and discuss with your doctor, who may check albumin, urine protein and liver function to find the cause.
fy.n: Your total protein is in the normal range, a reassuring sign of adequate nutrition, healthy liver production and no major protein loss through the kidneys. A balanced diet with enough protein (dal, dairy, eggs, fish, nuts) keeps it here.
fy.hi: Your total protein is raised. Most often this reflects mild dehydration on the day of the test. Persistently high values with a normal albumin usually mean increased globulins, which can occur with chronic infection, liver disease, autoimmune conditions or, less commonly, a plasma-cell disorder. Your doctor may repeat the test well hydrated and check the globulin fraction.

TLP-073.notes: Falls by about 1 g/dL in the second and third trimester of pregnancy due to dilution. Prolonged tourniquet use and upright posture raise values slightly. Children under 3 have slightly lower values.
TLP-073.src: CLSI adult reference interval; Tietz Textbook of Clinical Chemistry
TLP-073.retest: If high, repeat well hydrated; if persistently abnormal, request protein electrophoresis.

TLP-074.name: Albumin
TLP-074.meas: The most abundant protein in your blood, made by the liver, which maintains fluid balance and carries hormones, drugs and nutrients.
TLP-074.sig: A robust indicator of liver synthetic capacity and nutritional state over the previous few weeks. Low albumin causes fluid to leak into tissues and is a strong marker of illness severity.
TLP-074.ind: Low albumin points to chronic liver disease, malnutrition, kidney protein loss (nephrotic syndrome), protein-losing gut disease, chronic inflammation or severe illness. High albumin almost always reflects dehydration.

fy.lo: Your albumin is low, which suggests your liver is making less of it, your diet is short of protein, or you are losing protein through the kidneys or gut. Long-standing inflammation can also lower it. Swelling of the ankles is a common sign. Please discuss with your doctor, who may check urine protein and liver function.
fy.n: Your albumin is in the normal range, which confirms good liver production, adequate protein nutrition and no significant protein loss. Maintain it with a balanced diet containing enough protein at each meal.
fy.hi: Your albumin is slightly above normal, which almost always means you were a little dehydrated when the sample was taken (for example after fasting overnight in hot weather). It is not a sign of disease. Drink normally and it will settle; no follow-up is usually needed.

TLP-074.notes: Falls by 0.5–1 g/dL in pregnancy due to haemodilution. Slightly lower in adults over 70. Bromocresol green method may read 0.3–0.5 g/dL higher than bromocresol purple in liver disease.
TLP-074.src: CLSI adult reference interval; Tietz Textbook of Clinical Chemistry
TLP-074.retest: Repeat in 4–6 weeks after nutritional improvement, or with liver and urine tests if low.

TLP-075.name: Globulin
TLP-075.meas: The non-albumin proteins in your blood, including antibodies (immunoglobulins), transport proteins and clotting factors, calculated as total protein minus albumin.
TLP-075.sig: Largely reflects immune activity. A rise signals the body is producing extra antibodies in response to chronic infection, inflammation or liver disease, or in rare cases an abnormal antibody-producing cell clone.
TLP-075.ind: High globulin suggests chronic infection (tuberculosis, HIV, hepatitis), chronic liver disease, autoimmune conditions (lupus, rheumatoid arthritis) or a plasma-cell disorder such as multiple myeloma. Low globulin points to immune deficiency, kidney or gut protein loss, or steroid therapy.

fy.lo: Your globulin is low, which can reflect reduced antibody production (some immune deficiencies or steroid treatment) or loss of protein through the kidneys or gut. If you get frequent infections, mention this to your doctor, who may measure the individual immunoglobulin classes.
fy.n: Your globulin is in the normal range, indicating a healthy balance of antibodies and other immune and transport proteins without signs of chronic infection or inflammation. No action is needed.
fy.bhi: Your globulin is mildly raised, which usually means your immune system is somewhat activated. Recent or ongoing infection, gum or skin infection, fatty liver or an autoimmune tendency are common reasons. Your doctor may repeat the test in a few weeks and, if it stays up, look at the albumin-globulin ratio and a protein electrophoresis.
fy.hi: Your globulin is clearly raised, which is consistent with a chronic infection, long-standing liver disease, an autoimmune condition or, less commonly, an abnormal antibody-producing cell line. Please discuss with your doctor, who will likely arrange a protein electrophoresis to identify which globulin is responsible.

TLP-075.notes: Calculated value, so it inherits any error in total protein or albumin. Rises with age and in chronic inflammatory states common in India (tuberculosis, chronic hepatitis). Falls in pregnancy dilution.
TLP-075.src: CLSI adult reference interval; Tietz Textbook of Clinical Chemistry
TLP-075.retest: If persistently above 3.5 g/dL, request serum protein electrophoresis.

TLP-076.name: A/G Ratio
TLP-076.meas: Your albumin divided by your globulin, showing the balance between the liver's main protein and the immune proteins.
TLP-076.sig: A quick screen for a shift in protein balance: a low ratio means albumin has fallen or globulins have risen, which points to liver disease, kidney protein loss or an over-active immune system before either alone is obviously abnormal.
TLP-076.ind: A low ratio suggests chronic liver disease, nephrotic syndrome, chronic infection, autoimmune disease or multiple myeloma. A high ratio is uncommon and usually reflects low globulins from immune deficiency or steroid treatment, or dehydration.

fy.lo: Your albumin-to-globulin ratio is low, meaning globulins outweigh albumin. This is consistent with chronic liver disease, protein loss through the kidneys, or a long-standing infection or immune condition raising antibody levels. Your doctor will look at the individual albumin and globulin values and may arrange protein electrophoresis, liver and urine tests.
fy.blo: Your albumin-to-globulin ratio is at the lower edge of normal, which can be an early hint of increased immune protein or slightly low albumin. Recent infection, fatty liver or a marginal protein intake are common reasons. It is usually worth repeating in 4–6 weeks rather than acting on a single value.
fy.n: Your albumin-to-globulin ratio is in the normal range, indicating a healthy balance between liver-made albumin and immune globulins. This makes chronic liver disease, kidney protein loss and abnormal antibody production unlikely.
fy.hi: Your albumin-to-globulin ratio is high, which is uncommon. It usually means globulins are low, as can happen with some immune deficiencies, steroid treatment or protein loss, or that you were dehydrated at the time of sampling. Your doctor may repeat the test and, if it persists, measure the individual immunoglobulins.

TLP-076.notes: Calculated from albumin and globulin, so method-dependent; some labs quote a normal range of 1.0–2.5. Interpret together with the absolute values rather than in isolation.
TLP-076.src: Tietz Textbook of Clinical Chemistry; CLSI adult reference interval
TLP-076.retest: Repeat with protein electrophoresis if persistently below 1.0.

TLP-077.name: FIB-4 Score (Calculated)
TLP-077.meas: A calculated index combining your age, AST, ALT and platelet count to estimate the likelihood of significant scarring (fibrosis) in the liver.
TLP-077.sig: Scarring, not fat, is what determines the long-term outcome of fatty liver disease, and FIB-4 is the recommended first-line tool to identify who needs a liver stiffness scan. A low score reliably rules out advanced fibrosis.
TLP-077.ind: A high score indicates a substantial probability of advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis from fatty liver, hepatitis B or C, or alcohol. A low score makes advanced fibrosis unlikely. The score can be raised falsely by a low platelet count from other causes or by muscle-related AST elevation.

fy.n: Your FIB-4 score is low, which makes advanced liver scarring unlikely even if you have fatty liver. This is reassuring, though fat in the liver can still progress, so continue with weight control, exercise and limited alcohol. Recheck every 1–3 years if you have diabetes or fatty liver.
fy.bhi: Your FIB-4 score falls in the indeterminate zone, which does not confirm scarring but cannot rule it out. This is common over the age of 50 because age is part of the formula. Your doctor may arrange a liver stiffness scan (FibroScan or elastography) to settle the question, particularly if you have diabetes or fatty liver.
fy.hi: Your FIB-4 score is high, suggesting a meaningful chance of advanced liver scarring. It is a screening estimate, not a diagnosis, and can be pushed up by a low platelet count or muscle injury.
