Please see your doctor or a liver specialist for a stiffness scan and further tests; if scarring is confirmed, treatment and monitoring can slow or reverse it.

TLP-077.notes: Formula: age (years) × AST / (platelets (10^9/L) × √ALT). Validated for ages 35–65; over-estimates fibrosis in people over 65 (upper cut-off of 2.0 for the low-risk band is used in that group) and is unreliable below 35. Not for use in acute hepatitis.
TLP-077.src: Sterling et al. 2006; AASLD 2023 / EASL 2021 NAFLD guidelines
TLP-077.retest: Every 1–3 years if low risk with fatty liver or diabetes; proceed to elastography if indeterminate or high.

TLP-078.name: NAFLD Fibrosis Score
TLP-078.sample: Calculated (age, BMI, diabetes status, AST, ALT, platelets, albumin)
TLP-078.meas: A calculated score using age, body mass index, diabetes status, AST/ALT ratio, platelet count and albumin to estimate the probability of advanced scarring in a fatty liver.
TLP-078.sig: Developed specifically for fatty liver disease, it separates people who can safely be reassured from those who need a liver stiffness scan or specialist review. It complements FIB-4 and is most useful when the two agree.
TLP-078.ind: A high score indicates a high probability of advanced fibrosis (F3–F4) in fatty liver disease. A low score effectively excludes it. Intermediate scores are inconclusive and require imaging. Low albumin or platelets from other causes can inflate the score.

fy.n: Your NAFLD fibrosis score is low, which makes advanced scarring of the liver unlikely. Fat in the liver may still be present, and it responds well to 7–10% weight loss, regular exercise, controlling diabetes and avoiding alcohol. Recheck the score every 1–3 years.
fy.bhi: Your NAFLD fibrosis score is in the indeterminate range, so scarring can neither be confirmed nor excluded from blood tests alone. Older age, diabetes and a higher BMI all push the score up. Your doctor may arrange a liver stiffness scan to clarify; meanwhile weight loss and good sugar control are the most effective steps.
fy.hi: Your NAFLD fibrosis score is high, suggesting a significant likelihood of advanced liver scarring from fatty liver disease. This is a screening estimate rather than a diagnosis. Please see your doctor or a liver specialist for a stiffness scan and assessment; identifying and treating fibrosis early can prevent progression to cirrhosis.

TLP-078.notes: Formula: −1.675 + 0.037 × age + 0.094 × BMI + 1.13 × (diabetes/IFG = 1) + 0.99 × AST/ALT − 0.013 × platelets (10^9/L) − 0.66 × albumin (g/dL). Requires BMI and diabetes status. Less accurate in people over 65 and in lean NAFLD, which is common in South Asians.
TLP-078.src: Angulo et al. 2007; AASLD 2023 / EASL 2021 NAFLD guidelines
TLP-078.retest: Every 1–3 years if low; proceed to elastography if indeterminate or high.

TLP-079.name: APRI (AST to Platelet Ratio)
TLP-079.alias: AST to Platelet Ratio Index, APRI score
TLP-079.meas: A simple calculated index that compares your AST (as a multiple of its upper limit) with your platelet count to estimate liver scarring.
TLP-079.sig: A low-cost fibrosis screen recommended by the WHO for hepatitis B and C in resource-limited settings; also used in fatty liver. It relies on the fact that scarring raises AST and lowers platelets.
TLP-079.ind: A high APRI suggests significant fibrosis or cirrhosis from chronic hepatitis B or C, alcohol or fatty liver. A low APRI makes cirrhosis unlikely. Acute hepatitis, muscle injury or a low platelet count from other causes can falsely elevate the score.

fy.n: Your APRI score is low, which makes significant liver scarring unlikely. It is a rough screen rather than a scan, so if you carry hepatitis B or C or have fatty liver, continue regular follow-up; otherwise, a healthy weight and limited alcohol are all that is needed.
fy.bhi: Your APRI score is in the indeterminate range, meaning it cannot rule scarring in or out. This can happen with a temporary rise in AST from exercise, medicines or alcohol, or a mildly low platelet count. Your doctor may repeat the test and combine it with FIB-4 or a liver stiffness scan for a clearer answer.
fy.hi: Your APRI score is high, which is consistent with a meaningful chance of advanced scarring or cirrhosis, especially if you have hepatitis B or C, drink alcohol regularly or have long-standing fatty liver. It is not a diagnosis, but please see your doctor or a liver specialist for a stiffness scan and further evaluation.

TLP-079.notes: Formula: (AST / upper limit of normal for AST) × 100 / platelets (10^9/L). Cut-offs per WHO 2015: < 0.5 rules out significant fibrosis, > 1.5 suggests significant fibrosis, > 2.0 suggests cirrhosis. Less accurate than FIB-4 in fatty liver; invalid in acute hepatitis.
TLP-079.src: Wai et al. 2003; WHO 2015 hepatitis B/C guidelines
TLP-079.retest: Repeat with each liver review; proceed to elastography if indeterminate or high.

TLP-080.name: Amylase
TLP-080.meas: An enzyme that digests starch, produced by the pancreas and the salivary glands.
TLP-080.sig: A traditional marker of pancreatic inflammation: it rises within hours of an attack of acute pancreatitis. Because salivary glands also make amylase, it is less specific than lipase and is best read alongside it.
TLP-080.ind: High amylase suggests acute or chronic pancreatitis, a blocked pancreatic duct, gallstones, salivary gland disease (mumps, stones), bowel perforation or obstruction, kidney failure (reduced clearance), or the harmless macroamylasaemia. Low values are seen in advanced chronic pancreatitis where the gland has burnt out, and in cystic fibrosis.

fy.lo: Your amylase is low. This is usually of no concern in a healthy person, but in someone with long-standing pancreatic disease, diabetes or alcohol-related illness it can mean the pancreas has lost much of its enzyme-producing tissue. If you have loose, greasy stools or weight loss, mention this to your doctor.
fy.n: Your amylase is in the normal range, which suggests your pancreas and salivary glands are not inflamed. Protect your pancreas by keeping alcohol moderate, triglycerides controlled and gallstones treated if they cause symptoms.
fy.bhi: Your amylase is mildly raised, up to about three times normal. Without abdominal pain this is often from salivary glands, mild kidney impairment, medicines or a benign condition called macroamylasaemia rather than the pancreas. Your doctor may check lipase, which is more pancreas-specific, and repeat the test.
fy.hi: Your amylase is more than three times normal, which is consistent with acute pancreatitis, especially if you have severe upper abdominal pain radiating to the back with nausea. Gallstones and alcohol are the commonest triggers. Please seek medical attention promptly; lipase and an ultrasound or CT scan will confirm the diagnosis.

TLP-080.notes: Reference intervals vary widely by method (some labs use up to 110–120 U/L). Rises with kidney failure because amylase is cleared by the kidneys. In acute pancreatitis the level peaks at 24–48 hours and may already be falling after 3–5 days, so a normal value does not exclude an older attack.
TLP-080.src: CLSI adult reference interval; ACG 2013 acute pancreatitis guideline
TLP-080.retest: Repeat with lipase if symptoms suggest pancreatitis; recheck after recovery to confirm normalisation.

TLP-081.name: Lipase
TLP-081.meas: An enzyme made almost exclusively by the pancreas to digest fats.
TLP-081.sig: The preferred blood test for acute pancreatitis: more specific than amylase and staying raised for longer (up to 1–2 weeks), so it catches attacks that amylase may miss.
TLP-081.ind: High lipase suggests acute pancreatitis (gallstones, alcohol, high triglycerides, some medicines), chronic pancreatitis flare, pancreatic duct obstruction or tumour, and to a lesser degree bowel obstruction, kidney failure or cholecystitis. Low values may indicate burnt-out chronic pancreatitis with poor fat digestion.

fy.lo: Your lipase is low. In most healthy people this has no significance. In someone with a history of pancreatitis, heavy alcohol use or diabetes, a very low level can indicate that the pancreas is no longer producing enough enzyme to digest fat, which shows up as bulky, pale stools and weight loss. Discuss with your doctor if that applies to you.
fy.n: Your lipase is in the normal range, suggesting your pancreas is not inflamed. This effectively rules out acute pancreatitis if you have had abdominal pain in the last week. Keep alcohol moderate and triglycerides controlled to protect the gland.
fy.bhi: Your lipase is mildly raised, less than three times the upper limit. Mild rises occur with kidney impairment, certain medicines, gut inflammation or a recent minor pancreatic irritation, and are not diagnostic of pancreatitis on their own. Your doctor may repeat the test and arrange an ultrasound if you have any abdominal symptoms.
fy.hi: Your lipase is more than three times normal, which in the setting of upper abdominal pain is consistent with acute pancreatitis. Gallstones, alcohol and very high triglycerides are the usual triggers. Please seek prompt medical attention; imaging will confirm the diagnosis and guide treatment, and the pancreas usually recovers fully with appropriate care.

TLP-081.notes: Reference intervals differ considerably between methods (upper limits of 51–67 U/L are common). A rise above three times the upper limit is the diagnostic threshold for acute pancreatitis. Persists 7–14 days after an attack. Mildly raised in kidney failure.
TLP-081.src: CLSI adult reference interval; ACG 2013 and revised Atlanta classification of acute pancreatitis
TLP-081.retest: Repeat after recovery from any pancreatic episode; a persistent rise needs imaging of the pancreas.

TLP-082.name: NT-proBNP
TLP-082.meas: A hormone fragment released by the heart muscle when its chambers are stretched by high pressure or fluid overload.
TLP-082.sig: The best blood marker of heart failure: a low value virtually rules it out, and a high value signals the heart is under strain, often before symptoms are obvious. Useful in breathlessness, uncontrolled blood pressure and screening older adults.
TLP-082.ind: High NT-proBNP suggests heart failure, but also rises with atrial fibrillation, valve disease, pulmonary embolism, kidney failure, severe anaemia, sepsis and advancing age. Low values indicate the heart is not under strain; obesity can lower it artificially.

fy.n: Your NT-proBNP is low, which makes heart failure very unlikely: your heart is not under significant strain. This is reassuring even if you sometimes feel breathless, which then more likely has a lung, fitness or anaemia cause. Keep your heart healthy with blood pressure control, exercise and not smoking.
fy.bhi: Your NT-proBNP is in the grey zone. Values here become more common with age, kidney impairment, an irregular heart rhythm or uncontrolled blood pressure, and do not necessarily mean heart failure. Your doctor may arrange an ECG and an echocardiogram (heart ultrasound) to check how your heart is pumping.
fy.hi: Your NT-proBNP is raised, which is consistent with the heart working under strain, as in heart failure, significant valve disease or an irregular rhythm; kidney disease and severe anaemia can also contribute. Please see your doctor soon for an ECG and echocardiogram, particularly if you have breathlessness, ankle swelling or difficulty lying flat.

TLP-082.notes: Age-adjusted cut-offs apply for acute breathlessness: < 300 pg/mL rules out acute heart failure; rule-in thresholds are 450 (< 50 years), 900 (50–75) and 1800 pg/mL (> 75). Values rise with kidney disease and age; obesity lowers them. The 125 pg/mL threshold is the ESC rule-out cut-off in the non-acute setting.
TLP-082.retest: Repeat if new or worsening breathlessness or swelling; used serially to monitor treatment in known heart failure.

TLP-083.name: Troponin I (hs)
TLP-083.dn: High-sensitivity Troponin I (heart muscle injury marker)
TLP-083.meas: A protein found only in heart muscle cells, detected in tiny amounts with a highly sensitive assay; it leaks into the blood when heart muscle is injured.
TLP-083.sig: The definitive blood marker of heart muscle injury and the cornerstone of heart attack diagnosis. In a well person without chest pain, a low value is reassuring while a persistently detectable rise flags silent cardiac stress and future risk.
TLP-083.ind: High troponin indicates heart muscle injury: acute heart attack, myocarditis, heart failure, very fast heart rhythms, pulmonary embolism, severe kidney disease or extreme exertion. In stable people, chronically mildly raised values are associated with structural heart disease and higher long-term risk. Low values are normal.

fy.n: Your high-sensitivity troponin is within the normal range, which means there is no detectable ongoing injury to your heart muscle. In a person without chest pain this is a reassuring finding. Continue to manage blood pressure, cholesterol and sugar, as these protect the heart long term.
fy.hi: Your troponin is above the 99th-percentile cut-off, indicating some injury to heart muscle. If you have chest pain, breathlessness or sweating right now, treat this as an emergency and go to the nearest hospital. Without symptoms, it may reflect strain from high blood pressure, kidney disease or recent intense exertion, but it still needs prompt review by your doctor with an ECG and echocardiogram.

TLP-083.notes: Cut-offs are assay-specific 99th-percentile values (the figures here are for a common hs-TnI platform, e.g. Abbott Architect: 34 ng/L men, 16 ng/L women) and must match the lab's platform. A single value cannot diagnose or exclude a heart attack; serial testing at 0 and 1–3 hours is required in chest pain. Chronic kidney disease raises baseline values. Not a screening test for blocked arteries.
TLP-083.src: Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction 2018; ESC 2023 ACS guideline
TLP-083.retest: Any raised value needs a repeat within 1–3 hours in an emergency setting if symptomatic; otherwise discuss with a cardiologist for further evaluation.

TLP-084.name: Homocysteine
TLP-084.profile: ADD-ON · EXTENDED CV RISK; ADD-ON · THROMBOPHILIA WORK-UP (on VTE history only)
TLP-084.sample: EDTA plasma (separated within 1 hour, on ice)
TLP-084.meas: An amino acid produced during protein metabolism that the body normally recycles using vitamins B12, B6 and folate.
TLP-084.sig: Raised homocysteine damages the lining of blood vessels and promotes clotting, and is linked with heart disease, stroke, venous thrombosis and pregnancy loss. In India it is often high because of vegetarian diets low in vitamin B12.
TLP-084.ind: High homocysteine most commonly indicates vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, or a common genetic variant (MTHFR); other causes are kidney disease, hypothyroidism, smoking, coffee, alcohol and some medicines (methotrexate, anti-epileptics, metformin). Low values are of no clinical concern.

fy.n: Your homocysteine is in the normal range, suggesting your vitamin B12, folate and B6 status is adequate and that this pathway is not adding to your vascular or clotting risk. A diet with enough B vitamins (dairy, eggs, green leafy vegetables, legumes) will keep it here.
fy.bhi: Your homocysteine is moderately raised. In most people this reflects low vitamin B12 or folate, especially on a vegetarian diet, or a common inherited variant that slows the recycling pathway. It adds modestly to heart, stroke and clotting risk. Your doctor may check B12 and folate; correcting a deficiency usually normalises it within 2–3 months.
fy.hi: Your homocysteine is high, which is consistent with a significant B12 or folate deficiency, kidney impairment or an inherited metabolic variant, and is associated with increased risk of blood clots, heart disease and pregnancy complications. Please review with your doctor, who will check vitamin levels and kidney function and guide appropriate supplementation and monitoring.

TLP-084.notes: Fasting sample preferred; values rise after a protein-rich meal. Sample must be separated promptly (red cells release homocysteine) or results are falsely high. Values are lower in pregnancy and higher in men, older adults and with kidney disease. Some labs use an upper limit of 12 µmol/L; values > 100 µmol/L suggest homocystinuria.
TLP-084.src: AHA scientific statement on homocysteine; ISTH thrombophilia guidance
TLP-084.retest: Repeat 8–12 weeks after starting B12/folate correction to confirm normalisation.

TLP-085.name: Hepatitis A IgM
TLP-085.meas: IgM-class antibodies against the hepatitis A virus, which appear within days of infection and persist for a few months.
TLP-085.sig: The test that confirms a recent or current hepatitis A infection, a food- and water-borne cause of acute jaundice that is very common in India, particularly in the monsoon. A positive result explains fever with jaundice and guides household precautions.
TLP-085.ind: A positive result indicates acute or recent hepatitis A infection (within roughly the past 3–6 months). A negative result makes hepatitis A the cause of current jaundice unlikely. Rarely, a false positive can occur with rheumatoid factor or recent hepatitis A vaccination.

fy.n: Your hepatitis A IgM is negative, meaning there is no evidence of a recent hepatitis A infection. If you have jaundice or liver enzyme elevation, another cause such as hepatitis E, B or a medicine will be considered. If you have never had hepatitis A or been vaccinated, the vaccine gives long-lasting protection.
fy.bhi: Your hepatitis A IgM result is equivocal, which means the signal was too weak to call clearly positive or negative. This can occur very early in an infection, during recovery, or occasionally after recent vaccination. Your doctor will usually repeat the test in 1–2 weeks alongside liver enzymes to clarify.
fy.hi: Your hepatitis A IgM is positive, which is consistent with a recent or current hepatitis A infection. This is a self-limiting illness in almost everyone: rest, fluids, a light diet and avoiding alcohol and unnecessary medicines are the mainstay. Wash hands carefully, avoid preparing food for others for a week after jaundice starts, and see your doctor if you develop confusion or bleeding.

TLP-085.notes: IgM appears 5–10 days before symptoms and persists 3–6 months; a positive result therefore does not always mean the current illness is due to hepatitis A. Recent vaccination can give transient IgM positivity. Anti-HAV IgG (total) is used to check immunity, not this test.
TLP-085.src: CDC / WHO viral hepatitis guidance; manufacturer's chemiluminescent immunoassay cut-off
TLP-085.retest: Repeat in 1–2 weeks if equivocal or if tested very early in a febrile illness.

TLP-086.name: Hepatitis E IgM
TLP-086.meas: IgM-class antibodies against the hepatitis E virus, which appear early in infection and fade within a few months.
TLP-086.sig: Confirms recent hepatitis E, the commonest cause of acute viral hepatitis in Indian adults, spread through contaminated water. It matters most in pregnancy, where hepatitis E can be severe, and in people with existing liver disease.
TLP-086.ind: A positive result indicates acute or recent hepatitis E infection. A negative result makes hepatitis E an unlikely cause of current jaundice, though very early testing can be falsely negative. Cross-reactivity with other viral infections occasionally causes false positives.

fy.n: Your hepatitis E IgM is negative, meaning there is no evidence of recent hepatitis E infection. If you have fever with jaundice, other causes such as hepatitis A, dengue, malaria, typhoid or medicines will be considered. Drinking safe water and avoiding raw street food are the best protection.
fy.bhi: Your hepatitis E IgM result is equivocal, meaning the antibody signal was borderline. This can happen in the first days of infection, during recovery, or from cross-reaction with another recent viral illness. Your doctor will usually repeat the test in 1–2 weeks together with liver enzymes, and may add HEV RNA testing if the picture is unclear.
fy.hi: Your hepatitis E IgM is positive, which is consistent with a recent hepatitis E infection. Most people recover fully within a few weeks with rest, fluids and avoiding alcohol and unnecessary medicines. Pregnant women and people with existing liver disease need closer monitoring, so please inform your doctor promptly. Boil or filter drinking water to protect your household.

TLP-086.notes: IgM persists for 3–6 months after infection. In pregnancy, especially the third trimester, hepatitis E carries a substantially higher risk of severe disease and needs specialist care. Immunocompromised patients may develop chronic infection and require HEV RNA testing.
TLP-086.src: WHO / EASL 2018 hepatitis E guidance; manufacturer's ELISA cut-off
TLP-086.retest: Repeat in 1–2 weeks if equivocal or if tested in the first few days of illness.

TLP-087.name: Pre-Albumin
TLP-087.meas: A liver-made transport protein with a short lifespan of about two days, so it reflects protein nutrition over the past week rather than the past month.
TLP-087.sig: The most responsive blood marker of recent protein-energy nutrition, changing within days of a dietary shortfall or recovery. Useful in unexplained hair loss, skin changes and frailty in older adults, but falls with any inflammation, so it is read alongside CRP.
TLP-087.ind: Low pre-albumin indicates recent inadequate protein intake, malabsorption, liver disease, or the acute-phase response to infection, inflammation or surgery; it also falls with hyperthyroidism. High values are uncommon and seen with kidney failure, steroid use or dehydration.

fy.lo: Your pre-albumin is well below normal, which suggests significant recent protein depletion or an active inflammatory process. Poor appetite, restrictive diets, gut absorption problems, liver disease or a recent illness are common reasons. Please discuss with your doctor, who will check CRP to separate nutrition from inflammation and may involve a dietitian.
fy.blo: Your pre-albumin is mildly low, an early sign that your protein intake over the last week or two has not kept pace with your body's needs, or that a recent infection or inflammation has pulled it down. Increasing protein at each meal (dal, paneer, eggs, fish, nuts) usually restores it within 1–2 weeks. Recheck after that period.
fy.n: Your pre-albumin is in the normal range, showing that your recent protein nutrition is adequate and there is no significant inflammatory drain on your reserves. This is a good sign for skin, hair and muscle maintenance. Keep protein spread across your meals to stay here.
fy.hi: Your pre-albumin is above the usual range. This is rarely a problem in itself; it is seen with reduced kidney clearance, steroid medicines, or mild dehydration at the time of sampling. Your doctor may simply repeat it with kidney function tests if there is any concern.

TLP-087.notes: A negative acute-phase reactant: falls in any infection, inflammation or after surgery, so interpret with CRP. Reference intervals vary by method (typically 18–38 or 20–40 mg/dL). Lower in children under 5 and in pregnancy. Some labs report in mg/L (multiply mg/dL by 10).
TLP-087.src: ASPEN nutrition assessment guidance; CLSI adult reference interval
TLP-087.retest: Repeat every 1–2 weeks while nutrition is being corrected; it responds within days to adequate protein intake.

TLP-088.name: Serum Creatinine
TLP-088.meas: The level of creatinine, a waste product of normal muscle turnover that healthy kidneys clear from the blood at a steady rate.
TLP-088.sig: Creatinine is the everyday marker of how well your kidneys filter. Because it rises only after roughly half of kidney function is lost, it is read together with eGFR and urine albumin to catch damage early.
TLP-088.ind: A raised creatinine points to reduced kidney filtration from dehydration, uncontrolled diabetes or blood pressure, kidney disease, urinary obstruction or certain medicines; a low value usually reflects low muscle mass, pregnancy or a very low-protein diet rather than disease.

fy.lo: A creatinine below the usual range is rarely a kidney problem. It is most often seen with low muscle mass, a small build, pregnancy, or a very low-protein diet. No action is usually needed; if you have been losing weight or strength unintentionally, mention it to your doctor.
fy.n: Your creatinine sits in the healthy range, which suggests your kidneys are filtering waste normally. Staying well hydrated, keeping blood pressure and sugar in check, and avoiding regular use of over-the-counter painkillers are the best ways to keep it there.
fy.bhi: A mildly raised creatinine can simply reflect dehydration, a heavy-protein meal, intense exercise or a muscular build, but it can also be an early sign of kidney strain. Drink normally and repeat the test, and check your eGFR and urine albumin alongside it. Your doctor may review your blood pressure and any regular medicines.
fy.hi: A clearly raised creatinine suggests your kidneys are filtering less efficiently than they should. Common causes include long-standing diabetes or high blood pressure, dehydration, painkiller overuse, or a blockage in the urinary tract. Please discuss this with your doctor soon; a repeat test, eGFR and a urine albumin check will show whether it is temporary or ongoing.

TLP-088.notes: Children have lower values (roughly 0.3–0.7 mg/dL) and pregnancy lowers creatinine by 20–30%; very muscular people, body-builders on creatine supplements, and elderly people with low muscle mass sit at the ends of the range without kidney disease.
TLP-088.src: KDIGO 2024 CKD guideline; CLSI adult reference intervals (Jaffe/enzymatic, IDMS-traceable)
TLP-088.retest: If raised, repeat after 1–2 weeks of normal hydration together with eGFR and urine albumin-creatinine ratio; chronic kidney disease is defined only when abnormalities persist beyond 3 months.

TLP-089.name: Blood Urea
TLP-089.meas: The amount of urea, the nitrogen waste your liver makes from protein breakdown, circulating in the blood before the kidneys remove it.
TLP-089.sig: Urea rises when the kidneys clear less or when the body is short of water, so it is a sensitive but non-specific kidney and hydration marker. It is most informative when read alongside creatinine.
TLP-089.ind: High urea points to dehydration, a high-protein diet, bleeding in the gut, muscle breakdown, heart failure or reduced kidney function; low urea is seen with a low-protein diet, over-hydration, pregnancy or advanced liver disease.

fy.lo: A low urea usually means you are eating little protein, drinking a lot of fluid, or are pregnant, and it is seldom a concern on its own. Rarely it reflects a liver that is making less urea. If your liver tests are also off, or you feel unwell, let your doctor know.
fy.n: Your urea is in the healthy range, which suggests a good balance between the protein you eat, the water you drink and the waste your kidneys clear. Regular hydration and a balanced protein intake will keep it steady.
fy.bhi: A mildly raised urea is most often due to not drinking enough, a protein-heavy diet or protein supplements, or a recent bout of vomiting or diarrhoea. If your creatinine is normal, kidney function is probably fine. Hydrate well for a few days and repeat; if it stays up, your doctor may look further.
fy.hi: A clearly raised urea suggests either significant dehydration or that your kidneys are not clearing waste as they should, especially if creatinine is also high. Heart failure, bleeding in the stomach or bowel, and some medicines can contribute. Please see your doctor promptly so the cause can be sorted out and treated.

TLP-089.notes: Reference interval varies slightly by method (some laboratories quote 13–43 mg/dL); elderly people run slightly higher and pregnant women lower. Urea is reported here as urea, not blood urea nitrogen (BUN).
TLP-089.src: CLSI adult reference intervals; Tietz Textbook of Clinical Chemistry
TLP-089.retest: Repeat after 3–5 days of normal fluid and protein intake if raised without a matching creatinine rise; otherwise follow the creatinine/eGFR plan.

TLP-090.name: BUN
TLP-090.meas: The nitrogen portion of urea in the blood, calculated from the urea result (urea in mg/dL divided by 2.14).
TLP-090.sig: BUN is the international way of expressing urea and is the figure used in most kidney-function ratios. Like urea it climbs with dehydration, high protein turnover or falling kidney clearance.
TLP-090.ind: A high BUN points to dehydration, heavy protein intake, gastrointestinal bleeding, heart failure or reduced kidney function; a low BUN reflects low protein intake, over-hydration, pregnancy or severe liver disease.

fy.lo: A low BUN is usually a sign of a light protein intake, plenty of fluids, or pregnancy, and is not harmful in itself. In rare cases it points to a liver that is struggling to make urea. If you are on a restrictive diet or have known liver trouble, mention it to your doctor.
fy.n: Your BUN is within the healthy range, suggesting your kidneys are clearing protein waste efficiently and you are reasonably well hydrated. Keeping fluid intake steady and protein intake moderate helps it stay there.
fy.bhi: A slightly raised BUN most often reflects mild dehydration, a high-protein diet or supplements, or a recent stomach upset, especially when creatinine is normal. Drink normally for a few days and recheck. If it remains high or creatinine is also raised, your doctor may assess kidney function further.
fy.hi: A clearly raised BUN suggests marked dehydration or that your kidneys are clearing waste poorly, particularly when creatinine is high too. Heart failure, internal bleeding, high-dose steroids or certain medicines can also drive it up. Please consult your doctor soon for a fuller kidney assessment.

TLP-090.notes: Calculated from serum urea (BUN = urea / 2.14); elderly people run slightly higher and pregnant women lower. Children have a slightly lower upper limit (about 18 mg/dL).
TLP-090.src: CLSI adult reference intervals; Tietz Textbook of Clinical Chemistry
TLP-090.retest: Follows the urea result; repeat after correcting hydration if isolated, or with creatinine and eGFR if both are raised.

TLP-091.name: BUN/Creatinine Ratio
TLP-091.meas: How much urea nitrogen is present for each unit of creatinine, calculated from the two blood results.
TLP-091.sig: Urea and creatinine usually rise together when the kidneys fail, but urea alone climbs with dehydration or bleeding. The ratio therefore helps tell a 'pre-kidney' cause such as fluid loss from true kidney damage.
TLP-091.ind: A high ratio suggests dehydration, reduced blood flow to the kidneys, gut bleeding, high protein intake or steroid use; a low ratio suggests low protein intake, liver disease, muscle breakdown or over-hydration.

fy.lo: A low ratio means creatinine is relatively high compared with urea. This is common in people with a lot of muscle, on a low-protein diet, drinking large volumes of fluid, or with liver disease that reduces urea production. It is rarely a concern by itself; your doctor will interpret it with the individual values.
fy.n: Your BUN and creatinine are in proportion to each other, which suggests any variation in either is not driven by dehydration or bleeding. Nothing extra is needed beyond keeping the individual kidney markers in range.
fy.hi: A high ratio suggests urea is rising faster than creatinine, which typically happens with dehydration, a heavy protein diet, steroid medicines or bleeding in the gut rather than kidney damage. Drink adequately and recheck; if you have black stools, dizziness or feel unwell, see your doctor promptly.

TLP-091.notes: Only meaningful when both BUN and creatinine are expressed in mg/dL; very low creatinine (small build, pregnancy) inflates the ratio without any disease.
TLP-091.src: Tietz Textbook of Clinical Chemistry; Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
TLP-091.retest: No separate retest; it updates whenever urea and creatinine are repeated.

TLP-092.name: Urea / Creatinine Ratio
TLP-092.meas: How much urea is present for each unit of creatinine, calculated from the two blood results in mg/dL.
TLP-092.sig: The urea-based version of the BUN-creatinine ratio, used in India and the UK. It separates a fluid-loss or bleeding cause of raised urea from actual kidney injury, where both markers rise in step.
TLP-092.ind: A high ratio points to dehydration, poor kidney blood flow, gut bleeding, high protein intake or steroids; a low ratio points to low protein intake, liver disease, rhabdomyolysis or over-hydration.

fy.lo: A low urea-creatinine ratio means creatinine is relatively high for the amount of urea, as seen with a muscular build, low protein intake, generous fluid intake, or a liver that makes less urea. On its own it is seldom worrying; your doctor will look at the separate values before deciding anything.
fy.n: Your urea and creatinine are in balance with each other, which suggests any change in kidney markers is not being driven by dehydration or bleeding. Keep up normal hydration and focus on the individual kidney results.
fy.hi: A high ratio suggests urea has risen out of proportion to creatinine, usually from dehydration, a protein-rich diet, steroid medicines, or bleeding in the stomach or bowel, rather than from kidney damage. Restore fluid intake and repeat. If you notice black stools or feel faint, see your doctor without delay.

TLP-092.notes: Valid only when urea and creatinine are both in mg/dL (a ratio of 40–100 is normal when urea is in mmol/L and creatinine in µmol/L); low creatinine from small muscle mass or pregnancy inflates the ratio.
TLP-092.src: Tietz Textbook of Clinical Chemistry; Oxford Handbook of Clinical Medicine
TLP-092.retest: No separate retest; it recalculates whenever urea and creatinine are repeated.

TLP-093.name: eGFR
TLP-093.alias: Estimated glomerular filtration rate, eGFR (CKD-EPI creatinine)
TLP-093.meas: An estimate of how many millilitres of blood your kidneys filter each minute, calculated from creatinine, age and sex using the CKD-EPI 2021 equation.
TLP-093.sig: eGFR turns a creatinine value into a percentage-style score of kidney function and is the number used worldwide to stage chronic kidney disease. Falling eGFR is silent for years, so tracking it is the earliest practical warning.
TLP-093.ind: A reduced eGFR indicates diminished kidney filtration from diabetes, high blood pressure, glomerular or inherited kidney disease, obstruction, dehydration or medicines; a very high value has no clinical significance except in early diabetes where 'hyperfiltration' may precede damage.

fy.lo: An eGFR in this band suggests your kidneys are filtering at well below full capacity. If it persists for three months it meets the definition of chronic kidney disease, most often from long-standing diabetes or high blood pressure. Please see your doctor soon; repeat testing, a urine albumin check and a review of blood pressure, sugar and medicines are the usual next steps.
fy.blo: A mildly reduced eGFR is common after age 50 and is often simply age-related. It becomes significant only if urine albumin is raised or it keeps falling. Stay well hydrated, avoid regular painkiller use, keep blood pressure and sugar controlled, and repeat the test with a urine albumin-creatinine ratio in about three months.
fy.n: Your estimated filtration rate is in the normal range, which suggests your kidneys are working at full capacity. Protecting them is straightforward: good hydration, controlled blood pressure and sugar, not smoking, and using painkillers sparingly. A yearly check is enough for most people.

TLP-093.notes: eGFR declines naturally by about 1 mL/min per year after age 40; the equation is not validated for children (use Schwartz), pregnancy, very high or low muscle mass, amputees or acute kidney injury, where creatinine is changing rapidly.
TLP-093.src: KDIGO 2024 CKD guideline; CKD-EPI 2021 creatinine equation (race-free)
TLP-093.retest: Chronic kidney disease requires eGFR below 60 (or albuminuria) on tests at least 3 months apart; if under 60 for the first time, repeat within 2–4 weeks to exclude an acute cause, then at 3 months.

TLP-094.name: Uric Acid
TLP-094.meas: The level of uric acid, the end product of purine breakdown from your own cells and from foods such as red meat, seafood and alcohol.
TLP-094.sig: Uric acid above its solubility limit can crystallise in joints (gout) and kidneys (stones), and a raised level tracks closely with insulin resistance, fatty liver, high blood pressure and cardiovascular risk. It is a modifiable metabolic risk marker, not only a gout test.
TLP-094.ind: High uric acid suggests overproduction or under-excretion from a purine-rich diet, alcohol, obesity, metabolic syndrome, reduced kidney function, diuretics or rapid cell turnover; low uric acid is seen with some medicines, liver disease, pregnancy or rare inherited conditions.

fy.lo: A low uric acid is uncommon and usually harmless. It can result from a very low-purine or vegan diet, certain medicines (including some for gout, diabetes or high cholesterol), pregnancy, or liver disease. No specific action is needed, though if you are on long-term medication it is worth mentioning to your doctor.
fy.n: Your uric acid is in the healthy range, which means crystals are unlikely to form in your joints or kidneys and it is not adding to your metabolic risk. Staying hydrated, moderating alcohol and sugary drinks, and keeping weight in check will keep it there.
fy.bhi: Your uric acid is at the upper edge of normal, close to the level at which crystals can begin to form. This is often linked to red meat, seafood, alcohol, sugary drinks, weight gain or mild insulin resistance. Increasing water intake, cutting back on these and losing a little weight usually brings it down; recheck in three months.
fy.hi: A raised uric acid suggests a real tendency to gout attacks and uric acid kidney stones, and is a marker of insulin resistance and cardiovascular risk. Common drivers are diet, alcohol, obesity, diuretic tablets and reduced kidney function. Please discuss with your doctor, especially if you have had joint pain or stones; lifestyle change is the first step and treatment is available if needed.

TLP-094.notes: Uric acid rises in women after menopause towards male values; children have lower levels (about 2–5.5 mg/dL). Gout treatment targets a level below 6 mg/dL regardless of sex.
TLP-094.src: ACR 2020 gout guideline; CLSI adult reference intervals
TLP-094.retest: If raised, repeat after 3 months of dietary change; during a gout flare uric acid can be falsely normal, so test 2–4 weeks after the flare settles.

TLP-095.name: Cystatin C
TLP-095.meas: The level of cystatin C, a small protein produced by all cells at a constant rate and cleared almost entirely by kidney filtration.
TLP-095.sig: Unlike creatinine, cystatin C does not depend on muscle mass, diet or sex, so it detects early kidney decline in the elderly, very thin or very muscular people, and confirms whether a borderline creatinine-based eGFR is real. KDIGO recommends it when creatinine eGFR is 45–59 with no other kidney markers.
TLP-095.ind: A raised cystatin C indicates reduced kidney filtration; levels can also be nudged up by thyroid overactivity, high-dose steroids, obesity, smoking and inflammation. A low value has no clinical significance.

fy.n: Your cystatin C is in the normal range, which is reassuring evidence that your kidneys are filtering well, independent of your muscle mass or diet. If your creatinine-based eGFR was borderline, this result makes true kidney disease less likely. Continue the usual kidney-friendly habits.
fy.bhi: A mildly raised cystatin C suggests early or mild reduction in kidney filtration, though thyroid overactivity, steroid medicines, obesity and smoking can also lift it slightly. Compare it with your creatinine eGFR and urine albumin, and repeat in about three months. Your doctor may check thyroid function if the picture does not fit.
fy.hi: A clearly raised cystatin C suggests your kidneys are filtering noticeably less than normal, and because it is not affected by muscle mass this is a reliable signal. Diabetes, high blood pressure and long-term painkiller use are the usual causes. Please see your doctor; the cystatin-based eGFR and a urine albumin test will help stage the problem and plan care.

TLP-095.notes: Reference interval is method-dependent (roughly 0.5–1.0 mg/L for IFCC-standardised assays); values are higher in infants under 1 year and in people over 70, and are raised by hyperthyroidism and glucocorticoids without any kidney change.
TLP-095.src: KDIGO 2024 CKD guideline; manufacturer IFCC-standardised reference interval
TLP-095.retest: Repeat with creatinine in 3 months if borderline; a persistent cystatin-C eGFR below 60 confirms chronic kidney disease.

TLP-096.name: eGFR from Cystatin C
TLP-096.meas: An estimate of kidney filtration rate calculated from cystatin C, age and sex using the CKD-EPI 2012 cystatin C equation.
TLP-096.sig: This eGFR is free of the muscle-mass bias that affects the creatinine version, so it is used to confirm or rule out chronic kidney disease when the creatinine eGFR is borderline. Averaging both estimates gives the most accurate non-invasive measure available.
TLP-096.ind: A reduced value indicates diminished kidney filtration from the same causes as the creatinine eGFR; discordance between the two estimates points to unusual muscle mass, thyroid disease, steroid use or inflammation rather than kidney change.

fy.lo: A cystatin-based eGFR in this band suggests kidney filtration is genuinely reduced, because this estimate is not distorted by muscle mass. If it persists for three months it confirms chronic kidney disease. Please see your doctor soon to review blood pressure, sugar, medicines and urine albumin, and to plan how often to monitor.
fy.blo: A mildly reduced cystatin-based eGFR suggests a small drop in filtration, which is common with age and only concerning if urine albumin is also raised or the number keeps falling. Keep hydrated, control blood pressure and sugar, avoid regular painkillers, and repeat with a urine albumin-creatinine ratio in three months.
fy.n: Your cystatin-based eGFR is normal, which is strong reassurance that your kidneys are filtering at full capacity regardless of your body build. If your creatinine eGFR was lower, that difference is probably due to muscle mass rather than kidney disease. Maintain the usual kidney-friendly habits and recheck yearly.

TLP-096.notes: Not validated in children, pregnancy, thyroid disease, high-dose steroid therapy or acute kidney injury; when creatinine and cystatin eGFR disagree by more than 15–20 units, the combined creatinine-cystatin equation is preferred.
TLP-096.src: KDIGO 2024 CKD guideline; CKD-EPI 2012 cystatin C equation
TLP-096.retest: As for creatinine eGFR: confirm any value below 60 on a second sample at least 3 months apart before labelling chronic kidney disease.

TLP-097.name: Sodium
TLP-097.meas: The concentration of sodium in the blood, which reflects the balance between salt and water in the body rather than salt intake alone.
TLP-097.sig: Sodium controls the water content of every cell, including brain cells, and even modest shifts cause confusion, fatigue or seizures. It is the most frequently abnormal electrolyte in older adults and in people taking diuretics or antidepressants.
TLP-097.ind: Low sodium suggests excess water relative to salt from diuretics, heart, liver or kidney disease, SIADH, hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency or drinking very large volumes; high sodium suggests water loss from fever, diarrhoea, poor fluid access, uncontrolled diabetes or diabetes insipidus.

fy.lo: A sodium at this level means your body is holding too much water relative to salt, which can cause nausea, headache, confusion or unsteadiness. Common causes are water tablets, certain antidepressants, heart, liver or kidney conditions, low thyroid or adrenal function, or drinking very large amounts of water. Please contact your doctor promptly; this needs assessment rather than just extra salt.
fy.blo: A mildly low sodium is common and often caused by diuretic tablets, some antidepressants or painkillers, a recent stomach upset, drinking a lot of plain water, or an under-active thyroid. It is usually symptom-free but is worth correcting. Review your medicines and fluid intake with your doctor and repeat the test within a couple of weeks.
fy.n: Your sodium is within the normal range, which suggests your body is regulating water and salt well. Drinking to thirst rather than to a target, and replacing fluids sensibly during heat, exercise or illness, will keep it stable.
fy.bhi: A mildly raised sodium usually means you are somewhat short of water, for example after fever, diarrhoea, heavy sweating or simply not drinking enough, and high blood sugar can add to it. Increase plain fluid intake over the next day or two and repeat; if you have unusual thirst or pass very large volumes of urine, tell your doctor.
fy.hi: A clearly raised sodium suggests significant water loss or inadequate intake, and can cause thirst, weakness, confusion or drowsiness. Causes include severe diarrhoea or vomiting, uncontrolled diabetes, and rarely a condition called diabetes insipidus. Please see your doctor promptly, as this needs supervised correction, especially in older adults.

TLP-097.notes: Reference interval is the same in children and adults; pregnancy lowers sodium by 3–5 mmol/L; very high blood sugar or lipids can lower the measured value artificially (pseudohyponatraemia).
TLP-097.src: European Society of Endocrinology hyponatraemia guideline 2014; CLSI adult reference intervals
TLP-097.retest: Mild abnormalities: repeat within 1–2 weeks after reviewing medicines and fluid intake; values below 125 or above 155 mmol/L warrant same-day medical review.

TLP-098.name: Potassium
TLP-098.meas: The concentration of potassium in the blood, the mineral that sets the electrical rhythm of heart and muscle cells.
TLP-098.sig: Potassium has the narrowest safe window of any electrolyte: both low and high levels can trigger dangerous heart rhythms with little warning. It is essential to monitor in anyone on diuretics, blood-pressure tablets of the ACE-inhibitor or ARB class, or with kidney disease.
TLP-098.ind: Low potassium suggests loss through vomiting, diarrhoea, diuretics or excess aldosterone (a cause of secondary hypertension), or a shift into cells from insulin or stress; high potassium suggests reduced kidney excretion, ACE-inhibitor or potassium-sparing diuretic use, adrenal insufficiency, tissue breakdown, or most commonly a haemolysed or delayed sample.

fy.lo: A potassium at this level can cause muscle weakness, cramps, constipation and irregular heartbeats. It usually follows vomiting, diarrhoea, water tablets, or laxative overuse, and occasionally an adrenal hormone excess that also raises blood pressure. Please contact your doctor today; potassium replacement and a check of the cause are needed.
fy.blo: A mildly low potassium is common with diuretic tablets, a recent stomach bug, heavy sweating, or a diet low in fruit and vegetables. It rarely causes symptoms but is worth correcting, particularly if you have heart disease or high blood pressure. Increase potassium-rich foods such as bananas, coconut water and beans, review medicines with your doctor and repeat in a week or two.
fy.n: Your potassium is within the normal range, which suggests your kidneys and hormones are keeping this crucial electrolyte steady. A diet rich in fruit, vegetables and pulses helps maintain it, particularly if you take blood-pressure medicines.
fy.bhi: A mildly raised potassium most often comes from the sample itself, when blood cells break during collection or the sample stands too long before testing. Genuine causes include kidney impairment, ACE-inhibitor or ARB blood-pressure tablets, potassium supplements or salt substitutes. Repeat the test with a fresh, promptly processed sample, and mention your medicines to your doctor.
fy.hi: A clearly raised potassium can affect heart rhythm and needs prompt attention, unless it is a sample artefact, which is common. Real causes include reduced kidney function, certain blood-pressure tablets, potassium-sparing diuretics, adrenal insufficiency or muscle injury. Please contact your doctor today; an urgent repeat sample, and often an ECG, are the first steps.

TLP-098.notes: Some methods quote an upper limit of 5.1–5.3 mmol/L; newborns run higher (up to 6.0). A haemolysed sample, fist clenching during collection, or a delay of more than 2 hours before separation raises the result artificially.
TLP-098.src: CLSI adult reference intervals; KDIGO 2024 CKD guideline; ESC 2021 heart failure guideline (monitoring thresholds)
TLP-098.retest: Any unexpected abnormal value should be repeated on a fresh, non-haemolysed sample processed within 2 hours; values below 3.0 or above 5.5 mmol/L need same-day medical review.

TLP-099.name: Chloride
TLP-099.meas: The concentration of chloride, the main negatively charged ion in blood that pairs with sodium and helps regulate acid-base balance.
TLP-099.sig: Chloride usually moves in step with sodium, so a chloride that deviates on its own signals a disturbance of the body's acid-base balance. It is used to calculate the anion gap, which uncovers hidden acid build-up.
TLP-099.ind: Low chloride points to prolonged vomiting, diuretic use, metabolic alkalosis or fluid overload; high chloride points to dehydration, excessive saline, kidney tubular disorders, diarrhoea or metabolic acidosis.

fy.lo: A low chloride usually accompanies a low sodium or follows repeated vomiting, water tablets, or drinking large volumes of fluid, and it can signal that the blood has become slightly too alkaline. It seldom causes symptoms of its own. Your doctor will interpret it alongside sodium and bicarbonate; a repeat after any recent illness settles is sensible.
fy.n: Your chloride is within the normal range and in balance with your sodium, which suggests your acid-base status and fluid balance are well regulated. No specific action is needed.
fy.hi: A raised chloride most commonly reflects dehydration or diarrhoea, and can also indicate the blood is slightly too acidic, as happens with some kidney tubular conditions or after large volumes of saline. Rehydrate and repeat; if bicarbonate is low as well, your doctor may look into acid-base balance further.

TLP-099.notes: Reference interval is broadly the same across ages; some methods quote 96–106 mmol/L. Bromide-containing medicines can give a falsely high reading on some analysers.
TLP-099.src: CLSI adult reference intervals; Tietz Textbook of Clinical Chemistry
TLP-099.retest: Repeat together with sodium and bicarbonate once any acute vomiting, diarrhoea or dehydration has resolved.

TLP-100.name: Bicarbonate
TLP-100.meas: The concentration of bicarbonate, the main buffer that neutralises acid in the blood, measured as total carbon dioxide in serum.
TLP-100.sig: Bicarbonate is the simplest window on acid-base balance: it falls when acid accumulates (kidney failure, uncontrolled diabetes, diarrhoea) and rises with vomiting, diuretics or chronic lung disease. In chronic kidney disease a low bicarbonate accelerates bone and muscle loss and is treated.
TLP-100.ind: Low bicarbonate indicates metabolic acidosis from kidney disease, diabetic ketoacidosis, severe diarrhoea, lactic acidosis, some medicines, or compensation for over-breathing; high bicarbonate indicates metabolic alkalosis from vomiting, diuretics, excess aldosterone, or compensation for chronic lung disease.

fy.lo: A low bicarbonate suggests your blood is carrying more acid than usual. Common causes are reduced kidney function, poorly controlled diabetes, prolonged diarrhoea, certain medicines, or a sample that stood open too long. If your kidney tests are also abnormal or you have diabetes, please discuss this with your doctor soon; otherwise a repeat on a fresh sample is the first step.
fy.n: Your bicarbonate is within the normal range, which suggests your kidneys and lungs are keeping the acid-base balance of your blood steady. Nothing further is needed.
fy.hi: A raised bicarbonate suggests your blood is slightly more alkaline than usual, most often from water tablets, repeated vomiting, or long-standing lung disease that traps carbon dioxide. Excess of the adrenal hormone aldosterone is a less common cause, particularly if potassium is low and blood pressure is high. Your doctor will review your medicines and, if needed, check further.

TLP-100.notes: Serum total CO2 runs 1–2 mmol/L above true bicarbonate; some laboratories quote 23–29 mmol/L. Samples left uncapped lose CO2 and read falsely low; children under 2 years have a lower range (17–25).
TLP-100.src: CLSI adult reference intervals; KDIGO 2024 CKD guideline (treatment threshold < 22 mmol/L)
TLP-100.retest: Repeat on a promptly processed, capped sample if unexpectedly low; in chronic kidney disease it is monitored with each kidney panel.

TLP-101.name: Calcium
TLP-101.meas: The total amount of calcium in the blood, roughly half of which is bound to albumin and half free and active.
TLP-101.sig: Blood calcium is tightly controlled by parathyroid hormone and vitamin D, so an abnormal value usually reflects a gland or vitamin problem rather than diet. Persistent mild elevation is the commonest clue to an overactive parathyroid gland, a treatable cause of bone loss and kidney stones.
TLP-101.ind: High calcium suggests primary hyperparathyroidism, excess vitamin D or calcium supplements, thiazide diuretics, prolonged immobility or, less often, malignancy; low calcium suggests vitamin D deficiency, low albumin, chronic kidney disease, low magnesium, or underactive parathyroid glands after neck surgery.

fy.lo: A calcium at this level can cause tingling around the mouth and fingers, muscle cramps or spasms, and needs attention. Causes include marked vitamin D deficiency, chronic kidney disease, low magnesium, or underactive parathyroid glands, sometimes after thyroid surgery. Please see your doctor soon; vitamin D, PTH, magnesium and albumin will usually be checked together.
fy.blo: A mildly low calcium is often simply a reflection of low albumin in the blood, and the corrected value may be normal. Genuine mild lowering is most commonly due to vitamin D deficiency, which is very common in India. Check your vitamin D and albumin, ensure adequate dairy or calcium-rich foods, and repeat the test after correction.
fy.n: Your total calcium is within the normal range, which suggests your parathyroid glands and vitamin D are keeping bone and blood calcium well balanced. Adequate dietary calcium, vitamin D from sunlight or supplements, and weight-bearing exercise will support bone health long term.
fy.bhi: A mildly raised calcium is often due to dehydration at the time of sampling, calcium or vitamin D supplements, or thiazide blood-pressure tablets. If it persists on a repeat, the commonest cause is a mildly overactive parathyroid gland. Pause supplements for a few days, hydrate and repeat with a PTH and vitamin D level; discuss the results with your doctor.
fy.hi: A clearly raised calcium can cause thirst, frequent urination, constipation, bone pain, tiredness or low mood, and warrants prompt evaluation. The usual causes are an overactive parathyroid gland or excess vitamin D; less commonly it is linked to other conditions your doctor will want to exclude. Please see your doctor soon and stop any calcium or vitamin D supplements until reviewed.

TLP-101.notes: Correct for albumin: add 0.8 mg/dL for every 1 g/dL that albumin is below 4.0 g/dL. Children and adolescents run slightly higher (up to 10.8 mg/dL); pregnancy lowers total calcium with albumin while ionised calcium stays normal; some methods quote 8.6–10.3 mg/dL.
TLP-101.src: Endocrine Society / Fourth International Workshop on asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism 2014; CLSI adult reference intervals
TLP-101.retest: Any abnormal value should be repeated with albumin (or ionised calcium), PTH and 25-OH vitamin D; a persistently raised calcium with non-suppressed PTH points to hyperparathyroidism.

TLP-102.name: Magnesium
TLP-102.meas: The concentration of magnesium in the blood, a mineral essential for over 300 enzyme reactions, muscle relaxation, heart rhythm and blood sugar control.
TLP-102.sig: Magnesium deficiency is common yet easily missed: it causes cramps, palpitations, fatigue and resistant low potassium or calcium. Long-term acid-suppressing tablets, diuretics, diabetes and alcohol all deplete it, and low magnesium worsens insulin resistance.
TLP-102.ind: Low magnesium suggests poor intake, chronic diarrhoea or malabsorption, alcohol excess, diuretics, proton-pump inhibitors, uncontrolled diabetes or kidney tubular loss; high magnesium is rare and suggests kidney failure or excess magnesium-containing antacids or laxatives.

fy.lo: A low magnesium suggests your body's stores are depleted, which can show up as cramps, twitching, palpitations, tiredness, or as low potassium and calcium that will not correct. Long-term antacid tablets, water tablets, alcohol, diarrhoea or poorly controlled diabetes are the usual reasons. Increase green vegetables, nuts, seeds and whole grains, review medicines with your doctor, and recheck in a few weeks.
fy.n: Your magnesium is within the normal range, which suggests adequate intake and normal kidney handling. Because blood levels stay normal until stores are quite depleted, a diet with leafy greens, nuts, pulses and whole grains remains worthwhile, especially if you take acid-suppressing tablets or diuretics.
fy.hi: A raised magnesium is uncommon and almost always occurs when the kidneys cannot excrete it, especially if you are taking magnesium-containing antacids, laxatives or supplements. It can cause weakness, low blood pressure or a slow pulse at high levels. Stop any magnesium supplements and discuss with your doctor, particularly if your kidney tests are also abnormal.

TLP-102.notes: Some laboratories quote 1.6–2.6 mg/dL; the same interval applies to children. Serum magnesium reflects only about 1% of body stores, so a low-normal value does not exclude deficiency in someone with symptoms or risk factors.
TLP-102.src: CLSI adult reference intervals; Tietz Textbook of Clinical Chemistry
TLP-102.retest: Recheck 4–6 weeks after dietary change or stopping a depleting medicine; test alongside potassium and calcium when those are low.

TLP-103.name: Phosphorus
TLP-103.meas: The level of inorganic phosphate in the blood, a mineral that partners calcium in bone and powers every cell's energy currency (ATP).
TLP-103.sig: Phosphate rises early when kidneys lose the ability to excrete it and drives the vascular calcification and bone disease of chronic kidney disease. Low phosphate, from vitamin D deficiency or refeeding, weakens muscle and bone.
TLP-103.ind: High phosphorus suggests reduced kidney function, underactive parathyroid glands, excess vitamin D, or cell breakdown; low phosphorus suggests vitamin D deficiency, overactive parathyroid glands, malnutrition or refeeding, alcohol excess, antacid overuse, or kidney tubular loss.

fy.lo: A low phosphorus suggests your body is short of this mineral, which can cause muscle weakness, bone aches or tiredness. Vitamin D deficiency and an overactive parathyroid gland are the usual causes, along with poor nutrition, alcohol, or regular aluminium-containing antacids. Check your vitamin D and calcium, eat dairy, eggs, pulses and nuts, and discuss the result with your doctor.
fy.n: Your phosphorus is within the normal range, which suggests your kidneys, parathyroid glands and vitamin D are handling bone minerals well. A balanced diet provides all the phosphate you need; no supplements are required.
fy.hi: A raised phosphorus most often reflects reduced kidney clearance, and in that setting it can promote calcium deposits in blood vessels over time. Other causes include underactive parathyroid glands, excess vitamin D, or a haemolysed sample. If your kidney tests are abnormal, your doctor may advise limiting processed foods and colas, which are high in phosphate additives, and will review the result with calcium and PTH.

TLP-103.notes: Children and adolescents have higher values (about 4.0–7.0 mg/dL) because of bone growth; levels fall slightly with age and are lower after a carbohydrate meal, so a fasting morning sample is preferred. Haemolysis raises the result artificially.
TLP-103.src: KDIGO 2017 CKD-MBD guideline; CLSI adult reference intervals
TLP-103.retest: Repeat fasting with calcium, PTH and vitamin D if abnormal; in chronic kidney disease it is monitored every 3–12 months depending on stage.

TLP-104.name: Calcium (Ionised)
TLP-104.meas: The biologically active, unbound fraction of calcium in the blood, measured directly rather than estimated from total calcium and albumin.
TLP-104.sig: Ionised calcium is the fraction that actually drives nerve, muscle and hormone signalling, and it stays accurate when albumin is low, in kidney disease, or when acid-base balance is disturbed. It is the definitive test when total calcium is borderline or unreliable.
TLP-104.ind: A high ionised calcium suggests primary hyperparathyroidism, excess vitamin D or malignancy-related hypercalcaemia; a low value suggests vitamin D deficiency, hypoparathyroidism, low magnesium, chronic kidney disease, or acute illness such as pancreatitis.

fy.lo: A low ionised calcium means the active form of calcium is genuinely reduced, not just an artefact of low protein. This can cause tingling, cramps or muscle spasm, and usually stems from vitamin D deficiency, underactive parathyroid glands, low magnesium or kidney disease. Please see your doctor; vitamin D, PTH and magnesium will guide treatment.
fy.n: Your ionised calcium is within the normal range, confirming that the active calcium available to your nerves, muscles and bones is adequate, even if total calcium looked borderline. Maintain calcium-rich foods and adequate vitamin D to keep it there.
fy.hi: A raised ionised calcium confirms true hypercalcaemia, which most commonly indicates an overactive parathyroid gland or excess vitamin D intake. Symptoms can include thirst, frequent urination, constipation, tiredness and kidney stones. Please see your doctor soon and pause any calcium or vitamin D supplements until reviewed; a PTH level is the key next test.

TLP-104.notes: Reference interval is method- and pH-dependent (some analysers quote 1.16–1.32 mmol/L); the sample must be collected anaerobically and analysed promptly, as exposure to air raises pH and lowers the result. Values are slightly higher in children and unchanged in pregnancy.
TLP-104.src: Endocrine Society / Fourth International Workshop on asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism 2014; manufacturer ion-selective electrode reference interval
TLP-104.retest: Repeat with PTH and 25-OH vitamin D if abnormal; ensure prompt, anaerobic sample handling on any repeat.

TLP-105.name: PTH (Intact)
TLP-105.meas: The level of intact parathyroid hormone, released by four small glands in the neck to raise blood calcium by acting on bone, kidney and vitamin D activation.
TLP-105.sig: PTH is only interpretable together with calcium: a high PTH with high calcium points to an overactive parathyroid gland, while a high PTH with low or normal calcium usually means the glands are working overtime to compensate for vitamin D deficiency or kidney disease. It is central to diagnosing the cause of osteoporosis, kidney stones or abnormal calcium.
TLP-105.ind: High PTH suggests primary hyperparathyroidism (with high calcium) or secondary hyperparathyroidism from vitamin D deficiency, low calcium intake or chronic kidney disease (with low or normal calcium); low PTH suggests hypoparathyroidism after neck surgery, autoimmune gland damage, low magnesium, or appropriate suppression by high calcium from other causes.

fy.lo: A low PTH means your parathyroid glands are releasing little hormone. If your calcium is high, this is the correct response and points to another cause of high calcium such as excess vitamin D; if your calcium is low, it suggests underactive glands, often after thyroid or neck surgery, or low magnesium. Your doctor will interpret it with your calcium and magnesium results.
fy.n: Your PTH is within the normal range, which together with a normal calcium suggests your parathyroid glands are regulating calcium and bone turnover correctly. Keeping vitamin D replete and calcium intake adequate prevents the glands from having to work harder over time.
fy.bhi: A mildly raised PTH most commonly means your glands are compensating for low vitamin D or low dietary calcium, which is extremely common in India, or for a mild drop in kidney function. If your calcium is also high, an overactive gland becomes more likely. Check your vitamin D and calcium, correct any deficiency, and repeat PTH in about three months.
fy.hi: A clearly raised PTH suggests your parathyroid glands are significantly overactive. With a high calcium this is consistent with primary hyperparathyroidism, a treatable cause of bone loss, stones and fatigue; with a low or normal calcium it suggests severe vitamin D deficiency or chronic kidney disease driving the glands. Please see your doctor or an endocrinologist to review calcium, vitamin D, kidney function and bone density.

TLP-105.notes: Reference interval is assay-specific (second-generation intact assays typically 15–65 pg/mL; some quote 10–65). PTH rises with age and with vitamin D deficiency, and in chronic kidney disease higher targets (2–9 times upper limit in dialysis) are accepted. Sample should be drawn fasting in the morning with calcium on the same draw.
TLP-105.src: Endocrine Society / Fourth International Workshop on asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism 2014; KDIGO 2017 CKD-MBD guideline
TLP-105.retest: Always repeat with a simultaneous calcium and 25-OH vitamin D; recheck 3 months after correcting vitamin D deficiency before diagnosing a gland problem.

TLP-106.name: Urine Microalbumin
TLP-106.alias: Urine albumin, Microalbuminuria, Spot urine albumin
TLP-106.meas: The concentration of albumin, the main blood protein, leaking into the urine in amounts too small for a routine dipstick to detect.
TLP-106.sig: Albumin in the urine is the earliest detectable sign of kidney damage from diabetes or high blood pressure, appearing years before creatinine changes. It is also an independent predictor of heart attack and stroke, and treatment at this stage can reverse the leak.
TLP-106.ind: A raised urine albumin suggests early diabetic or hypertensive kidney damage, glomerular disease or generalised blood-vessel damage; transient rises occur with fever, urinary infection, heavy exercise, menstruation, heart failure or poor sugar control. A low value has no significance.

fy.n: No significant albumin is leaking into your urine, which suggests the fine filters of your kidneys are intact and, if you have diabetes or high blood pressure, they have not yet caused kidney damage. Keeping sugar and blood pressure well controlled and repeating this test yearly is the best protection.
fy.bhi: A small amount of albumin is leaking into your urine. This is the earliest, and reversible, stage of kidney damage, most often from diabetes or high blood pressure, but it can also be a temporary effect of fever, infection, heavy exercise or menstruation. Repeat the test twice over the next 3–6 months on a first-morning sample; if it persists, your doctor may tighten blood pressure and sugar control with kidney-protective medicines.
fy.hi: A large amount of albumin is leaking into your urine, which suggests established kidney damage or a glomerular disease, and it raises cardiovascular risk. Please see your doctor soon; a urine albumin-creatinine ratio, kidney function tests and blood pressure review are needed, and treatments that reduce the leak and protect your kidneys are available.

TLP-106.notes: Concentration in mg/L depends on how dilute the urine is, so the albumin-creatinine ratio is the preferred measure; avoid testing during fever, urinary infection, menstruation or within 24 hours of strenuous exercise. Not for use in pregnancy screening, where 24-hour protein or PCR is used.
TLP-106.src: ADA Standards of Care 2024; KDIGO 2024 CKD guideline
TLP-106.retest: Albuminuria is confirmed only when 2 of 3 samples over 3–6 months are raised; screen annually in diabetes and hypertension.

TLP-107.name: Urine Micro Albumin/Creatinine ratio
TLP-107.meas: The amount of albumin in the urine for every gram of creatinine, which corrects the albumin level for how concentrated or dilute the urine is.
TLP-107.sig: UACR is the standard test for kidney damage recommended yearly for everyone with diabetes or hypertension. It stages chronic kidney disease alongside eGFR, and even values in the upper-normal range predict heart and kidney risk.
TLP-107.ind: A raised UACR indicates albuminuria from diabetic or hypertensive kidney disease, glomerulonephritis or systemic vascular damage; transient elevation occurs with fever, infection, exercise, menstruation or heart failure. Very low values are normal.

fy.n: Your albumin-creatinine ratio is in the normal range, which suggests your kidney filters are not leaking protein and any diabetes or high blood pressure has not damaged them. Continue good sugar and blood pressure control and repeat the test once a year.
fy.bhi: Your ratio shows moderately increased albumin loss, the earliest stage of kidney damage, usually from diabetes or high blood pressure, and a marker of higher cardiovascular risk. It can be temporary after fever, exercise or infection, so repeat it twice within 3–6 months. If confirmed, your doctor may start or adjust kidney-protective blood pressure or diabetes medicines, which can reduce the leak.
fy.hi: Your ratio shows severely increased albumin loss, consistent with significant kidney damage or a glomerular disease, and it carries a high risk of progression if untreated. Please see your doctor or a kidney specialist soon; kidney function, blood pressure and possibly further tests will be arranged, and effective treatments exist to slow or halt the damage.

TLP-107.notes: Values 10–29 mg/g are 'high-normal' and carry some added risk. The ratio underestimates albuminuria in muscular people (high urine creatinine) and overestimates it in the elderly or very thin. Avoid testing during fever, urinary infection, menstruation or after strenuous exercise; not validated for pregnancy screening.
TLP-107.src: KDIGO 2024 CKD guideline; ADA Standards of Care 2024
TLP-107.retest: Confirm with 2 of 3 first-morning samples over 3–6 months; then monitor yearly (normal) or every 3–6 months (raised).

TLP-108.name: Urine Protein
TLP-108.alias: Spot urine protein, Urine total protein
TLP-108.meas: The concentration of total protein (albumin plus other proteins) in a single urine sample, measured chemically rather than by dipstick.
TLP-108.sig: Healthy kidneys let almost no protein through. A measurable amount signals damage to the kidney filters or tubules, but the concentration alone is heavily affected by how dilute the urine is, so it is chiefly used to calculate the protein-creatinine ratio.
TLP-108.ind: Raised urine protein suggests glomerular disease, diabetic or hypertensive kidney damage, urinary infection, or overflow of abnormal proteins as in myeloma; transient rises occur with fever, exercise, dehydration or prolonged standing. A very low value is normal.

fy.n: Your urine protein is at the very low level expected from healthy kidneys, which suggests the kidney filters are not leaking protein. Keeping blood pressure and sugar in check and staying hydrated maintains this.
fy.hi: Protein is present in your urine above the usual trace amount. In a concentrated sample this can be exaggerated, and fever, heavy exercise or a urinary infection can cause a temporary rise. The protein-creatinine ratio on this report gives the truer picture; if that is also raised, repeat on a first-morning sample and discuss kidney function and blood pressure with your doctor.

TLP-108.notes: Spot concentration varies several-fold with hydration, so interpret only with the protein-creatinine ratio; 24-hour excretion below 150 mg/day is the reference standard. Some laboratories quote an upper limit of 10 or 20 mg/dL depending on the method (pyrogallol red or benzethonium chloride).
TLP-108.src: KDIGO 2024 CKD guideline; Tietz Textbook of Clinical Chemistry
TLP-108.retest: Repeat on an early-morning sample, avoiding exercise and fever, and rely on the protein-creatinine ratio for follow-up.

TLP-109.name: Urine Creatinine
TLP-109.meas: The concentration of creatinine in a single urine sample, which reflects how concentrated the urine is and the person's muscle mass.
TLP-109.sig: On its own urine creatinine says little about kidney health; its job is to standardise other urine measurements. Dividing urine albumin or protein by creatinine cancels out dilution, turning a spot sample into a reliable estimate of daily loss.
TLP-109.ind: A low value indicates dilute urine (high fluid intake, diuretics) or low muscle mass; a high value indicates concentrated urine (dehydration, first-morning sample) or high muscle mass. Neither is a disease marker by itself.

fy.lo: Your urine was quite dilute at the time of sampling, usually because you had been drinking plenty of fluid or take water tablets; people with low muscle mass also have lower values. This is not a kidney problem, but very dilute urine can make albumin and protein ratios less accurate, so a first-morning sample is better for any repeat.
fy.n: Your urine creatinine is in the typical range, which means the sample was neither too dilute nor too concentrated and the albumin and protein ratios on this report can be trusted. No action is needed for this value itself.
fy.hi: Your urine was concentrated at the time of sampling, typically a first-morning or dehydrated sample, or you have a high muscle mass. This is not a disease sign. Be aware that a concentrated sample can make the albumin-creatinine ratio read slightly lower than usual; keep normal hydration and rely on the ratios, not the raw concentrations.

TLP-109.notes: Spot values range widely (roughly 20–300 mg/dL) with hydration and muscle mass and carry no diagnostic cut-off; a value below 20 mg/dL suggests a sample too dilute for reliable ratios. Daily excretion is about 15–25 mg/kg in men and 10–20 mg/kg in women.
TLP-109.src: Tietz Textbook of Clinical Chemistry; KDIGO 2024 CKD guideline (ratio methodology)
TLP-109.retest: No retest for its own sake; if a ratio needs repeating, collect a first-morning midstream sample.

TLP-110.name: Urine Protein/creatinine Ratio
TLP-110.meas: The amount of total protein in the urine for every gram of creatinine, which estimates daily protein loss from a single sample.
TLP-110.sig: The ratio closely tracks 24-hour urine protein without the inconvenience of a full-day collection. It quantifies the severity of kidney protein leak, distinguishes nephrotic-range loss, and is the standard measure used in pregnancy and glomerular disease.
TLP-110.ind: A raised ratio suggests glomerular disease, diabetic or hypertensive nephropathy, tubular disease or overflow proteinuria; values above 3,000–3,500 mg/g indicate nephrotic-range loss. Transient rises follow fever, exercise, infection or prolonged standing.

fy.n: Your protein-creatinine ratio is in the normal range, which suggests your kidney filters are retaining protein as they should. If you have diabetes or high blood pressure, this is reassuring; keep them well controlled and repeat yearly.
fy.bhi: Your ratio shows a mild protein leak from the kidneys. This can be temporary after fever, vigorous exercise, a urinary infection or a long day on your feet, but if it persists it points to early kidney damage from diabetes, high blood pressure or a filter disorder. Repeat on a first-morning sample within a few weeks; if still raised, your doctor may check the albumin-creatinine ratio, kidney function and blood pressure.
fy.hi: Your ratio shows a significant protein leak, consistent with kidney filter damage that needs proper evaluation. Causes include diabetic or hypertensive kidney disease and inflammatory conditions of the kidney filters; very high values can cause swelling of the legs and face. Please see your doctor or a kidney specialist soon for blood tests, blood pressure review, and possibly an ultrasound or further investigation.

TLP-110.notes: Roughly equivalent to mg of protein per day; some laboratories report mg/mg (divide by 1,000) or use 200 mg/g as the upper limit. In pregnancy a ratio of 300 mg/g or more (30 mg/mmol) defines significant proteinuria for pre-eclampsia assessment. Less accurate at very high or low muscle mass.
TLP-110.src: KDIGO 2024 CKD guideline; NICE NG133 (pregnancy proteinuria threshold)
TLP-110.retest: Confirm a raised ratio on a first-morning sample after excluding fever, exercise and infection; monitor every 3–6 months once kidney disease is established.

TLP-111.name: Colour (Urine)
TLP-111.meas: The visual colour of the urine sample, which is determined mainly by the pigment urochrome and how concentrated the urine is.
TLP-111.sig: Colour is a quick clue to hydration and to the presence of blood, bile pigments, or unusual substances. A strikingly abnormal colour often prompts the chemical and microscopic tests that follow.
TLP-111.ind: Dark yellow or amber suggests concentrated urine from dehydration; red, pink or brown suggests blood, haemoglobin, myoglobin, beetroot or certain drugs; deep yellow-brown or orange suggests bilirubin, rifampicin or B-vitamins; milky suggests pus, fat or phosphates; very pale suggests dilute urine or diabetes.

rng.n: Pale yellow / straw / yellow (Pale yellow to yellow)
rng.hi: Dark amber, red, brown, orange, milky or other (Abnormal colour)

fy.n: Your urine colour is in the normal pale-to-yellow range, which suggests you are reasonably well hydrated and there is no visible blood or bile pigment. Drinking enough to keep it pale yellow through the day is a simple hydration guide.
fy.hi: Your urine colour is outside the usual range. Dark amber usually means concentrated urine from not drinking enough; orange can follow vitamin B or rifampicin; red or brown can come from beetroot, some medicines, or blood and bile pigments; milky urine may contain pus or phosphate crystals. Check the blood, bilirubin and microscopy results on this report; if they are abnormal, or the colour persists after good hydration, see your doctor.

TLP-111.notes: Colour depends heavily on hydration and time of day (first-morning urine is darker); many foods, dyes and medicines (rifampicin, nitrofurantoin, phenazopyridine, B-complex vitamins) change colour harmlessly. Samples should be examined within 2 hours of collection.
TLP-111.src: CLSI GP16 urinalysis guideline; Strasinger Urinalysis and Body Fluids
TLP-111.retest: Repeat after 24 hours of normal fluid intake and avoiding coloured foods or supplements if the cause is unclear; persistent red or brown colour needs a repeat with microscopy.

any.label: Abnormal colour
any.text: Dark amber, red, brown, orange, milky or other

TLP-112.name: Appearance
TLP-112.meas: How clear or cloudy the urine sample looks when held against light.
