TLP-112.sig: Fresh normal urine is clear. Cloudiness suggests suspended cells, bacteria, crystals or mucus and directs attention to the microscopy findings, though harmless phosphate crystals in alkaline urine are the commonest cause.
TLP-112.ind: Turbid urine suggests urinary infection (pus cells, bacteria), blood, crystals, mucus, contamination with vaginal secretions or semen, or rarely fat or lymph; hazy urine is often due to phosphates, urates or mucus with no disease.

fy.n: Your urine was clear, which suggests no significant excess of cells, bacteria or crystals in the sample. This is what healthy, well-hydrated urine looks like; nothing further is needed for this item.
fy.bhi: Your urine was slightly hazy. The most common reasons are harmless phosphate or urate crystals that form as the sample cools, a little mucus, or minor contamination during collection. If pus cells, bacteria and nitrite on this report are normal, no action is needed. If you have burning or frequency, tell your doctor.
fy.hi: Your urine was cloudy, which usually means it contained pus cells, bacteria, blood or abundant crystals. A urinary infection is the commonest cause, especially with burning, urgency or lower abdominal discomfort. Look at the leucocyte, nitrite and microscopy results; if they are abnormal or you have symptoms, see your doctor, who may send a urine culture. Some cloudiness is simply from phosphate crystals and is harmless.

TLP-112.notes: Urine becomes cloudy on standing or refrigeration as crystals precipitate, so freshly voided samples examined within 2 hours are needed; a contaminated non-midstream sample is a frequent cause of turbidity in women.
TLP-112.src: CLSI GP16 urinalysis guideline; Strasinger Urinalysis and Body Fluids
TLP-112.retest: Repeat with a clean-catch midstream sample examined within 2 hours if microscopy is abnormal or symptoms are present.

TLP-113.name: Volume
TLP-113.meas: The amount of urine received in the container for this test, not your total daily urine output.
TLP-113.sig: A routine urinalysis needs about 10–15 mL to allow both chemical strip testing and microscopy of a properly centrifuged sediment. Sample volume is a quality check rather than a health measure; daily urine output is assessed separately when needed.
TLP-113.ind: A volume below the minimum means microscopy may be less reliable or incomplete. It carries no diagnostic meaning about kidney function; true low or high daily output (oliguria or polyuria) requires a timed collection.

fy.lo: The sample you provided was smaller than the amount ideally needed for a full urinalysis, so the microscopy part may be less complete than usual. This says nothing about your kidneys or your urine output. If any result on this report is unclear or unexpectedly abnormal, a repeat with a larger midstream sample will settle it.
fy.n: The sample volume was adequate for complete chemical and microscopic testing, so the urinalysis results on this report are reliable. This figure reflects only what was collected, not how much urine you pass in a day.

TLP-113.notes: This is the volume received by the laboratory (a minimum of 10–12 mL is required; 30–50 mL is ideal) and is unrelated to 24-hour urine output, which normally ranges 800–2,000 mL/day in adults.
TLP-113.src: CLSI GP16 urinalysis guideline; Strasinger Urinalysis and Body Fluids
TLP-113.retest: If insufficient, repeat with a 30–50 mL clean-catch midstream sample.

TLP-114.name: Specific Gravity
TLP-114.meas: How concentrated the urine is compared with pure water, reflecting the amount of dissolved salts and waste.
TLP-114.sig: Specific gravity shows whether your kidneys can concentrate or dilute urine appropriately, and reveals hydration status at the time of the sample. Persistently dilute urine despite dehydration is an early sign of tubular kidney damage or diabetes insipidus.
TLP-114.ind: Low specific gravity suggests high fluid intake, diuretics, diabetes insipidus or loss of kidney concentrating ability; high specific gravity suggests dehydration, glucose or protein in the urine, contrast dye, or the hormone SIADH. A fixed value around 1.010 regardless of intake suggests chronic kidney disease.

fy.lo: Your urine was very dilute, which most often simply means you had been drinking a lot of fluid or take water tablets. It becomes significant only if you pass unusually large volumes and are constantly thirsty, which can indicate diabetes insipidus or a kidney concentrating problem. If that sounds familiar, or a first-morning sample is also dilute, discuss it with your doctor.
fy.n: Your urine concentration is in the normal range, which suggests your kidneys are adjusting water balance appropriately and you were reasonably hydrated. No action is needed; a first-morning sample would normally sit towards the higher end of this range.
fy.hi: Your urine was very concentrated, which usually indicates you were dehydrated at the time of sampling, as after an overnight fast, sweating, vomiting or diarrhoea. Glucose or protein in the urine, or recent X-ray contrast dye, can also raise it. Drink adequately and repeat if needed; if glucose was also detected, see the glucose result and discuss with your doctor.

TLP-114.notes: Random samples span 1.003–1.035; first-morning urine is normally 1.015 or above. Dipstick methods do not register glucose or contrast and read low in alkaline urine; refractometer values are raised by glucose, protein and contrast. Infants concentrate less well (upper limit about 1.020).
TLP-114.src: CLSI GP16 urinalysis guideline; Strasinger Urinalysis and Body Fluids
TLP-114.retest: Repeat on a first-morning sample if persistently low; a concentrating ability test may be arranged by your doctor if it stays below 1.010.

TLP-115.name: pH
TLP-115.meas: How acidic or alkaline the urine is, on a scale where 7 is neutral.
TLP-115.sig: The kidneys excrete the day's acid load in the urine, so pH reflects diet, acid-base balance and the kidneys' ability to acidify. It matters most for kidney-stone risk (acidic urine favours uric acid stones, alkaline urine favours phosphate stones) and for spotting certain infections.
TLP-115.ind: Alkaline urine suggests a vegetarian diet, a urinary infection with urea-splitting bacteria, alkalinising medicines, kidney tubular acidosis or a sample left standing; strongly acidic urine suggests a high-protein diet, metabolic acidosis, uncontrolled diabetes, diarrhoea, gout tendency or starvation.

fy.lo: Your urine was unusually acidic. This can follow a high-protein or meat-heavy diet, fasting, diarrhoea or poorly controlled diabetes, and persistently acidic urine increases the risk of uric acid kidney stones. Drinking more water, adding fruit and vegetables and moderating meat helps; if ketones were also present or you have diabetes, discuss the result with your doctor.
fy.n: Your urine pH is within the normal range, which suggests your kidneys are handling your daily acid load appropriately. Most people run mildly acidic urine, and it shifts naturally with meals, so no action is needed.
fy.hi: Your urine was strongly alkaline. The commonest reason is a sample that stood for a while before testing, but a urinary infection with certain bacteria, a largely vegetarian diet, antacids or citrate medicines, or a kidney tubular disorder can cause it. Alkaline urine can promote phosphate crystals and stones. Check the nitrite and leucocyte results; if they are positive or you have symptoms, see your doctor and repeat on a fresh sample.

TLP-115.notes: Normal urine can fall anywhere from 4.5 to 8.0 depending on diet and timing; first-morning urine is usually 5.0–6.0. Delay beyond 2 hours before testing raises pH as bacteria break down urea. Vegetarian diets, common in India, produce more alkaline urine without disease.
TLP-115.src: CLSI GP16 urinalysis guideline; Strasinger Urinalysis and Body Fluids
TLP-115.retest: Repeat on a fresh sample tested within 2 hours if strongly alkaline; if kidney tubular acidosis is suspected, your doctor may order blood bicarbonate and a first-morning urine pH.

TLP-116.name: Protein (Urine)
TLP-116.meas: A chemical strip estimate of protein, mainly albumin, in the urine, graded from negative through trace to 4+.
TLP-116.sig: The dipstick is a quick screen for significant protein leak from the kidneys, though it misses the small amounts that define early diabetic kidney disease and can over-read in concentrated or alkaline urine. Any positive result should be quantified with a protein-creatinine ratio.
TLP-116.ind: A positive dipstick suggests glomerular or tubular kidney disease, urinary infection, hypertension-related kidney damage, or transient proteinuria from fever, exercise or standing; in pregnancy it raises the question of pre-eclampsia. Negative does not exclude microalbuminuria.

fy.n: No protein was detected on the strip test, which suggests there is no significant leak from your kidney filters. If you have diabetes or high blood pressure, note that this strip cannot detect the very small albumin losses of early kidney damage, so the albumin-creatinine ratio remains the better yearly check.
fy.bhi: A trace of protein was detected. This is frequently a false alarm from concentrated or alkaline urine, or a temporary leak after fever, vigorous exercise, or a long day standing. Repeat on a first-morning sample after a normal day; if still present, a protein-creatinine ratio will show whether it is significant, and your doctor can review blood pressure and kidney function.
fy.hi: Protein was clearly detected on the strip. This suggests your kidney filters are letting protein through, which can result from diabetes, high blood pressure, kidney inflammation or a urinary infection; occasionally it is temporary after fever or exercise. Please have a protein-creatinine ratio and kidney blood tests, and see your doctor, especially if you have swelling of the legs or face or, in pregnancy, headache or high blood pressure.

TLP-116.notes: The strip detects mainly albumin and reads falsely positive in alkaline (pH above 8) or very concentrated urine and after antiseptic contamination, and falsely negative in dilute urine or when the protein is a light chain (myeloma). In pregnancy, 1+ or more should prompt quantification and blood pressure measurement.
TLP-116.src: CLSI GP16 urinalysis guideline; KDIGO 2024 CKD guideline; NICE NG133
TLP-116.retest: Any trace or positive result should be repeated on a first-morning sample and confirmed with a urine protein-creatinine or albumin-creatinine ratio.

TLP-117.name: Glucose (Urine)
TLP-117.meas: A chemical strip test for glucose spilling into the urine, graded from negative through trace to 4+.
TLP-117.sig: Glucose appears in urine only when blood sugar exceeds the kidney's reabsorption threshold, about 180 mg/dL, or when the kidney tubules themselves leak glucose. A positive result is a strong pointer to undiagnosed or uncontrolled diabetes, though a negative result never rules diabetes out.
TLP-117.ind: Positive urine glucose suggests diabetes mellitus with high blood sugar, SGLT2-inhibitor diabetes tablets (which deliberately cause it), pregnancy (lowered kidney threshold), or a benign kidney tubular leak (renal glycosuria); rarely it follows a very large sugar load or Cushing's syndrome.

fy.n: No glucose was detected in your urine, which suggests your blood sugar stayed below the level at which the kidneys spill sugar. This does not exclude pre-diabetes or mild diabetes, so your fasting glucose and HbA1c remain the tests to watch.
fy.bhi: A trace of glucose was found in your urine. If you take an SGLT2-type diabetes tablet this is expected. Otherwise it may reflect a temporarily high blood sugar after a large meal, pregnancy, or a harmless tendency of the kidneys to leak small amounts of sugar. Check your fasting glucose and HbA1c on this report and repeat the urine test fasting; discuss with your doctor if either blood test is raised.
fy.hi: Glucose was clearly present in your urine, which suggests your blood sugar has been running high enough to overflow into the urine, consistent with diabetes that is undiagnosed or not well controlled, unless you are on an SGLT2 diabetes tablet where this is expected. Please review your blood glucose and HbA1c and see your doctor soon; if ketones are also present, seek attention the same day.

TLP-117.notes: The kidney threshold falls in pregnancy, so mild glycosuria is common in healthy pregnant women; SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) cause marked glycosuria by design. High-dose vitamin C can cause a false-negative strip; bleach contamination a false positive.
TLP-117.src: CLSI GP16 urinalysis guideline; ADA Standards of Care 2024
TLP-117.retest: A positive result should be followed by fasting plasma glucose and HbA1c rather than a repeat urine test; if blood glucose is normal, your doctor may consider renal glycosuria.

TLP-118.name: Blood (Urine)
TLP-118.meas: A chemical strip test that detects the haem pigment from red blood cells, free haemoglobin or muscle myoglobin in the urine.
TLP-118.sig: Blood in the urine, even when invisible, can be the only early sign of kidney inflammation, stones, infection or, in older adults and smokers, a bladder or kidney tumour. A positive strip needs confirmation by microscopy, because it also reacts to haemoglobin and myoglobin without intact cells.
TLP-118.ind: A positive result suggests urinary infection, kidney or bladder stones, glomerulonephritis, prostate enlargement, strenuous exercise, menstrual contamination, or urinary-tract tumours; a strip positive without red cells on microscopy suggests haemolysis or muscle breakdown (myoglobinuria).

fy.n: No blood was detected in your urine, which suggests there is no bleeding or inflammation anywhere along the urinary tract at the time of sampling. Nothing further is needed for this item.
fy.bhi: A trace of blood was detected on the strip. This is often due to menstrual contamination, recent vigorous exercise, mild dehydration, or a sample collected during a urinary infection, and the strip can react even when very few cells are present. Check the RBC count on microscopy; repeat on a fresh midstream sample away from menstruation, and see your doctor if it persists.
fy.hi: Blood was clearly detected in your urine. Common causes include urinary infection, kidney or bladder stones, an enlarged prostate, or inflammation of the kidney filters; in people over 40 or who smoke, a bladder or kidney growth must also be excluded. Please see your doctor even if you have no symptoms; a repeat urinalysis with microscopy, kidney tests and often an ultrasound are the usual next steps.

TLP-118.notes: False positives occur with menstrual blood, dehydration, strenuous exercise, bleach or bacterial peroxidase; false negatives with high-dose vitamin C or very high specific gravity. Persistent microscopic haematuria (3 or more RBC/hpf on 2 of 3 samples) warrants urological evaluation, particularly over age 40 or with smoking history.
TLP-118.src: AUA/SUFU 2020 microhaematuria guideline; CLSI GP16 urinalysis guideline
TLP-118.retest: Repeat on a clean midstream sample away from menstruation and 48 hours after heavy exercise; persistent positivity needs microscopy, kidney tests and referral.

TLP-119.name: Bilirubin
TLP-119.meas: A strip test for conjugated bilirubin, the water-soluble bile pigment that only reaches the urine when the liver or bile ducts are affected.
TLP-119.sig: Bilirubin in urine appears before the skin turns yellow, making it an early warning of liver inflammation or bile duct blockage. It is always abnormal, and its combination with the urobilinogen result helps distinguish a blocked duct from liver cell damage.
TLP-119.ind: A positive result suggests viral or drug-induced hepatitis, biliary obstruction from gallstones or tumour, cirrhosis, or other causes of conjugated jaundice; it is negative in haemolytic jaundice and Gilbert's syndrome, where bilirubin is unconjugated.

fy.n: No bilirubin was detected in your urine, which is the expected result and suggests your liver is processing bile pigment normally and the bile ducts are not blocked. Nothing further is needed for this item.
fy.hi: Bilirubin was detected in your urine, which is always worth investigating as it suggests the liver is inflamed or bile flow is obstructed, for instance by hepatitis, certain medicines, alcohol or gallstones. You may notice dark urine, pale stools or yellowing of the eyes. Please see your doctor promptly; liver function blood tests and usually an ultrasound of the liver and bile ducts are the next steps.

TLP-119.notes: Bilirubin breaks down in light and on standing, so samples must be fresh and protected from light; phenazopyridine and rifampicin colour the strip and can give false positives, and high vitamin C or nitrite can cause false negatives.
TLP-119.src: CLSI GP16 urinalysis guideline; Strasinger Urinalysis and Body Fluids
TLP-119.retest: A positive result should prompt serum bilirubin and liver function tests within days rather than a repeat urine strip.

TLP-120.name: Urobilinogen
TLP-120.meas: A strip estimate of urobilinogen, a colourless substance formed when gut bacteria break down bile and a small amount of which is normally recycled and excreted in urine.
TLP-120.sig: Urobilinogen rises when the liver is overwhelmed by pigment from red-cell breakdown or cannot re-clear what the gut returns, and it disappears when bile flow is fully blocked. Read with urine bilirubin it helps separate haemolytic, hepatic and obstructive causes of jaundice.
TLP-120.ind: Increased urobilinogen suggests haemolytic anaemia, hepatitis, cirrhosis or congestive liver, and can be raised by constipation or a heavy-meal sample; absent urobilinogen with positive bilirubin suggests complete bile-duct obstruction, and broad-spectrum antibiotics can also abolish it.

fy.n: Your urine urobilinogen is at the normal, small amount, which suggests bile is flowing into the gut and being recycled normally and there is no excess breakdown of red blood cells. Nothing further is needed for this item.
fy.hi: Your urine urobilinogen is increased, which suggests either more bile pigment is being produced than usual, as with increased red-cell breakdown, or the liver is not clearing the recycled pigment efficiently, as in hepatitis or cirrhosis. Constipation and an afternoon sample can raise it mildly. Please have liver function tests and a blood count, and discuss with your doctor, particularly if urine bilirubin is also positive or you feel unwell.

TLP-120.notes: Strips cannot reliably detect the absence of urobilinogen, so complete biliary obstruction is inferred from a positive bilirubin with 'normal' urobilinogen rather than a 'low' reading. Levels peak in the early afternoon; sulphonamides, nitrite and formalin interfere, and samples must be fresh as urobilinogen oxidises in light.
TLP-120.src: CLSI GP16 urinalysis guideline; Strasinger Urinalysis and Body Fluids
TLP-120.retest: Follow up an increased result with serum bilirubin, liver enzymes and a complete blood count rather than a repeat strip.

TLP-121.name: Ketone Bodies
TLP-121.meas: A strip test for ketones, the acids produced when the body burns fat for fuel instead of glucose.
TLP-121.sig: Ketones in the urine mean the body is short of usable glucose. In a fasting person that is a normal metabolic response, but in a person with diabetes and high blood sugar it warns of diabetic ketoacidosis, a medical emergency.
TLP-121.ind: Ketones suggest prolonged fasting, a very low-carbohydrate or ketogenic diet, vomiting or febrile illness, pregnancy with morning sickness, strenuous exercise, or, with high blood glucose, insulin deficiency and impending ketoacidosis; SGLT2 diabetes tablets can trigger ketosis with near-normal sugar.

fy.n: No ketones were detected in your urine, which suggests your body is fuelling itself normally on glucose and, if you have diabetes, you are not short of insulin. Nothing further is needed for this item.
fy.bhi: A small amount of ketones was detected. This is common after an overnight fast for blood tests, a low-carbohydrate diet, skipped meals, vomiting or a fever, and it clears once you eat normally. If you have diabetes and your glucose is high, or you take an SGLT2 tablet and feel nauseated or unwell, contact your doctor today rather than waiting.
fy.hi: A moderate to large amount of ketones was detected. If you have diabetes, especially with a high blood glucose, thirst, vomiting, abdominal pain or rapid breathing, this can signal diabetic ketoacidosis and you should seek medical care the same day. If you do not have diabetes, it usually reflects prolonged fasting, a strict ketogenic diet, or a vomiting illness; eat and drink, and see your doctor if you are unwell.

TLP-121.notes: The strip detects acetoacetate and acetone but not beta-hydroxybutyrate, the main ketone in ketoacidosis, so blood ketone testing is preferred in diabetic emergencies. Fasting samples for health checks frequently show trace ketones; levodopa, captopril and phenolic dyes can cause false positives.
TLP-121.src: ADA Standards of Care 2024; CLSI GP16 urinalysis guideline
TLP-121.retest: Repeat after a normal meal if trace; in diabetes with moderate or large ketones, check blood glucose and blood ketones immediately rather than repeating the urine strip.

TLP-122.name: Nitrites
TLP-122.meas: A strip test for nitrite, a chemical produced when common urinary bacteria such as E. coli convert dietary nitrate in urine that has sat in the bladder for a few hours.
TLP-122.sig: A positive nitrite is a highly specific pointer to a bacterial urinary infection, even before a culture result. A negative result is less reassuring, because some bacteria do not make nitrite and frequent urination gives them too little time to do so.
TLP-122.ind: A positive nitrite indicates bacteriuria with nitrate-reducing organisms (most gram-negative bacteria); a negative result does not exclude infection with enterococci, staphylococci or in dilute, frequently voided urine.

fy.n: Nitrite was not detected in your urine, which makes a bacterial urinary infection less likely, though not impossible if you had passed urine recently or the bacteria are of a type that does not produce nitrite. If leucocytes or pus cells are raised and you have symptoms, a urine culture is still worthwhile.
fy.hi: Nitrite was detected in your urine, which strongly suggests bacteria are present and multiplying in the urinary tract. With burning, urgency, frequency or lower abdominal pain this is consistent with a urinary infection; without symptoms it may represent harmless bacterial colonisation or a contaminated sample. Please see your doctor, who will usually send a urine culture before deciding whether treatment is needed; drink plenty of water meanwhile.

TLP-122.notes: Best on a first-morning sample held in the bladder for at least 4 hours; false negatives with dilute urine, vegetarian diets low in nitrate, high vitamin C or non-nitrate-reducing bacteria; false positives with samples left standing, or phenazopyridine. Asymptomatic bacteriuria is generally not treated except in pregnancy.
TLP-122.src: IDSA 2019 asymptomatic bacteriuria guideline; CLSI GP16 urinalysis guideline
TLP-122.retest: Confirm a positive result with a urine culture on a clean midstream (ideally first-morning) sample rather than a repeat strip.

TLP-123.name: Leucocytes
TLP-123.meas: A strip test for leucocyte esterase, an enzyme released by white blood cells, indicating white cells in the urine even if they have broken down.
TLP-123.sig: White cells in urine mean inflammation somewhere in the urinary tract, most often infection. Combined with nitrite it makes a urinary infection very likely, while a positive leucocyte result with a negative culture points to conditions such as stones, kidney inflammation or sexually transmitted infections.
TLP-123.ind: A positive result suggests urinary tract infection, kidney inflammation (pyelonephritis, interstitial nephritis), stones, tuberculosis of the urinary tract, urethritis, or vaginal contamination; it is negative in most non-inflammatory conditions.

fy.n: No white cells were detected by the strip, which suggests there is no significant inflammation or infection in your urinary tract at present. Nothing further is needed for this item.
fy.bhi: A trace of white cells was detected. This often reflects mild contamination from the skin or vaginal secretions during collection, or a very early or resolving infection. If you have no urinary symptoms and nitrite is negative, simply repeat with a careful midstream sample; if you have burning or frequency, see your doctor for a urine culture.
fy.hi: White cells were clearly detected, which suggests inflammation in the urinary tract, most commonly a bacterial infection, particularly if nitrite is also positive or you have burning, urgency or fever. In some people the culture is negative and the cause is a stone, a sexually transmitted infection, or, rarely, tuberculosis. Please see your doctor for a urine culture and further assessment; drink plenty of fluids in the meantime.

TLP-123.notes: False positives from vaginal contamination, trichomonas or formalin; false negatives with high glucose, high specific gravity, high vitamin C or some antibiotics (cephalexin, tetracycline). Sterile pyuria warrants evaluation for stones, interstitial nephritis, chlamydia or genitourinary tuberculosis, which remains relevant in India.
TLP-123.src: IDSA 2019 asymptomatic bacteriuria guideline; CLSI GP16 urinalysis guideline
TLP-123.retest: Repeat on a clean midstream sample; a positive result with symptoms should go to culture, and a persistently positive result with negative cultures needs specialist review.

TLP-124.name: Microscopy (Sediment)
TLP-124.meas: The overall impression from examining the centrifuged urine deposit under a microscope for cells, casts, crystals and organisms.
TLP-124.sig: Microscopy confirms what the chemical strips suggest and reveals what they cannot: the kind of cells present, casts that pinpoint kidney disease, and crystals that predict stones. It is the part of a urinalysis that directs further investigation.
TLP-124.ind: An abnormal sediment may show pus cells and bacteria (infection), red cells and red-cell casts (glomerular bleeding), granular or waxy casts (kidney disease), abundant or unusual crystals (stone risk, metabolic disorders), or yeast and epithelial cells (contamination or fungal infection).

fy.n: Your urine deposit showed nothing significant under the microscope, which suggests no infection, bleeding, kidney-filter damage or crystal build-up at the time of testing. This is a reassuring baseline; drinking enough water keeps the urinary tract flushed and healthy.
fy.hi: Your urine deposit showed one or more abnormal findings, which are broken down in the individual items below. Raised pus cells and bacteria usually point to infection; red cells to bleeding from anywhere in the tract; casts to a process within the kidney itself; and crystals to concentrated urine or stone risk. Read the specific items, and discuss any that are flagged with your doctor, who may repeat the test or arrange a culture or ultrasound.

TLP-124.notes: Findings depend on collection technique and delay; samples over 2 hours old lose casts and cells and gain crystals. Menstruation, vaginal discharge and non-midstream collection commonly contaminate samples from women.
TLP-124.src: CLSI GP16 urinalysis guideline; European Urinalysis Guidelines (ECLM 2000)
TLP-124.retest: Repeat on a fresh first-morning, clean-catch midstream sample examined within 2 hours if any finding is unexpected.

TLP-125.name: RBC
TLP-125.alias: Urine RBC, Red cells /hpf, Microscopic haematuria
TLP-125.meas: The number of red blood cells seen per high-power microscope field in the centrifuged urine deposit.
TLP-125.sig: Counting red cells confirms true haematuria and separates it from pigment reactions on the strip. Three or more per field on repeated samples is the accepted definition of microscopic haematuria, which needs a cause to be found, particularly in older adults and smokers.
TLP-125.ind: Raised red cells suggest urinary infection, kidney or bladder stones, glomerulonephritis (often with misshapen cells or red-cell casts), enlarged prostate, trauma, strenuous exercise, menstrual contamination, or tumours of the kidney, bladder or prostate.

fy.n: The number of red cells in your urine is within the normal range, which suggests there is no bleeding from the kidneys, bladder or urinary passages. Nothing further is needed for this item.
fy.bhi: A few more red cells than usual were seen. This can follow menstruation, vigorous exercise, mild infection, or sample contamination, but it meets the threshold at which repeated findings should be investigated. Repeat on a clean midstream sample away from menstruation and exercise; if red cells persist on two of three samples, your doctor will check kidney function, urine protein and usually arrange an ultrasound.
fy.hi: A clearly increased number of red cells was seen in your urine, which indicates bleeding somewhere in the urinary tract. Infection, stones, prostate enlargement and kidney-filter inflammation are the common causes, but in people over 40 or with a smoking history a bladder or kidney growth must be excluded. Please see your doctor promptly for kidney tests, urine protein assessment and imaging; a urology referral may be advised.

TLP-125.notes: Menstrual contamination is the commonest artefact in women; dysmorphic red cells or red-cell casts point to a glomerular (kidney-filter) source. Counts are lower in dilute or old samples where cells lyse. AUA defines microhaematuria as 3 or more RBC/hpf on a properly collected sample.
TLP-125.src: AUA/SUFU 2020 microhaematuria guideline; CLSI GP16 urinalysis guideline
TLP-125.retest: Confirm with 2 further clean-catch midstream samples over several weeks, avoiding menstruation and heavy exercise; persistence on 2 of 3 samples warrants evaluation.

TLP-126.name: Pus Cells (Urine)
TLP-126.dn: Pus cells in urine (white cells, microscopy)
TLP-126.meas: The number of white blood cells (pus cells) seen per high-power microscope field in the centrifuged urine deposit.
TLP-126.sig: Pus cells are the microscope's confirmation of inflammation in the urinary tract. More than a handful per field, particularly with bacteria and symptoms, indicates infection, while pus cells without bacteria raise the possibility of stones, kidney inflammation or tuberculosis.
TLP-126.ind: Raised pus cells suggest urinary tract infection (cystitis, pyelonephritis, prostatitis), stones, interstitial nephritis, urethritis from sexually transmitted infection, genitourinary tuberculosis, or contamination from vaginal secretions.

fy.n: The number of pus cells in your urine is within the normal range, which suggests no infection or inflammation in your urinary tract at present. Nothing further is needed for this item.
fy.bhi: A slightly increased number of pus cells was seen. Without symptoms this is often due to contamination from the skin or vaginal area during collection, or a mild, self-limiting irritation. If you have burning, frequency or lower abdominal discomfort, or if nitrite or bacteria are also flagged, see your doctor for a urine culture; otherwise repeat on a careful midstream sample.
fy.hi: A clearly increased number of pus cells was seen, which indicates active inflammation in the urinary tract, most commonly a bacterial infection, especially with bacteria, positive nitrite, or symptoms such as burning, urgency, fever or back pain. If cultures come back negative, stones, kidney inflammation, a sexually transmitted infection or tuberculosis may need to be considered. Please see your doctor for a urine culture and treatment; drink plenty of water meanwhile.

TLP-126.notes: Some laboratories quote 0–2/hpf as normal for men; counts above 10/hpf with symptoms are strongly suggestive of infection. Vaginal contamination (with many epithelial cells) is the commonest cause of false pyuria in women. Sterile pyuria in India should raise the possibility of genitourinary tuberculosis.
TLP-126.src: IDSA 2019 asymptomatic bacteriuria guideline; European Urinalysis Guidelines (ECLM 2000)
TLP-126.retest: Repeat on a clean midstream first-morning sample; with symptoms or bacteria, send a urine culture; persistent sterile pyuria needs specialist evaluation.

TLP-127.name: Epithelial Cells (Urine)
TLP-127.meas: The number of cells shed from the lining of the urinary tract or genital skin seen per high-power microscope field.
TLP-127.sig: A few epithelial cells are normal shedding. Many squamous cells indicate the sample picked up cells from the skin or vagina, which means the pus cell and bacteria counts may be contaminated and a repeat midstream sample is needed. Renal tubular cells, by contrast, suggest kidney injury.
TLP-127.ind: Many squamous epithelial cells indicate a contaminated, non-midstream sample; increased transitional cells may follow catheterisation or bladder inflammation; renal tubular epithelial cells suggest acute tubular injury, viral infection or kidney transplant rejection.

fy.n: Only an occasional epithelial cell was seen, which is normal shedding from the lining of the urinary tract and also tells us the sample was well collected, so the other microscopy results are reliable. Nothing further is needed for this item.
fy.hi: Many epithelial cells were seen in your urine. Most often these are skin-type squamous cells that entered the sample during collection, which means the pus cell and bacteria findings may be overstated and, if those are abnormal, a repeat clean-catch midstream sample is advisable. Rarely the cells are of kidney-tubule type, which suggests kidney injury; your doctor will note if the report specifies this.

TLP-127.notes: Squamous cells above 5/hpf (or 'many') generally indicate contamination and may invalidate a culture; renal tubular cells at more than 2/hpf are significant in any number. Counts are naturally higher in women and in non-midstream samples.
TLP-127.src: European Urinalysis Guidelines (ECLM 2000); CLSI GP16 urinalysis guideline
TLP-127.retest: Repeat with a clean-catch midstream sample (cleanse the area, discard the first stream) if other microscopy items are abnormal.

TLP-128.name: Crystals
TLP-128.meas: The presence and type of mineral crystals seen in the urine deposit under the microscope.
TLP-128.sig: Most crystals are harmless precipitates that form as concentrated urine cools, but persistent crystals of the same type signal the chemistry behind kidney stones, and a few rare crystal types (cystine, tyrosine, leucine, drug crystals) point directly to inherited metabolic disorders, liver failure or medication toxicity.
TLP-128.ind: Calcium oxalate crystals suggest concentrated urine, high oxalate intake or stone tendency; uric acid crystals suggest acidic urine and high urate; triple phosphate crystals suggest alkaline urine or infection with urea-splitting bacteria; cystine crystals indicate cystinuria; tyrosine or leucine crystals indicate severe liver disease; sulphonamide or aciclovir crystals indicate drug precipitation.

rng.bhi: Few calcium oxalate, urate or phosphate crystals (Few common crystals)
rng.hi: Abundant crystals, or cystine / tyrosine / leucine / drug crystals (Abundant or abnormal)

fy.n: No crystals were seen in your urine, which suggests your urine was not overly concentrated and the minerals in it were well dissolved. Drinking enough water throughout the day is the simplest way to keep it that way.
fy.bhi: A few common crystals, such as calcium oxalate, uric acid or phosphate, were seen. These usually form because the urine was concentrated or cooled before examination and are harmless in themselves, though if they appear repeatedly they hint at a tendency to kidney stones. Increase your water intake, moderate salt and, for oxalate, foods such as spinach and nuts; if you have had stones or pain, discuss with your doctor.
fy.hi: Abundant crystals, or a type that is never normal, were seen in your urine. Large numbers of calcium oxalate or uric acid crystals suggest significant stone risk and warrant a review of hydration, diet and blood uric acid or calcium. Cystine, tyrosine, leucine or drug crystals point to an inherited disorder, liver disease or medication build-up and need medical attention. Please share this report with your doctor for further evaluation.

TLP-128.notes: Crystals form readily in samples left standing or refrigerated and in first-morning concentrated urine, so a few common crystals in a delayed sample are of no significance; the crystal type is more important than the amount. Certain drugs (sulphonamides, aciclovir, indinavir, high-dose vitamin C causing oxalate) produce characteristic crystals.
TLP-128.src: European Urinalysis Guidelines (ECLM 2000); Strasinger Urinalysis and Body Fluids
TLP-128.retest: Repeat on a fresh, well-hydrated midstream sample examined within 2 hours; persistent crystals of one type merit blood calcium, uric acid and a kidney ultrasound.

any.label: Few common crystals
any.text: Few calcium oxalate, urate or phosphate crystals

any.label: Abundant or abnormal
any.text: Abundant crystals, or cystine / tyrosine / leucine / drug crystals

TLP-129.name: Cast
TLP-129.meas: Cylindrical moulds of protein, sometimes containing trapped cells, that form inside the kidney tubules and are washed out in the urine.
TLP-129.sig: Because casts can only form inside the kidney, they localise a problem to the kidney itself rather than the bladder or urethra. The type of cast is diagnostic: red-cell casts mean glomerular inflammation, white-cell casts mean kidney infection, granular and waxy casts mean established kidney disease, while a few hyaline casts are normal.
TLP-129.ind: Hyaline casts occur with dehydration, exercise, fever or diuretics and are benign in small numbers; red-cell casts indicate glomerulonephritis; white-cell casts indicate pyelonephritis or interstitial nephritis; granular, waxy or broad casts indicate acute tubular injury or chronic kidney disease; fatty casts indicate nephrotic syndrome.

rng.hi: Cellular, granular, waxy, fatty or numerous casts (Pathological casts)

fy.n: No casts were seen in your urine, which suggests there is no active inflammation or injury within the kidney tubules and filters. This is the expected finding in healthy kidneys; nothing further is needed for this item.
fy.bhi: An occasional hyaline cast was seen. These clear protein casts are common after dehydration, exercise, fever or water tablets and, in small numbers, are not a sign of kidney disease. Ensure normal hydration and repeat if you wish; no action is needed unless protein, blood or other casts are also present.
fy.hi: Casts containing cells or granular material, or casts in large numbers, were seen in your urine. Because these form inside the kidney, they suggest a process affecting the kidney itself: red-cell casts point to inflammation of the filters, white-cell casts to kidney infection, and granular or waxy casts to tubular injury or longer-standing kidney disease. Please see your doctor or a kidney specialist soon for kidney function tests, urine protein quantification and further evaluation.

TLP-129.notes: Casts dissolve in alkaline or dilute urine and in samples over 2 hours old, so absence in a delayed sample is not fully reassuring. Up to 2 hyaline casts per low-power field is normal, and numbers rise transiently after strenuous exercise.
TLP-129.src: European Urinalysis Guidelines (ECLM 2000); Brenner and Rector's The Kidney
TLP-129.retest: Repeat on a fresh first-morning sample examined within 2 hours; any cellular, granular or waxy cast should prompt kidney function tests and specialist review.

any.label: Pathological casts
any.text: Cellular, granular, waxy, fatty or numerous casts

TLP-130.name: Yeast
TLP-130.meas: The presence of yeast cells, usually Candida, seen in the urine deposit under the microscope.
TLP-130.sig: Yeast in urine most often reflects contamination from a vaginal yeast infection or harmless colonisation, especially in people with diabetes, on antibiotics, or with a urinary catheter. True fungal urinary infection is uncommon but matters in people with poorly controlled diabetes or weakened immunity.
TLP-130.ind: Yeast suggests vaginal candidiasis contaminating the sample, colonisation after antibiotics or in diabetes (glucose in urine feeds yeast), catheter-associated colonisation, or, with symptoms and pus cells, a fungal urinary tract infection; in immunocompromised people it can signal invasive candidiasis.

fy.n: No yeast was seen in your urine, which is the expected finding and suggests no fungal overgrowth in or around the urinary tract. Nothing further is needed for this item.
fy.hi: Yeast cells were seen in your urine. In women this is most commonly from a vaginal yeast infection contaminating the sample, and in anyone it can follow a course of antibiotics or reflect sugar in the urine from diabetes, which yeast feeds on. Itching, discharge or burning support a genital yeast infection that is easily treated. Check your glucose results, repeat with a careful midstream sample, and see your doctor if you have symptoms, diabetes or a weakened immune system.

TLP-130.notes: Yeast is a common contaminant and is rarely treated unless symptomatic, or in pregnancy, immunosuppression, neutropenia, kidney transplant, or before urological procedures. Glycosuria from diabetes or SGLT2 inhibitors markedly increases genital yeast infections.
TLP-130.src: IDSA 2016 candidiasis guideline; CLSI GP16 urinalysis guideline
TLP-130.retest: Repeat with a clean-catch midstream sample after treating any vaginal infection; a fungal culture is sent if yeast persists with symptoms or pus cells.

TLP-131.name: Bacteria
TLP-131.meas: The amount of bacteria seen in the urine deposit under the microscope, graded from absent to plenty.
TLP-131.sig: Normal urine in the bladder is sterile, so bacteria seen in a fresh, properly collected sample suggest infection, particularly alongside pus cells and nitrite. Bacteria alone can also reflect contamination or harmless colonisation, which is why culture and symptoms decide treatment.
TLP-131.ind: Moderate to plenty of bacteria with pus cells suggest urinary tract infection; bacteria without pus cells suggest contamination, a delayed sample, or asymptomatic bacteriuria, which is common in older adults and people with diabetes and generally does not need treatment outside pregnancy.

rng.hi: Moderate to plenty (2+ to 4+) (Moderate to plenty)

fy.n: No significant bacteria were seen in your urine, which suggests no urinary infection at the time of sampling. Nothing further is needed for this item.
fy.bhi: A few bacteria were seen. In a sample that was not midstream or was tested after a delay this usually represents contamination or harmless colonisation rather than infection, especially if pus cells and nitrite are normal. If you have burning, frequency or lower abdominal pain, see your doctor for a urine culture; otherwise a repeat on a fresh clean-catch sample is enough.
fy.hi: A moderate to large amount of bacteria was seen in your urine. Together with raised pus cells, positive nitrite or leucocytes, or symptoms such as burning, urgency, fever or back pain, this is consistent with a urinary tract infection that usually needs treatment. Without symptoms it may be harmless colonisation, which is generally left alone except in pregnancy. Please see your doctor, who will send a urine culture to identify the organism and the right antibiotic; drink plenty of water meanwhile.

TLP-131.notes: Bacteria multiply rapidly in samples left at room temperature, so counts are reliable only within 2 hours of collection or with refrigeration. Asymptomatic bacteriuria is not treated except in pregnancy and before urological surgery (IDSA 2019). Culture, not microscopy, is the definitive test.
TLP-131.src: IDSA 2019 asymptomatic bacteriuria guideline; CLSI GP16 urinalysis guideline
TLP-131.retest: Send a urine culture on a fresh clean-catch midstream sample before starting antibiotics; repeat microscopy is not needed on its own.

TLP-132.name: Cortisol (AM)
TLP-132.alias: Serum cortisol 8 AM, Basal cortisol, Cortisol (morning)
TLP-132.profile: ADD-ON · SECONDARY-HYPERTENSION WORK-UP; ADRENAL FUNCTION PROFILE
TLP-132.meas: The level of cortisol, the adrenal gland's main stress and energy hormone, measured at its natural morning peak.
TLP-132.sig: Morning cortisol is the first-line screen for adrenal underactivity: a clearly low value at the hormone's daily peak suggests Addison's disease or pituitary failure, while a robust value largely excludes it. It is also part of the secondary hypertension work-up, though excess cortisol (Cushing's) is better detected by late-night or suppression tests than by a morning level.
TLP-132.ind: Low morning cortisol suggests adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease, pituitary disease) or suppression from recent steroid tablets, inhalers or creams; high morning cortisol suggests physical or emotional stress, acute illness, depression, alcohol excess, oral contraceptives (raised binding protein), or Cushing's syndrome.

fy.lo: A morning cortisol this low, at the time of day when it should be at its peak, suggests your adrenal glands are not producing enough hormone, or have been switched off by recent steroid medicines including tablets, injections, inhalers, or skin creams. Symptoms can include profound tiredness, weight loss, dizziness on standing, salt craving or darkened skin. Please see your doctor promptly; a confirmatory stimulation test and treatment are important and should not be delayed.
fy.blo: Your morning cortisol is in an indeterminate range: too low to fully rule out adrenal underactivity, but not low enough to confirm it. Sampling later than 9 AM, night-shift work, or recent steroid use in any form can produce this. Your doctor may repeat the test at 8 AM or arrange a short stimulation test, particularly if you have fatigue, low blood pressure or unexplained weight loss.
fy.n: Your morning cortisol is in the normal range, which suggests your adrenal glands are producing an appropriate amount of stress hormone and adrenal underactivity is unlikely. Regular sleep, managing chronic stress and avoiding unnecessary steroid medicines help keep this hormone system balanced.
fy.bhi: Your morning cortisol is at the upper edge of normal. This is common after a stressful night, poor sleep, an early-morning journey to the lab, acute illness, or in women taking oral contraceptive pills, which raise the protein that carries cortisol. It rarely indicates disease on its own. If you have unexplained weight gain around the middle, easy bruising, high blood pressure or high sugar, your doctor may consider a late-night salivary cortisol or a dexamethasone suppression test.
fy.hi: A clearly raised morning cortisol suggests either a significant stress response, from illness, pain, anxiety, alcohol or depression, or the effects of oral contraceptives on cortisol-binding protein; less commonly it points to Cushing's syndrome, especially with central weight gain, purple stretch marks, muscle weakness, high blood pressure or diabetes. Please discuss with your doctor; a specific test such as late-night salivary cortisol or overnight dexamethasone suppression will be needed before any conclusion is drawn.

TLP-132.notes: Reference interval is assay-specific (Roche ECLIA 7–10 AM: 6.2–19.4 µg/dL; other immunoassays quote roughly 5–25). Endocrine Society thresholds: below 3 µg/dL strongly suggests adrenal insufficiency; above 15 µg/dL makes it unlikely. Oestrogen therapy, pregnancy and oral contraceptives raise total cortisol; night-shift workers and samples drawn after 9 AM are lower. A morning cortisol cannot diagnose or exclude Cushing's syndrome.
TLP-132.src: Endocrine Society 2016 adrenal insufficiency guideline; Endocrine Society 2008 Cushing's syndrome guideline; manufacturer reference interval
TLP-132.retest: Repeat strictly between 7 and 9 AM after normal sleep and at least 24 hours off any hydrocortisone-type steroid if borderline; further testing (ACTH stimulation or dexamethasone suppression) is arranged by your doctor rather than a simple repeat.

TLP-133.name: TSH
TLP-133.meas: The pituitary signal that tells the thyroid gland how much hormone to make.
TLP-133.sig: TSH is the single most sensitive screen for thyroid over- or under-activity; it moves early and in the opposite direction to thyroid hormone, so even mild dysfunction is caught before symptoms appear.
TLP-133.ind: A raised TSH points to an under-active thyroid (hypothyroidism, most often autoimmune Hashimoto's disease in India, or iodine-related). A suppressed TSH suggests an over-active thyroid (Graves' disease, toxic nodule, thyroiditis) or excess thyroxine tablets.

fy.lo: A suppressed TSH suggests your thyroid is over-active or you are taking more thyroxine than needed. Common causes include Graves' disease, an overactive nodule or a temporary thyroiditis. Your doctor will look at FT4/FT3 alongside this and may examine your neck; do not stop or change thyroid tablets on your own.
fy.blo: A mildly low TSH with normal thyroid hormones is called subclinical hyperthyroidism. It can be a passing change (recent illness, early pregnancy, a slightly high thyroxine dose) or the first sign of an over-active gland. It usually deserves a repeat in 6–8 weeks and a chat with your doctor if it persists.
fy.n: Your TSH is in the healthy range, which means the thyroid is producing hormone at the rate your body is asking for. Thyroid disorders are common in Indian adults, especially women, so a normal result now is a useful baseline; repeat every 1–2 years or sooner if you notice weight, energy or mood changes.
fy.bhi: A mildly raised TSH with normal FT4 is subclinical hypothyroidism - the gland is working a little harder to keep up. Early autoimmune thyroiditis is the usual cause, and about a third of such results settle on their own. Your doctor may repeat TSH in 6–12 weeks with anti-TPO antibodies before deciding whether treatment is needed.
fy.hi: A clearly raised TSH is consistent with an under-active thyroid, most often due to Hashimoto's (autoimmune) thyroiditis. Tiredness, weight gain, dry skin, cold intolerance and irregular periods are typical. This level usually calls for treatment with thyroxine, which is safe and effective; please see your doctor rather than waiting for a repeat.

TLP-133.notes: Pregnancy: trimester-specific upper limits apply (roughly 2.5 mIU/L in the first trimester, 3.0 in the second and third); TSH rises modestly with age, and a level up to 6–7 mIU/L can be acceptable over 70. Non-fasting sample is fine; biotin supplements can falsely lower TSH on some immunoassays.
TLP-133.src: ATA 2014/2017 guidelines; Indian Thyroid Society consensus
TLP-133.retest: Repeat abnormal results in 6–8 weeks before starting treatment; on treatment, recheck 6–8 weeks after any dose change and then annually.

TLP-134.name: FT4
TLP-134.meas: The unbound, biologically available fraction of thyroxine, the main hormone released by the thyroid gland.
TLP-134.sig: FT4 shows how much thyroid hormone is actually available to your tissues, and read together with TSH it tells whether a thyroid problem is mild (subclinical) or established (overt).
TLP-134.ind: Low FT4 with high TSH confirms overt hypothyroidism; low FT4 with a low or normal TSH suggests a pituitary (central) cause. High FT4 with suppressed TSH indicates hyperthyroidism; high FT4 with normal or raised TSH may reflect assay interference, thyroxine over-replacement or, rarely, a pituitary tumour.

fy.lo: A low FT4 means your body is getting less thyroid hormone than it needs. Together with a raised TSH this confirms an under-active thyroid; with a normal or low TSH it points to the pituitary instead. Either way this is a result to discuss with your doctor soon, as treatment is straightforward and restores energy, metabolism and mood.
fy.n: Your free T4 is in the normal range, so the amount of active thyroid hormone reaching your cells is adequate. If your TSH is also normal, your thyroid axis is functioning well. If TSH is mildly off while FT4 is normal, the change is subclinical and your doctor will usually watch rather than treat immediately.
fy.hi: A raised FT4 means your body is exposed to more thyroid hormone than it needs. With a suppressed TSH this is consistent with an over-active thyroid (Graves' disease, a hot nodule or thyroiditis) or too high a thyroxine dose. Palpitations, weight loss, tremor, heat intolerance and anxiety are typical; your doctor may add FT3, TRAb and a thyroid scan.

TLP-134.notes: Reference interval is method-dependent (typically 0.8–1.8 ng/dL on chemiluminescent assays); pregnancy lowers measured FT4 in the second and third trimesters, and heparin, biotin and some anticonvulsants interfere. Multiply by 12.87 for pmol/L.
TLP-134.retest: Repeat with TSH in 6–8 weeks after any thyroxine or anti-thyroid dose change; take the sample before the morning thyroxine tablet.

TLP-135.name: FT3
TLP-135.meas: The unbound fraction of triiodothyronine, the more potent thyroid hormone made partly by the thyroid and mostly by conversion of T4 in the tissues.
TLP-135.sig: FT3 is most useful when hyperthyroidism is suspected, because some over-active glands push out excess T3 before T4 rises (T3-toxicosis); in hypothyroidism it stays normal until late, so it adds little there.
TLP-135.ind: High FT3 with suppressed TSH indicates hyperthyroidism (Graves' disease, toxic nodule, early thyroiditis, or liothyronine intake). Low FT3 is most often the 'sick euthyroid' pattern seen during any serious illness, crash dieting or starvation rather than true thyroid failure.

fy.lo: A low FT3 on its own is most often your body's normal response to another illness, fasting or very low-calorie dieting, which slows T4-to-T3 conversion to save energy. It also occurs in established hypothyroidism. If you are otherwise well, a repeat after recovery usually normalises it; discuss with your doctor if TSH is also abnormal.
fy.n: Your FT3 is in the healthy range, so the most active form of thyroid hormone is being produced and converted properly. Together with a normal TSH and FT4 this confirms a well-balanced thyroid. Adequate selenium, iodine and calories all support this conversion.
fy.hi: A raised FT3 is consistent with an over-active thyroid, and a T3-predominant pattern is typical of Graves' disease or an autonomous nodule. Symptoms include palpitations, weight loss despite good appetite, sweating and anxiety. Your doctor will interpret this with TSH and FT4, and may request TRAb antibodies or an uptake scan to find the cause.

TLP-135.notes: Method-dependent (2.3–4.2 pg/mL is typical for chemiluminescent assays; multiply by 1.536 for pmol/L). Children run slightly higher; acute illness, amiodarone, beta-blockers and steroids lower FT3 without thyroid disease.
TLP-135.src: ATA 2016 hyperthyroidism guideline; manufacturer reference intervals
TLP-135.retest: Repeat with TSH and FT4 in 4–6 weeks if abnormal, or after recovery from an intercurrent illness.

TLP-136.name: Anti-TPO Antibody
TLP-136.alias: Thyroid peroxidase antibody, TPOAb, Anti-microsomal antibody
TLP-136.meas: Antibodies the immune system has made against thyroid peroxidase, an enzyme inside thyroid cells.
TLP-136.sig: Anti-TPO is the best marker of autoimmune thyroid disease; a positive result explains a raised TSH and predicts who with subclinical hypothyroidism will progress, and who is at risk of thyroid problems in pregnancy or after delivery.
TLP-136.ind: Raised levels indicate Hashimoto's thyroiditis (most common), and are also found in Graves' disease and in 10–15% of healthy women, who then carry a higher lifetime risk of hypothyroidism, miscarriage and postpartum thyroiditis. There is no 'low' abnormal.

fy.n: No significant thyroid antibodies were detected, so an autoimmune attack on the thyroid is unlikely at present. If your TSH is normal, your risk of developing hypothyroidism in the next few years is low. A negative result does not need repeating unless thyroid function changes.
fy.bhi: A low-positive antibody level shows some immune activity against the thyroid, which is seen in a minority of healthy people as well as in early Hashimoto's disease. It does not need treatment by itself. Your doctor may check TSH yearly, and more closely in pregnancy or when planning one, because the thyroid may not cope with the extra demand.
fy.hi: A clearly positive anti-TPO is consistent with autoimmune (Hashimoto's) thyroiditis. If your TSH is already raised this explains it and supports starting thyroxine; if TSH is still normal you have roughly a 4% per year chance of becoming hypothyroid, so annual TSH checks are sensible. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning pregnancy, as monitoring is closer then.

TLP-136.notes: Cut-offs are assay-specific (34 IU/mL on Roche, 9 IU/mL on some others); titres fluctuate and do not track disease activity, so serial measurement has little value. Levels can be transiently positive after viral thyroiditis or with interferon and amiodarone therapy.
TLP-136.src: ATA 2017 pregnancy guideline; Endocrine Society; manufacturer cut-off
TLP-136.retest: No routine repeat; recheck only if thyroid function changes, or once before pregnancy if previously borderline.

TLP-137.name: DHEA-S
TLP-137.meas: The sulphated form of DHEA, a weak androgen made almost entirely by the adrenal glands, that circulates in large stable amounts.
TLP-137.sig: DHEA-S is the cleanest read-out of adrenal androgen production: it separates adrenal from ovarian causes of excess hair or acne in women, and its steady decline with age makes it a marker of adrenal reserve in older adults.
TLP-137.ind: High values point to adrenal over-production - PCOS with an adrenal component, non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia, Cushing's or, if very high, an adrenal tumour. Low values are seen in adrenal insufficiency, long-term steroid use, chronic illness and normal ageing.

fy.lo: A low DHEA-S means the adrenal glands are producing less of this androgen than expected for your age. Long-term steroid tablets or inhalers, chronic illness, pituitary under-activity and simple ageing are the usual reasons; true adrenal failure is rare. Your doctor may check a morning cortisol if you feel unusually fatigued or dizzy on standing.
fy.n: Your DHEA-S is within the expected range for your age and sex, which suggests the adrenal glands are contributing a normal share of androgens. In women with acne or excess hair, a normal DHEA-S points away from the adrenals and towards the ovaries as the source. No action is needed; levels fall gently each decade.
fy.bhi: A mildly raised DHEA-S suggests a modest adrenal contribution to androgen excess, most often as part of PCOS, stress-related adrenal activation or non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia. It is not dangerous in itself. Your doctor may pair it with 17-OH progesterone and testosterone, and a repeat morning sample helps confirm it is persistent.
fy.hi: A clearly raised DHEA-S is consistent with significant adrenal androgen over-production. Common causes are non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia and PCOS, but very high levels (several times the upper limit) can indicate an adrenal tumour and need imaging. Please discuss with your doctor promptly, especially if symptoms such as hair growth, acne or voice change came on quickly.

TLP-137.notes: Strongly age-dependent: peaks at 20–30 and falls by about 2% a year, so a 60-year-old's lower limit is roughly half the adult value quoted; paediatric and adrenarche ranges differ entirely. Not affected by time of day or menstrual cycle. Multiply by 0.0271 for µmol/L.
TLP-137.src: Endocrine Society hirsutism guideline 2018; manufacturer age-stratified intervals
TLP-137.retest: Repeat only if raised, ideally with 17-OHP and testosterone in the early-follicular phase; very high values warrant adrenal imaging rather than a repeat.

TLP-138.name: Cortisol:DHEA Ratio
TLP-138.meas: The morning cortisol level divided by the DHEA-S level, both converted to molar units, giving the balance between the adrenal 'stress' hormone and the 'anabolic' adrenal androgen.
TLP-138.sig: Cortisol and DHEA-S are made from the same precursor, and prolonged stress, ageing and chronic illness push production towards cortisol; the ratio is used in wellness and athlete panels as a rough index of chronic stress load and recovery.
TLP-138.ind: A high ratio (cortisol up, DHEA-S down) is associated with chronic stress, over-training, depression, poor sleep, ageing and illness. A low ratio suggests the opposite balance - relative adrenal androgen excess (PCOS, adrenal hyperplasia) or low cortisol output.

fy.blo: A low ratio means your DHEA-S is high relative to cortisol. In younger adults this is common and harmless; in women it can reflect an adrenal contribution to PCOS or hair and acne concerns, and occasionally a low morning cortisol. Look at the two individual results with your doctor rather than the ratio alone.
fy.n: Your cortisol and DHEA-S are in proportion, which suggests the adrenal glands are handling day-to-day stress without tipping into a chronically 'stressed' pattern. Regular sleep, steady training loads and not over-restricting calories keep this balance; the ratio is a wellness indicator, not a diagnostic test.
fy.bhi: A mildly raised ratio shows cortisol running a little ahead of DHEA-S, a pattern often seen with sustained work or training stress, poor sleep, recent illness or normal ageing. It is not a diagnosis. Reviewing sleep, recovery days and caffeine, then repeating an early-morning sample in 2–3 months, is a reasonable next step.
fy.hi: A clearly raised ratio suggests a strong cortisol-dominant pattern: chronic stress, over-training, depression, or an illness that has lowered DHEA-S. Rarely it reflects true cortisol excess. If you have weight gain around the middle, easy bruising, high blood pressure or persistent exhaustion, discuss with your doctor, who may check cortisol more formally.

TLP-138.notes: There is no universally accepted reference range - the ratio is method- and unit-dependent (usually calculated as morning cortisol in nmol/L divided by DHEA-S in µmol/L) and is not validated for diagnosing adrenal disease; TrustLab flags it against its own laboratory-derived interval. Requires a 7–9 am sample; steroid medicines, oral contraceptives and shift work invalidate it.
TLP-138.src: Research literature on cortisol/DHEA-S balance (e.g. Kudielka & Kirschbaum); not a guideline-endorsed test
TLP-138.retest: Repeat after 8–12 weeks of lifestyle change on a rested 8 am sample; interpret with the individual cortisol and DHEA-S results.

TLP-139.name: Testosterone Total
TLP-139.meas: The total amount of testosterone in the blood, including the fractions bound to SHBG and albumin.
TLP-139.sig: In men, total testosterone is the first-line test for hypogonadism - low levels underlie fatigue, low libido, muscle loss and low bone density; in women it is the main screen for androgen excess behind acne, hirsutism and irregular periods (PCOS).
TLP-139.ind: In men, low levels indicate testicular failure (primary) or pituitary under-activity (secondary), obesity, diabetes, opioid or steroid use, or ageing. In women, raised levels point to PCOS or, if markedly high, an ovarian or adrenal tumour; high levels in men usually reflect supplement or steroid use.

fy.lo: A low testosterone suggests your body is producing less of this hormone than it should. In men this is consistent with hypogonadism from the testes or pituitary, worsened by obesity, diabetes, poor sleep and some medicines; in women a low level is rarely significant. Please confirm with a second early-morning sample and discuss LH, FSH and prolactin with your doctor.
fy.blo: A borderline-low testosterone sits in a grey zone where symptoms matter more than the number. Weight gain, sleep apnoea, heavy drinking, stress and chronic illness all pull the level down temporarily. Your doctor will usually repeat the test on another morning and add free testosterone or SHBG before deciding whether treatment is warranted.
fy.n: Your total testosterone is within the expected range for your sex, which supports normal muscle, bone, energy and reproductive function in men, and argues against a significant androgen excess in women. Regular exercise, a healthy weight and 7–8 hours of sleep are the best ways to keep it there.
fy.bhi: A mildly raised testosterone in a woman is most often part of polycystic ovary syndrome, particularly if periods are irregular or there is acne or excess hair. It is not harmful in itself. Your doctor may check SHBG, DHEA-S, 17-OHP and an ovarian ultrasound, and a repeat early in the next cycle helps confirm the finding.
fy.hi: A clearly raised testosterone needs a proper look. In women a level this high goes beyond typical PCOS and your doctor will want to exclude an ovarian or adrenal source, especially if symptoms have appeared quickly. In men it usually reflects testosterone injections, gels or anabolic supplements; please tell your doctor about any such use.

TLP-139.notes: Sample must be drawn between 7 and 10 am (levels fall through the day) and ideally fasting; men over 60 have lower normal levels but the treatment threshold stays at about 300 ng/dL. Immunoassays are unreliable at the low female values, where LC-MS/MS is preferred. Multiply by 0.0347 for nmol/L.
TLP-139.src: Endocrine Society 2018 hypogonadism guideline (harmonised threshold 264–300 ng/dL); Endocrine Society hirsutism guideline 2018
TLP-139.retest: Confirm any low value with a second 8–10 am fasting sample on a different day before labelling hypogonadism; in women, sample in days 3–7 of the cycle.

TLP-140.name: Estradiol
TLP-140.meas: The most potent oestrogen, produced mainly by the ovaries in women and in small amounts from testosterone in men.
TLP-140.sig: In women estradiol reflects ovarian activity across the cycle and confirms menopause when combined with FSH; in men a raised estradiol relative to testosterone contributes to breast enlargement, low libido and fat gain.
TLP-140.ind: Low levels in women indicate menopause, premature ovarian insufficiency, hypothalamic suppression (low weight, over-exercise, stress) or pituitary disease. High levels occur at mid-cycle, in pregnancy, on hormonal treatment or, rarely, with oestrogen-producing tumours. In men high estradiol reflects obesity, liver disease, testosterone therapy or anabolic steroid use.

fy.lo: A low estradiol means the ovaries (or, in men, conversion from testosterone) are producing little oestrogen. In women this is expected after menopause, but before 40 it may signal premature ovarian insufficiency, very low weight, intense training or a pituitary problem. Low oestrogen affects bone density, so discuss FSH, cycle history and bone health with your doctor.
fy.n: Your estradiol is in the expected range for your sex and, in women, for the phase of the cycle sampled. This is consistent with normally functioning ovaries or, in men, a healthy balance between testosterone and oestrogen. Maintaining a healthy weight helps, since fat tissue is a major site of oestrogen production.
fy.bhi: A level in this range in a woman is normal around ovulation, when the leading follicle releases a surge of oestrogen, and is also seen on fertility medicines or hormone therapy. It only needs attention if the sample was taken early in the cycle or you are post-menopausal; in that case your doctor may repeat it with an ultrasound.
fy.hi: A raised estradiol in a man suggests increased conversion of testosterone to oestrogen, commonly from excess body fat, liver disease, testosterone injections or anabolic steroids, and can cause breast tenderness and low libido. In a woman outside mid-cycle or pregnancy, a high level may reflect ovarian cysts, hormone medicines or, rarely, an oestrogen-producing tumour; discuss with your doctor.

TLP-140.notes: Female ranges vary with cycle phase (follicular 20–150, ovulatory 150–400, luteal 40–250 pg/mL) and drop below 20 after menopause; state the cycle day when giving the sample. Standard immunoassays are imprecise below 20 pg/mL, so LC-MS/MS is preferred in men, children and post-menopausal women. Multiply by 3.67 for pmol/L.
TLP-140.retest: Repeat on day 2–4 of the cycle with FSH when assessing ovarian reserve or menopause; in men, repeat with testosterone in the early morning.

TLP-141.name: FSH
TLP-141.meas: The pituitary hormone that drives egg-follicle growth in women and sperm production in men.
TLP-141.sig: FSH rises when the ovaries or testes stop responding, so it is the classic marker of declining ovarian reserve, menopause and testicular failure; a low FSH instead points to a pituitary or hypothalamic cause of infertility or low hormones.
TLP-141.ind: Raised FSH indicates primary gonadal failure - menopause or premature ovarian insufficiency in women, and testicular damage or Klinefelter syndrome in men. Low FSH with low sex hormones suggests hypothalamic-pituitary suppression (stress, low weight, prolactin excess, pituitary disease, anabolic steroid use).

fy.lo: A low FSH suggests the pituitary is sending a weak signal to the ovaries or testes. Stress, very low body weight, heavy exercise, high prolactin, hormonal contraception or testosterone use are common causes; a pituitary problem is less common. Your doctor will read it with LH, sex hormones and prolactin, and may repeat it off hormonal medicines.
fy.n: Your FSH is in the expected range, which suggests the pituitary and the ovaries or testes are communicating normally. In women sampled on day 2–4, this is reassuring about ovarian reserve for the moment; in men it supports normal sperm-producing tissue. No action needed beyond routine follow-up if you are trying to conceive.
fy.bhi: A moderately raised FSH means the pituitary is working harder to stimulate the ovaries or testes. In women this is consistent with reduced ovarian reserve or approaching menopause; in men it suggests some impairment of sperm production. It is not a diagnosis on its own - AMH or a semen analysis adds clarity, and a repeat next cycle confirms the trend.
fy.hi: A clearly raised FSH indicates the ovaries or testes are no longer responding well. In women this is the pattern of menopause, or of premature ovarian insufficiency if you are under 40; in men it points to primary testicular failure. This deserves a proper consultation to discuss bone protection, hormone replacement where appropriate and, if relevant, fertility options.

TLP-141.notes: Female values depend on cycle phase (mid-cycle surge up to 20–25, luteal 1.5–8, post-menopausal 25–130 mIU/mL) - a day 2–4 sample is required for ovarian-reserve interpretation; hormonal contraception suppresses FSH. Prepubertal children have values below 4.
TLP-141.src: ESHRE/ASRM ovarian reserve consensus; Endocrine Society; manufacturer intervals
TLP-141.retest: Repeat on day 2–4 of a subsequent cycle if raised; a single raised value does not confirm ovarian insufficiency - two values over 25 four weeks apart are required.

TLP-142.name: LH
TLP-142.meas: The pituitary hormone that triggers ovulation in women and stimulates testosterone production in men.
TLP-142.sig: LH read together with FSH separates ovarian/testicular problems from pituitary ones, flags the LH-dominant pattern typical of PCOS, and in men explains whether a low testosterone is due to the testes (LH high) or the pituitary (LH low).
TLP-142.ind: Raised LH suggests primary gonadal failure (menopause, ovarian insufficiency, testicular damage) or, in a woman with a normal FSH, PCOS. Low LH indicates hypothalamic-pituitary suppression from stress, weight loss, high prolactin, anabolic steroids or pituitary disease.

fy.lo: A low LH means the pituitary is under-stimulating the ovaries or testes. Common causes are the combined pill or other hormonal treatment, testosterone or anabolic use, significant weight loss, intense training, stress and high prolactin; a pituitary cause is less common. If your sex hormones are also low, your doctor may check other pituitary hormones.
fy.n: Your LH is in the expected range, which supports a normal signal from the pituitary to the ovaries or testes. In women this, together with a normal FSH and LH:FSH ratio, argues against the hormonal pattern of PCOS; in men it means a normal testosterone is being maintained without extra pituitary effort.
fy.bhi: A moderately raised LH in a woman is either the natural mid-cycle surge (if sampled near ovulation) or, on a day 2–4 sample with normal FSH, the LH-dominant pattern often seen in PCOS. In a man it suggests the testes need extra stimulation to maintain testosterone. Your doctor will interpret it with FSH, sex hormones and your cycle history.
fy.hi: A clearly raised LH, especially with a high FSH, indicates that the ovaries or testes are no longer responding normally - the menopausal pattern in women, premature ovarian insufficiency if under 40, or primary testicular failure in men. This is worth a proper consultation to discuss hormone replacement, bone health and, where relevant, fertility options.

TLP-142.notes: Female values vary strongly with cycle phase (mid-cycle surge 14–96, luteal 1–11, post-menopausal 8–60 mIU/mL) - specify cycle day; sample on day 2–4 for PCOS or reserve assessment. Hormonal contraception suppresses LH. Prepubertal children have values under 0.3.
TLP-142.src: Rotterdam/Endocrine Society PCOS guidance; Endocrine Society hypogonadism 2018; manufacturer intervals
TLP-142.retest: Repeat on day 2–4 of the next cycle if raised; in men, repeat with an 8–10 am testosterone.

TLP-143.name: Prolactin
TLP-143.meas: The pituitary hormone responsible for breast milk production, which also suppresses the reproductive hormones when raised.
TLP-143.sig: Excess prolactin is one of the most common treatable causes of irregular periods, infertility, low libido and, in men, low testosterone; it is also the first clue to a benign pituitary tumour (prolactinoma) or to a medication side effect.
TLP-143.ind: Raised prolactin suggests a prolactinoma, antipsychotic or anti-nausea medicines, hypothyroidism, pregnancy or breastfeeding, kidney failure, chest-wall irritation or simple stress at venepuncture. Low prolactin is rarely significant, except after pituitary damage or with dopamine-agonist drugs.

fy.lo: A low prolactin is seldom a health concern. It is most often seen in people taking dopamine-type medicines (for Parkinson's disease or to lower prolactin), and occasionally after pituitary damage, when other pituitary hormones would also be low. If you have no other symptoms, no action is needed; otherwise your doctor may check the rest of the pituitary hormones.
fy.n: Your prolactin is in the normal range, which makes a prolactin-driven cause of irregular periods, infertility, low libido or milky nipple discharge unlikely. It also argues against a common pituitary tumour. Prolactin is sensitive to stress, sleep and food, so a normal rested-morning result is reassuring.
fy.bhi: A mildly raised prolactin is common and usually has a benign explanation: stress or a difficult blood draw, recent exercise, food, breast stimulation, an under-active thyroid, or medicines such as antipsychotics, antidepressants and domperidone. Your doctor may repeat it rested and fasting, check TSH and ask about medicines; a persistent rise may lead to a pituitary MRI.
fy.hi: A prolactin this high is consistent with a prolactinoma, a benign growth of prolactin-producing pituitary cells, particularly if you have missed periods, milky discharge, headaches or vision changes. Certain medicines can also push it this high. This is very treatable, usually with tablets, so please see an endocrinologist rather than waiting; a pituitary MRI is the usual next step.

TLP-143.notes: Pregnancy and breastfeeding raise prolactin to 200 ng/mL or more physiologically. Draw the sample 2–3 hours after waking, rested for 20 minutes, without recent breast examination or intercourse. Very high values on a small tumour can read falsely low (hook effect), and 'macroprolactin' (a harmless large form) can cause a falsely raised result - ask the lab to check if symptoms are absent. Multiply by 21.2 for mIU/L.
TLP-143.src: Endocrine Society 2011 hyperprolactinaemia guideline; Pituitary Society 2023
TLP-143.retest: Repeat a mildly raised result once on a rested, fasting morning sample before imaging; ask for macroprolactin screening if raised without symptoms.

TLP-144.name: CEA
TLP-144.meas: A protein normally made in fetal life that can be re-expressed by some adult cancers, chiefly of the bowel.
TLP-144.sig: CEA is mainly a monitoring test for people already treated for colorectal cancer, where a rising level flags recurrence months before scans; as a screening test in healthy people it is weak, since many benign conditions and smoking raise it and early cancers often do not.
TLP-144.ind: Raised CEA is associated with colorectal, pancreatic, gastric, lung, breast and medullary thyroid cancers, but also with smoking, liver disease, pancreatitis, inflammatory bowel disease, COPD and hypothyroidism. A low or undetectable level has no significance.

fy.n: Your CEA is in the normal range. This is reassuring but does not rule out cancer, because early tumours often release little or no CEA; if you are over 45, the recommended bowel-cancer screen remains a stool blood test or colonoscopy, not this marker. No repeat is needed unless your doctor is monitoring a known condition.
fy.bhi: A mildly raised CEA is most commonly due to smoking, which alone can lift it into this range, or to benign conditions such as fatty liver, chronic bronchitis, pancreatitis or inflammatory bowel disease. It is not a cancer diagnosis. Your doctor may repeat it in 4–6 weeks; a stable or falling level is reassuring, a steady rise prompts further tests.
fy.hi: A clearly raised CEA needs follow-up but is not, by itself, proof of cancer - liver disease, heavy smoking and bowel inflammation can all cause it. Your doctor will ask about bowel habit, bleeding, weight loss or persistent cough, examine you and usually arrange a colonoscopy or imaging. If you have had bowel cancer before, contact your oncologist promptly.

TLP-144.notes: Smokers have a higher upper limit (up to about 5 ng/mL); the assay-specific cut-off varies between 2.5 and 5.0. Not recommended for population screening; its main validated role is post-treatment surveillance of colorectal cancer.
TLP-144.src: ASCO 2006 tumour marker guideline; NCCN colon cancer; EGTM
TLP-144.retest: Repeat in 4–6 weeks if mildly raised; in colorectal cancer follow-up, every 3–6 months for 5 years.

TLP-145.name: CA 19-9
TLP-145.meas: A sugar-protein released by cells lining the pancreas, bile ducts, stomach and bowel.
TLP-145.sig: CA 19-9 is the standard marker for monitoring pancreatic and bile-duct cancer, where the level tracks tumour burden and treatment response; it is not a screening test, because bile-duct blockage of any cause and many benign conditions raise it and 5–10% of people cannot make it at all.
TLP-145.ind: Raised levels are seen in pancreatic, bile duct, gastric and colorectal cancers, but also in gallstones with duct obstruction, jaundice, pancreatitis, cirrhosis, cholangitis, and even in benign ovarian or lung cysts.
