Very high levels (over 1000) are strongly suggestive of malignancy. Low levels have no significance.

fy.n: Your CA 19-9 is in the normal range. This does not fully exclude pancreatic disease - small tumours may not raise it and about one in ten people genetically cannot produce this marker - but it is reassuring in the absence of symptoms. Persistent upper abdominal pain, unexplained weight loss, new diabetes or jaundice should always be assessed regardless of this result.
fy.bhi: A mildly raised CA 19-9 most often reflects a benign cause: gallstones, recent pancreatitis, fatty liver or cirrhosis, thyroid disease, or a chest or urinary infection. Your doctor may check liver tests and an abdominal ultrasound, then repeat the marker in 4–6 weeks; a level that returns to normal once the underlying issue settles needs no further action.
fy.hi: A CA 19-9 in this range needs prompt evaluation. Bile-duct obstruction from gallstones or jaundice can produce very high values, but so can cancers of the pancreas and bile ducts, so your doctor will usually arrange liver tests and imaging (CT or MRCP) within days. Please seek review promptly, especially with pain, jaundice, dark urine or weight loss.

TLP-145.notes: People who are Lewis antigen-negative (about 5–10% of the population) cannot synthesise CA 19-9 and will read low even with cancer. Any degree of cholestasis or jaundice raises it disproportionately. Assay cut-off may be 27–37 U/mL depending on platform.
TLP-145.src: NCCN pancreatic adenocarcinoma; ESMO; EGTM tumour marker recommendations
TLP-145.retest: Repeat after treating any obstruction or infection; in known pancreatic cancer, every 1–3 months during treatment.

TLP-146.name: AFP
TLP-146.meas: A protein produced by the fetal liver and yolk sac that falls to very low levels after birth and re-appears with liver regeneration or certain tumours.
TLP-146.sig: AFP is the main blood marker for primary liver cancer (hepatocellular carcinoma) and for some testicular and ovarian germ-cell tumours; in people with hepatitis B, hepatitis C or cirrhosis, it is used with ultrasound for six-monthly surveillance.
TLP-146.ind: Raised AFP suggests hepatocellular carcinoma or non-seminomatous germ-cell tumours, but modest rises also occur with active hepatitis, cirrhosis and liver regeneration, and in pregnancy. Levels above 200–400 ng/mL in a person with liver disease are highly suggestive of cancer. Low levels have no significance outside pregnancy screening.

fy.n: Your AFP is in the normal range, which makes a liver or germ-cell tumour unlikely at this time. If you carry hepatitis B or C or have cirrhosis, keep up six-monthly AFP and ultrasound surveillance, since up to a third of early liver cancers do not raise AFP. Otherwise no repeat is needed.
fy.bhi: A mildly raised AFP is most often the liver 'regenerating' during active hepatitis (viral, alcohol- or fat-related) rather than cancer, and it is normal in pregnancy. Your doctor will usually check liver enzymes and hepatitis B/C status, arrange an ultrasound if you have known liver disease, and repeat the AFP in 4–8 weeks to see the trend.
fy.hi: A clearly raised AFP needs prompt attention. In someone with hepatitis B, hepatitis C or cirrhosis it raises real concern for liver cancer, and in a young man it may point to a testicular germ-cell tumour; it can still be a flare of hepatitis. Your doctor will arrange liver imaging and, in men, a testicular examination and beta-hCG, without delay.

TLP-146.notes: Physiologically raised throughout pregnancy (maternal serum screening uses MoM, not ng/mL) and in infants under 1 year. Assay cut-offs vary between 7 and 20 ng/mL. For HCC surveillance a rising trend on serial samples matters more than a single value.
TLP-146.retest: Repeat in 4–8 weeks if mildly raised; six-monthly with ultrasound for anyone with cirrhosis or chronic hepatitis B.

TLP-147.name: CA 125 (Female)
TLP-147.meas: A protein shed by the lining cells of the ovary, fallopian tube, peritoneum and pleura.
TLP-147.sig: CA 125 is the standard marker for monitoring epithelial ovarian cancer and for triaging a pelvic mass, especially after menopause; it is not a reliable screen in healthy women, because periods, endometriosis, fibroids and pelvic infection all raise it and half of early ovarian cancers do not.
TLP-147.ind: Raised CA 125 may reflect epithelial ovarian, fallopian tube or endometrial cancer, but far more often endometriosis, fibroids, pelvic inflammatory disease, menstruation, early pregnancy, ovarian cysts, liver disease, heart failure or any cause of fluid in the abdomen or chest. Low values have no significance.

fy.n: Your CA 125 is in the normal range. In a woman without symptoms this is reassuring, though it cannot exclude early ovarian cancer, which often releases little CA 125. Persistent bloating, pelvic pain, feeling full quickly or needing to pass urine often - especially after menopause - should still be checked with a pelvic ultrasound regardless of this result.
fy.bhi: A mildly raised CA 125 is very common in menstruating women and usually reflects a benign cause: your period, endometriosis, fibroids, an ovarian cyst, pelvic infection or early pregnancy. Your doctor may repeat it mid-cycle in 4–6 weeks and arrange a pelvic ultrasound; after menopause even a modest rise is taken more seriously and ultrasound is advised sooner.
fy.hi: A clearly raised CA 125 needs a pelvic ultrasound and specialist review, particularly if you are post-menopausal, where it raises the possibility of ovarian cancer. In younger women severe endometriosis, pelvic infection or a large benign cyst can produce similar levels, as can liver disease or abdominal fluid. Please see your doctor promptly rather than waiting for a repeat.

TLP-147.notes: Female-only parameter. Levels are higher during menstruation and in the first trimester; sample mid-cycle where possible. Post-menopausal women have a lower baseline, so any value above 35 warrants imaging (RMI/ROMA scoring). Also used with HE4 for pelvic-mass triage.
TLP-147.src: NICE CG122 ovarian cancer; ACOG; EGTM
TLP-147.retest: Repeat mid-cycle in 4–6 weeks if mildly raised in a pre-menopausal woman; every 3 months during ovarian cancer follow-up.

TLP-148.name: CA 15-3 (Female)
TLP-148.meas: A fragment of the MUC1 protein shed into the blood by breast duct cells.
TLP-148.sig: CA 15-3 is used to track treatment response and detect recurrence in women already diagnosed with breast cancer; it is normal in most early breast cancers and rises with several benign conditions, so it is not a substitute for mammography as a screening test.
TLP-148.ind: Raised CA 15-3 is associated with advanced or recurrent breast cancer, and less often with ovarian, lung, pancreatic and liver cancers, but also with benign breast disease, hepatitis, cirrhosis, hypothyroidism, sarcoidosis and pregnancy. Low values have no significance.

fy.n: Your CA 15-3 is in the normal range. This is reassuring but does not mean the breasts are free of disease, because early breast cancer rarely raises this marker - a normal result should not replace breast self-awareness and mammography from age 40. If you have had breast cancer, a stable normal value is a good sign.
fy.bhi: A mildly raised CA 15-3 usually has a benign explanation - benign breast lumps, liver disease, an under-active thyroid, pregnancy or a recent chest infection - and is not a cancer diagnosis on its own. Your doctor will examine the breasts, may arrange a mammogram or ultrasound, and repeat the marker in 4–6 weeks to check it is not rising.
fy.hi: A clearly raised CA 15-3 needs proper evaluation, particularly if you have a breast lump, previous breast cancer or bone pain, though it can still reflect liver disease or other benign causes. Your doctor will examine you and typically arrange breast imaging and, depending on findings, further scans. If you are under breast cancer follow-up, contact your oncologist promptly.

TLP-148.notes: Female-only parameter in TrustLab packages. Assay cut-off varies from 25 to 32 U/mL. Not recommended for screening or for diagnosing early breast cancer; its validated use is in monitoring metastatic disease, where a 25% change on serial samples is significant.
TLP-148.src: ASCO 2007 breast cancer tumour marker guideline; EGTM
TLP-148.retest: Repeat in 4–6 weeks if mildly raised; during metastatic breast cancer treatment, at each cycle or every 2–3 months.

TLP-149.name: PSA Total
TLP-149.meas: A protein made by prostate gland cells that leaks into the blood in larger amounts when the gland is enlarged, inflamed or cancerous.
TLP-149.sig: PSA is the only blood test that can flag prostate cancer before symptoms, but it is organ-specific rather than cancer-specific - most raised values in the 4–10 range are benign enlargement or prostatitis, which is why testing is a shared decision for men over 50.
TLP-149.ind: A raised PSA can indicate prostate cancer, but more commonly benign prostatic enlargement, prostatitis, urinary infection or retention, recent ejaculation, cycling or a prostate examination. A very low PSA is not a concern, though 5-alpha-reductase drugs (finasteride, dutasteride) halve the reading.

fy.n: Your PSA is below the conventional action level, which makes a significant prostate cancer unlikely for now. Age matters: a value near the top of this range is more notable at 45 than at 70, and a rising trend on repeat testing is more informative than any single number. Most men repeat PSA every 2–4 years.
fy.bhi: A PSA in the grey zone means roughly one man in four at this level has prostate cancer, while three in four have benign enlargement, prostatitis or a temporary rise from infection, ejaculation or cycling. Your doctor will check the free:total ratio, examine the prostate and may repeat PSA in 6–8 weeks; if still raised, a prostate MRI usually follows.
fy.hi: A PSA above 10 carries a higher likelihood of prostate cancer (around one in two) and should be evaluated without delay, though a large benign prostate or acute prostatitis can also cause it. Your doctor will examine the prostate and usually arrange an MRI and urology referral to discuss whether a biopsy is needed. Outcomes are good when found early.

TLP-149.notes: Age-specific upper limits are widely used: 40–49 years 2.5, 50–59 years 3.5, 60–69 years 4.5, over 70 years 6.5 ng/mL. Avoid ejaculation, vigorous cycling and rectal examination for 48 hours before sampling, and delay testing 6 weeks after a urinary infection. Finasteride/dutasteride halve PSA - double the reading for interpretation.
TLP-149.src: EAU 2024 prostate cancer guideline; AUA 2023 early detection; USPSTF 2018
TLP-149.retest: Repeat a grey-zone value in 6–8 weeks after excluding infection; otherwise every 2–4 years from 50 (45 with family history), stopping around 70–75.

TLP-150.name: PSA Free
TLP-150.meas: The portion of PSA circulating unattached to blood proteins, which is proportionately higher in benign enlargement than in cancer.
TLP-150.sig: Free PSA has no meaning on its own; it is measured so that the free-to-total ratio can be calculated, which helps decide whether a total PSA in the 4–10 grey zone is more likely benign or malignant and can spare men an unnecessary biopsy.
TLP-150.ind: A free PSA that is low relative to total PSA (low ratio) favours prostate cancer; a proportionately high free PSA favours benign prostatic enlargement. The absolute free PSA value is not interpreted against a reference range.

rng.n: Interpreted via free:total ratio (Reported for ratio only)

fy.n: This number is not judged as high or low by itself - it exists to be divided by your total PSA. Please look at the 'PSA Free:Total Ratio' line on this report, where the interpretation sits. A higher proportion of free PSA is the reassuring direction; a low proportion prompts closer assessment. Discuss the ratio with your doctor.

TLP-150.notes: No reference range is applied to free PSA alone; the ratio is only validated when total PSA is 4–10 ng/mL. Free PSA is unstable - the sample should be separated and analysed within 3 hours or frozen, otherwise the fraction falls and the ratio reads falsely low.
TLP-150.retest: Repeat together with total PSA whenever the total is repeated; a free PSA cannot be interpreted from a different day's sample.

TLP-151.name: PSA Free:Total Ratio
TLP-151.meas: Free PSA divided by total PSA, expressed as a percentage.
TLP-151.sig: In men whose total PSA is in the 4–10 grey zone, the free:total ratio roughly separates benign enlargement (high ratio) from cancer (low ratio): below 10% about half of men have cancer, above 25% fewer than one in ten - so it guides whether an MRI or biopsy is needed.
TLP-151.ind: A low ratio (little free PSA) points towards prostate cancer; a high ratio suggests benign prostatic hyperplasia or prostatitis. The ratio is not informative when total PSA is below 4 or above 10 ng/mL, and is lowered by delayed sample processing.

fy.lo: A low free:total ratio means most of your PSA is the bound form, the pattern more often seen with prostate cancer than benign enlargement - roughly half of men with a grey-zone PSA and a ratio this low have cancer. It is not a diagnosis. Your doctor will usually recommend a prostate MRI and urology review to decide about biopsy.
fy.blo: An intermediate ratio does not settle the question either way: benign enlargement and cancer both occur at this level. Your doctor will weigh it with your age, family history, prostate examination, the trend in total PSA and possibly PSA density on ultrasound or MRI. A repeat PSA panel in 6–12 weeks, with prompt sample handling, is often the next step.
fy.n: A high proportion of free PSA is the reassuring pattern - it suggests a raised total PSA is more likely due to benign enlargement or inflammation than cancer, with a cancer probability below about 10%. It does not remove the need for follow-up; your doctor will usually repeat PSA in 6–12 months and review earlier if urinary symptoms change.

TLP-151.notes: Validated only for total PSA between 4 and 10 ng/mL (some use 2.5–10) in men with a normal prostate examination; not used for men on finasteride/dutasteride without adjustment. Cut-offs of 15–25% are used in different guidelines; TrustLab uses 25% as the reassuring threshold and 10% as the high-risk threshold.
TLP-151.src: EAU 2024 prostate cancer guideline; Catalona et al. JAMA 1998
TLP-151.retest: Repeat with total PSA in 6–12 weeks when intermediate, ensuring the sample is processed within 3 hours.

TLP-152.name: Testosterone Free
TLP-152.alias: Calculated free testosterone, cFT, Unbound testosterone
TLP-152.sample: Serum (8–10 am, calculated from total testosterone, SHBG and albumin)
TLP-152.meas: The 1–3% of testosterone that circulates unbound to any protein and is freely available to enter cells.
TLP-152.sig: Free testosterone corrects for SHBG, so it clarifies borderline total testosterone results - it is the test that shows whether an obese, diabetic or older man with a 'low-normal' total is truly androgen-deficient, and whether a woman with a normal total testosterone still has androgen excess because her SHBG is low.
TLP-152.ind: Low free testosterone in men confirms hypogonadism, particularly when SHBG is high (ageing, liver disease, hyperthyroidism, anticonvulsants). Raised free testosterone in women points to PCOS or, if very high, an androgen-secreting tumour; in men it usually reflects supplement or steroid use.

fy.lo: A low free testosterone means the hormone actually available to your tissues is reduced, even if your total testosterone looked acceptable. In men this supports hypogonadism, often driven by weight, diabetes, sleep apnoea, ageing or medicines; in women a low value seldom needs treatment. Your doctor will confirm with a second morning sample and check LH, FSH and prolactin.
fy.blo: A borderline-low free testosterone is common in men over 50 and in those carrying extra weight or sleeping poorly. Whether it matters depends on symptoms - low energy, low libido, reduced morning erections, loss of muscle. Your doctor will usually repeat the test in a few weeks and address weight, sleep and alcohol first, as these can lift the level.
fy.n: Your free testosterone is in the expected range for your sex, which suggests that the amount of active hormone reaching your cells is adequate regardless of what SHBG is doing. In men this argues against androgen deficiency as a cause of tiredness; in women it argues against significant androgen excess. Strength training, healthy weight and good sleep keep it there.
fy.bhi: A mildly raised free testosterone in a woman - often with a normal total testosterone but low SHBG - is the most common laboratory pattern in polycystic ovary syndrome, particularly with insulin resistance or excess weight. It is not dangerous in itself. Your doctor may arrange an ovarian ultrasound and check glucose and insulin; even 5% weight loss lowers it noticeably.
fy.hi: A clearly raised free testosterone in a woman goes beyond the usual PCOS range and your doctor will want to exclude an ovarian or adrenal source, especially if hair growth, acne, voice deepening or missed periods have come on rapidly. In a man a level this high usually reflects testosterone treatment or anabolic supplements. Please discuss with your doctor promptly.

TLP-152.notes: Free testosterone results differ substantially between methods: values here are for calculated free testosterone (Vermeulen) or equilibrium dialysis; direct 'analogue' immunoassays give much lower numbers and are not recommended. Age lowers the male range - about 20% lower over 60. Multiply by 0.1 for ng/dL. Do not interpret in pregnancy or on hormonal contraception.
TLP-152.src: Endocrine Society 2018 hypogonadism guideline (cFT threshold ≈ 65 pg/mL); Vermeulen 1999; Endocrine Society hirsutism 2018
TLP-152.retest: Confirm a low male value with a second 8–10 am fasting sample; in women, sample on cycle day 3–7 off hormonal contraception for 3 months.

TLP-153.name: SHBG
TLP-153.alias: Sex hormone-binding globulin, Testosterone-oestradiol binding globulin
TLP-153.meas: A liver-made carrier protein that binds testosterone and oestradiol tightly, controlling how much of these hormones is free to act.
TLP-153.sig: SHBG is what makes total testosterone misleading: a low SHBG (typical of insulin resistance, obesity and PCOS) frees more testosterone even when the total looks normal, while a high SHBG (ageing, thyroid over-activity, liver disease, oestrogen therapy) can mask a genuine deficiency in men.
TLP-153.ind: Low SHBG is associated with obesity, type 2 diabetes and insulin resistance, PCOS, hypothyroidism, androgen or anabolic steroid use, Cushing's syndrome and nephrotic syndrome. High SHBG occurs with ageing, hyperthyroidism, liver cirrhosis, oestrogen (including the pill and pregnancy), anticonvulsants, anorexia and HIV.

fy.lo: A low SHBG usually signals insulin resistance - it is one of the earliest blood changes with excess weight, pre-diabetes and fatty liver, and in women it is the PCOS pattern that raises free testosterone. It is rarely a disease in itself. Losing weight, cutting refined carbohydrate and building muscle raise SHBG; your doctor may check glucose, HbA1c and thyroid function.
fy.n: Your SHBG is in the normal range, so the free and total testosterone results on this report can be read at face value without correction. A normal SHBG also argues against significant insulin resistance or liver or thyroid disturbance. It rises slowly with age, so a repeat is only needed if hormone results become hard to interpret.
fy.hi: A high SHBG binds more of your testosterone, so total testosterone can look normal while the free, active fraction is low. It is raised by an over-active thyroid, liver disease, low body weight, the pill, pregnancy and some epilepsy medicines. Your doctor will rely on free testosterone and may check TSH and liver tests.

TLP-153.notes: Female range assumes no hormonal contraception or pregnancy, both of which raise SHBG two- to four-fold; prepubertal children have higher values. SHBG rises about 1% per year in men after 40. Fasting is not required.
TLP-153.src: Endocrine Society 2018 hypogonadism guideline; manufacturer CLIA intervals
TLP-153.retest: Repeat only when re-evaluating testosterone; no routine interval.

TLP-154.name: Free Androgen Index
TLP-154.sample: Serum (calculated: total testosterone nmol/L x 100 / SHBG nmol/L)
TLP-154.meas: Total testosterone divided by SHBG, giving a simple estimate of how much testosterone is biologically active.
TLP-154.sig: FAI is the most practical marker of androgen excess in women - it detects the PCOS pattern of normal-total-testosterone with low SHBG that a total testosterone alone misses, and it correlates better with hirsutism and acne than total testosterone does.
TLP-154.ind: A raised FAI in a woman is consistent with PCOS, insulin resistance, non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia or, if very high, an androgen-secreting tumour. In men a low FAI suggests androgen deficiency, but the index is less reliable in men because SHBG is not the dominant binder at male testosterone levels.

fy.lo: A low free androgen index in a man suggests relatively little of your testosterone is free to act, usually because SHBG is high (ageing, thyroid over-activity, liver disease) or because total testosterone itself is low. Whether this matters depends on symptoms. Your doctor will look at calculated free testosterone, which is more reliable in men, on a morning sample.
fy.n: Your free androgen index is in the expected range, which means the balance between testosterone and its carrier protein is healthy. In women this argues against biochemical androgen excess even if you have some acne or hair concerns, which can be skin-level sensitivity rather than high hormones. In men it supports adequate available testosterone.
fy.bhi: A mildly raised FAI in a woman shows a shift towards more active testosterone, most often because SHBG is lowered by insulin resistance or excess weight - the typical laboratory picture in polycystic ovary syndrome. It is a useful early signal. Your doctor may check glucose, insulin and an ovarian ultrasound; modest weight loss brings it down.
fy.hi: A clearly raised FAI is consistent with significant androgen excess. In most women this is PCOS, but a rapid onset of symptoms or a very high value should prompt your doctor to check DHEA-S and 17-OH progesterone and consider imaging to exclude an ovarian or adrenal source. In men a high FAI usually reflects testosterone supplements or anabolic steroids.

TLP-154.notes: Cut-offs vary widely between laboratories (female upper limit 4.5–8, male range 30–150); FAI is unreliable in men, in pregnancy, on hormonal contraception (which raises SHBG and lowers FAI) and when SHBG is very low. Calculated free testosterone is preferred where available. Sample on cycle day 3–7 in women.
TLP-154.src: Rotterdam 2003 / International PCOS Guideline 2023; Endocrine Society hirsutism 2018
TLP-154.retest: Repeat in the early-follicular phase after 3 months off hormonal contraception if borderline; no routine interval otherwise.

TLP-155.name: Bio-available Testosterone
TLP-155.alias: Non-SHBG-bound testosterone, BAT, Free plus albumin-bound testosterone
TLP-155.sample: Serum (8–10 am, calculated from total testosterone, SHBG and albumin)
TLP-155.meas: The free testosterone plus the loosely albumin-bound fraction - together the roughly 30–40% of testosterone that can readily enter tissues.
TLP-155.sig: Bioavailable testosterone is considered the best single reflection of androgen action at the tissue level, particularly in older men and in men with abnormal SHBG, where it separates true deficiency from a total testosterone that merely looks low.
TLP-155.ind: Low bioavailable testosterone in men indicates hypogonadism (testicular or pituitary), or ageing and metabolic disease acting through high SHBG or reduced production. High values in women suggest PCOS or an androgen-secreting tumour; in men they usually reflect exogenous testosterone or anabolic steroids.

fy.lo: A low bioavailable testosterone means the hormone genuinely able to act on muscle, bone, brain and libido is reduced. In men this is the most convincing laboratory support for androgen deficiency, whether from the testes, the pituitary, or age and weight acting through SHBG. Your doctor will confirm on a second morning sample and check LH, FSH and prolactin.
fy.n: Your bioavailable testosterone is in the expected range, which suggests your tissues are receiving an adequate supply of active androgen even if total testosterone or SHBG looked unusual. In men this makes androgen deficiency an unlikely cause of fatigue or low mood; in women it argues against meaningful androgen excess. No action is needed.
fy.bhi: A mildly raised bioavailable testosterone in a woman is common in polycystic ovary syndrome and with insulin resistance, where low SHBG leaves more testosterone available. It is not dangerous but explains acne, oily skin or excess hair. Your doctor may check glucose and insulin and arrange an ovarian ultrasound; weight management and exercise are the most effective first steps.
fy.hi: A clearly raised bioavailable testosterone in a woman warrants a closer look beyond PCOS, particularly with rapidly progressing symptoms - your doctor will check DHEA-S and 17-OHP and may image the ovaries and adrenals. In a man a level this high usually indicates testosterone treatment or anabolic supplements, which can suppress natural production and fertility; please tell your doctor.

TLP-155.notes: No standardised reference interval exists - values depend on the calculation (Vermeulen or Sodergard) or measurement method (ammonium sulphate precipitation) and on the assays used for total testosterone and SHBG; the intervals here apply to calculated bioavailable testosterone and should be read alongside TrustLab's method note. Male values fall with age. Multiply by 0.0347 for nmol/L.
TLP-155.src: Endocrine Society 2018 hypogonadism guideline; Vermeulen 1999; Mayo Clinic reference intervals
TLP-155.retest: Confirm a low value with a second 8–10 am fasting sample on a different day; not needed routinely if total testosterone and SHBG are normal.

TLP-156.name: Androstenedione
TLP-156.sample: Serum (morning; day 3–7 of cycle in women)
TLP-156.meas: A weak androgen made in roughly equal amounts by the adrenal glands and the ovaries or testes, and converted in tissues to testosterone and oestrogen.
TLP-156.sig: Androstenedione picks up about one in ten women with PCOS-type androgen excess whose testosterone is normal, and is a key marker in congenital adrenal hyperplasia, where it tracks treatment control; it is also raised by some adrenal and ovarian tumours.
TLP-156.ind: Raised androstenedione suggests PCOS, non-classic or classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency), Cushing's syndrome, or an androgen-secreting ovarian or adrenal tumour; it is also raised by DHEA supplements. Low values are seen in adrenal insufficiency, ovarian failure and long-term glucocorticoid therapy.

fy.lo: A low androstenedione suggests reduced output from the adrenal glands or gonads. Long-term steroid tablets or inhalers are the most common cause; adrenal insufficiency, ovarian failure and pituitary under-activity are rarer. On its own it is seldom a problem. If you also have fatigue, dizziness or low blood pressure, your doctor may check a morning cortisol and DHEA-S.
fy.n: Your androstenedione is in the expected range, which suggests the adrenal glands and ovaries or testes are producing normal amounts of this precursor hormone. In a woman being assessed for acne, excess hair or irregular periods, a normal androstenedione alongside normal testosterone and DHEA-S makes significant androgen excess unlikely. No action is required.
fy.bhi: A mildly raised androstenedione is most often part of polycystic ovary syndrome, and sometimes reflects non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia, a mild inherited enzyme difference. It is not dangerous in itself. Your doctor will usually pair it with 17-OH progesterone, DHEA-S and testosterone on an early-cycle morning sample, and may arrange an ovarian ultrasound.
fy.hi: A clearly raised androstenedione goes beyond typical PCOS and your doctor will want to identify the source - congenital adrenal hyperplasia is likely if 17-OH progesterone is also high, whereas a very high level with rapid symptom onset needs imaging to exclude an adrenal or ovarian tumour. Please mention any DHEA or bodybuilding supplements, which can also cause this.

TLP-156.notes: Higher in the mid-cycle and luteal phases and lower after menopause; sample on day 3–7, in the morning, off hormonal contraception. Children before adrenarche have much lower values. Immunoassays can cross-react with other steroids; LC-MS/MS is preferred. Multiply by 0.0349 for nmol/L.
TLP-156.src: Endocrine Society 2018 CAH guideline; International PCOS Guideline 2023; manufacturer intervals
TLP-156.retest: Repeat with 17-OHP and DHEA-S on an 8 am, day 3–7 sample if raised; in treated CAH, monitor every 3–6 months.

TLP-157.name: 17-OH Progesterone
TLP-157.sample: Serum (8 am; follicular phase, day 3–7, in women)
TLP-157.meas: A steroid intermediate that builds up when the adrenal enzyme 21-hydroxylase is under-active.
TLP-157.sig: 17-OHP is the screening test for non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia, an inherited condition that mimics PCOS with acne, hirsutism and irregular periods but has different implications for fertility and for a couple's children; every woman being evaluated for androgen excess should have it once.
TLP-157.ind: A raised early-morning follicular 17-OHP suggests non-classic (late-onset) 21-hydroxylase deficiency; values above 1000 ng/dL are essentially diagnostic, 200–1000 need an ACTH stimulation test. Mild rises also occur in the luteal phase, PCOS and with adrenal or ovarian tumours. Low values are not clinically significant.

fy.n: Your 17-OH progesterone is below the screening threshold, which makes non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia very unlikely - provided the sample was taken in the early morning and, for women, in the first week of the cycle. This means any acne, excess hair or irregular periods are more likely explained by PCOS or another cause, and a repeat is not usually needed.
fy.bhi: A 17-OHP in this range is indeterminate: it can reflect non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia, but is also seen in PCOS, after ovulation, or later in the day. Your doctor will usually repeat it at 8 am on day 3–7 of the cycle and, if still raised, arrange a short ACTH stimulation test for a definite answer. This is not urgent.
fy.hi: A 17-OHP this high is consistent with non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia, an inherited enzyme difference that causes the adrenal glands to over-produce androgens. It is manageable, often with low-dose medication, and matters particularly if you are planning pregnancy, as your partner may be offered carrier testing. Please see an endocrinologist; genetic confirmation (CYP21A2) is usually offered.

TLP-157.notes: Levels rise in the luteal phase (up to 285 ng/dL is normal after ovulation) and are highest in the morning, so an 8 am follicular sample is essential; markedly raised throughout pregnancy and in premature newborns. Classic CAH is screened in newborns with different cut-offs. Multiply by 0.0303 for nmol/L.
TLP-157.src: Endocrine Society 2018 congenital adrenal hyperplasia guideline
TLP-157.retest: Repeat an indeterminate result at 8 am on cycle day 3–7; proceed to a 250 µg ACTH stimulation test if it remains 200–1000 ng/dL.

TLP-158.name: Progesterone
TLP-158.alias: Serum progesterone, Mid-luteal progesterone, Day 21 progesterone
TLP-158.sample: Serum (mid-luteal, about 7 days before the expected period)
TLP-158.meas: The hormone released by the corpus luteum after an egg has been released, which prepares the womb lining for pregnancy.
TLP-158.sig: A mid-luteal progesterone is the simplest way to confirm that ovulation has occurred - central to any fertility work-up - and its level indicates whether the luteal phase is strong enough to support implantation.
TLP-158.ind: A low mid-luteal progesterone suggests no ovulation in that cycle (PCOS, thyroid or prolactin disorders, low body weight, perimenopause) or mistimed sampling; an intermediate level suggests ovulation with a weak luteal phase. High levels are normal in pregnancy and on progesterone treatment. In men, progesterone is normally very low and raised values suggest adrenal or testicular tumour or supplement use.

fy.lo: A low progesterone on a mid-luteal sample suggests ovulation did not happen this cycle, or the sample was mistimed - in cycles longer than 28 days, 'day 21' can fall before ovulation. If it recurs, PCOS, thyroid or prolactin problems, stress or low weight are common causes; your doctor may repeat it 7 days before your expected period.
fy.blo: A progesterone in this range shows that ovulation probably occurred but the corpus luteum is producing a modest amount of hormone, or the sample was slightly early or late. This is common and does not by itself prevent pregnancy. Your doctor may repeat the test next cycle, timed 7 days before your expected period, before considering luteal support.
fy.n: For a woman, a progesterone at this level on a mid-luteal sample confirms that you ovulated this cycle and that the luteal phase can support an early pregnancy - a reassuring result in a fertility work-up. For a man, a value in the normal range simply reflects the small amount the adrenal glands and testes produce. No action is needed.
fy.hi: In a man a raised progesterone is unusual and may reflect adrenal enzyme differences, a testicular or adrenal tumour, or progesterone-containing supplements or creams; your doctor will repeat it with other adrenal hormones and examine you. In a woman, a high value usually means pregnancy or progesterone medication and is not a concern - but tell your doctor if neither applies.

TLP-158.notes: Timing is everything: sample 7 days after ovulation (7 days before the next expected period), not fixed 'day 21', in cycles longer than 28 days. Follicular phase values below 1.5 ng/mL are normal. In pregnancy first-trimester levels are 10–44 ng/mL and rise thereafter. Progesterone pessaries or injections make the result uninterpretable. Multiply by 3.18 for nmol/L.
TLP-158.src: NICE CG156 fertility; ASRM 2015 luteal phase; ESHRE
TLP-158.retest: Repeat in the next cycle, timed 7 days before the expected period, if low or intermediate; weekly sampling may be needed in irregular cycles.

TLP-159.name: AMH (Anti-Müllerian Hormone)
TLP-159.meas: A hormone released by the small growing follicles in the ovary, in proportion to how many eggs remain.
TLP-159.sig: AMH is the best single blood marker of ovarian reserve: it predicts how the ovaries will respond to IVF stimulation and roughly how many reproductive years remain, and a very high level supports a diagnosis of PCOS - but it does not predict natural fertility or egg quality.
TLP-159.ind: A low AMH indicates diminished ovarian reserve (age, previous ovarian surgery, chemotherapy, premature ovarian insufficiency, genetic causes) and predicts a poor response to IVF. A high AMH is typical of polycystic ovary syndrome and predicts a strong, sometimes excessive, response to stimulation.

fy.lo: A very low AMH indicates the pool of remaining eggs is small for your age, so the ovaries would respond weakly to IVF stimulation and the reproductive window may be shorter than average. It does not mean you cannot conceive naturally - one good egg a month is enough. If you are planning a family, see a fertility specialist soon.
fy.blo: A low AMH suggests your ovarian reserve is below average for your age. It says little about egg quality or your monthly chance of natural conception, but it predicts fewer eggs from IVF and suggests not delaying if you wish to have children. Your doctor may add an antral follicle count and day-3 FSH, and discuss options including egg freezing.
fy.n: Your AMH is in the normal range for reproductive-age women, which suggests a healthy number of remaining eggs and a typical response to fertility treatment if it is ever needed. AMH declines naturally with age, so a normal result at 25 is different from one at 38. Not smoking is the main modifiable factor that protects ovarian reserve.
fy.bhi: A high AMH means many small follicles are present - the pattern typical of polycystic ovaries, especially if your periods are irregular. It is good news for egg numbers but predicts an exaggerated response to IVF drugs, so clinics use gentler protocols. Your doctor may check LH, FSH, testosterone and an ultrasound; weight management helps restore regular ovulation.
fy.hi: A very high AMH strongly suggests polycystic ovary syndrome and, in IVF, a risk of ovarian hyper-stimulation unless protocols are adjusted - make sure your fertility clinic knows this result. Extremely high values, particularly after menopause or with virilising symptoms, can rarely come from a granulosa cell tumour of the ovary, which your doctor can exclude with an ultrasound.

TLP-159.notes: AMH falls steadily with age (median ≈ 3.0 ng/mL at 25, 1.5 at 35, 0.5 at 42), so the band should be read against age; values on the combined pill or GnRH agonists read 20–30% lower, and vitamin D deficiency lowers it slightly. Assay-dependent (Roche/Beckman automated assays are harmonised; older ELISA differ). Multiply by 7.14 for pmol/L. In men and children AMH has different uses (testicular function, disorders of sex development).
TLP-159.src: ESHRE 2019 ovarian stimulation guideline; International PCOS Guideline 2023 (AMH ≥ 3.5–4 ng/mL supports PCOS); Bologna criteria
TLP-159.retest: No routine repeat - AMH changes slowly; recheck in 12 months when planning fertility treatment or if the first result was on hormonal contraception.

TLP-160.name: LH:FSH Ratio
TLP-160.meas: Luteinising hormone divided by follicle stimulating hormone on an early-cycle sample.
TLP-160.sig: In the early follicular phase LH and FSH are normally roughly equal; a ratio of 2 or more reflects the LH-dominant pituitary drive seen in about half of women with polycystic ovary syndrome, so it supports - though never makes - that diagnosis.
TLP-160.ind: A raised ratio is associated with PCOS, particularly the lean, oligo-ovulatory type. A very low ratio (FSH much higher than LH) points to declining ovarian reserve or menopause. The ratio is uninterpretable at mid-cycle, on hormonal contraception or in men.

fy.n: Your LH and FSH are in normal proportion on this sample, which argues against the LH-dominant pattern of polycystic ovary syndrome. This does not exclude PCOS - about half of women with the condition have a normal ratio - so your doctor will rely more on cycle history, androgen levels and ultrasound. If FSH is much higher, see the FSH interpretation.
fy.bhi: A ratio in this range shows LH running ahead of FSH, a pattern seen in many women with polycystic ovary syndrome, particularly if periods are infrequent. It is a supporting clue rather than a diagnosis, and a sample taken near ovulation can mimic it. Your doctor will interpret it with testosterone, AMH and ultrasound, and may repeat it next cycle.
fy.hi: A markedly raised LH:FSH ratio on a properly timed early-cycle sample is a strong hormonal indicator of polycystic ovary syndrome and often goes with irregular or absent ovulation. PCOS is very manageable. Your doctor will add androgen tests, glucose and insulin, and an ultrasound; weight management and ovulation support restore regular cycles in most women.

TLP-160.notes: Not part of the Rotterdam or 2023 International PCOS diagnostic criteria - it is a supportive marker only. Valid only on a day 2–4 sample in a woman not on hormonal contraception; a mid-cycle LH surge falsely raises the ratio, and it has no established interpretation in men.
TLP-160.retest: Repeat on day 2–4 of a later cycle if the sample timing was uncertain; otherwise no routine repeat.

TLP-161.name: PAPP-A
TLP-161.meas: A protein made by the placenta, reported as a multiple of the median (MoM) for the exact gestational age.
TLP-161.sig: PAPP-A is one half of the first-trimester dual marker test: combined with free beta-hCG, nuchal translucency and maternal age it gives a personal risk figure for Down syndrome and trisomies 18 and 13, and a low level is also an early warning of a placenta that may underperform later.
TLP-161.ind: A low PAPP-A (below 0.4 MoM) is associated with trisomies 21, 18 and 13, and independently with later pre-eclampsia, growth restriction, preterm birth and stillbirth. A high PAPP-A has no adverse association. The value is meaningful only within the combined risk calculation.

fy.lo: A low PAPP-A means the placenta is producing less of this protein than typical for your stage. It nudges the combined screening risk upwards and, independently, marks a somewhat higher chance of pre-eclampsia or a smaller baby later on. Your obstetrician may recommend low-dose aspirin from 12–16 weeks and extra growth scans; please review the combined risk figure together.
fy.n: Your PAPP-A is in the expected range for your gestation, which is reassuring both for the chromosomal screen and for placental function later in pregnancy. Remember that this figure is only one input - the combined risk on your screening report is what your doctor uses to decide whether any further testing (NIPT or a diagnostic test) is needed.

TLP-161.notes: Valid only between 11 and 13+6 weeks with an accurate crown-rump length; MoM is adjusted for maternal weight, ethnicity, smoking, diabetes, IVF conception and multiple pregnancy, so the raw MoM should not be compared between labs. The 0.4 MoM threshold (5th centile) is used for placental risk; the combined risk cut-off for offering further testing is usually 1 in 150–250.
TLP-161.src: Fetal Medicine Foundation combined screening; ACOG Practice Bulletin 226; FOGSI
TLP-161.retest: Not repeated - screening is a one-off calculation; a high-risk result is followed by NIPT or diagnostic testing (CVS/amniocentesis), not a repeat blood test.

TLP-162.name: Free β-hCG
TLP-162.alias: Free beta human chorionic gonadotropin, fβ-hCG
TLP-162.meas: The unattached beta subunit of the pregnancy hormone hCG, reported as a multiple of the median for the exact gestational age.
TLP-162.sig: Free beta-hCG is the second dual-marker analyte: a high level with a low PAPP-A is the classic Down syndrome pattern, while a low level with low PAPP-A points towards trisomy 18 or 13 - together with the nuchal translucency scan the test detects around 90% of Down syndrome pregnancies.
TLP-162.ind: A raised free beta-hCG (above 2.0 MoM) is associated with trisomy 21 and, if very high, with molar or multiple pregnancy. A low free beta-hCG (below 0.5 MoM) is associated with trisomies 18 and 13 and with some later placental complications. Interpretation is only valid within the combined risk.

fy.lo: A low free beta-hCG, especially alongside a low PAPP-A, shifts the screening risk for trisomy 18 or 13 upwards and slightly raises the chance of placental problems later. On its own it does not mean anything is wrong - most pregnancies with this pattern are healthy. Your doctor will read the combined risk with you and may offer NIPT.
fy.n: Your free beta-hCG is in the expected range for your gestation, which is reassuring as part of the combined first-trimester screen. Please read this together with the PAPP-A and the nuchal translucency measurement - the overall risk figure on your screening report, not any single marker, is what guides whether further testing is suggested.
fy.hi: A raised free beta-hCG contributes to a higher combined risk for Down syndrome, particularly when PAPP-A is low, and can also be seen with twins or a molar pregnancy. Many such pregnancies are entirely normal. Your doctor will discuss the overall risk figure and, if it exceeds the cut-off, offer NIPT or a diagnostic test such as CVS.

TLP-162.notes: Valid only between 11 and 13+6 weeks with accurate dating; MoM is adjusted for maternal weight, ethnicity, smoking, diabetes and IVF conception. Free beta-hCG is unstable at room temperature - samples must reach the laboratory promptly. In twins each fetus contributes, so the combined risk uses different algorithms.
TLP-162.src: Fetal Medicine Foundation combined screening; ACOG Practice Bulletin 226
TLP-162.retest: Not repeated - a high-risk combined result is followed by NIPT or diagnostic testing rather than a second blood sample.

TLP-163.name: TSH Receptor Antibody (TRAb)
TLP-163.alias: TRAb, TSI, Thyroid stimulating immunoglobulin, TBII
TLP-163.meas: Antibodies that bind the TSH receptor on thyroid cells and, in Graves' disease, switch the gland permanently 'on'.
TLP-163.sig: TRAb is the specific test for Graves' disease - it tells apart Graves' from other causes of an over-active thyroid without a scan, predicts whether the disease will relapse after tablets, and in pregnancy warns of the risk to the baby's thyroid.
TLP-163.ind: A positive TRAb confirms Graves' disease as the cause of hyperthyroidism (or of thyroid eye disease); the level falls with successful treatment and rising or persistently high values predict relapse. It can also be low-positive in Hashimoto's thyroiditis. There is no 'low' abnormal.

fy.n: No TSH receptor antibodies were detected, which makes Graves' disease an unlikely explanation for an over-active thyroid. If your TSH is suppressed, a hot nodule, a temporary thyroiditis or excess thyroxine are more likely, and your doctor may arrange an uptake scan. If you are being treated for Graves' disease, a negative result is a good sign for stopping tablets.
fy.hi: A positive TRAb is consistent with Graves' disease, an autoimmune condition in which the antibodies drive the thyroid to over-produce hormone. It is very treatable with anti-thyroid tablets, radioiodine or surgery, and the level helps judge when treatment can safely stop. If you are pregnant or planning to be, tell your doctor: high levels need fetal thyroid monitoring.

TLP-163.notes: Cut-off is assay-specific (1.75 IU/L for Roche Elecsys third-generation assay; some kits quote a grey zone of 1.2–1.8). Measure at diagnosis, before stopping anti-thyroid drugs and at 20–24 weeks of pregnancy in any woman with current or past Graves' disease. Values above 5 IU/L (about three times the cut-off) in pregnancy indicate high fetal risk.
TLP-163.src: ATA 2016 hyperthyroidism guideline; ATA 2017 pregnancy guideline; ETA 2018
TLP-163.retest: Repeat after 12–18 months of anti-thyroid treatment before stopping; in pregnancy, at booking and 18–22 weeks if positive.

TLP-164.name: Semen Analysis (WHO 6th Edition, 2021)
TLP-164.alias: Seminogram, Spermogram, Sperm count and motility
TLP-164.sample: Semen (2–7 days abstinence, examined within 1 hour)
TLP-164.meas: The volume, sperm concentration, total count, motility, morphology, vitality and pH of an ejaculate, compared with WHO 6th edition reference limits.
TLP-164.sig: Semen analysis is the cornerstone of the male fertility work-up - a male factor contributes to about half of couples' infertility, and this single test tells whether sperm are being produced, delivered and are able to swim, guiding everything from lifestyle advice to IVF/ICSI.
TLP-164.ind: Abnormal results are described as oligozoospermia (low count), asthenozoospermia (poor motility), teratozoospermia (abnormal shapes), or azoospermia (no sperm), alone or combined. Causes include varicocele, infection, heat, smoking, obesity, hormonal disorders, genetic conditions, blocked ducts, medicines and anabolic steroids. There is no 'too good' result.

rng.n: Volume ≥ 1.4 mL; concentration ≥ 16 million/mL; total ≥ 39 million; progressive motility ≥ 30%; total motility ≥ 42%; normal forms ≥ 4%; vitality ≥ 54% (Within WHO 2021 reference limits)
rng.bhi: Single parameter just below the 5th-centile limit (One parameter mildly below reference)
rng.hi: One or more parameters clearly below reference, or no sperm seen (Abnormal)

fy.n: All the main measures of your semen - count, movement, shape and volume - are at or above the WHO reference limits, so a male factor is unlikely to be the main barrier to conception. These limits describe fertile men, not a guarantee, so if pregnancy has not occurred after a year the female evaluation matters too.
fy.bhi: One measure sits just below the reference limit while the others are normal. Semen quality varies a lot between samples, and a recent fever, short or very long abstinence, heat exposure or stress can pull a single value down; this rarely prevents conception on its own. A repeat in 8–12 weeks (one full sperm production cycle) usually clarifies the picture.
fy.hi: Your sample shows a significant reduction in sperm number, movement or shape, or no sperm at all (azoospermia). This does not mean you cannot father a child, but it needs proper assessment - a repeat sample, hormone tests (FSH, LH, testosterone) and an examination for varicocele or blockage. Many causes are treatable, and ICSI can succeed with very few sperm.

TLP-164.notes: WHO 2021 limits are the 5th centile of recent fathers, not a fertile/infertile cut-off; values below them raise probability of subfertility but do not exclude conception. Requires 2–7 days' abstinence, complete collection, and analysis within 60 minutes; results vary 20–30% between samples, so two samples 4–12 weeks apart are needed before any diagnosis. Azoospermia must be confirmed on a centrifuged pellet.
TLP-164.src: WHO Laboratory Manual for the Examination and Processing of Human Semen, 6th edition (2021); EAU 2024 sexual and reproductive health
TLP-164.retest: Repeat any abnormal result after 8–12 weeks; two abnormal samples are required before treatment decisions.

any.label: Within WHO 2021 reference limits
any.text: Volume ≥ 1.4 mL; concentration ≥ 16 million/mL; total ≥ 39 million; progressive motility ≥ 30%; total motility ≥ 42%; normal forms ≥ 4%; vitality ≥ 54%

any.label: One parameter mildly below reference
any.text: Single parameter just below the 5th-centile limit

any.label: Abnormal
any.text: One or more parameters clearly below reference, or no sperm seen

TLP-165.name: Semen Culture
TLP-165.alias: Semen bacteriology, Seminal fluid culture and sensitivity
TLP-165.meas: Whether bacteria grow from the semen sample, and in what quantity, with antibiotic sensitivities if significant.
TLP-165.sig: Bacterial infection of the prostate, seminal vesicles or epididymis can lower sperm motility, raise white cells and DNA damage, and can be passed to a partner; a culture identifies the organism so that targeted treatment is given rather than blind antibiotics.
TLP-165.ind: Significant growth (usually ≥ 10,000 CFU/mL of a recognised pathogen such as E. coli, Enterococcus, Klebsiella, Staphylococcus aureus or Ureaplasma/Mycoplasma on special media) suggests male accessory gland infection. Low counts of skin or urethral flora usually represent contamination. No growth is normal.

rng.n: No growth, or < 1,000 CFU/mL commensal flora (No significant growth)
rng.bhi: 1,000 – 10,000 CFU/mL or mixed skin flora (Low-count / possible contaminant)
rng.hi: ≥ 10,000 CFU/mL of a single pathogen (Significant growth)

fy.n: No significant bacteria grew from your semen, which makes an infection of the prostate, seminal vesicles or epididymis unlikely as a cause of reduced sperm quality. Note that some organisms, such as Chlamydia and Mycoplasma, do not grow on routine culture and need a separate PCR test if there are symptoms or a raised white-cell count in the semen.
fy.bhi: A small number of bacteria grew, of a type usually found on the skin or at the urethral opening, which most often reflects contamination during collection rather than true infection and generally does not need antibiotics. If your semen also showed many white cells, or you have pain or discharge, your doctor may repeat the culture with careful washing first.
fy.hi: A significant growth of bacteria suggests an infection of the male reproductive tract, which can reduce sperm motility and quality and may affect your partner. The report lists which antibiotics the organism is sensitive to, so your doctor can prescribe a targeted course; your partner may be advised to be tested. Repeat the culture about 3 months after treatment.

TLP-165.notes: No universal CFU threshold - 10,000 CFU/mL of a single pathogen (or 1,000 CFU/mL of Ureaplasma) is commonly used; interpretation should account for the leucocyte count (> 1 million/mL) on the semen analysis. Sexually transmitted organisms (Chlamydia, Neisseria, Mycoplasma genitalium) require PCR, not culture.
TLP-165.src: WHO 2021 semen manual (Chapter 2); EAU 2024 male accessory gland infection
TLP-165.retest: Repeat 3 months after completing antibiotics, or immediately with improved collection technique if contamination is suspected.

any.label: No significant growth
any.text: No growth, or < 1,000 CFU/mL commensal flora

TLP-166.name: Expanded Carrier Screening (500+ gene NGS panel)
TLP-166.alias: ECS, Preconception carrier panel, Recessive gene carrier test
TLP-166.sample: EDTA whole blood (or saliva) - both partners recommended
TLP-166.meas: Whether you silently carry a faulty copy of any of several hundred genes for recessive or X-linked conditions that could affect a child if your partner carries the same one.
TLP-166.sig: Most of us carry two to four recessive gene faults without knowing; when both partners carry the same one, each pregnancy has a 25% chance of an affected child - conditions such as thalassaemia, spinal muscular atrophy and cystic fibrosis. Screening before pregnancy allows informed choices (IVF with embryo testing, prenatal diagnosis) rather than surprises.
TLP-166.ind: A positive (carrier) result means one copy of a disease-causing variant was found - you are healthy but can pass it on; only when both partners carry variants in the same gene is a pregnancy at high risk. A negative result reduces but does not eliminate carrier risk. Variants of uncertain significance are usually not reported or are flagged separately.

rng.bhi: VUS or X-linked/AD finding needing review (Variant of uncertain significance / partner testing advised)
rng.hi: Positive - one or more genes (Carrier (pathogenic variant detected))

fy.n: No disease-causing variants were found in the genes tested, which lowers - but does not fully remove - the chance that you carry one of these conditions, since the test looks for known variants and cannot see every possible change. If your partner is a carrier, your doctor may still discuss the small residual risk.
fy.bhi: A variant of uncertain significance is a gene change whose effect is not yet known - it may be harmless or may later prove disease-causing as evidence accumulates. It is not a carrier result. A genetic counsellor can explain the current evidence, and the laboratory can reclassify it later; in most cases no action is needed for pregnancy planning.
fy.hi: You carry one faulty copy of a gene for a recessive condition. This does not affect your own health - most people screened are carriers of something. What matters is whether your partner carries a variant in the same gene, so partner testing is the next step; a genetic counsellor will explain the risk and options, including IVF with embryo testing.

TLP-166.notes: No reference range - results are qualitative and gene-specific; residual risk after a negative result depends on ethnicity and the detection rate for each gene. Panels differ between laboratories; not all include haemoglobinopathy or SMA copy-number analysis unless stated. Results have implications for blood relatives, and genetic counselling before and after testing is recommended.
TLP-166.src: ACMG 2021 carrier screening practice resource; ACOG Committee Opinion 690/691; ICMR guidelines for genetic testing
TLP-166.retest: No repeat needed - a germline result does not change; reclassification of any VUS may be requested after 2–3 years.

any.label: Variant of uncertain significance / partner testing advised
any.text: VUS or X-linked/AD finding needing review

TLP-167.name: Semen Analysis — Strict Morphology (Kruger)
TLP-167.alias: Kruger strict criteria, Tygerberg morphology, Percent normal forms
TLP-167.meas: The percentage of sperm with a perfectly normal head, mid-piece and tail when judged against strict (Tygerberg) criteria.
TLP-167.sig: Sperm shape correlates with their ability to bind and penetrate the egg; strict morphology was developed in IVF laboratories to predict fertilisation rates, and a very low percentage helps decide between standard IVF and ICSI (injecting a single sperm into the egg).
TLP-167.ind: A low percentage of normal forms (teratozoospermia) is associated with varicocele, heat exposure, smoking, infection, oxidative stress, genetic causes and some medicines, and predicts reduced fertilisation with conventional IVF. There is no 'too high' result.

fy.lo: Fewer than 4% of your sperm have a strictly normal shape - the 'poor prognosis' pattern in Kruger's original IVF studies. Under strict criteria most sperm from every man are classed abnormal, so this does not mean you cannot conceive naturally, but if IVF is planned the laboratory will usually recommend ICSI.
fy.blo: Between 4% and 14% normal forms is the intermediate zone - above the WHO reference limit of 4% but below the level at which standard IVF fertilisation is most reliable. Natural conception is entirely possible. Your fertility team will weigh this with your sperm count and motility; a repeat in 8–12 weeks after addressing heat, smoking and weight often shows improvement.
fy.n: More than 14% of your sperm have a strictly normal shape, which is a good result under these demanding criteria and predicts normal fertilisation in conventional IVF. Morphology varies from sample to sample, so this reflects the current three-month production cycle; keeping cool, not smoking and a balanced diet rich in antioxidants help maintain it.

TLP-167.notes: Kruger's original thresholds (> 14% normal, 4–14% intermediate, < 4% poor) predate WHO 2010/2021, which set the lower reference limit at 4%. Highly observer-dependent - laboratories should report their internal quality control. Requires the same abstinence and timing rules as the routine semen analysis.
TLP-167.src: Kruger et al. 1986/1988 (Tygerberg strict criteria); WHO 2021 semen manual (LRL 4%)
TLP-167.retest: Repeat after 8–12 weeks alongside a full semen analysis; single low values should not drive treatment choice.

TLP-168.name: Anti-sperm Antibody (MAR, direct)
TLP-168.alias: Mixed antiglobulin reaction test, ASA, Sperm-bound IgG/IgA
TLP-168.meas: The percentage of motile sperm that have antibodies (IgG or IgA) stuck to their surface, shown by their binding to coated latex beads.
TLP-168.sig: When the immune system has been exposed to sperm - after vasectomy reversal, testicular injury, infection or surgery - antibodies coat the sperm and make them clump, swim poorly and fail to pass cervical mucus or bind the egg; the MAR test identifies this immunological cause of infertility, which changes treatment towards IUI or ICSI.
TLP-168.ind: 50% or more antibody-bound motile sperm indicates clinically significant immunological infertility; 10–49% is a borderline finding of uncertain impact. Causes include vasectomy reversal, obstruction, torsion, biopsy, trauma, orchitis, varicocele and cryptorchidism. There is no 'low' abnormal.

fy.n: Fewer than 10% of your motile sperm carry antibodies, which is a negative result - an immune reaction against your own sperm is not contributing to fertility problems. If sperm were seen clumping together on the routine analysis, that is more likely due to infection or a high sperm concentration than to antibodies, and no further immunological testing is needed.
fy.bhi: Some of your motile sperm are coated with antibodies, but fewer than half. The significance of this borderline level is uncertain - it may slightly reduce the sperm's ability to swim through cervical mucus, but many men at this level conceive normally. Your doctor may repeat the test in 2–3 months and consider it when planning treatment.
fy.hi: Half or more of your motile sperm are antibody-coated, which is consistent with immunological infertility. The antibodies usually arise after a vasectomy reversal, injury, infection or surgery to the testes, and they impair the sperm's ability to reach and enter the egg. This is very treatable: sperm washing with IUI, or IVF with ICSI, bypasses the problem.

TLP-168.notes: The direct MAR test requires at least 100 motile sperm - it cannot be performed in severe oligo- or asthenozoospermia, when an indirect test on serum or seminal plasma is used. WHO 2021 no longer provides a reference limit; 50% is the long-standing clinical threshold and 10–40% is variously labelled borderline. IgA-bound sperm carry greater clinical weight than IgG.
TLP-168.src: WHO 2021 semen manual; EAU 2024 male infertility guideline; ESHRE
TLP-168.retest: Repeat borderline results after 2–3 months; a positive result is usually confirmed once before treatment planning.

TLP-169.name: Sperm DNA Fragmentation Index (SCD/SCSA)
TLP-169.alias: DFI, Sperm chromatin dispersion test, SCSA, Halo test
TLP-169.meas: The percentage of sperm whose DNA contains breaks, assessed by chromatin dispersion (SCD) or flow-cytometric chromatin structure assay (SCSA).
TLP-169.sig: A sperm can look and swim normally yet carry damaged DNA; high fragmentation is linked with longer time to pregnancy, lower IVF blastocyst rates and roughly a doubled risk of miscarriage, so the DFI adds information the routine semen analysis cannot, especially in recurrent loss and repeated implantation failure.
TLP-169.ind: A raised DFI reflects oxidative stress on sperm from varicocele, smoking, obesity, heat, infection, advanced paternal age, chemotherapy, some medicines and long abstinence. A low DFI is desirable; there is no 'too low'.

fy.n: Fewer than 15% of your sperm show DNA damage, which is a good result and suggests that sperm DNA integrity is not contributing to difficulty conceiving or to pregnancy loss. Keeping this level is helped by not smoking, avoiding heat to the testes (laptops, hot baths, tight clothing), a healthy weight and shorter abstinence before intercourse or sample collection.
fy.bhi: A moderate level of DNA fragmentation may modestly reduce the chance of natural conception and IVF success and slightly increase miscarriage risk, though many men at this level father healthy children. Oxidative stress is the usual driver. Your doctor may look for a varicocele or infection, advise antioxidants, stopping smoking and shorter abstinence, and repeat the test after 3 months.
fy.hi: A high DNA fragmentation index is associated with lower fertilisation and implantation rates and a higher chance of miscarriage, and is a recognised contributor to unexplained infertility and recurrent loss. It is often improvable: treating a varicocele or infection, quitting smoking, weight loss and antioxidants can bring it down over 3 months.

TLP-169.notes: Thresholds are assay-specific: SCSA uses < 15% good, 15–25/30% fair, > 25–30% poor; SCD (Halosperm) commonly uses 30%. Results rise with abstinence beyond 2–3 days and with delays before processing. Not recommended as a routine first-line test; its main indications are recurrent pregnancy loss, repeated IVF failure, varicocele and unexplained infertility.
TLP-169.src: Evenson SCSA thresholds; Agarwal et al. 2020 clinical practice guidelines on SDF; EAU 2024
TLP-169.retest: Repeat after 3 months of lifestyle change or varicocele repair; keep abstinence to 2–3 days for the repeat sample.

TLP-170.name: Y-chromosome Microdeletion (AZFa, AZFb, AZFc)
TLP-170.alias: YCMD, AZF deletion analysis, Yq microdeletion PCR
TLP-170.meas: Whether small segments of the long arm of the Y chromosome that hold the sperm-production genes (AZFa, AZFb, AZFc) are missing.
TLP-170.sig: Y microdeletions are the second commonest genetic cause of severe male infertility, found in about 1 in 12 men with no sperm or fewer than 5 million/mL; the region deleted predicts whether sperm can be found surgically for ICSI, and a deletion is passed on to every son, so the result shapes both treatment and counselling.
TLP-170.ind: An AZFc deletion (most common) causes azoospermia or severe oligozoospermia but sperm can often be retrieved; complete AZFa or AZFb deletions predict no sperm production and make surgical retrieval futile. Partial deletions (e.g. gr/gr) have a milder, variable effect. No deletion is the normal result.

rng.n: AZFa, AZFb and AZFc regions intact (No deletion detected)
rng.bhi: Partial AZFc deletion (Partial deletion (e.g. gr/gr, b2/b3))
rng.hi: Complete AZFa, AZFb or AZFc deletion (Deletion detected)

fy.n: No microdeletion was found in the AZFa, AZFb or AZFc regions of your Y chromosome, so this common genetic cause of very low or absent sperm has been excluded. Other causes - hormonal, obstructive, varicocele, previous infection or a chromosome rearrangement on a karyotype - remain possible, and your fertility specialist will continue to look for them.
fy.bhi: A partial deletion within the AZFc region (such as gr/gr) was found. These are also present in some fertile men and their effect on sperm production is variable and often mild, but they may lower sperm count and can be passed to sons. This does not prevent treatment. A genetic counsellor can explain what is known.
fy.hi: A complete deletion was found in one of the AZF regions. If it is AZFc, sperm can frequently still be found in the testis for ICSI; if it is a complete AZFa or AZFb deletion, sperm retrieval is very unlikely to succeed and donor sperm is the realistic path. Any son would inherit the deletion.

TLP-170.notes: Qualitative test - no reference range; performed by multiplex PCR against the EAA/EMQN standard marker set. Indicated only when sperm concentration is below 5 million/mL or in azoospermia; not useful in men with normal counts. A normal karyotype should be checked alongside. Deletions are inherited by all sons but do not affect daughters.
TLP-170.src: EAA/EMQN 2023 best practice guidelines for Y-chromosomal microdeletion analysis; EAU 2024 male infertility
TLP-170.retest: No repeat - a germline result does not change; confirm laboratory used the EMQN marker set if a result is unexpected.

any.label: No deletion detected
any.text: AZFa, AZFb and AZFc regions intact

any.label: Deletion detected
any.text: Complete AZFa, AZFb or AZFc deletion

TLP-171.name: CFTR Mutation Screen (35 common Indian variants)
TLP-171.alias: Cystic fibrosis mutation panel, CFTR carrier test, CBAVD gene test
TLP-171.meas: Whether any of 35 disease-causing variants most common in Indian populations (including F508del and the 5T/7T/9T poly-T tract) are present in the CFTR gene.
TLP-171.sig: Mild CFTR variants cause absence of the sperm-carrying tubes (congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens) in otherwise healthy men - the cause of about 1–2% of male infertility and most cases of obstructive azoospermia with low semen volume; because the variant can pass to a child, the partner must be tested before ICSI to avoid a baby with cystic fibrosis.
TLP-171.ind: Two variants (or one variant plus the 5T allele) explain CBAVD and carry a risk of cystic fibrosis in offspring if the partner is also a carrier; one variant means carrier status - healthy, but a 1 in 4 risk of an affected child if the partner carries one too. No variant detected reduces but does not exclude carrier status, since only 35 of over 2,000 known variants are tested.

rng.n: Negative for the 35-variant panel (No variant detected)
rng.hi: Compound heterozygous or homozygous (Two variants / variant + 5T)

fy.n: None of the 35 common CFTR variants were found, which makes a CFTR-related cause of infertility unlikely and lowers your chance of being a cystic fibrosis carrier considerably, though not to zero, because rarer variants are not covered. If your semen volume is low and the vas deferens cannot be felt on examination, your doctor may request full CFTR sequencing.
fy.bhi: One CFTR variant was found, which means you are a carrier. This does not affect your own health, but if your partner also carries a CFTR variant there is a 1 in 4 chance of a child with cystic fibrosis - so your partner should be tested before IVF or ICSI.
fy.hi: Two CFTR variants (or a variant plus 5T) were found, which explains an absent vas deferens and blocked sperm delivery. Sperm can almost always be retrieved surgically for ICSI, but your partner must be tested first, because if she also carries a variant, embryos could have cystic fibrosis - embryo testing can then be offered.

TLP-171.notes: Qualitative test; detection rate for the 35-variant Indian panel is roughly 60–70% of CFTR carriers in Indian populations - full gene sequencing is needed to exclude a rare variant in men with CBAVD. Indicated for obstructive azoospermia, semen volume < 1.5 mL with low pH, absent vas on examination, or when a partner is a known carrier.
TLP-171.src: ACMG carrier screening guidance; EAU 2024 male infertility; Indian CFTR variant spectrum studies (Sharma et al.)
TLP-171.retest: No repeat - germline result; request full CFTR sequencing if CBAVD is present and the panel is negative or shows only one variant.

TLP-172.name: NK Cell % (CD56+ CD16+) by flow cytometry
TLP-172.alias: Peripheral NK cells, CD56+ CD16+ lymphocytes, pNK
TLP-172.sample: EDTA whole blood (flow cytometry, analysed within 24 hours)
TLP-172.meas: The proportion of blood lymphocytes that are natural killer cells, identified by their CD56 and CD16 surface markers.
TLP-172.sig: NK cells in the womb lining help the placenta implant; blood NK cell numbers have been studied as a possible marker of an over-active immune response in recurrent miscarriage and repeated IVF failure, though blood and uterine NK cells behave differently and the link remains unproven - this is offered as an investigational test on request.
TLP-172.ind: A raised peripheral NK percentage has been reported in some women with recurrent pregnancy loss and implantation failure, but also occurs with stress, exercise, viral infection, smoking and normal variation. A low percentage is seen after chemotherapy, in some immunodeficiencies and with certain medicines. Neither is diagnostic of a reproductive immune problem.

fy.lo: A low proportion of NK cells is usually of no reproductive significance. It can follow a recent viral illness, chemotherapy or immune-suppressing medicines, and occasionally reflects a rare immune deficiency if you also have frequent or unusual infections. For pregnancy planning it does not indicate a problem; your doctor may simply repeat it if you were unwell at sampling.
fy.n: Your NK cell percentage is within the usual range for healthy adults. Given how uncertain the science is, a normal result mainly means there is no reason to consider immune-modulating treatments, which carry their own risks and are not recommended by major fertility bodies outside research studies. Continue with the established parts of your recurrent-loss work-up.
fy.hi: A raised blood NK cell percentage has been linked in some studies with recurrent miscarriage and implantation failure, but the evidence is inconsistent and blood NK cells do not reliably reflect what happens in the womb. Stress, smoking and infection can raise it. Discuss with your fertility specialist; guidelines advise against immune treatments based on this test alone.

TLP-172.notes: Unvalidated for reproductive use - no consensus cut-off exists (published thresholds range from 12% to 18% of lymphocytes); the interval given is a general adult flow-cytometry reference and TrustLab reports it as investigational. Results vary with time of day, exercise, stress, infection and menstrual phase. Uterine (endometrial biopsy) NK cells are a separate test. ESHRE 2023 and RCOG advise against routine NK testing in recurrent pregnancy loss.
TLP-172.src: ESHRE 2023 recurrent pregnancy loss guideline (recommends against routine use); RCOG Green-top 17; general adult lymphocyte subset reference intervals
TLP-172.retest: If repeated, sample at the same time of day, rested, in the follicular phase and free of infection; a single raised value should not drive treatment.

TLP-173.name: Day 7 Progesterone (window-of-implantation timing)
TLP-173.alias: LH+7 progesterone, Mid-luteal progesterone (timed), Implantation-window progesterone
TLP-173.sample: Serum, 7 days after the LH surge or ovulation trigger (or on the planned transfer day in a medicated cycle)
TLP-173.meas: The progesterone level at the point in the luteal phase when the womb lining is expected to be receptive to an embryo.
TLP-173.sig: Implantation depends on progesterone opening the 'window of implantation' around day 7 after ovulation; a low level at this exact time - whether in a natural cycle or on the day of a frozen embryo transfer - is associated with lower pregnancy and higher miscarriage rates, and in medicated cycles can be corrected by adjusting the progesterone dose.
TLP-173.ind: A low value indicates a weak corpus luteum, mis-timed sampling, no ovulation, or insufficient absorption of vaginal progesterone in a medicated frozen-transfer cycle. An intermediate value suggests ovulation with suboptimal luteal support. Adequate levels support normal receptivity; there is no upper concern except when levels are very high before ovulation (premature luteinisation).

fy.lo: A progesterone this low at the implantation window suggests that ovulation did not occur this cycle, that the sample was mistimed, or - in a medicated frozen-transfer cycle - that your progesterone is not being absorbed well enough. It does not mean future cycles will be the same. Your fertility team may re-time the test, adjust luteal support, or postpone a transfer.
fy.blo: Progesterone in this range shows the luteal phase is active but on the weaker side for the day of implantation. In natural cycles this is common and varies month to month; in a medicated transfer cycle it is the level at which many clinics add extra progesterone before transfer, as studies link it to lower pregnancy rates.
fy.n: Your progesterone at the implantation window is at a level associated with a receptive womb lining and good pregnancy rates, both in natural cycles and on the day of a frozen embryo transfer. No change to timing or luteal support is suggested by this result. If you are using progesterone medication, continue exactly as prescribed - do not stop early.

TLP-173.notes: Unvalidated / investigational add-on: thresholds are drawn from frozen-transfer studies (serum progesterone < 10 ng/mL on transfer day associated with lower live-birth rates; some clinics use 8–12 ng/mL) and from the ≥ 10 ng/mL mid-luteal convention; a single random luteal value varies with pulsatile secretion by up to 8-fold. Timing must be anchored to a documented LH surge, trigger injection or the transfer schedule, not a calendar day. Oral progesterone gives falsely low serum levels relative to effect; vaginal progesterone gives low serum but adequate uterine levels. Multiply by 3.18 for nmol/L.
TLP-173.src: Labarta et al. 2017/2021 (Human Reproduction) progesterone on FET day; ESHRE 2019 luteal phase support; ASRM 2015
TLP-173.retest: Repeat in the next cycle with documented ovulation timing, or 2–3 days after adjusting luteal support in a medicated cycle.

TLP-174.name: CRP
TLP-174.meas: A protein the liver releases into the blood within hours of inflammation, infection or tissue injury anywhere in the body.
TLP-174.sig: CRP rises and falls fast, so it tracks active inflammation in near real time. It tells you that something is inflamed, not where or why, which is why it is read alongside your symptoms and other results.
TLP-174.ind: High values point to bacterial infection, flare of an inflammatory or autoimmune condition, recent injury or surgery, or a chronic low-grade inflammatory state such as obesity. A low or undetectable value is normal and not a concern.

fy.n: No sign of significant active inflammation right now. That is reassuring for infection and for flares of joint or bowel conditions. Regular activity, a healthy weight and not smoking all help keep CRP low over the years.
fy.bhi: Slightly above the usual range, which suggests mild inflammation. A recent cold, a dental problem, a minor injury, being overweight or a poor night's sleep can all do this. If you feel well, a repeat in two to four weeks usually settles the question.
fy.hi: Clearly raised, which suggests active inflammation, most often an infection or a flare of an inflammatory condition. Fever, pain or swelling alongside this result should be discussed with your doctor promptly. Repeat once treated to confirm it has fallen back.

TLP-174.notes: Conventional CRP is for detecting active inflammation; for cardiovascular risk staging the separate hsCRP test (< 1, 1–3, > 3 mg/L) is used. Newborns and pregnancy have different behaviour; values are unaffected by sex.
TLP-174.src: CLSI adult reference interval; NICE / BSR guidance on acute-phase markers
TLP-174.retest: Repeat in 2–4 weeks if mildly raised without symptoms, or 48–72 hours into treatment for infection to confirm response.

TLP-175.name: ESR
TLP-175.meas: How quickly red cells settle in a tube over one hour, which speeds up when inflammatory proteins are present in the blood.
TLP-175.sig: ESR is a slow, indirect marker of inflammation that stays raised for days to weeks after CRP has normalised, so it is useful for chronic conditions such as arthritis, tuberculosis and some blood disorders. It rises naturally with age and in anaemia.
TLP-175.ind: A high ESR suggests chronic infection, autoimmune or inflammatory arthritis, tuberculosis, anaemia, kidney disease or, when very high, conditions such as myeloma or vasculitis. A very low ESR is seen in polycythaemia or sickle-cell disease and is rarely a concern on its own.

fy.n: Your red cells settle at a normal rate, which makes ongoing chronic inflammation unlikely. Together with a normal CRP this is a good sign for joints, gut and general immune health. No action is needed beyond your usual healthy routine.
fy.bhi: Mildly quicker settling than expected. Age, anaemia, being overweight, a recent infection or menstruation can all nudge ESR up without disease. If you have no joint pain, fever or weight loss, a repeat in four to six weeks is a sensible check.
fy.hi: Clearly raised, which suggests a persistent inflammatory process such as an infection, inflammatory arthritis, anaemia or, less commonly, a blood-protein disorder. Your doctor will interpret this with CRP, blood counts and your symptoms, and may order further tests to find the source.

TLP-175.notes: ESR rises with age: a rough upper limit is age/2 for men and (age+10)/2 for women. Pregnancy and anaemia raise ESR independently of inflammation; children typically run < 10 mm/hr.
TLP-175.src: ICSH Westergren method; Miller et al. age-adjusted limits
TLP-175.retest: Repeat after 4–6 weeks if mildly raised and asymptomatic; use it to monitor treatment response in chronic inflammatory conditions.

TLP-176.name: Anti-Thyroglobulin Antibody
TLP-176.profile: ADD-ON · URTICARIA — SECOND-LINE (only if first line negative); THYROID ANTIBODIES
