TLP-176.meas: Antibodies your immune system has made against thyroglobulin, the storage protein inside the thyroid gland.
TLP-176.sig: A marker of autoimmune thyroid disease (Hashimoto's or Graves') and, in chronic urticaria, a clue that hives are driven by an autoimmune process. Also needed to check whether thyroglobulin tumour-marker results are reliable after thyroid cancer.
TLP-176.ind: A positive result is consistent with autoimmune thyroiditis, autoimmune-type chronic urticaria or, occasionally, other autoimmune conditions; around one in ten healthy people carry low levels. There is no meaningful low result.

fy.n: No antibodies against thyroglobulin were detected, so an autoimmune attack on the thyroid is unlikely at present. If your TPO antibody is also negative, autoimmune thyroid disease is an improbable cause of hives, fatigue or hair changes.
fy.bhi: A small amount of antibody is present. This is common, is found in some healthy people, and does not by itself mean your thyroid is failing. Your doctor will look at TSH and TPO antibody together; a repeat in six to twelve months is usually all that is needed.
fy.hi: Clearly positive, which suggests your immune system is reacting against thyroid tissue, as in Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Many people keep normal thyroid function for years, so the practical step is yearly TSH monitoring. In chronic urticaria this pattern supports an autoimmune trigger, which can guide treatment choice.

TLP-176.notes: Cut-offs are strongly method-dependent (Roche < 115, Abbott < 4.1, Siemens < 40 IU/mL); TrustLab's platform cut-off applies. Antibody levels may fall temporarily in pregnancy and rebound after delivery.
TLP-176.src: ATA 2014/2016 thyroid guidelines; EAACI/GA2LEN urticaria guideline 2022
TLP-176.retest: Annual TSH if positive; repeat the antibody itself only if it changes management (e.g. thyroid cancer follow-up).

TLP-177.name: Vitamin D (25-OH)
TLP-177.meas: The circulating storage form of vitamin D, reflecting what you have gained from sunlight, food and supplements over the past few weeks.
TLP-177.sig: Vitamin D controls calcium absorption and bone strength and supports muscle and immune function. Deficiency is extremely common in urban India despite abundant sunshine because of indoor lifestyles, clothing and skin pigmentation.
TLP-177.ind: Low levels point to inadequate sun exposure, malabsorption, obesity, kidney or liver disease, or certain medicines, and contribute to bone pain, muscle weakness and osteoporosis. Very high levels almost always come from over-supplementation and can raise blood calcium.

fy.lo: Your vitamin D stores are depleted, which over time weakens bones, tires muscles and may worsen aches and low mood. Limited midday sun, covered skin, indoor work and higher body weight are the usual reasons. Your doctor can advise a replacement course; recheck after about three months.
fy.blo: Stores are below the level considered ideal for bone and muscle health, a very common finding in Indian adults. Fifteen to twenty minutes of midday sun on bare arms most days, vitamin-D-fortified milk or a modest daily supplement usually corrects it. Recheck in three months.
fy.n: Your vitamin D level is in the sufficient range, supporting healthy bones, muscles and immunity. Keep it there with regular sunlight and adequate dietary calcium; if you rely on a supplement, continue the maintenance dose your doctor suggested.
fy.hi: Higher than the safe range, which almost always reflects taking more supplement than needed. Very high levels can push up blood calcium and cause nausea, thirst and kidney strain. Stop supplements, discuss with your doctor and have calcium and vitamin D rechecked.

TLP-177.notes: To convert to nmol/L multiply by 2.5. Some bone societies accept ≥ 20 ng/mL as adequate for the general population; 30 ng/mL is the Endocrine Society target for those at risk. Pregnancy, breastfeeding and infancy have specific supplementation advice; immunoassays may read differently from LC-MS.
TLP-177.src: Endocrine Society 2011 (Holick et al.); ICMR/ESI India position
TLP-177.retest: Recheck 8–12 weeks after starting replacement; once sufficient, yearly or only if symptoms return.

TLP-178.name: Vitamin B12
TLP-178.meas: The amount of vitamin B12 in your blood, needed for red-cell production, nerve insulation and DNA synthesis.
TLP-178.sig: B12 deficiency is one of the most frequent nutritional problems in India, particularly among vegetarians, and it can damage nerves and memory long before anaemia appears. Catching it early prevents irreversible nerve injury.
TLP-178.ind: Low levels suggest low dietary intake, poor absorption from the stomach or small bowel (pernicious anaemia, metformin, acid-suppressing drugs, bariatric surgery) or heavy alcohol use. High levels usually reflect supplements or injections, and occasionally liver or blood disorders.

fy.lo: Your B12 is low enough to affect nerves and blood formation, showing as tiredness, tingling feet, poor balance, mouth ulcers or memory fog. Vegetarian diets, long-term acid-reducers or metformin, and absorption problems are common causes. Your doctor will usually recommend replacement and check for the underlying reason.
fy.blo: A grey-zone result: some people at this level are truly short of B12 and some are not. If you have numbness, fatigue or a mainly vegetarian diet, your doctor may add homocysteine or methylmalonic acid, or simply treat and recheck in three months.
fy.n: Your B12 is adequate for healthy blood and nerves. If you are vegetarian or over 50, keep an eye on it every year or two, since absorption falls with age and the vitamin is found almost only in animal foods, fortified products and supplements.
fy.hi: Above the usual range, most often because of B12 tablets or injections, which is harmless. If you are not taking any, your doctor may check liver and kidney function and a blood count, as high levels occasionally accompany liver or blood conditions.

TLP-178.notes: Serum B12 can read falsely normal with intrinsic-factor antibodies and falsely low in pregnancy, folate deficiency and on the oral contraceptive pill. Multiply by 0.738 to convert to pmol/L.
TLP-178.src: BSH 2014 guideline on cobalamin and folate disorders; WHO 2008
TLP-178.retest: Recheck about 3 months after starting treatment; in the borderline zone, add methylmalonic acid or homocysteine if symptoms are present.

TLP-179.name: Folate
TLP-179.alias: Folic acid, Serum folate, Vitamin B9
TLP-179.meas: The level of folate, a B vitamin from green vegetables, pulses and fortified grains that cells need to divide and make DNA.
TLP-179.sig: Folate works with B12 to build red cells and keep homocysteine low; deficiency causes anaemia and, in early pregnancy, raises the risk of neural-tube defects in the baby. Serum folate reflects intake over the past few days.
TLP-179.ind: Low folate suggests a diet poor in fresh vegetables and pulses, alcohol excess, malabsorption (coeliac disease), pregnancy demand, or drugs such as methotrexate and some anti-epileptics. High values simply reflect supplements and are not harmful, though they can mask B12 deficiency.

fy.lo: Your folate is low enough to interfere with red-cell production and may explain tiredness, breathlessness or a sore tongue. A diet light on greens and pulses, alcohol, gut malabsorption or certain medicines are typical causes. Your doctor will usually check B12 first, then start folate replacement.
fy.blo: Slightly under the comfortable range, suggesting recent intake has been marginal. More leafy greens, beans, lentils, citrus and fortified cereals for a few weeks usually corrects it. If you are planning pregnancy, a daily folic-acid supplement is advised regardless.
fy.n: Your folate is adequate for healthy blood cells and homocysteine control. Green vegetables, pulses and fortified grains keep it there; women planning a pregnancy should still take the recommended pre-conception folic-acid supplement.
fy.hi: Above the reference range, which almost always reflects a folic-acid supplement or fortified foods and is not harmful in itself. The one caution is that plenty of folate can hide a B12 deficiency, so make sure your B12 result is also adequate.

TLP-179.notes: Serum folate falls within days of poor intake; red-cell folate reflects the past 2–3 months. Pregnancy demand is higher and pre-conception supplementation is recommended irrespective of level. Multiply by 2.27 to convert to nmol/L.
TLP-179.retest: Recheck after 2–3 months of dietary change or supplementation; not needed routinely once normal.

TLP-180.name: Zinc
TLP-180.meas: The concentration of zinc in your blood, a mineral essential for immunity, wound healing, taste, skin and hair growth.
TLP-180.sig: Zinc deficiency is common where diets are cereal-based and low in animal protein, and it shows up as slow wound healing, hair loss, recurrent infections, acne-like rashes and poor growth in children. Serum zinc is an imperfect but practical screen.
TLP-180.ind: Low zinc suggests poor dietary intake, high-phytate vegetarian diets, chronic diarrhoea, liver disease, alcohol excess, or the acute-phase response of infection. High levels are rare and usually mean supplement excess or sample contamination.

fy.lo: Your zinc is low, which can slow wound healing, thin the hair, dull taste and make infections more frequent; in children it can hold back growth. A largely cereal-and-pulse diet, chronic diarrhoea or alcohol are common reasons. Your doctor may suggest a short supplement course and dietary changes.
fy.blo: Marginally low, suggesting your intake is not quite keeping pace. Meat, fish, eggs, dairy, pumpkin seeds and nuts are good sources, and soaking or sprouting pulses improves absorption. A repeat in two to three months, ideally fasting and without recent illness, will show if it has recovered.
fy.n: Your zinc level is adequate for normal immunity, skin and hair. A varied diet with some animal protein or seeds and nuts will keep it there; there is no benefit in taking extra zinc when the level is already normal.
fy.hi: Higher than expected, most often because of zinc supplements or a contaminated collection tube. Long-term excess zinc can lower copper and cause anaemia and nerve symptoms, so pause supplements and discuss a repeat with your doctor.

TLP-180.notes: Serum zinc falls by 10–20% after meals, with infection or inflammation, in pregnancy and on the oral contraceptive; collect fasting in a trace-element tube. Children under 10 have slightly lower cut-offs (< 65 µg/dL indicates deficiency).
TLP-180.retest: Repeat after 8–12 weeks of dietary change or supplementation; retest once inflammation has settled if CRP was raised.

TLP-181.name: Copper
TLP-181.meas: The amount of copper in your blood, most of it bound to the carrier protein ceruloplasmin.
TLP-181.sig: Copper is needed for iron handling, pigment, connective tissue and nerve function; deficiency causes anaemia, hair depigmentation and nerve problems, while excess is a feature of Wilson's disease and inflammation. It is best read together with ceruloplasmin.
TLP-181.ind: Low copper suggests malabsorption, bariatric surgery, excess zinc intake, malnutrition or Wilson's disease (where free copper is actually high). High copper is seen with inflammation, pregnancy, oestrogen use, liver disease and some cancers.

fy.lo: Your copper is low, which can cause anaemia that does not respond to iron, premature greying, brittle hair and numb feet. High-dose zinc supplements, gut surgery or malabsorption are the usual culprits; rarely it reflects Wilson's disease. Your doctor will review ceruloplasmin and your supplements before advising.
fy.blo: Slightly below the reference range, which may simply reflect a low-copper diet or extra zinc. Nuts, seeds, shellfish, whole grains and dark chocolate all supply copper. If ceruloplasmin is also low or you have liver or neurological symptoms, your doctor may look further.
fy.n: Your copper is within range, so a copper-related cause for anaemia, hair or nerve symptoms is unlikely, and there is no sign of the copper overload seen in Wilson's disease. No specific action is needed.
fy.hi: Above the usual range, most often because of inflammation, pregnancy or oestrogen-containing medicines, which raise the carrier protein and with it total copper. Less commonly it points to liver disease. Your doctor will read it alongside ceruloplasmin and CRP before deciding whether anything further is needed.

TLP-181.notes: Serum copper rises in pregnancy (up to 200 µg/dL by the third trimester) and on oral contraceptives; interpret with ceruloplasmin and CRP. Children have slightly higher values. Multiply by 0.157 to convert to µmol/L.
TLP-181.src: Tietz Textbook of Clinical Chemistry; AASLD 2022 Wilson disease guidance
TLP-181.retest: Repeat with ceruloplasmin and CRP if abnormal; recheck 3 months after correcting zinc excess or starting supplementation.

TLP-182.name: RA Factor
TLP-182.meas: An antibody directed against your own IgG antibodies, found in most people with rheumatoid arthritis and in some other conditions.
TLP-182.sig: RF is part of the classification criteria for rheumatoid arthritis and higher levels predict more aggressive joint disease. It is not specific: it also rises with age, chronic infections, hepatitis C and other autoimmune diseases, so it is interpreted with anti-CCP and symptoms.
TLP-182.ind: A positive RF is consistent with rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren's syndrome, cryoglobulinaemia, chronic infection (hepatitis C, tuberculosis, endocarditis) or simply advancing age; strong positives are far more likely to be rheumatoid arthritis. A negative result does not exclude arthritis.

fy.n: Rheumatoid factor was not detected. This makes rheumatoid arthritis less likely, though about one in five people with the condition test negative, so persistent joint swelling or morning stiffness still deserves a doctor's assessment.
fy.bhi: A low level of rheumatoid factor is present. This is found in a few percent of healthy people, more often with age, and after infections. If you have swollen or stiff joints your doctor may add anti-CCP and inflammatory markers; if you feel well, a repeat in a few months is reasonable.
fy.hi: A strong rheumatoid factor result, which is more likely to reflect rheumatoid arthritis or a related autoimmune condition, especially if joints are painful or swollen. Early treatment protects joints, so a rheumatologist review with anti-CCP, CRP and joint examination is the sensible next step.

TLP-182.notes: Cut-off is method-dependent (nephelometry commonly < 14 or < 20 IU/mL); ACR/EULAR define low positive as up to 3 times the upper limit and high positive above that. Positivity rises with age and after recent viral infection.
TLP-182.retest: Repeat with anti-CCP after 3–6 months if low positive and symptoms are unclear; not needed serially once diagnosis is established.

TLP-183.name: ASO
TLP-183.meas: Antibodies against streptolysin O, a toxin made by group A streptococcus, showing a recent or past throat or skin infection with that bacterium.
TLP-183.sig: ASO helps decide whether joint pain, fever, heart murmur or kidney inflammation could be a delayed reaction to a recent strep infection, as in rheumatic fever or post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. It rises one to three weeks after infection and can stay up for months.
TLP-183.ind: A raised titre points to a group A streptococcal infection in the past several weeks to months and supports rheumatic fever or reactive arthritis in the right setting. A normal titre does not exclude it, particularly early or after skin infections, where anti-DNase B is more reliable.

fy.n: No evidence of a recent streptococcal infection. If you have joint pain, this makes a post-strep cause such as rheumatic fever unlikely, and your doctor will look at other explanations. Nothing further is needed for this test.
fy.bhi: Mildly raised, which can follow an ordinary sore throat in the past few months and is common in school-age children and their parents. It does not mean active infection. If joint pain, fever or a new murmur is present, a repeat in two weeks to see whether the level is rising helps clarify.
fy.hi: Clearly raised, indicating a recent group A streptococcal infection. If you also have migrating joint pains, fever, a rash or breathlessness, your doctor will assess for rheumatic fever and may check the heart. Without symptoms, the level simply reflects a past infection and will fall over months.

TLP-183.notes: Upper limit is about 200 IU/mL in adults but up to 400 IU/mL in school-age children (5–15 years), in whom repeated exposure is common. Titre peaks 3–5 weeks after infection; paired samples 2 weeks apart showing a rise are more informative than a single value.
TLP-183.src: AHA 2015 Jones criteria revision; WHO rheumatic fever guidance
TLP-183.retest: Repeat in 2 weeks if rheumatic fever is suspected to demonstrate a rising titre; consider anti-DNase B if ASO is normal but suspicion remains.

TLP-184.name: Anti-CCP
TLP-184.alias: ACPA, Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide, CCP antibody
TLP-184.meas: Antibodies against citrullinated proteins, which are highly specific for rheumatoid arthritis and can appear years before joints become painful.
TLP-184.sig: Anti-CCP is the most specific blood test for rheumatoid arthritis (about 95%) and a positive result predicts more erosive disease, guiding earlier and more intensive treatment. It is far less affected by age, infection and other autoimmune diseases than rheumatoid factor.
TLP-184.ind: A positive anti-CCP is strongly consistent with rheumatoid arthritis, present or future; it is occasionally seen in psoriatic arthritis, tuberculosis or interstitial lung disease. A negative result lowers but does not remove the possibility, since about a third of patients are seronegative.

fy.n: Anti-CCP was not detected, which makes rheumatoid arthritis considerably less likely and, if it were present, points to a milder form. Ongoing joint swelling or prolonged morning stiffness still warrants a doctor's examination, as some people with rheumatoid arthritis are antibody-negative.
fy.bhi: A low positive result. Because this antibody is so specific, even a modest level raises the chance of rheumatoid arthritis, particularly with joint symptoms or a positive rheumatoid factor. A rheumatology review is worthwhile; if you have no symptoms, your doctor may repeat it in three to six months.
fy.hi: A strong positive result, which is highly consistent with rheumatoid arthritis, present now or likely to develop. This antibody pattern also predicts more joint damage if untreated, so early specialist assessment and, if confirmed, prompt treatment protects your joints for the long term. Not smoking helps too.

TLP-184.notes: Second-generation ELISA cut-off is typically 20 U/mL, but some platforms use 5 or 17 U/mL; low positive is defined as up to 3 times the upper limit. Smoking increases positivity and titre.
TLP-184.src: ACR/EULAR 2010 classification criteria; EULAR 2016 early arthritis recommendations
TLP-184.retest: Repeat in 3–6 months if low positive and symptoms uncertain; not needed for monitoring once diagnosed.

TLP-185.name: ANA
TLP-185.alias: Antinuclear antibody, ANA by IFA, ANA HEp-2
TLP-185.meas: Antibodies that react against the nucleus of your own cells, reported as a dilution titre and a staining pattern under the microscope.
TLP-185.sig: ANA is the entry test for connective-tissue diseases such as lupus, Sjögren's, scleroderma and myositis; a negative result makes lupus very unlikely. The titre and pattern determine whether more specific antibody tests (ENA, dsDNA) are needed.
TLP-185.ind: A positive ANA is consistent with lupus, Sjögren's syndrome, systemic sclerosis, mixed connective-tissue disease, autoimmune hepatitis or drug-induced lupus, but low titres occur in up to 15% of healthy people, especially women and the elderly. A negative result argues strongly against lupus.

fy.n: No antinuclear antibodies were found, which makes lupus and most connective-tissue diseases unlikely as a cause of your symptoms. A small number of conditions can still be ANA-negative, so persistent rashes, joint swelling or dry eyes should still be discussed with your doctor.
fy.bhi: A weak positive at the lowest reported dilution. This is common in healthy people, particularly women, and after infections, and usually has no consequence. Whether it matters depends on your symptoms; your doctor may check a specific antibody panel or simply repeat the test in six to twelve months.
fy.hi: A clearly positive result, meaning your immune system is producing antibodies against cell nuclei. This does not diagnose a disease on its own; the pattern reported alongside points to which specific tests come next (ENA, dsDNA, complement). A rheumatologist review is appropriate, especially with joint pain, rash, mouth ulcers or fatigue.

TLP-185.notes: Screening dilution 1:80 on HEp-2 cells per ACR/ICAP; the staining pattern (homogeneous, speckled, nucleolar, centromere) is reported and guides follow-up. Titres up to 1:160 are found in some healthy older adults. ELISA/CLIA screening assays report index values rather than titres.
TLP-185.src: ACR/EULAR 2019 SLE classification criteria (ANA ≥ 1:80 entry criterion); ICAP consensus
TLP-185.retest: Repeat only if symptoms evolve; a positive screen is followed by ENA, anti-dsDNA and complement rather than by repeating the ANA.

TLP-186.name: Immunoglobulins (IgG)
TLP-186.alias: Immunoglobulin G, Serum IgG, Total IgG
TLP-186.meas: The total amount of IgG, the most abundant antibody class, which provides lasting immunity after infections and vaccines.
TLP-186.sig: IgG level is the backbone of an immune-deficiency work-up when infections are frequent, and a raised level flags chronic infection, liver disease or autoimmune activity. Very high values may signal a plasma-cell disorder and lead on to electrophoresis.
TLP-186.ind: Low IgG suggests a primary antibody deficiency, protein loss through kidneys or gut, or the effect of steroids, immunosuppressants or lymphoma. High IgG is seen with chronic infections, autoimmune disease, chronic liver disease, HIV and monoclonal disorders such as myeloma.

fy.lo: Your IgG is markedly low, which reduces your protection against chest and sinus infections. Causes range from inherited antibody deficiency to protein loss from the kidneys or gut, or medicines that suppress immunity. An immunology review is important, as replacement antibody therapy can prevent lung damage.
fy.blo: Mildly below the reference range. This can follow steroid or immunosuppressant use, viral illness or protein loss, and is often harmless. If you get more than the usual number of infections, your doctor may check vaccine antibody responses and IgG subclasses; otherwise a repeat in three months is sensible.
fy.n: Your IgG is within range, indicating a normal ability to make and keep long-term antibodies. This makes a significant antibody deficiency unlikely as a cause of recurrent infections and shows no sign of excess antibody production.
fy.hi: Raised IgG, which usually reflects your immune system working hard against a long-standing infection, autoimmune condition or chronic liver disease. Occasionally it comes from a single clone of cells, so your doctor may request protein electrophoresis to check whether the increase is broad-based or from one source.

TLP-186.notes: Children have age-specific ranges (lower in infancy, rising to adult by about 6 years). Multiply by 0.01 to convert to g/L. Falls with high-dose steroids and rituximab; rises in pregnancy-associated liver disease.
TLP-186.src: CLSI adult reference intervals (nephelometry); ESID primary immunodeficiency criteria
TLP-186.retest: Repeat in 3 months if borderline; if raised, follow with serum protein electrophoresis.

TLP-187.name: Immunoglobulins (IgA)
TLP-187.alias: Immunoglobulin A, Serum IgA, Total IgA
TLP-187.meas: The amount of IgA, the antibody that guards the lining of the gut, airways and other mucous surfaces.
TLP-187.sig: Selective IgA deficiency is the commonest inherited immune deficiency and it makes coeliac antibody tests (which are IgA-based) falsely negative, so total IgA must be known to interpret them. Raised IgA points to gut, liver or kidney (IgA nephropathy) conditions.
TLP-187.ind: Low IgA suggests selective IgA deficiency or a broader antibody deficiency, and is linked with recurrent sinus and chest infections, coeliac disease and autoimmunity. High IgA is seen in chronic liver disease, especially alcohol-related, chronic infections, IgA nephropathy and IgA myeloma.

fy.lo: Your IgA is almost absent, a pattern called selective IgA deficiency that affects about one in 500 people. Many stay perfectly well; some have more sinus or chest infections, allergies or coeliac disease. Importantly, coeliac antibody tests need an IgG-based version for you, and you should mention this before blood transfusions.
fy.blo: IgA is below the usual range but not absent. This partial deficiency is often harmless and may be transient after illness or with some medicines. Because it can weaken coeliac antibody screening, your doctor may use IgG-based coeliac tests, and a repeat in a few months will show whether it persists.
fy.n: Your IgA is within range, so your mucosal defences are intact and the IgA-based coeliac antibody results on this report can be trusted. No action is needed for this test.
fy.hi: Raised IgA, most commonly a response to ongoing gut or airway infection, or to liver strain, particularly from alcohol. Occasionally it accompanies IgA nephropathy or a plasma-cell disorder, so your doctor may review liver tests, urine protein and, if the rise is large, protein electrophoresis.

TLP-187.notes: Selective IgA deficiency is defined as < 7 mg/dL in a person over 4 years with normal IgG and IgM. Children have lower age-specific ranges, reaching adult levels in the teens. Multiply by 0.01 to convert to g/L.
TLP-187.src: ESID 2019 diagnostic criteria; CLSI adult reference intervals
TLP-187.retest: Confirm deficiency on a repeat sample; if low, request IgG-based tTG/DGP for coeliac screening.

TLP-188.name: Immunoglobulins (IgM)
TLP-188.alias: Immunoglobulin M, Serum IgM, Total IgM
TLP-188.meas: The amount of IgM, the large antibody your body makes first when it meets a new infection.
TLP-188.sig: IgM completes the immunoglobulin picture: low levels contribute to a diagnosis of antibody deficiency, while a marked rise raises the question of a chronic infection or a plasma-cell disorder such as Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia.
TLP-188.ind: Low IgM suggests common variable immunodeficiency, protein loss, lymphoma or the effect of immunosuppressive drugs. High IgM is found in acute and chronic infections, primary biliary cholangitis, hyper-IgM syndrome and Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia.

fy.lo: Your IgM is below the reference range. On its own this is often not significant, especially if IgG and IgA are normal, but combined with low IgG it can indicate an antibody deficiency. Immunosuppressant medicines and protein loss are other causes. Your doctor will decide whether an immunology assessment is needed.
fy.n: Your IgM is within range, meaning your first-line antibody response is intact. Together with normal IgG and IgA, this makes an inherited antibody deficiency very unlikely and shows no sign of an abnormal antibody-producing clone.
fy.hi: Raised IgM, which most often means your immune system is responding to a recent or ongoing infection. Persistent or marked elevation can occasionally come from liver disease or from a single antibody-producing clone, so your doctor may add protein electrophoresis and a blood count, and repeat the test in a few months.

TLP-188.notes: Women tend to run slightly higher IgM than men; children have age-specific ranges. Multiply by 0.01 to convert to g/L. Very high IgM can make blood viscous, which is why large rises prompt electrophoresis.
TLP-188.retest: Repeat in 3 months if abnormal; add serum protein electrophoresis if markedly raised.

TLP-189.name: Ceruloplasmin
TLP-189.meas: The liver-made protein that carries most of the copper in your blood and helps move iron around the body.
TLP-189.sig: A low ceruloplasmin is the key screening clue for Wilson's disease, an inherited copper-overload disorder that damages the liver and brain but is treatable if caught early. It is also an acute-phase protein, so inflammation and oestrogens push it up.
TLP-189.ind: Low levels point to Wilson's disease, severe copper deficiency, protein-losing states, liver failure or the rare inherited aceruloplasminaemia. High levels are non-specific and reflect inflammation, pregnancy, oestrogen therapy, liver disease or cancer.

fy.lo: Your ceruloplasmin is markedly low. This is a recognised pointer to Wilson's disease, especially in younger people with unexplained liver test changes, tremor or mood symptoms, although severe copper deficiency and heavy protein loss can also cause it. Your doctor will usually arrange serum copper, 24-hour urine copper and an eye examination.
fy.blo: Mildly below the reference range, a grey zone found in some healthy people, in copper-poor diets and in around one in five carriers of a Wilson's gene. If liver tests or neurological symptoms are abnormal, further copper studies are worthwhile; otherwise a repeat with serum copper is a reasonable next step.
fy.n: Your ceruloplasmin is within range, which makes Wilson's disease unlikely and suggests your copper transport is working normally. If serum copper is also normal, no further copper studies are needed.
fy.hi: Above the usual range, which nearly always reflects inflammation, pregnancy, oestrogen-containing medicines or liver irritation rather than a copper problem. It is rarely important on its own; your doctor will read it alongside CRP and liver tests, and it does not need specific treatment.

TLP-189.notes: Normal ceruloplasmin does not fully exclude Wilson's disease (5–10% of cases), and oestrogen or inflammation can mask a low value. Infants under 6 months have physiologically low levels; pregnancy roughly doubles it. Multiply by 10 to convert to mg/L.
TLP-189.src: AASLD 2022 Wilson disease practice guidance; EASL 2012
TLP-189.retest: If low, follow with serum copper, 24-hour urinary copper and slit-lamp examination; repeat when inflammation settles if borderline.

TLP-190.name: C3
TLP-190.meas: The level of C3, the central protein of the complement system, a cascade of blood proteins that helps antibodies clear infections and immune complexes.
TLP-190.sig: In lupus and related diseases, complement is consumed during flares, so a falling C3 signals active disease, especially kidney involvement, and a recovering C3 shows treatment is working. It is an activity marker rather than a diagnostic test.
TLP-190.ind: Low C3 suggests active lupus (especially nephritis), post-infectious or membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, cryoglobulinaemia, severe liver disease or an inherited deficiency. High C3 is an acute-phase response to infection or inflammation and has little diagnostic weight.

fy.lo: Your C3 is low, which suggests complement proteins are being used up, as happens during an active lupus flare, some kidney inflammations or certain infections. If C4 and anti-dsDNA are also abnormal, this pattern points to active disease. Your doctor will usually check urine for protein and blood, and review your treatment.
fy.n: Your C3 is within range, which is reassuring: it argues against active complement-consuming disease such as a lupus flare or immune-complex kidney inflammation at this time. In someone with known lupus, a stable normal C3 is one of the markers of good control.
fy.hi: A raised C3 usually just means your body is mounting a general inflammatory response, for example to an infection, injury or an inflammatory condition. It is not a marker of complement disease and does not need treatment on its own; your doctor will look at CRP and your symptoms.

TLP-190.notes: Reference intervals vary slightly by platform (roughly 80–90 to 160–180 mg/dL); interpret trends against the same laboratory. Newborns have lower values. Complement is heat-labile, so delayed sample handling can falsely lower results.
TLP-190.src: ACR/EULAR 2019 SLE classification criteria; CLSI adult reference intervals
TLP-190.retest: Repeat every 3–6 months in lupus, or sooner during a suspected flare, together with C4, anti-dsDNA and urinalysis.

TLP-191.name: C4
TLP-191.meas: The level of C4, an early component of the classical complement pathway that is consumed when antibodies bind their targets.
TLP-191.sig: C4 is the more sensitive of the two complements for immune-complex diseases: it tends to fall earlier than C3 in lupus flares and is characteristically low in hereditary angioedema and cryoglobulinaemia. Some people are born with partially absent C4 genes, which lowers baseline values.
TLP-191.ind: Low C4 points to active lupus, hereditary or acquired angioedema, cryoglobulinaemia, immune-complex vasculitis or inherited C4 gene deficiency. High C4 is a mild acute-phase response and rarely significant.

fy.lo: Your C4 is low, meaning the classical complement pathway is being activated or is genetically reduced. In lupus this suggests active disease; with recurrent swelling attacks it raises the question of hereditary angioedema; with a purpuric rash it can point to cryoglobulins. Your doctor will match it to your symptoms and to C3.
fy.n: Your C4 is within range. This argues against an active immune-complex process and against most forms of hereditary angioedema (where C4 is almost always low during and between attacks). In known lupus, normal C4 alongside normal C3 supports quiet disease.
fy.hi: A mildly raised C4 is a common, non-specific finding during inflammation or infection and has no particular disease association. It does not need treatment or follow-up in its own right; your doctor will interpret it alongside CRP and your symptoms.

TLP-191.notes: Platform ranges vary (roughly 10–16 to 40–45 mg/dL). Inherited C4A or C4B null alleles are common and cause persistently low-normal C4 without disease. A normal C4 during an angioedema attack makes hereditary angioedema very unlikely.
TLP-191.src: ACR/EULAR 2019 SLE classification criteria; WAO/EAACI HAE guideline 2021
TLP-191.retest: Repeat with C3 and anti-dsDNA every 3–6 months in lupus or at any flare; in angioedema, recheck with C1-inhibitor studies.

TLP-192.name: Immunoglobulins (IgE)
TLP-192.meas: The total amount of IgE, the antibody class behind allergic reactions, asthma, eczema and defence against parasites.
TLP-192.sig: A raised total IgE supports an allergic (atopic) tendency in eczema, asthma, rhinitis or hives, and very high levels prompt a look for parasitic infection or rarer immune conditions. A normal level does not rule out allergy to a specific substance.
TLP-192.ind: High IgE is consistent with atopic eczema, allergic asthma or rhinitis, parasitic worm infection, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, or rare hyper-IgE syndromes. A low or undetectable IgE is normal and only occasionally hints at a broader antibody deficiency.

fy.n: Your total IgE is in the normal range, so a strong allergic constitution is less likely. You can still be allergic to individual things (foods, dust mite, pollen) with a normal total, so if symptoms suggest a trigger, specific IgE testing is the more useful next step.
fy.bhi: Mildly raised, which suggests some allergic tendency, common in people with hay fever, mild eczema or a family history of allergy. It does not identify what you react to. If symptoms are troublesome, your doctor may test specific IgE to likely triggers or refer for skin-prick testing.
fy.hi: Clearly raised, consistent with a significant allergic tendency such as atopic eczema, asthma or allergic rhinitis, or with a parasitic gut infection, which is common in India. Your doctor may check stool for parasites, an eosinophil count and specific IgE, and will use the level as one guide to treatment choice in eczema and urticaria.

TLP-192.notes: Age-specific: infants < 15, children under 10 about < 50–90, adults < 100 IU/mL. Smokers and some healthy adults run higher; levels do not correlate with allergy severity. In chronic urticaria a raised IgE predicts response to omalizumab.
TLP-192.src: EAACI allergy diagnosis position papers; CLSI adult reference intervals
TLP-192.retest: Not usually repeated; move to specific IgE or skin testing when a trigger is suspected. Recheck after treating parasites if very high.

TLP-193.name: Anti-tTG IgA (tissue transglutaminase)
TLP-193.alias: Tissue transglutaminase IgA, tTG-IgA, Coeliac antibody
TLP-193.meas: IgA antibodies against tissue transglutaminase, the gut enzyme targeted by the immune system in coeliac disease.
TLP-193.sig: This is the first-line blood test for coeliac disease, with sensitivity and specificity both above 95% while you are still eating gluten. Very high levels (over ten times the cut-off) can allow diagnosis without biopsy in children; it is only reliable if your total IgA is normal.
TLP-193.ind: A positive result is consistent with coeliac disease, an immune reaction to gluten that damages the small bowel and causes diarrhoea, bloating, anaemia, osteoporosis or fatigue; occasional low positives occur in type 1 diabetes, autoimmune liver disease or IgA nephropathy. A negative result while on gluten makes coeliac disease unlikely.

fy.n: No coeliac antibodies were found. Provided you were eating gluten normally in the weeks before the test and your total IgA is normal, coeliac disease is unlikely to explain your gut or nutritional symptoms. If you had already cut out gluten, the test can be falsely negative and would need repeating after re-introduction.
fy.bhi: A weak positive that sits in the equivocal zone. This can be an early or mild coeliac reaction, or a non-specific finding in type 1 diabetes or liver disease. Do not stop gluten yet: your doctor may add endomysial antibody or repeat in three to six months, and may consider a gastroscopy if symptoms persist.
fy.hi: A positive coeliac antibody, which strongly suggests your immune system is reacting to gluten and damaging the small bowel. Keep eating gluten for now, because the confirmatory endoscopy and biopsy need it. Once confirmed, a strict gluten-free diet reverses the damage and its complications, so a gastroenterology referral is the next step.

TLP-193.notes: Cut-offs are assay-specific (Euroimmun ≥ 20, Inova ≥ 20, others ≥ 7–10 U/mL); interpret with the total IgA on this report. ESPGHAN 2020 allows biopsy-free diagnosis in children with tTG ≥ 10× upper limit plus positive EMA. Levels fall on a gluten-free diet and are used to monitor adherence.
TLP-193.retest: Repeat 6–12 months after starting a gluten-free diet to confirm the level is falling; retest after gluten re-challenge if the first sample was taken while gluten-free.

TLP-194.name: Anti-Endomysial Antibody (IgA Or IgG)
TLP-194.meas: Antibodies that stain the connective tissue around smooth muscle on a microscope slide, a highly specific sign of coeliac disease.
TLP-194.sig: Endomysial antibody is the most specific coeliac test (close to 100%) and is used to confirm a positive or equivocal tTG result; a positive EMA with a very high tTG can avoid biopsy in children. It is read by eye, so results are reported as positive or negative with a titre.
TLP-194.ind: A positive EMA is almost always due to coeliac disease or dermatitis herpetiformis (its skin form). A negative EMA with a negative tTG makes coeliac disease very unlikely while on gluten; IgA-deficient people need the IgG version.

fy.n: Endomysial antibody was not detected. Combined with a negative tTG, this makes coeliac disease very unlikely as long as you were eating gluten before the test. If tTG was weakly positive but EMA is negative, the tTG result was probably not significant, though your doctor may still repeat both in a few months.
fy.hi: Endomysial antibody is positive, which is a very specific marker of coeliac disease. Together with a raised tTG this is strong evidence, and in children with a tTG above ten times the cut-off it may be enough for diagnosis without biopsy. Keep eating gluten until your gastroenterologist has completed the assessment.

TLP-194.notes: Indirect immunofluorescence on monkey oesophagus or human umbilical cord; titre ≥ 1:5 or 1:10 is reported as positive depending on substrate. IgG-EMA is used when total IgA is deficient. Sensitivity is lower in children under 2 years.
TLP-194.retest: Not routinely repeated; used once to confirm a positive tTG. Becomes negative after 6–12 months of a strict gluten-free diet.

TLP-195.name: Anti-Deamidated Gliadin
TLP-195.alias: DGP, Anti-DGP IgG/IgA, Gliadin peptide antibody
TLP-195.meas: Antibodies against gliadin, the gluten protein, after it has been chemically modified in the gut lining, in its IgG and IgA forms.
TLP-195.sig: DGP antibodies add value where tTG can miss coeliac disease: in children under two, in people with IgA deficiency (using the IgG form) and in some seronegative adults. It replaced the older, less specific gliadin antibody test.
TLP-195.ind: A positive DGP supports coeliac disease and, when IgG-DGP is positive with a deficient total IgA, is the main coeliac screen. Low positives can be non-specific, especially in the IgA form, and are less meaningful without a positive tTG or EMA.

fy.n: No antibodies to deamidated gliadin were found. Together with a negative tTG this makes coeliac disease unlikely, including in the situations where tTG alone can miss it, such as low total IgA or very young children. Ordinary gluten sensitivity without coeliac disease is not detected by this test.
fy.bhi: A weak positive in the equivocal zone. On its own, particularly if tTG and EMA are negative, this is often not significant and can be seen in other gut conditions. Continue eating gluten; your doctor may repeat the coeliac panel in three to six months or proceed to biopsy if symptoms are marked.
fy.hi: A positive result, which supports coeliac disease. It is particularly meaningful if this is the IgG form and your total IgA is low, or if you are a young child, because those are the cases the usual tTG test can miss. Keep gluten in your diet until a gastroenterologist confirms the diagnosis, then a gluten-free diet is the treatment.

TLP-195.notes: Cut-offs are assay-specific (commonly 20 U/mL negative, 20–30 equivocal). IgG-DGP is the recommended screen in IgA deficiency; IgA-DGP alone has lower specificity. Levels normalise more slowly than tTG on a gluten-free diet.
TLP-195.retest: Repeat in 3–6 months if equivocal and still on gluten; use IgG-DGP to monitor diet adherence in IgA-deficient patients.

TLP-196.name: H. pylori Antigen (Stool)
TLP-196.profile: ADD-ON · URTICARIA — SECOND-LINE (only if first line negative); H. PYLORI PROFILE
TLP-196.meas: Protein fragments of Helicobacter pylori shed into the stool, showing that the bacterium is currently living in your stomach.
TLP-196.sig: H. pylori infects over half of Indian adults and is the main cause of gastric and duodenal ulcers and a risk factor for stomach cancer; in chronic urticaria it is a recognised, treatable trigger in some people. The stool antigen detects current infection, unlike blood antibodies, which stay positive after cure.
TLP-196.ind: A positive result means active H. pylori infection, which may underlie dyspepsia, ulcers, iron deficiency, B12 deficiency or, in some cases, chronic hives. A negative result makes current infection unlikely, provided you have not taken acid-suppressants or antibiotics in the previous two to four weeks.

fy.n: No H. pylori antigen was found in your stool, so current infection is unlikely. If you were taking a proton-pump inhibitor, bismuth or antibiotics in the two to four weeks before the sample, the test can miss the bacterium and a repeat off those medicines would be more reliable.
fy.hi: H. pylori is present in your stomach. This is very common and often silent, but it raises the risk of ulcers and, over decades, stomach cancer, and it may be contributing to indigestion, low iron or chronic hives. Your doctor will usually prescribe a course of eradication treatment and recheck the stool test at least four weeks after finishing it.

TLP-196.notes: Monoclonal antigen assays have sensitivity and specificity above 90%. Stop proton-pump inhibitors for 2 weeks and antibiotics or bismuth for 4 weeks before testing to avoid false negatives. Watery stool can also lower sensitivity.
TLP-196.src: Maastricht VI/Florence 2022 consensus; ACG 2017 H. pylori guideline
TLP-196.retest: Test of cure ≥ 4 weeks after finishing treatment and ≥ 2 weeks off proton-pump inhibitors.

TLP-197.name: Procalcitonin
TLP-197.meas: A precursor of the hormone calcitonin that many tissues release into the blood in response to bacterial toxins and severe systemic inflammation.
TLP-197.sig: Procalcitonin rises within hours in serious bacterial infection and sepsis but stays low in most viral illnesses, so it helps decide whether fever needs antibiotics and how severe an infection is. Falling levels over days show that treatment is working.
TLP-197.ind: High values point to bacterial infection, particularly bloodstream infection, pneumonia, pyelonephritis or sepsis; very high values also occur after major surgery, burns, severe trauma and some cancers. Low values favour viral or localised infection and are not a concern in themselves.

fy.n: Procalcitonin is at a normal level, which makes a serious bacterial infection or sepsis unlikely. If you have fever, a viral cause or a localised problem is more probable. Your doctor may still treat based on the overall picture, and a repeat in 6–24 hours is useful if you remain unwell.
fy.bhi: A mild rise, which sits in a grey zone: it can be seen in early or localised bacterial infection, in some viral illnesses with a strong inflammatory response, after surgery or in kidney disease. Together with your symptoms, CRP and cultures, your doctor will decide whether antibiotics are needed; a repeat within 24 hours shows the direction.
fy.hi: Clearly raised, which suggests a significant bacterial infection or a body-wide inflammatory response. This level usually calls for prompt medical assessment, cultures and treatment. Once therapy starts, the level should fall by roughly half every one to two days; your doctor may use serial results to guide how long antibiotics continue.

TLP-197.notes: Sepsis thresholds: < 0.5 unlikely, 0.5–2 possible, > 2 likely, > 10 septic shock. Newborns under 72 hours have a physiological peak; chronic kidney disease, major surgery, burns and medullary thyroid cancer raise PCT without infection. Localised infections (abscess, empyema) may not raise it.
TLP-197.src: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021; PCT-guided antibiotic stewardship trials (PRORATA, ProACT)
TLP-197.retest: Repeat every 24–48 hours in a treated infection; a fall of ≥ 80% from peak or a level < 0.5 supports stopping antibiotics.

TLP-198.name: Lupus Anticoagulant (dRVVT + APTT-based)
TLP-198.meas: Whether antibodies in your blood interfere with phospholipid-dependent clotting tests, detected by two different clotting assays with confirmation steps.
TLP-198.sig: Lupus anticoagulant is the antiphospholipid antibody most strongly linked to blood clots and to recurrent pregnancy loss, so it is central to the antiphospholipid syndrome work-up in thrombosis, IVF failure and recurrent miscarriage. Despite the name, it makes blood clot more, not less, and is not confined to lupus.
TLP-198.ind: A persistent positive (confirmed at least 12 weeks apart) is consistent with antiphospholipid syndrome, particularly with a history of clots or pregnancy complications; transient positives follow infections and some medicines. A negative result reduces but does not exclude the syndrome, as the other antibodies can be positive alone.

fy.n: No lupus anticoagulant was detected on either clotting test. This makes the antiphospholipid syndrome less likely as a cause of clots or pregnancy loss, though your anticardiolipin and beta-2-glycoprotein results are needed to complete the picture. If you are on a blood thinner, the result can be affected and your doctor may repeat it.
fy.bhi: The clotting tests gave a mixed or borderline picture that could not be classed as clearly positive or negative. This often happens with anticoagulant medicines, recent infection or sample problems. It is not a diagnosis; a repeat sample after twelve weeks, ideally off interfering medicines, usually resolves it.
fy.hi: A lupus anticoagulant was detected. This is the antiphospholipid antibody most linked to clots and pregnancy complications, but it must be confirmed on a second sample at least twelve weeks later, because infections can produce temporary positives. If confirmed, your doctor, and in pregnancy your obstetrician, will discuss preventive treatment.

TLP-198.notes: Testing must follow ISTH three-step method (screen, mix, confirm) on both dRVVT and a sensitive APTT. Warfarin, heparin and direct oral anticoagulants cause false positives or negatives; test before starting anticoagulation or after a suitable washout. Acute thrombosis and infection can give transient positives.
TLP-198.src: ISTH 2020 lupus anticoagulant guideline; Sydney 2006 / ACR-EULAR 2023 APS criteria
TLP-198.retest: Confirm any positive or indeterminate result ≥ 12 weeks later; retest off anticoagulants where possible.

TLP-199.name: Anti-cardiolipin IgG
TLP-199.alias: aCL IgG, ACA IgG, Cardiolipin antibody IgG
TLP-199.meas: IgG antibodies directed against cardiolipin, a phospholipid on cell membranes, which can promote abnormal clotting.
TLP-199.sig: Anticardiolipin IgG is one of the three laboratory criteria for antiphospholipid syndrome, a treatable cause of clots, stroke in young people, recurrent miscarriage and IVF failure. Medium-to-high levels carry the clinical risk; low levels are common and usually harmless.
TLP-199.ind: A persistent medium or high positive is consistent with antiphospholipid syndrome, on its own or as part of lupus. Low positives and transient rises occur after infections (including syphilis, hepatitis C, HIV) and with some drugs, and do not meet criteria on their own.

fy.n: No significant anticardiolipin IgG antibodies were found. Together with negative lupus anticoagulant and beta-2-glycoprotein results, this makes antiphospholipid syndrome an unlikely explanation for clots or pregnancy complications. No action is needed for this test.
fy.bhi: A low level of antibody is present. This is a common finding after infections and in healthy people, and on its own it does not meet the criteria for antiphospholipid syndrome. Your doctor will look at the other antibodies and your history; a repeat after twelve weeks shows whether it persists or fades.
fy.hi: A medium or high level of anticardiolipin IgG, which is a criterion for antiphospholipid syndrome if it persists on a repeat at least twelve weeks later. If you have had a clot, a stroke or pregnancy losses, this result is important and your doctor will discuss anticoagulant or aspirin-based prevention, particularly around pregnancy or surgery.

TLP-199.notes: Sydney criteria define positivity as > 40 GPL or > 99th percentile of the local assay; ACR/EULAR 2023 weight moderate (40–79) and high (≥ 80) differently. Results are not standardised between ELISA kits; compare only within the same laboratory. Transient positives follow infections.
TLP-199.src: Sydney 2006 revised APS criteria; ACR/EULAR 2023 APS classification criteria
TLP-199.retest: Confirm any positive ≥ 12 weeks later on the same platform; no serial monitoring needed once persistence is established.

TLP-200.name: Anti-cardiolipin IgM
TLP-200.alias: aCL IgM, ACA IgM, Cardiolipin antibody IgM
TLP-200.meas: IgM antibodies against cardiolipin, the early-response antibody class, which can also be produced by infections.
TLP-200.sig: Anticardiolipin IgM completes the antiphospholipid antibody set, but it is the least specific member: isolated IgM positives are more often triggered by infections or rheumatoid factor than by true antiphospholipid syndrome. It carries most weight when IgG or lupus anticoagulant is also positive.
TLP-200.ind: A persistent medium or high IgM supports antiphospholipid syndrome, especially alongside other positive antibodies. Isolated low IgM is frequently a transient post-infectious finding or an artefact of rheumatoid factor, and has weak association with clots or pregnancy loss.

fy.n: Anticardiolipin IgM was not detected at a significant level. This is the expected result and, if the IgG antibody, beta-2-glycoprotein antibodies and lupus anticoagulant are also negative, the antiphospholipid syndrome is effectively excluded at this time.
fy.bhi: A low IgM antibody level, which by itself is a weak finding: recent viral infections, vaccinations and rheumatoid factor commonly cause it, and it usually disappears within weeks. Your doctor will interpret it with the other antibody results and may simply repeat it after twelve weeks.
fy.hi: A medium or high anticardiolipin IgM. Because IgM can rise temporarily after infections, this needs confirming on a second sample at least twelve weeks later before it counts towards antiphospholipid syndrome. Its significance is greatest if the IgG antibody or lupus anticoagulant is also positive and you have a history of clots or pregnancy loss.

TLP-200.notes: Positivity > 40 MPL or > 99th percentile (Sydney); ACR/EULAR 2023 give IgM less weight than IgG. Rheumatoid factor and cryoglobulins can cause false-positive IgM. Kits are not interchangeable.
TLP-200.src: Sydney 2006 revised APS criteria; ACR/EULAR 2023 APS classification criteria
TLP-200.retest: Confirm any positive ≥ 12 weeks later; isolated low IgM rarely needs further follow-up if the repeat is negative.

TLP-201.name: Anti-β2-glycoprotein-I IgG
TLP-201.alias: Anti-β2GPI IgG, Beta-2 glycoprotein antibody IgG, aβ2GPI IgG
TLP-201.meas: IgG antibodies against beta-2-glycoprotein I, the plasma protein that most clot-promoting antiphospholipid antibodies actually bind.
TLP-201.sig: Anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I IgG is the most specific of the antiphospholipid antibodies for true antiphospholipid syndrome, and being positive for all three (with lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin) marks the highest risk of clots and pregnancy complications.
TLP-201.ind: A persistent positive is consistent with antiphospholipid syndrome, particularly with a history of venous or arterial clots, recurrent miscarriage, late pregnancy loss or pre-eclampsia. It is occasionally positive in lupus without clinical events and rarely after infection.

fy.n: No antibodies to beta-2-glycoprotein I were detected. This is reassuring, because this antibody is the most specific marker of the antiphospholipid syndrome; with negative anticardiolipin and lupus anticoagulant results the syndrome is very unlikely.
fy.bhi: A low positive level. Low levels of this antibody are less clearly linked to clotting than higher ones and can be transient. Your doctor will review it alongside the other antiphospholipid tests and your history, and will usually repeat it after twelve weeks to see whether it persists.
fy.hi: A clear positive for anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I IgG, which is a strong marker of antiphospholipid syndrome if confirmed on a repeat at least twelve weeks apart. Being positive for this together with lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin identifies the highest-risk pattern, so your doctor will plan clot prevention, particularly for pregnancy, surgery or long travel.

TLP-201.notes: Positivity is > 99th percentile of the local assay (commonly 20 U/mL); ACR/EULAR 2023 treat ≥ 40 as moderate and ≥ 80 as high. Domain-I-specific antibodies carry the most risk but are not routinely reported. Not standardised across kits.
TLP-201.src: Sydney 2006 revised APS criteria; ACR/EULAR 2023 APS classification criteria
TLP-201.retest: Confirm persistence ≥ 12 weeks after the first positive; serial testing is not needed after that.

TLP-202.name: Anti-β2-glycoprotein-I IgM
TLP-202.alias: Anti-β2GPI IgM, Beta-2 glycoprotein antibody IgM, aβ2GPI IgM
TLP-202.meas: IgM antibodies against beta-2-glycoprotein I, the early-response class of the most specific antiphospholipid antibody.
TLP-202.sig: The IgM form of anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I is included in the criteria for antiphospholipid syndrome but has a weaker link with clotting than IgG; it matters mainly when it is persistent, at medium-to-high levels, or accompanied by other positive antibodies.
TLP-202.ind: A persistent positive supports antiphospholipid syndrome, especially in combination with IgG antibodies or lupus anticoagulant. Isolated low IgM is often transient after infections and has limited clinical significance.

fy.n: Anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I IgM was not detected. This completes a negative antiphospholipid screen if the IgG form, anticardiolipin antibodies and lupus anticoagulant are also negative, and makes this syndrome an unlikely cause of your clotting or pregnancy history.
fy.bhi: A low IgM antibody level. On its own this is a weak signal, commonly appearing for a few weeks after an infection or vaccination. It does not meet criteria for antiphospholipid syndrome by itself; a repeat after twelve weeks, read with the other antibodies, will clarify whether it persists.
fy.hi: A medium or high IgM level. Its meaning depends on persistence and company: confirmed on a second sample twelve weeks later and paired with IgG antibodies or lupus anticoagulant, it supports antiphospholipid syndrome; alone and transient, it is less concerning. Your doctor will weigh it against your history of clots or pregnancy complications.

TLP-202.notes: Positivity > 99th percentile of the assay (commonly 20 U/mL). IgM carries less weight than IgG in ACR/EULAR 2023 criteria. Rheumatoid factor can cause false-positive IgM results.
TLP-202.src: Sydney 2006 revised APS criteria; ACR/EULAR 2023 APS classification criteria
TLP-202.retest: Confirm ≥ 12 weeks after a positive; if the repeat is negative and other antibodies are negative, no further testing is needed.

TLP-203.name: ENA Panel (Sm, RNP, Ro/SSA, La/SSB, Scl-70, Jo-1, Centromere)
TLP-203.alias: Extractable nuclear antigen antibodies, ENA profile, ANA profile
TLP-203.meas: A set of antibodies against seven named proteins inside the cell nucleus, each of which is linked to a particular autoimmune connective-tissue disease.
TLP-203.sig: Where ANA says that autoantibodies are present, the ENA panel says which ones: anti-Sm points to lupus, anti-RNP to mixed connective-tissue disease, Ro/La to Sjögren's and neonatal lupus risk, Scl-70 and centromere to the two forms of scleroderma, and Jo-1 to myositis with lung involvement. It turns a screening result into a diagnosis pathway.
TLP-203.ind: A positive component is consistent with the disease it is linked to (Sm: lupus; RNP: mixed connective-tissue disease or lupus; Ro/SSA and La/SSB: Sjögren's, subacute cutaneous lupus, neonatal heart block risk; Scl-70: diffuse systemic sclerosis; centromere: limited systemic sclerosis; Jo-1: antisynthetase syndrome). A fully negative panel makes these conditions less likely but does not exclude them.

fy.n: None of the seven specific antibodies was found. If your ANA was positive, this suggests it is not driven by the antibodies that define lupus, Sjögren's, scleroderma or myositis, which makes those diagnoses less likely. Your doctor will still weigh your symptoms, and may look at anti-dsDNA and complement separately.
fy.bhi: One or more antibodies came back in the weak or borderline range. Weak signals are common, can be non-specific and sometimes disappear on repeat. They are worth noting rather than acting on; your doctor may repeat the panel in three to six months or use a second method to confirm, guided by whether you have matching symptoms.
fy.hi: At least one specific antibody is clearly positive; the report names which. Each antibody points towards a particular connective-tissue disease, for example Ro/La towards Sjögren's or Scl-70 towards scleroderma, but diagnosis needs matching symptoms and examination. A rheumatologist review is the right next step, and women planning pregnancy should mention a positive Ro/La result.

TLP-203.notes: Each antigen is reported separately as negative, borderline or positive (immunoblot or ELISA indices vary by kit). Anti-Sm is highly specific but present in only 10–30% of lupus; Ro/SSA can be positive with a negative ANA. Anti-Ro/La positivity in pregnancy requires fetal heart monitoring from 16 weeks.
TLP-203.src: ACR/EULAR 2019 SLE criteria; ACR/EULAR 2013 systemic sclerosis criteria; ACR/EULAR 2016 Sjögren's criteria
TLP-203.retest: Not repeated routinely; repeat borderline results in 3–6 months or confirm by a second method.

TLP-204.name: Component-Resolved Diagnostics (CRD)
TLP-204.alias: Molecular allergy testing, Allergen component IgE, ISAC / ALEX component panel
TLP-204.meas: Specific IgE against individual allergen proteins (components) rather than whole extracts, reported per molecule, such as Ara h 2 in peanut or Der p 2 in dust mite.
TLP-204.sig: Component testing separates true, potentially severe allergy from harmless cross-reactivity: for example, IgE to peanut storage proteins predicts real reactions, whereas IgE to the pollen-like Ara h 8 usually means only an itchy mouth. In eczema and food allergy it helps decide which foods must be avoided and which can be safely reintroduced.
TLP-204.ind: Positive IgE to a stable, species-specific component (storage proteins, Der p 1/2, Fel d 1) points to genuine sensitisation with risk of systemic reactions; positivity limited to cross-reactive components (profilins, PR-10 proteins, CCDs) suggests pollen-related cross-reactivity with low risk. A negative panel does not exclude allergy to something not on the panel.

fy.n: No IgE was detected against the allergen components tested, so a true allergy to those specific molecules is unlikely. Symptoms after a food or exposure can still have other causes (intolerance, irritation, or an allergen not on the panel), so keep a symptom diary and discuss any clear pattern with your allergist.
fy.bhi: A low level of IgE against one or more components. Low-grade sensitisation often does not cause symptoms, particularly if it is to cross-reactive proteins such as profilin or PR-10. Do not remove foods on this basis alone; your allergist will match the components to your history and may suggest a supervised food challenge.
fy.hi: Clear sensitisation to one or more components; the report names them. Sensitisation to stable, species-specific proteins (for example peanut Ara h 2, egg Gal d 1, milk Bos d 8, dust-mite Der p 2) carries real risk and guides avoidance and emergency planning, whereas cross-reactive components usually mean milder symptoms. An allergist should translate this into a personal plan.

TLP-204.notes: Multiplex platforms (ISAC) report in ISU-E with a cut-off of 0.3; singleplex ImmunoCAP components report in kUA/L with 0.35 cut-off. Sensitisation is not the same as clinical allergy; interpretation requires the exposure history. Paediatric patterns evolve, so results are usually re-evaluated every 1–2 years.
TLP-204.retest: Re-evaluate every 12–24 months in children to detect outgrowing of egg or milk allergy; repeat before considering food reintroduction.

TLP-205.name: Specific IgE — Paediatric Panel
TLP-205.alias: Child allergy panel, Paediatric food and inhalant IgE panel, sIgE panel
TLP-205.meas: IgE antibodies against a set of common childhood allergens, typically milk, egg, wheat, soy, peanut, fish, dust mite, cockroach, pet dander and moulds, each reported separately.
TLP-205.sig: Blood specific-IgE testing identifies which allergens a child is sensitised to without stopping antihistamines or needing skin pricks, guiding avoidance in eczema, wheeze, rhinitis and suspected food allergy. Higher values raise the likelihood that exposure will actually cause symptoms.
TLP-205.ind: A positive allergen indicates sensitisation; the probability that it causes symptoms rises with the level, and allergen-specific thresholds exist for egg, milk and peanut. Negative results make IgE-mediated allergy to those allergens unlikely but do not exclude non-IgE reactions such as delayed cow's-milk protein intolerance.

fy.n: No IgE was found against the allergens on this panel, so an immediate-type allergy to these foods or airborne triggers is unlikely to be driving your child's symptoms. Delayed reactions, such as some forms of milk intolerance, are not IgE-based and are assessed by history and elimination rather than this test.
fy.bhi: A low level of IgE against one or more allergens on the panel. At this level many children have no symptoms on exposure, so foods should not be cut out on the blood test alone. Your paediatrician or allergist will match each result to what your child actually reacts to and may suggest a supervised challenge.
fy.hi: Clear sensitisation to one or more allergens, named in the report. The higher the level, the more likely exposure triggers symptoms, and for egg, milk and peanut there are recognised thresholds that predict reactions. An allergist can turn this into an avoidance plan, an emergency plan if needed, and a schedule for rechecking as many children outgrow food allergies.

TLP-205.notes: Classes: 0 (< 0.35), 1 (0.35–0.69), 2 (0.7–3.49), 3 (3.5–17.4), 4 (17.5–49.9), 5 (50–99.9), 6 (≥ 100 kUA/L). Sensitisation is not allergy; whole-extract results may need component testing to distinguish cross-reactivity. Total IgE affects interpretation in eczema, where broad low-level positives are common.
TLP-205.src: EAACI food allergy guideline 2023; NIAID 2010 food allergy guidelines
TLP-205.retest: Recheck every 12–24 months for egg, milk, wheat and soy in children, as levels falling below 2 kUA/L may indicate tolerance and suitability for a challenge.

TLP-206.name: Complement C3
TLP-206.profile: ADD-ON · URTICARIA — SECOND-LINE (only if first line negative)
TLP-206.meas: The concentration of C3, the most abundant complement protein, whose consumption marks immune-complex activation in the skin and blood vessels.
TLP-206.sig: In chronic urticaria that has not responded to first-line treatment, a low C3 is a red flag that the hives may actually be urticarial vasculitis or an underlying lupus-like disease, which are managed differently from ordinary urticaria. Normal complements support a diagnosis of simple chronic spontaneous urticaria.
TLP-206.ind: Low C3 in a patient with hives suggests hypocomplementaemic urticarial vasculitis, lupus, cryoglobulinaemia or a post-infectious immune-complex process. Normal or raised C3 argues against these and points back to chronic spontaneous urticaria, where C3 may be mildly high as an acute-phase protein.

fy.lo: Your C3 is low, which in someone with persistent hives raises the possibility that the rash is a form of blood-vessel inflammation (urticarial vasculitis) or part of a lupus-like condition, rather than ordinary urticaria. Wheals that last over 24 hours, bruise or hurt strengthen this suspicion. A dermatology or rheumatology review, and possibly a skin biopsy, are the next steps.
fy.n: Your C3 is normal, which is reassuring in chronic hives: it makes urticarial vasculitis and lupus-related urticaria unlikely and supports the more common, non-dangerous chronic spontaneous urticaria. This helps your doctor concentrate on antihistamine-based and, if needed, biologic treatment.
fy.hi: A slightly raised C3 reflects a general inflammatory response, which can accompany active urticaria, infection or other inflammation. It carries no specific diagnostic meaning for hives and does not need treatment; your doctor may simply note it alongside CRP.

TLP-206.notes: Same assay and interval as the rheumatology C3 (platform ranges roughly 80–90 to 160–180 mg/dL); interpret with C4 and C1q in suspected urticarial vasculitis. Samples must be separated promptly to avoid falsely low values.
TLP-206.src: EAACI/GA2LEN/EuroGuiDerm urticaria guideline 2022; Jachiet et al. urticarial vasculitis series
TLP-206.retest: Repeat with C4 and C1q if low, or if hives change character (painful, lasting > 24 h, leaving bruising).

TLP-207.name: Complement C4
TLP-207.profile: ADD-ON · URTICARIA — SECOND-LINE (only if first line negative)
TLP-207.meas: The concentration of C4, a classical-pathway complement protein that is consumed both in immune-complex disease and, uncontrolled, in C1-inhibitor deficiency.
TLP-207.sig: For hives and swelling that resist first-line antihistamines, C4 does double duty: a low value points either to urticarial vasculitis (with low C3) or, when swelling occurs without wheals, to hereditary or acquired angioedema, where C4 is low in over 95% of cases. A normal C4 during an attack nearly excludes C1-inhibitor deficiency.
TLP-207.ind: Low C4 suggests hereditary or acquired angioedema, urticarial vasculitis, lupus, cryoglobulinaemia or an inherited C4 gene deletion. Normal C4 makes C1-inhibitor-related angioedema very unlikely and favours histamine-mediated urticaria.

fy.lo: Your C4 is low. If your main problem is swelling of the face, hands, gut or throat without itchy wheals, this points towards hereditary or acquired angioedema, which needs specific treatment rather than antihistamines. If you have long-lasting, painful hives, it suggests urticarial vasculitis. Either way, C1-inhibitor testing and a specialist review are needed.
fy.n: Your C4 is normal, which is helpful: it makes hereditary angioedema very unlikely as the cause of swelling episodes and, together with a normal C3, argues against urticarial vasculitis. This supports a histamine-driven urticaria, which usually responds to optimised antihistamine or biologic therapy.
fy.hi: A mildly raised C4 is a non-specific sign of inflammation and has no particular link to urticaria or angioedema. It does not need any action on its own; your doctor will interpret it in the context of your symptoms and other results.

TLP-207.notes: Same assay and interval as the rheumatology C4 (platform ranges roughly 10–16 to 40–45 mg/dL). Ideally sample during or soon after a swelling attack. Common C4 null alleles cause low-normal values without disease; ACE-inhibitor angioedema has normal C4.
TLP-207.src: WAO/EAACI hereditary angioedema guideline 2021; EAACI/GA2LEN urticaria guideline 2022
TLP-207.retest: If low with angioedema, proceed to C1-inhibitor quantitative and functional assays; repeat during an attack if the first sample was taken while well.

TLP-208.name: Serum Tryptase (basal)
TLP-208.alias: Baseline tryptase, Total tryptase, Mast cell tryptase
TLP-208.profile: ADD-ON · URTICARIA — SECOND-LINE (only if first line negative); SINGLE MARKERS
TLP-208.meas: An enzyme stored in mast cells, the cells that release histamine; the resting level reflects your total mast-cell load rather than an acute reaction.
TLP-208.sig: A raised baseline tryptase in someone with hives, flushing, unexplained anaphylaxis or angioedema raises the possibility of an underlying mast-cell disorder (mastocytosis or hereditary alpha-tryptasaemia) and predicts more severe allergic reactions, particularly to insect stings. It also helps tell true mast-cell activation from other causes of swelling.
TLP-208.ind: Persistently high tryptase suggests systemic mastocytosis, hereditary alpha-tryptasaemia, a myeloid blood disorder or advanced chronic kidney disease; a rise measured within hours of a reaction indicates anaphylaxis. A low or low-normal value is normal and carries no concern.

fy.n: Your resting tryptase is normal, which makes a mast-cell disorder such as mastocytosis an unlikely cause of hives, flushing or swelling attacks. If you have had a severe allergic reaction, this baseline value is also useful for comparison with a level drawn during any future episode.
fy.bhi: Mildly above the usual range. About one in twenty people carry extra copies of the tryptase gene (hereditary alpha-tryptasaemia), which produces this pattern and can be linked to more troublesome allergic symptoms; kidney impairment and age also raise it slightly. Your doctor may repeat it and consider genetic or allergy specialist review.
fy.hi: Clearly raised at baseline, which is one of the criteria for systemic mastocytosis and also prompts a check for hereditary alpha-tryptasaemia or a bone-marrow condition. Flushing, itching, bone pain, gut symptoms or severe sting reactions alongside this result warrant referral to an allergist or haematologist, who may advise a bone-marrow examination.

TLP-208.notes: Baseline sample should be taken when symptom-free; a level > 20 µg/L is a minor WHO criterion for systemic mastocytosis. For suspected anaphylaxis, an acute sample 1–4 hours after onset is compared with baseline (significant rise: > 1.2 × baseline + 2). Chronic kidney disease and hereditary alpha-tryptasaemia raise baseline values.
TLP-208.src: WHO 2022 mastocytosis criteria; EAACI anaphylaxis guideline 2021
TLP-208.retest: Repeat a raised value on a symptom-free day; draw an acute sample within 1–4 hours of any severe reaction for comparison.

TLP-209.name: C1 Esterase Inhibitor — functional
TLP-209.alias: C1-INH function, Functional C1 esterase inhibitor, C1-INH activity
TLP-209.meas: How well your C1-inhibitor protein actually works at blocking the enzymes that generate bradykinin, the chemical behind hereditary angioedema swelling.
TLP-209.sig: The functional assay is what distinguishes type II hereditary angioedema, where the protein is present but faulty, from type I, where it is simply low. Combined with the quantitative level and C4 it confirms or excludes C1-inhibitor deficiency in recurrent swelling attacks that do not respond to antihistamines.
TLP-209.ind: Low function points to hereditary angioedema (type I if the level is also low, type II if the level is normal or high) or to acquired C1-inhibitor deficiency in older adults with lymphoproliferative or autoimmune disease. Normal function with normal C4 essentially excludes C1-inhibitor-related angioedema.

fy.lo: Your C1-inhibitor is not working properly, which with a low C4 is consistent with hereditary angioedema or, if it began later in life, an acquired form. Attacks are driven by bradykinin, not histamine, so antihistamines and steroids do not help but specific treatments do. An immunologist or allergist referral is next, and close family may need testing.
fy.blo: Function is in a borderline zone that can occur with sample handling problems, mild acquired deficiency or an early or partial hereditary form. It should not be dismissed if you have recurrent swelling without hives. Your doctor will usually repeat the test on a fresh, properly frozen sample together with the quantitative level and C4.
fy.n: Your C1-inhibitor is working normally. With a normal C4 this rules out hereditary and acquired C1-inhibitor deficiency as the cause of swelling episodes, which points instead to histamine-driven angioedema, medication effects (such as ACE inhibitors) or the rarer normal-C1-inhibitor form, which is assessed by history and genetics.

TLP-209.notes: Chromogenic assay reference ≥ 68–70% (lab-specific); < 50% is diagnostic in the right context. Sample must be separated and frozen quickly, as function degrades and gives falsely low results. Levels in infants under 1 year are unreliable; repeat after 12 months. Oestrogens can lower function.
TLP-209.src: WAO/EAACI hereditary angioedema guideline 2021; US HAEA 2020 guideline
TLP-209.retest: Confirm any abnormal result on a second sample; test first-degree relatives if hereditary angioedema is confirmed.

TLP-210.name: C1 Esterase Inhibitor — quantitative
TLP-210.alias: C1-INH antigen, C1 esterase inhibitor level, C1-INH quantitative
TLP-210.meas: The amount of C1-inhibitor protein in your blood, regardless of whether it is working.
TLP-210.sig: A low C1-inhibitor level with low C4 defines type I hereditary angioedema, which accounts for about 85% of cases, and a low level appearing in later life suggests the acquired form linked to lymphoma or autoimmunity. It is read together with the functional assay to classify the disorder.
TLP-210.ind: Low levels indicate type I hereditary angioedema or acquired C1-inhibitor deficiency. A normal or raised level with low function indicates type II; a raised level alone is an acute-phase response to inflammation and is not clinically significant.

fy.lo: Your C1-inhibitor protein level is low. With low C4 and low function, this fits type I hereditary angioedema, an inherited cause of unpredictable swelling of skin, gut or airway that needs specific treatment and an emergency plan. If it started after age 40, an acquired cause is sought. Specialist referral and family screening are the next steps.
fy.blo: The level is just under the reference range. This can be seen in carriers, in early or mild hereditary angioedema, with oestrogen-containing medicines, or simply as normal variation. Your doctor will interpret it with the functional assay and C4, and repeat the tests if you have a history of swelling without hives.
fy.n: Your C1-inhibitor protein level is normal. If its function and your C4 are also normal, C1-inhibitor deficiency is excluded. Note that a normal level with low function still indicates type II hereditary angioedema, so the functional result on this report is the one to check alongside.
fy.hi: A raised C1-inhibitor level simply reflects that it is an acute-phase protein that rises with inflammation or infection, and it has no disease significance on its own. It does not exclude type II hereditary angioedema if function is low, so read the two results together.

TLP-210.notes: Reference approximately 21–39 mg/dL (0.21–0.39 g/L) by nephelometry; type I HAE usually shows < 50% of normal. Values are unreliable in infants under 12 months. Androgens raise and oestrogens lower the level.
TLP-210.src: WAO/EAACI hereditary angioedema guideline 2021; US HAEA 2020 guideline
TLP-210.retest: Confirm abnormal results on a second sample at least 1 month apart; screen first-degree relatives if hereditary angioedema is diagnosed.

TLP-211.name: Anti-Parietal Cell Antibody
TLP-211.alias: APCA, Gastric parietal cell antibody, PCA
TLP-211.meas: Antibodies against the acid-producing parietal cells of the stomach lining, specifically their proton pump.
TLP-211.sig: Parietal cell antibodies are the sensitive screen for autoimmune gastritis, which destroys the cells that make acid and intrinsic factor and leads to B12 and iron deficiency and pernicious anaemia. Vitiligo, thyroid autoimmunity and type 1 diabetes cluster with it, which is why it is tested in those conditions.
TLP-211.ind: A positive result is consistent with autoimmune atrophic gastritis and pernicious anaemia, and is more common in people with vitiligo, Hashimoto's or Addison's disease; up to 10% of healthy older adults are positive without disease. A negative result makes autoimmune gastritis less likely but does not exclude it.

fy.n: No parietal cell antibodies were found, which makes autoimmune gastritis an unlikely cause of low B12 or iron. Because a minority of cases are antibody-negative, your doctor may still check B12, iron and, if symptoms persist, gastrin or an endoscopy.
fy.bhi: A borderline result, which is common in older adults and in people with other autoimmune conditions such as vitiligo or thyroid disease, and often has no consequence.
