The practical step is to make sure B12, iron and a blood count are normal, and to repeat the antibody in six to twelve months.
fy.hi: Parietal cell antibodies are present, suggesting your immune system is targeting the stomach lining. Over years this can reduce acid, B12 and iron absorption, and slightly raises the risk of stomach growths. Your doctor will check B12, iron and intrinsic-factor antibody, may arrange an endoscopy, and B12 supplementation is often started early.

TLP-211.notes: Detected by indirect immunofluorescence (rodent stomach, positive ≥ 1:40) or ELISA against H+/K+-ATPase; ELISA is more specific. Positivity increases with age. Long-term proton-pump inhibitor use does not cause the antibody but does lower B12.
TLP-211.src: BSG 2019 guideline on gastric adenocarcinoma risk / autoimmune gastritis; Lahner & Annibale reviews
TLP-211.retest: If positive, check B12, ferritin, gastrin and intrinsic-factor antibody; monitor B12 yearly and discuss endoscopic surveillance.

TLP-212.name: Anti-Intrinsic Factor Antibody
TLP-212.alias: IFAb, Intrinsic factor blocking antibody, IF antibody
TLP-212.meas: Antibodies against intrinsic factor, the stomach protein that binds vitamin B12 so it can be absorbed in the small intestine.
TLP-212.sig: Intrinsic factor antibody is highly specific for pernicious anaemia: a positive result explains B12 deficiency that will not respond to ordinary oral doses and commits the person to lifelong B12 replacement. It is less sensitive than parietal cell antibody, so the two are read together.
TLP-212.ind: A positive result is diagnostic of pernicious anaemia in a person with low B12, and is often accompanied by other autoimmune diseases such as vitiligo and thyroiditis. A negative result does not exclude pernicious anaemia, since only about half of cases are antibody-positive.

fy.n: No intrinsic factor antibodies were found. This lowers the chance of pernicious anaemia but does not rule it out, as around half of people with the condition test negative. If your B12 is low, your doctor will consider the parietal cell antibody result, your diet and any medicines before deciding on treatment.
fy.bhi: A borderline result that may become clearly positive or negative over time. If your B12 is low, it is safest to treat and to repeat the antibody in a few months; if B12 is normal, simply recheck B12 and the antibody in six to twelve months.
fy.hi: Intrinsic factor antibodies are present, which is a specific marker of pernicious anaemia: your stomach cannot absorb B12 from food efficiently. This is very treatable with regular B12 injections or high-dose oral B12, usually for life, which prevents anaemia and nerve damage. Your doctor may also check for related thyroid or gastric conditions.

TLP-212.notes: Type 1 (blocking) antibodies are detected by ELISA; recent B12 injection can cause false positives, so sample before treatment or at least 48 hours after. Sensitivity is ~50–70%, specificity > 95%.
TLP-212.src: BSH 2014 guideline on cobalamin and folate disorders; BSG 2019
TLP-212.retest: Repeat borderline results after 3–6 months, sampled before any B12 injection; no need to repeat a confirmed positive.

TLP-213.name: Anti-dsDNA
TLP-213.alias: Anti-double-stranded DNA, dsDNA antibody, Anti-native DNA
TLP-213.meas: Antibodies against double-stranded DNA, the genetic material in the cell nucleus, which are highly characteristic of systemic lupus.
TLP-213.sig: Anti-dsDNA is one of the most specific lupus antibodies and, unlike most autoantibodies, its level tracks disease activity, rising before kidney flares and falling with treatment. It is used both to support the diagnosis and to monitor established lupus alongside complement.
TLP-213.ind: A positive result is strongly consistent with systemic lupus, particularly lupus nephritis; low positives can occur in autoimmune hepatitis, drug-induced lupus and occasionally after some biologic treatments. A negative result does not exclude lupus, as about a third of patients are negative, especially in skin-limited disease.

fy.n: No anti-dsDNA antibodies were found. This makes systemic lupus, and particularly lupus affecting the kidneys, less likely, though skin-limited lupus is often negative for this antibody. If you have known lupus, a negative result is one sign of quiet disease.
fy.bhi: A low-level result in the borderline zone. This can be an early or mild lupus signal, a non-specific finding in other autoimmune conditions, or an assay effect. Your doctor will weigh it with ANA, complement, a urine test and your symptoms, and may confirm with a second method or a repeat in three months.
fy.hi: A clear positive, which strongly supports systemic lupus if you have matching symptoms such as joint pain, rash, mouth ulcers, fatigue or protein in the urine. In known lupus, a rising level with falling complement warns of a flare, particularly of the kidneys. A rheumatologist review with urine and complement testing is the sensible next step.

TLP-213.notes: Cut-offs are method-specific (ELISA/CLIA commonly < 30 IU/mL negative; Crithidia IFA reported as titre; Farr assay < 7 IU/mL). Positivity by a high-specificity method (Crithidia or Farr) carries more weight in ACR/EULAR 2019 criteria. Some biologics (anti-TNF) induce transient positivity.
TLP-213.src: ACR/EULAR 2019 SLE classification criteria; EULAR 2023 SLE management recommendations
TLP-213.retest: In lupus, monitor every 3–6 months with C3, C4 and urinalysis; repeat borderline results in 3 months or confirm by Crithidia IFA.

TLP-214.name: Anti-Histone
TLP-214.meas: Antibodies against histones, the proteins that package DNA in the cell nucleus.
TLP-214.sig: Anti-histone antibodies are found in over 95% of drug-induced lupus, where a medicine (hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid, minocycline, anti-TNF biologics) triggers a lupus-like illness that resolves when the drug is stopped. They also appear in about half of people with systemic lupus, so they are interpreted with anti-dsDNA and the medication history.
TLP-214.ind: A positive result with a negative anti-dsDNA in someone taking a culprit medicine is consistent with drug-induced lupus; a positive alongside anti-dsDNA is simply part of the antibody profile of systemic lupus. Low levels occur in rheumatoid arthritis, autoimmune hepatitis and some healthy people.

fy.n: No anti-histone antibodies were detected. If you are taking a medicine known to trigger lupus-like symptoms, this makes drug-induced lupus unlikely as the explanation. It does not affect the likelihood of ordinary systemic lupus, which is judged from the other antibodies on this report.
fy.bhi: A weak signal in the borderline zone, which is seen in some healthy people and in several autoimmune conditions without specific meaning. Your doctor will consider whether you take any of the medicines associated with drug-induced lupus and may repeat the test in a few months if joint pains or rashes continue.
fy.hi: Anti-histone antibodies are present. If you are on a medicine such as hydralazine, isoniazid, minocycline or an anti-TNF biologic and have new joint pain, rash or fever with a negative anti-dsDNA, this pattern suggests drug-induced lupus, which usually settles after the drug is changed. If anti-dsDNA is also positive, it is simply part of a systemic lupus profile.

TLP-214.notes: ELISA cut-offs vary by kit (e.g. < 20 U/mL or index < 1.0); reported qualitatively. Drug-induced lupus typically shows anti-histone positive, anti-dsDNA and complement normal. Never stop a prescribed medicine on the basis of this result without medical advice.
TLP-214.src: ACR/EULAR 2019 SLE criteria; Vedove et al. drug-induced lupus review
TLP-214.retest: Repeat 3–6 months after stopping a suspected culprit drug; antibodies usually decline with symptom resolution.

TLP-215.name: Anti-Scl-70 (Topoisomerase I)
TLP-215.meas: Antibodies against DNA topoisomerase I, an enzyme inside the nucleus, which are characteristic of systemic sclerosis (scleroderma).
TLP-215.sig: Anti-Scl-70 is one of the three antibodies in the scleroderma classification criteria and predicts the diffuse skin form with a higher risk of interstitial lung disease, so a positive result prompts lung function testing and CT screening from the outset. It is almost never found in healthy people.
TLP-215.ind: A positive result is strongly consistent with systemic sclerosis, usually the diffuse cutaneous type, and identifies people who need lung surveillance; it can precede skin thickening in patients with Raynaud's phenomenon. A negative result does not exclude scleroderma, as other antibodies (centromere, RNA polymerase III) define different subsets.

fy.n: No anti-Scl-70 antibodies were found, which makes the diffuse, lung-prone form of scleroderma less likely. Scleroderma can still be present with other antibodies, so your centromere and RNA polymerase III results, and your symptoms such as Raynaud's or skin tightening, complete the picture.
fy.bhi: A borderline signal, which sometimes reflects assay noise rather than true antibody and can be seen weakly in lupus. If you have Raynaud's, puffy fingers or heartburn, your doctor may confirm the result by a second method (immunoblot or immunofluorescence pattern) and arrange nailfold capillary examination.
fy.hi: Anti-Scl-70 antibodies are present, a specific marker of systemic sclerosis with a tendency to involve the skin widely and the lungs. Even before skin changes, this result justifies a rheumatology referral with baseline lung function tests, a high-resolution chest CT and an echocardiogram, because early detection of lung involvement allows treatment that slows it.

TLP-215.notes: Detected by ELISA/CLIA or immunoblot with kit-specific cut-offs, often confirmed by a speckled/nucleolar ANA pattern. Anti-Scl-70 and anti-centromere are almost mutually exclusive. Rare positives occur in lupus overlap.
TLP-215.src: ACR/EULAR 2013 systemic sclerosis classification criteria; EULAR 2023 SSc recommendations
TLP-215.retest: No need to repeat a confirmed positive; confirm borderline results by a second method. Annual lung function testing if positive.

TLP-216.name: Anti-Centromere
TLP-216.meas: Antibodies against centromere proteins of the chromosomes, seen as a distinctive dotted pattern on the ANA slide or measured by ELISA.
TLP-216.sig: Anti-centromere antibody identifies the limited cutaneous form of systemic sclerosis (formerly CREST), which spares the trunk but carries a long-term risk of pulmonary arterial hypertension, so a positive result directs regular heart and lung screening rather than lung fibrosis surveillance.
TLP-216.ind: A positive result is consistent with limited systemic sclerosis and predicts calcinosis, Raynaud's, oesophageal reflux, telangiectasia and, over years, pulmonary hypertension; it also occurs in primary biliary cholangitis and Sjögren's overlap. A negative result does not exclude scleroderma.

fy.n: No anti-centromere antibodies were found, which makes the limited form of scleroderma less likely. If you have Raynaud's phenomenon without any other scleroderma antibody and normal nailfold capillaries, the chance of progressing to scleroderma is low, and a yearly review is usually sufficient.
fy.bhi: A borderline result that may represent a low level of true antibody or assay noise. Because the ANA slide pattern for centromere is very characteristic, your doctor may confirm it that way. If you have Raynaud's, reflux or telangiectasia, a rheumatology review is worthwhile; if not, a repeat in six to twelve months is reasonable.
fy.hi: Anti-centromere antibodies are present, a specific marker of limited scleroderma. This form progresses slowly and mainly affects fingers, face and gullet, but it carries a risk of high pressure in the lung arteries over the years, so a rheumatology referral with an annual echocardiogram and lung function tests is recommended, along with treatment for Raynaud's and reflux.

TLP-216.notes: IFA shows a discrete speckled (centromere) pattern; ELISA targets CENP-B with kit-specific cut-offs. Also positive in ~10–20% of primary biliary cholangitis. Nearly mutually exclusive with anti-Scl-70.
TLP-216.src: ACR/EULAR 2013 systemic sclerosis classification criteria; DETECT pulmonary hypertension screening algorithm
TLP-216.retest: A confirmed positive does not need repeating; annual echocardiography and pulmonary function tests are the follow-up.

TLP-217.name: Anti-RNA Polymerase III
TLP-217.dn: Anti-RNA polymerase III antibody (scleroderma renal-crisis marker)
TLP-217.alias: Anti-RNAP III, RNA pol III antibody, ARA
TLP-217.meas: Antibodies against RNA polymerase III, an enzyme in the nucleus, which define a distinct subset of systemic sclerosis.
TLP-217.sig: Anti-RNA polymerase III marks rapidly progressive diffuse skin thickening with the highest risk of scleroderma renal crisis, a sudden dangerous rise in blood pressure and kidney failure; it is also linked with a modestly increased chance of cancer around the time scleroderma begins. Knowing it early changes monitoring and drug choices.
TLP-217.ind: A positive result is consistent with diffuse systemic sclerosis and indicates a need for close blood pressure and kidney monitoring and age-appropriate cancer screening; it is rarely found in other diseases or in healthy people. A negative result does not exclude scleroderma.

fy.n: No anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies were found. This makes the subset of scleroderma with rapid skin thickening and kidney crisis less likely. Your Scl-70 and centromere results, and your symptoms, will guide whether further scleroderma assessment is needed.
fy.bhi: A weak signal in the borderline zone. Low-level results on this test can be non-specific and are usually confirmed by a second method before being acted on. If you have new skin tightening or Raynaud's, your doctor will arrange confirmation and a rheumatology review; otherwise a repeat in three to six months is sensible.
fy.hi: Anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies are present, a specific marker of scleroderma that tends to affect the skin quickly and can affect the kidneys suddenly. Regular home blood-pressure checks, prompt reporting of headaches or breathlessness, and avoiding high-dose steroids are important, and your doctor will discuss age-appropriate cancer screening. An early rheumatology referral is strongly advised.

TLP-217.notes: ELISA/CLIA cut-offs vary (e.g. < 20 U/mL negative, 20–39 weak); ANA is often only weakly positive with a fine speckled pattern, so this antibody must be requested specifically. Renal crisis risk is greatest in the first 4 years; steroid doses above 15 mg/day prednisolone increase it.
TLP-217.src: ACR/EULAR 2013 systemic sclerosis classification criteria; EULAR 2023 SSc recommendations
TLP-217.retest: A confirmed positive is not repeated; monitor blood pressure at least weekly at home in the first years and check kidney function every 3 months.

TLP-218.name: Scleroderma Overlap Panel (PM-Scl, U3-RNP, Th/To, Ku)
TLP-218.alias: Extended scleroderma antibodies, Anti-PM-Scl / fibrillarin / Th-To / Ku panel, Scleroderma immunoblot
TLP-218.meas: Four less common antibodies that define scleroderma variants overlapping with muscle inflammation or with prominent lung and pulmonary-vascular involvement.
TLP-218.sig: When the main scleroderma antibodies are negative, this panel catches the rarer subsets: PM-Scl and Ku point to scleroderma–myositis overlap, U3-RNP (fibrillarin) to diffuse disease with pulmonary hypertension and heart involvement, and Th/To to limited disease with lung fibrosis. Each changes what organs are screened.
TLP-218.ind: A positive component is consistent with a specific scleroderma subset: PM-Scl (myositis overlap, calcinosis, good prognosis), U3-RNP (diffuse disease, pulmonary hypertension, cardiac involvement), Th/To (limited skin, interstitial lung disease, pulmonary hypertension), Ku (myositis–scleroderma or lupus overlap). A negative panel does not exclude scleroderma.

fy.n: None of the four overlap antibodies was detected. Combined with negative Scl-70, centromere and RNA polymerase III results, an antibody-defined form of scleroderma is unlikely, although a small number of people have scleroderma without any recognised antibody, so your doctor will still be guided by examination and nailfold capillary findings.
fy.bhi: A weak band on the immunoblot for one of the antibodies. Weak bands are frequent and often not meaningful; they are usually confirmed by checking the ANA pattern (nucleolar staining supports PM-Scl, U3-RNP or Th/To) or repeating the blot. If you have muscle weakness, breathlessness or skin changes, mention them to your rheumatologist.
fy.hi: One or more overlap antibodies is positive; the report names which. PM-Scl or Ku suggests scleroderma with muscle inflammation, so muscle enzymes and strength will be checked; U3-RNP or Th/To suggests lung or pulmonary-artery involvement, so an echocardiogram, lung function tests and chest CT are arranged. A rheumatologist will build a monitoring plan around the specific antibody.

TLP-218.notes: Detected by line immunoassay (immunoblot) with band intensities graded negative, borderline (+), positive (++/+++); a nucleolar ANA pattern supports PM-Scl, U3-RNP and Th/To. These antibodies are not part of the 2013 classification criteria but guide organ screening.
TLP-218.src: EULAR 2023 SSc recommendations; EUSTAR / Nihtyanova & Denton antibody-subset reviews
TLP-218.retest: Confirm borderline bands with the ANA pattern or a repeat blot; a confirmed positive does not need serial testing.

TLP-219.name: Vitamin A (Retinol)
TLP-219.meas: The amount of retinol, the active form of vitamin A, circulating in your blood bound to its carrier protein.
TLP-219.sig: Vitamin A is essential for night vision, skin and mucous-membrane health and immune defence; deficiency causes night blindness, dry eyes and rough follicular skin, while excess from supplements is toxic to the liver and bones and dangerous in pregnancy. Serum retinol is held steady by liver stores, so it only falls once stores are nearly exhausted.
TLP-219.ind: Low retinol suggests dietary deficiency, fat malabsorption (coeliac disease, pancreatic or liver disease), zinc deficiency or the acute-phase response of infection. High levels almost always come from supplements, retinoid medicines or high-dose cod-liver oil, occasionally from kidney failure.

fy.lo: Your vitamin A is in the deficient range, which can cause poor night vision, dry gritty eyes, rough bumpy skin and more frequent infections. A diet low in yellow-orange vegetables, dairy and eggs, or a gut condition that hinders fat absorption, is usually behind it. Your doctor will guide replacement; avoid large self-prescribed doses, especially if pregnant.
fy.blo: Marginally low, which suggests your liver stores of vitamin A are running down. Carrots, pumpkin, sweet potato, dark leafy greens, milk, eggs and liver all top it up; a recent infection can also depress the reading temporarily. A repeat in two to three months after improving intake is the sensible check.
fy.n: Your vitamin A is within the healthy range, supporting normal vision, skin renewal and immunity. A varied diet keeps it there; avoid high-dose vitamin A supplements, which add nothing when the level is normal and can be harmful, especially in pregnancy.
fy.hi: Above the reference range, which nearly always reflects vitamin A supplements, cod-liver oil or retinoid medicines rather than diet. Persistent excess can cause headaches, dry peeling skin, hair loss, liver strain and bone thinning, and is harmful to an unborn baby. Stop any vitamin A supplement and discuss a repeat with your doctor.

TLP-219.notes: WHO defines deficiency as < 20 µg/dL (0.7 µmol/L); children under 5 use the same cut-off. Serum retinol falls transiently with infection (check CRP) and rises in chronic kidney disease. Protect the sample from light. Multiply by 0.0349 to convert to µmol/L.
TLP-219.src: WHO 2011 serum retinol indicators; Tietz Textbook of Clinical Chemistry
TLP-219.retest: Repeat 8–12 weeks after dietary change or supplementation, ideally when CRP is normal.

TLP-220.name: Vitamin E (α-Tocopherol)
TLP-220.meas: The concentration of alpha-tocopherol, the main active form of vitamin E, a fat-soluble antioxidant carried in the blood on lipoproteins.
TLP-220.sig: Vitamin E protects cell membranes and nerves from oxidative damage; deficiency is rare on a normal diet but occurs with fat malabsorption and causes nerve damage, unsteadiness and anaemia. Because it travels with cholesterol, the level should be read against your lipid results.
TLP-220.ind: Low vitamin E points to fat malabsorption (coeliac disease, cystic fibrosis, cholestatic liver disease, bariatric surgery), very low-fat diets or rare inherited transport defects. High levels reflect supplements, and very high intake can increase bleeding tendency, especially with anticoagulants.

fy.lo: Your vitamin E is low, which is uncommon and usually signals difficulty absorbing fats rather than a poor diet. Over time it can affect nerves and balance and make red cells fragile. Your doctor will look for a gut, pancreatic or liver cause and advise replacement; nuts, seeds, vegetable oils and green leaves are the main dietary sources.
fy.n: Your vitamin E is within the reference range, so antioxidant protection of your cells and nerves is adequate and fat absorption is likely to be normal. A diet including nuts, seeds and vegetable oils maintains this; extra vitamin E supplements offer no proven benefit when the level is normal.
fy.hi: Above the usual range, which in practice means a vitamin E supplement or a high blood-fat level carrying more of the vitamin. Large supplement doses can increase bleeding risk, particularly if you take blood thinners or aspirin, so review any supplement with your doctor and check your lipid results alongside.

TLP-220.notes: Deficiency threshold about 5 mg/L (12 µmol/L); vitamin E rises with cholesterol and triglycerides, so a tocopherol:cholesterol ratio < 2.2 mg/g better defines deficiency in hyperlipidaemia. Children have slightly lower values. Multiply by 2.32 to convert to µmol/L.
TLP-220.src: Tietz Textbook of Clinical Chemistry; ESPEN micronutrient guideline 2022
TLP-220.retest: Repeat with a lipid profile after 3 months of supplementation if deficient; not needed routinely once normal.

TLP-221.name: Selenium
TLP-221.meas: The concentration of selenium, a trace mineral built into antioxidant enzymes and the enzymes that activate thyroid hormone.
TLP-221.sig: Selenium supports thyroid hormone conversion, antioxidant defence, immunity, hair and nails; deficiency occurs with poor soil selenium, malabsorption and long-term tube or parenteral feeding, while excess from supplements causes hair loss, brittle nails and a garlic odour. It is checked in nutritional skin and hair conditions and in thyroid autoimmunity.
TLP-221.ind: Low selenium suggests inadequate intake, malabsorption, chronic kidney disease, cirrhosis or the acute-phase response of illness, and can contribute to hair loss, white nail bands and muscle weakness. High levels reflect supplement excess or occupational exposure.

fy.lo: Your selenium is in the deficient range, which can show as hair thinning, whitened or brittle nails, muscle aches and a sluggish thyroid response. Low-selenium soils, a restricted diet, gut malabsorption or kidney disease are typical causes. Your doctor may suggest a short supplement course; two or three Brazil nuts a day is a well-known dietary source.
fy.blo: Slightly under the optimal range, suggesting intake is marginal. Fish, eggs, poultry, whole grains, sunflower seeds and Brazil nuts raise it, and a recent illness can lower the reading temporarily. A repeat in two to three months after improving intake will show whether it has recovered.
fy.n: Your selenium is in the healthy range, adequate for antioxidant enzymes, thyroid hormone activation and hair and nail growth. A varied diet keeps it there; extra selenium supplements above dietary needs give no benefit and can be harmful.
fy.hi: Higher than the safe range, which almost always comes from supplements or very heavy Brazil-nut intake. Persistent excess can cause hair loss, nail changes, nausea, a garlic-like breath odour and nerve symptoms. Stop selenium-containing supplements, review your intake with your doctor and repeat the test in a few months.

TLP-221.notes: Reference intervals vary by region and method (roughly 60–70 to 130–150 µg/L); optimal glutathione-peroxidase activity is reached at about 90 µg/L. Serum selenium falls with inflammation, pregnancy and in chronic kidney disease. Multiply by 0.0127 to convert to µmol/L.
TLP-221.src: ESPEN micronutrient guideline 2022; Tietz Textbook of Clinical Chemistry
TLP-221.retest: Repeat after 8–12 weeks of dietary change or supplementation; interpret with CRP if recently unwell.

TLP-222.name: Vitamin B complex (B1/B2/B3/B6)
TLP-222.dn: Vitamin B complex panel (B1, B2, B3, B6)
TLP-222.alias: Thiamine / riboflavin / niacin / pyridoxine panel, B-vitamin profile
TLP-222.sample: EDTA whole blood and serum (protect from light)
TLP-222.meas: The status of four B vitamins, thiamine (B1), riboflavin (B2), niacin (B3) and pyridoxine (B6), each measured by its own assay and reported against its own reference interval.
TLP-222.sig: These B vitamins drive energy metabolism and skin, nerve and mucous-membrane health; deficiencies overlap in cracked lips, sore tongue, seborrhoeic-type rashes, pellagra-like sun-exposed dermatitis and tingling nerves, so they are assessed together in unexplained skin and neurological symptoms. Alcohol excess, malabsorption, isoniazid and dialysis are frequent causes.
TLP-222.ind: Low B1 suggests alcohol misuse, prolonged vomiting or refeeding and risks heart and brain injury; low B2 causes angular cheilitis and a scaly facial rash; low B3 causes pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia); low B6 causes a similar rash, neuropathy and anaemia, often from isoniazid or hydralazine. High B6 from supplements can itself cause nerve damage.

fy.lo: At least one of your B vitamins is deficient; the report shows which. Low B1, B2, B3 or B6 can cause cracked lips, a sore red tongue, scaly rashes on the face or sun-exposed skin, tingling feet or low energy. Alcohol, restricted diets, malabsorption and some medicines are common causes. Your doctor will advise targeted replacement and seek the cause.
fy.blo: One or more B vitamins is at the lower edge of normal, suggesting intake is only just keeping pace. Whole grains, pulses, dairy, eggs, meat, fish and green vegetables supply all four; if you drink alcohol regularly or follow a restrictive diet, that is the likely explanation. A repeat in two to three months after improving intake is reasonable.
fy.n: All four B vitamins are within their reference ranges, so a B-vitamin deficiency is unlikely to be behind your skin, mouth or nerve symptoms. A varied diet maintains this; high-dose B-complex supplements add nothing when levels are normal, and excess B6 can actually harm nerves.
fy.hi: One or more B vitamins is above its reference range, almost always because of supplements, energy drinks or fortified products. B1, B2 and B3 excess is generally harmless and excreted, but high vitamin B6 over months can cause numbness and unsteadiness. Review any supplement with your doctor and repeat the panel after stopping.

TLP-222.notes: No single unit: B1 as whole-blood thiamine diphosphate (approx. 70–180 nmol/L), B2 as whole-blood riboflavin or EGRAC (< 1.3 adequate), B3 as plasma niacin/nicotinamide or urinary N-methylnicotinamide, B6 as plasma pyridoxal-5-phosphate (approx. 20–125 nmol/L, deficient < 20). Ranges are method-specific and each component carries its own interval on the detailed report; inflammation lowers plasma B6.
TLP-222.src: ESPEN micronutrient guideline 2022; WHO/FAO vitamin requirements; Tietz
TLP-222.retest: Repeat the abnormal component(s) 8–12 weeks after replacement or after stopping supplements.

TLP-223.name: Essential Fatty Acid Profile
TLP-223.dn: Essential fatty acid profile (omega-3 / omega-6 balance)
TLP-223.alias: Fatty acid profile, Omega-3 index panel, Plasma / RBC fatty acids
TLP-223.meas: The proportions of individual fatty acids in your blood, including linoleic and alpha-linolenic acid (the true essentials), the omega-3s EPA and DHA, arachidonic acid, and the omega-6 to omega-3 ratio and omega-3 index derived from them.
TLP-223.sig: Essential fatty acid deficiency causes a scaly dermatitis, hair loss and poor wound healing and is seen with fat malabsorption, very low-fat diets and long-term parenteral nutrition; beyond deficiency, a low omega-3 index or a high omega-6 to omega-3 ratio reflects a pro-inflammatory pattern linked with eczema, dry skin and cardiovascular risk.
TLP-223.ind: A deficiency pattern (low linoleic acid, raised Mead acid, triene:tetraene ratio > 0.2) indicates true essential fatty acid deficiency from malabsorption or inadequate fat intake. An imbalance pattern (omega-3 index < 4%, omega-6:omega-3 ratio > 10) indicates low fish or omega-3 intake and high refined-oil intake. A balanced profile suggests adequate essential fat status.

rng.blo: Low omega-3 index / high omega-6:3 ratio (Suboptimal omega-3)
rng.hi: Very high omega-3 / supplement excess (Excess pattern)

fy.lo: Your profile shows a true essential fatty acid deficiency, which is uncommon and usually points to difficulty absorbing fat or a diet very low in fat, and can cause a dry scaly rash, hair thinning and slow healing. Your doctor will look for a gut, pancreatic or liver cause and advise on dietary fat or supplementation to restore the balance.
fy.blo: Your essential fats are adequate but the omega-3 share is low relative to omega-6, a pattern common with refined vegetable oils and little oily fish, and associated with a more inflammatory tendency in skin and blood vessels. Two portions of oily fish a week, or flaxseed, walnuts and chia for vegetarians, shift the balance within a few months.
fy.n: Your fatty acid profile is balanced: essential fats are adequate and the omega-3 to omega-6 proportion is in the healthy range, which supports skin barrier function and cardiovascular health. Keep it there with oily fish, nuts, seeds and limited deep-fried and refined-oil foods.
fy.hi: Your omega-3 fatty acids are well above the usual range, which reflects high-dose fish-oil supplementation rather than diet. Very high intake can prolong bleeding slightly and cause loose stools, so discuss the dose with your doctor, particularly if you take blood thinners or have surgery planned.

TLP-223.notes: No universal reference range; results are reported as percentage of total fatty acids by gas chromatography with lab-specific intervals. Key indices: omega-3 index (EPA+DHA in red cells) < 4% low, 4–8% intermediate, > 8% optimal; triene:tetraene ratio > 0.2 indicates essential fatty acid deficiency. Recent meals affect plasma more than red-cell profiles.
TLP-223.src: Harris & von Schacky omega-3 index; Holman triene:tetraene ratio; ESPEN 2022
TLP-223.retest: Recheck after 3–4 months of dietary change or supplementation, as red-cell fatty acids turn over slowly.

any.label: Suboptimal omega-3
any.text: Low omega-3 index / high omega-6:3 ratio

TLP-224.name: Serum Protein Electrophoresis (SPEP)
TLP-224.meas: The separation of your blood proteins into albumin and four globulin fractions on a gel, revealing whether any single abnormal antibody protein (an M-band or paraprotein) is present.
TLP-224.sig: Electrophoresis is the primary screen for plasma-cell disorders such as myeloma, MGUS and amyloidosis, which in older adults can present with unexplained itching, bone pain, anaemia, kidney impairment or recurrent infections. It also shows the broad, polyclonal rise of chronic inflammation or liver disease, and the low albumin of malnutrition and protein loss.
TLP-224.ind: A monoclonal band indicates a clone of plasma cells: most often MGUS (a benign precursor needing monitoring), less often myeloma, Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia or amyloidosis. A polyclonal gamma increase indicates chronic infection, autoimmune or liver disease; a low gamma region indicates antibody deficiency; low albumin indicates liver, kidney or nutritional causes.

rng.n: Normal pattern, no monoclonal band (Normal pattern)
rng.bhi: Polyclonal increase / equivocal band / other fraction abnormal (Non-specific abnormality)

fy.n: Your protein pattern is normal, with no sign of an abnormal antibody-producing clone and normal albumin. This makes myeloma and related conditions unlikely as a cause of itching, bone pain or anaemia. If suspicion remains, free light chains on this report add a further check.
fy.bhi: The pattern is altered but no single abnormal band is present. A broad rise in the antibody region usually reflects long-standing inflammation, infection or liver disease; a low albumin points to nutrition, liver or kidney causes; a faint uncertain band needs immunofixation to characterise it. Your doctor will decide which follow-up test fits.
fy.hi: A monoclonal band was found, meaning one clone of plasma cells is producing a single antibody protein. Most people with this have MGUS, a benign condition needing only periodic monitoring, but some have myeloma or a related disorder. Your doctor will arrange immunofixation, free light chains, a blood count, calcium and kidney tests, and a haematology referral.

TLP-224.notes: Reported as a pattern with fraction percentages and, when present, the M-protein quantity in g/dL (or g/L). Normal fractions approximately: albumin 3.5–5.0, alpha-1 0.2–0.4, alpha-2 0.5–0.9, beta 0.6–1.1, gamma 0.7–1.6 g/dL. Any suspected band is confirmed by immunofixation. Small bands can be missed in the beta region; free light chains improve sensitivity.
TLP-224.src: IMWG 2014 myeloma criteria; BSH 2013 guideline on investigation of paraproteins
TLP-224.retest: MGUS: repeat with free light chains at 6 months, then every 1–2 years if stable; sooner if bone pain, anaemia or kidney impairment develops.

any.label: Non-specific abnormality
any.text: Polyclonal increase / equivocal band / other fraction abnormal

TLP-225.name: Serum Free Light Chains
TLP-225.alias: sFLC, Free kappa and lambda, Freelite, Kappa/lambda ratio
TLP-225.meas: The amounts of free kappa and free lambda light chains, antibody fragments released into the blood by plasma cells, and the ratio between them, which is the key result.
TLP-225.sig: Because a plasma-cell clone makes only one light chain type, an abnormal kappa/lambda ratio detects clonal disease that electrophoresis can miss, especially light-chain myeloma and amyloidosis, and helps stage MGUS risk. It is also the most sensitive marker for tracking treatment response.
TLP-225.ind: A ratio above range (kappa excess) or below range (lambda excess) suggests a monoclonal plasma-cell disorder: MGUS, myeloma, AL amyloidosis or light-chain deposition disease. Both chains raised with a normal ratio reflects reduced kidney clearance or polyclonal activation from inflammation.

fy.lo: Your free lambda light chains are out of proportion to kappa, which suggests a clone of plasma cells making lambda chains. This ranges from harmless MGUS to conditions such as amyloidosis or myeloma. Your doctor will review it with the electrophoresis, a blood count, calcium and kidney function, and a haematology referral is usually the next step.
fy.n: Your kappa/lambda ratio is normal, which makes a clonal plasma-cell disorder unlikely, including the light-chain-only forms that electrophoresis can miss. If both chains are mildly raised together, that usually reflects kidney function or inflammation rather than a clone, and is not a concern in itself.
fy.hi: Your free kappa light chains are out of proportion to lambda, which suggests a clone of plasma cells producing kappa chains. Most often this is MGUS, which needs monitoring rather than treatment, but myeloma and amyloidosis must be considered, particularly with bone pain, anaemia, kidney impairment or unexplained itching. A haematology review with further tests is advised.

TLP-225.notes: Freelite reference: kappa 3.3–19.4 mg/L, lambda 5.7–26.3 mg/L, ratio 0.26–1.65; other platforms (N Latex) differ and are not interchangeable. In chronic kidney disease the renal reference range for the ratio is 0.37–3.1. A ratio ≥ 100 with involved chain ≥ 100 mg/L is a myeloma-defining event (IMWG 2014).
TLP-225.src: IMWG 2009/2014 free light chain guidelines; Katzmann et al. reference intervals
TLP-225.retest: Repeat with electrophoresis every 6–12 months in MGUS; every cycle during myeloma treatment to gauge response.

TLP-226.name: Serum β2-Microglobulin
TLP-226.meas: A small protein shed from the surface of almost all cells, especially white cells, which is filtered by the kidneys; its level reflects cell turnover and kidney clearance.
TLP-226.sig: In myeloma and lymphoma, beta-2-microglobulin reflects how much disease is present and is a core part of staging (it is the first factor in the International Staging System). Outside cancer it rises with reduced kidney filtration and with immune activation from infections or autoimmune disease.
TLP-226.ind: High levels point to myeloma, lymphoma or leukaemia, chronic kidney disease, chronic viral infections (HIV, hepatitis), autoimmune diseases or, occasionally, on dialysis, amyloid deposits. A low level has no clinical significance.

fy.n: Your beta-2-microglobulin is within range, which suggests no large burden of abnormal plasma cells or lymphocytes and normal kidney clearance. If a monoclonal protein was found elsewhere on this report, a normal value here is a favourable sign.
fy.bhi: Mildly raised, which most often reflects reduced kidney filtration (common with age, diabetes or high blood pressure) or general immune activation from a chronic infection or autoimmune condition. If a paraprotein is present, this level falls in the lower-risk staging group; your doctor will interpret it alongside your kidney function.
fy.hi: Clearly raised. In someone with a monoclonal protein this indicates a larger disease burden and places them in a higher staging group, prompting a haematology assessment. In someone without a paraprotein it usually reflects significant kidney impairment or a chronic inflammatory or viral condition, which your doctor will check with creatinine, eGFR and the wider picture.

TLP-226.notes: Reference approximately 0.8–2.4 mg/L (platform-dependent, some up to 2.7). Rises steeply as eGFR falls, so interpret with creatinine. International Staging System for myeloma: < 3.5 (stage I with albumin ≥ 3.5 g/dL), 3.5–5.5 (stage II), > 5.5 mg/L (stage III).
TLP-226.src: IMWG International Staging System (Greipp 2005 / R-ISS 2015); Tietz
TLP-226.retest: Repeat at diagnosis and staging of any plasma-cell disorder and with each reassessment; not needed serially otherwise.

TLP-227.name: Hydroxychloroquine Whole-Blood Level (LC-MS)
TLP-227.alias: HCQ level, Hydroxychloroquine concentration, Whole-blood HCQ
TLP-227.meas: The concentration of hydroxychloroquine in your whole blood, measured by mass spectrometry, reflecting how much of the medicine you have been taking over the past several weeks.
TLP-227.sig: Hydroxychloroquine levels vary widely between people on the same dose. A very low level reveals missed doses or poor absorption before disease flares, while a high level identifies those at greatest risk of the drug's rare retinal toxicity, so the test guides dose adjustment and eye-screening intensity in lupus, rheumatoid arthritis and cutaneous lupus.
TLP-227.ind: Undetectable or very low levels indicate non-adherence or malabsorption and are associated with disease flares. Levels above the target zone indicate accumulation, most often from dosing above 5 mg/kg/day or reduced kidney clearance, and are linked to higher retinopathy risk.

fy.lo: Very little hydroxychloroquine is in your blood, which almost always means doses have been missed over the past weeks, or occasionally that the tablets are not being absorbed. Without a steady level the medicine cannot protect you from flares. Please talk openly with your doctor about any difficulties taking it; a pill organiser or timing change often solves it.
fy.blo: Your level is below the range associated with the best disease control, suggesting some doses are missed, absorption is reduced, or the dose is on the low side for your body weight. Your doctor may review your dosing schedule or adherence and repeat the level in two to three months rather than adding other medicines.
fy.n: Your hydroxychloroquine level is in the target range, which means you are taking it consistently and the dose suits your body. This is the zone with the best balance of flare protection and low eye-toxicity risk. Keep taking it as prescribed and attend your routine annual eye screening.
fy.bhi: Slightly above the target range. This is not immediately dangerous, but levels in this zone are associated with a somewhat higher long-term risk to the retina, especially if kidney function is reduced or you have been on the drug for many years. Your doctor may fine-tune the dose and will ensure eye screening is up to date.
fy.hi: Your level is high, indicating the drug is accumulating, usually because the dose exceeds about 5 mg per kg of body weight or the kidneys clear it more slowly. This raises the risk of retinal damage, so your doctor will likely reduce the dose and may bring forward your eye examination. Do not stop the medicine on your own.

TLP-227.notes: No universally agreed therapeutic range; the 750–1200 ng/mL target derives from lupus cohort studies (Costedoat-Chancy, Durcan, Jorge) and the 2020 whole-blood consensus, with > 1500 ng/mL associated with higher retinopathy risk (Petri 2020). Levels reach steady state after about 3–6 months; sample at trough before the morning dose. Plasma/serum values are much lower and not comparable.
TLP-227.src: Petri et al. 2020 (Arthritis Rheumatol); Garg et al. 2021 systematic review; EULAR 2023 SLE recommendations
TLP-227.retest: Recheck 2–3 months after any dose change or adherence discussion; annually alongside eye screening in long-term users.

TLP-228.name: Cyclosporine Trough (C0)
TLP-228.alias: Ciclosporin trough, CsA C0, Cyclosporine pre-dose level
TLP-228.meas: The concentration of cyclosporine in whole blood taken just before the next dose, reflecting the lowest level your body reaches between doses.
TLP-228.sig: Cyclosporine has a narrow margin between effective and toxic, and its absorption varies widely, so trough monitoring keeps the level high enough to control psoriasis, eczema or urticaria while limiting the kidney damage and high blood pressure that rise with higher levels. It is read alongside creatinine and blood pressure at each visit.
TLP-228.ind: Low or undetectable levels suggest missed doses, poor absorption or an interacting drug that speeds metabolism (rifampicin, some anticonvulsants). High levels suggest a dose above requirements, reduced clearance or an interacting drug that slows metabolism (azoles, macrolides, calcium-channel blockers, grapefruit) and predict kidney toxicity.

fy.lo: Very little cyclosporine is in your blood before the dose, which suggests doses are being missed, the medicine is not being absorbed, or another drug is clearing it quickly. At this level it is unlikely to be controlling your skin condition. Discuss timing, missed doses and any new medicines with your doctor before any dose change.
fy.blo: Your trough is below the range usually aimed for in skin conditions. If your rash is well controlled, your doctor may be happy to keep the dose low, which is kinder to the kidneys; if it is not, a modest dose adjustment or a check on absorption and interacting medicines is the likely next step.
fy.n: Your cyclosporine level is in the range typically used for psoriasis, eczema and urticaria, balancing effect against kidney and blood-pressure side effects. Keep taking it at the same times each day, have creatinine and blood pressure checked as scheduled, and avoid grapefruit and new medicines without checking for interactions.
fy.bhi: Your level is above the usual range for skin conditions, which increases the chance of kidney strain, raised blood pressure, tremor and gum swelling. Common reasons are a dose at the higher end for your weight or a newly started interacting medicine such as an antifungal or antibiotic. Your doctor will review the dose and check creatinine and blood pressure.
fy.hi: Your level is high enough to carry a real risk of kidney injury and high blood pressure. This usually results from an interacting medicine, reduced kidney function or a dose above requirements. Contact your doctor soon for a dose review and a creatinine check; do not adjust or stop the medicine yourself.

TLP-228.notes: No universal therapeutic range: the 100–200 ng/mL band reflects usual practice for low-dose (2.5–5 mg/kg/day) dermatology use, whereas transplant targets are higher (150–300 ng/mL early, 50–150 later) and depend on the organ and time since transplant. Sample exactly 12 hours after the last dose, before the morning dose; LC-MS and immunoassay values differ. Interpret with creatinine (a rise > 30% from baseline prompts dose reduction).
TLP-228.src: BAD 2019 ciclosporin guideline (dermatology); transplant consensus (Ekberg/CAESAR) for comparison
TLP-228.retest: Check 1–2 weeks after starting or changing dose or after adding an interacting drug; every 4–8 weeks once stable, together with creatinine and blood pressure.

TLP-229.name: HBsAg - ELISA
TLP-229.alias: Hepatitis B surface antigen, Australia antigen, HBsAg screen
TLP-229.meas: Detects the outer-coat protein of the hepatitis B virus circulating in blood, which is present whenever the virus is actively replicating.
TLP-229.sig: HBsAg is the primary marker of current hepatitis B infection, whether recent or long-standing. Detecting it early allows monitoring of the liver, protection of household contacts and, in pregnancy, steps that prevent passing the virus to the baby.
TLP-229.ind: A reactive result indicates current hepatitis B infection – acute if recent, chronic if it persists beyond 6 months. A non-reactive result rules out active infection in most people; a low value has no meaning.

fy.n: A non-reactive result means no hepatitis B surface antigen was found, so there is no sign of active hepatitis B infection right now. If you have never been vaccinated, a simple three-dose course gives long-lasting protection – worth discussing at your next visit.
fy.bhi: Your result fell in the assay's grey zone – neither clearly negative nor positive. This usually reflects a very low signal or a non-specific reaction rather than true infection. The lab normally repeats the test and, if still unclear, your doctor may add a confirmatory or HBV DNA test.
fy.hi: A reactive result is consistent with hepatitis B infection in your blood. Many people feel entirely well; the virus may have been acquired years ago. Your doctor will usually add liver enzymes, HBV DNA and further markers, screen close contacts, and decide whether treatment or simply regular monitoring is right for you.

TLP-229.notes: In pregnancy a reactive result triggers newborn vaccine plus immunoglobulin at birth; recent hepatitis B vaccination (within ~3 weeks) can give a transient weak positive; S/CO cut-offs are assay-specific and initially reactive samples are repeated in duplicate before reporting.
TLP-229.src: WHO Hepatitis B guidelines 2024; CDC; NACO India testing guidelines
TLP-229.retest: If reactive, repeat HBsAg after 6 months – persistence defines chronic infection. Grey-zone results are repeated within 2–4 weeks.

TLP-230.name: Anti-HCV - ELISA
TLP-230.alias: HCV antibody, Hepatitis C screen, HCV Ab
TLP-230.meas: Detects antibodies your immune system has made against the hepatitis C virus, indicating exposure at some point.
TLP-230.sig: Hepatitis C is a silent, blood-transmitted infection that can scar the liver over decades yet is now curable with short oral treatment. Antibody screening is the first step in finding people who would benefit from that cure.
TLP-230.ind: A reactive antibody indicates past or present hepatitis C exposure; only an HCV RNA test can tell whether the virus is still active (about 1 in 4 people clear it spontaneously). False positives occur in low-risk populations and autoimmune conditions.

fy.n: No hepatitis C antibodies were detected, which makes past or current hepatitis C infection very unlikely. Antibodies take up to 8–12 weeks to appear, so if you had a possible exposure very recently your doctor may suggest repeating the test after that window.
fy.bhi: Your result sits in the indeterminate zone, which most often reflects a weak non-specific reaction rather than true infection. The sensible next step is an HCV RNA (PCR) test, which directly detects the virus and settles the question one way or the other.
fy.hi: A reactive antibody suggests you have been exposed to hepatitis C at some point. It does not by itself mean the virus is still present – roughly a quarter of people clear it on their own. Your doctor will order an HCV RNA test; if the virus is active, modern tablets cure over 95% of cases in 8–12 weeks.

TLP-230.notes: Antibody may be absent in the first 2–3 months after exposure and in severely immunosuppressed patients; a low S/CO (< 3–5, assay-dependent) has a higher false-positive rate and always needs RNA confirmation.
TLP-230.src: WHO Hepatitis C guidelines 2022; CDC 2020 HCV testing recommendations
TLP-230.retest: Reactive or indeterminate: HCV RNA within 2–4 weeks. Negative after a recent exposure: repeat at 12 weeks.

TLP-231.name: HIV - ELISA
TLP-231.alias: HIV Ag/Ab combo, HIV 4th generation ELISA, HIV I & II
TLP-231.meas: Detects antibodies to HIV-1 and HIV-2 together with the p24 viral protein, picking up infection from about 2–4 weeks after exposure.
TLP-231.sig: HIV is now a manageable long-term condition when found early, and treatment brings the virus to undetectable levels so it cannot be passed on. Screening in pregnancy, before marriage or before immune-suppressing treatment is standard practice.
TLP-231.ind: A reactive screen suggests HIV infection but must be confirmed by a second and third different assay (India's NACO three-test strategy) before any diagnosis is made. Non-reactive within the window period does not exclude very recent infection.

fy.n: Your screen is non-reactive – no HIV antibodies or antigen were found. With a 4th-generation test this is reliable from about 4 weeks after any exposure; if a possible exposure was more recent than that, a repeat at 6 weeks and 3 months gives full reassurance.
fy.bhi: An indeterminate result is not a diagnosis; it usually comes from a non-specific reaction, pregnancy, recent vaccination or autoimmune conditions. The lab will repeat the test and your doctor may add a different confirmatory assay or HIV RNA. Please do not draw conclusions until that is done.
fy.hi: A reactive screen means HIV infection is possible but not yet confirmed – screening tests are deliberately sensitive, and a small share of reactive results turn out to be false. The lab will run confirmatory tests; if confirmed, today's once-daily treatment gives a normal life expectancy. Counselling is available and results are strictly confidential.

TLP-231.notes: Window period 2–4 weeks for 4th-generation assays; babies under 18 months carry maternal antibody and need HIV DNA PCR instead; reactive results are only reported as positive after confirmation per NACO guidelines with pre- and post-test counselling.
TLP-231.src: NACO National HIV Testing Guidelines 2024; WHO consolidated HIV testing guidelines 2019; CDC
TLP-231.retest: Negative after a recent exposure: repeat at 6 weeks and 12 weeks. Reactive: confirmatory testing immediately, not a repeat of the same test.

TLP-232.name: VDRL / RPR
TLP-232.alias: Venereal Disease Research Laboratory test, Rapid Plasma Reagin, Non-treponemal syphilis test
TLP-232.meas: Detects non-specific 'reagin' antibodies produced during syphilis infection, reported as reactive or non-reactive with a titre if reactive.
TLP-232.sig: Syphilis is easily cured with penicillin but, untreated, can damage the heart, nerves and an unborn baby. Because the test titre rises and falls with disease activity, it is used both to screen and to follow treatment response.
TLP-232.ind: A reactive result suggests syphilis and must be confirmed with a treponemal test (TPHA/FTA-ABS). Biological false positives (usually low titre ≤ 1:8) occur in pregnancy, autoimmune disease, malaria, viral infections and older age.

fy.n: A non-reactive result means no syphilis antibodies were found, which is reassuring. Very early infection (first 3–4 weeks after a chancre) can be missed, so if you have had a recent exposure or a genital ulcer, your doctor may suggest repeating the test in a few weeks.
fy.bhi: Your screen is weakly reactive. At low titres this is often a 'biological false positive' from pregnancy, a recent viral illness, autoimmune conditions or age – but it can also be early or treated syphilis. A confirmatory treponemal test (TPHA) is the next step; please wait for it before worrying.
fy.hi: A clearly reactive result at this titre is consistent with active syphilis and will be confirmed with a treponemal test. If confirmed, treatment is straightforward and highly effective, partners should be tested, and the titre is rechecked over the following months to prove the infection has cleared.

TLP-232.notes: Reactive sera are titrated; a four-fold titre fall after treatment indicates cure. In pregnancy a reactive result requires urgent confirmation and treatment; a prozone (false negative at very high antibody levels) can occur in secondary syphilis – the lab dilutes samples when suspected.
TLP-232.src: CDC STI Treatment Guidelines 2021; NACO STI/RTI guidelines; WHO syphilis testing guidance
TLP-232.retest: Reactive: confirm with TPHA now and repeat titre at 6 and 12 months after treatment. Negative with recent exposure: repeat at 6 weeks.

TLP-233.name: Varicella IgG
TLP-233.alias: VZV IgG, Varicella zoster antibody, Chickenpox immunity
TLP-233.meas: Measures long-lasting IgG antibodies to varicella-zoster virus, showing whether you are immune to chickenpox from past infection or vaccination.
TLP-233.sig: Chickenpox during pregnancy can harm the baby and is more severe in adults, so knowing your immunity before conception, IVF or immune-suppressing treatment lets you be vaccinated in time. Immunity, once established, is usually lifelong.
TLP-233.ind: A positive IgG indicates immunity and requires no action. A negative result indicates susceptibility – vaccination is advised before pregnancy or before starting immunosuppressive drugs. Equivocal results are repeated or treated as non-immune.

fy.lo: No chickenpox antibodies were detected, so you are not currently protected. Some people who remember having chickenpox still test negative. If you are planning a pregnancy, IVF or immune-suppressing treatment, two doses of varicella vaccine, completed at least a month before conception, is the usual advice.
fy.blo: Your antibody level is borderline – too low to be sure you are protected. This can follow a single vaccine dose or a mild childhood infection long ago. Guidelines treat equivocal results as non-immune, so your doctor may repeat the test or simply recommend vaccination for certainty.
fy.n: A positive IgG confirms you are immune to chickenpox, from past infection or vaccination, and this protection is generally lifelong. No vaccine is needed. Immunity to chickenpox does not prevent shingles later in life, which is a separate consideration for adults over 50.

TLP-233.notes: Varicella vaccine is live and must not be given during pregnancy; a non-immune pregnant woman exposed to chickenpox should contact her doctor within 96 hours for immunoglobulin. Index cut-offs are assay-specific.
TLP-233.src: ACIP varicella recommendations 2007; RCOG Green-top Guideline 13; CDC
TLP-233.retest: Equivocal: repeat in 2–4 weeks or proceed to vaccination. Immune results need no repeat.

TLP-234.name: Rubella IgG
TLP-234.alias: Rubella antibody IgG, German measles immunity, Rubella immune status
TLP-234.meas: Quantifies long-term IgG antibodies to the rubella virus, showing whether past infection or MMR vaccination has left you protected.
TLP-234.sig: Rubella in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy causes congenital rubella syndrome – deafness, heart defects and cataracts – in most affected babies. Confirming immunity before conception is one of the most cost-effective preventive checks in prenatal care.
TLP-234.ind: IgG ≥ 10 IU/mL indicates immunity. Below 10 IU/mL indicates susceptibility and a need for MMR vaccination (before, never during, pregnancy). A high IgG on its own does not indicate recent infection – IgM and avidity testing are needed for that.

fy.lo: No protective rubella antibodies were found, so an infection during early pregnancy could harm a baby. The fix is simple: one dose of MMR vaccine, given at least 4 weeks before trying to conceive. If you are already pregnant, avoid contact with anyone with a rash-fever illness and have the vaccine after delivery.
fy.blo: Your rubella antibody is in the equivocal zone – present, but not clearly at a protective level. This often means waning immunity from childhood vaccination. Most guidelines advise a single MMR dose before pregnancy rather than repeated testing; your doctor can confirm which suits you.
fy.n: Your rubella IgG is at a protective level, so you are immune and a baby would be safe from congenital rubella. This immunity usually lasts a lifetime and needs no booster. There is no need to repeat this test in future pregnancies once immunity has been documented.

TLP-234.notes: MMR is a live vaccine and is avoided in pregnancy; women vaccinated should wait 4 weeks before conceiving. Some assays report 10–14.9 IU/mL as low-positive; a small number of vaccinated people never exceed 10 IU/mL despite being protected – re-vaccination beyond two documented doses is not recommended.
TLP-234.src: WHO rubella position paper 2020; ACOG; RCOG; CDC MMR recommendations
TLP-234.retest: Equivocal: retest 4–6 weeks after MMR, or accept vaccination without retest. Immune: no repeat needed.

TLP-235.name: Toxoplasma IgG
TLP-235.alias: Toxoplasmosis IgG, Toxo IgG, Toxoplasma gondii antibody
TLP-235.meas: Measures long-lasting IgG antibodies to Toxoplasma gondii, a parasite acquired from undercooked meat, unwashed produce or cat litter.
TLP-235.sig: Toxoplasma infection acquired for the first time during pregnancy can cross the placenta and affect the baby's brain and eyes, whereas infection before pregnancy is protective. IgG status therefore tells a woman whether she needs to take precautions or is already immune.
TLP-235.ind: A positive IgG indicates past infection with lasting immunity (or, with a positive IgM, possible recent infection – avidity testing then distinguishes). A negative IgG indicates susceptibility and a need for food and hygiene precautions in pregnancy.

fy.n: No toxoplasma antibodies were found, meaning you have never been infected and are not immune. That is the commonest result and nothing is wrong – it simply means that in pregnancy you should cook meat thoroughly, wash fruit and vegetables well, wear gloves for gardening and let someone else change the cat litter.
fy.bhi: Your IgG is equivocal – a low signal that could be very early infection, an old faint response or a non-specific reaction. If you are pregnant or planning to be, the test is repeated in 2–3 weeks along with IgM; a rise would suggest recent infection, a stable low result usually reflects past exposure.
fy.hi: A positive IgG shows you have had toxoplasma infection at some point – often years ago and without symptoms, as is common in India. If your IgM is negative this is old, immune-conferring exposure and poses no risk to a pregnancy. If IgM is also positive, an avidity test will help date the infection.

TLP-235.notes: IgG cut-offs vary by assay (values shown are for common CLIA platforms). In pregnancy a positive IgG with negative IgM needs no further action; IgG seroconversion between two samples during pregnancy indicates acute infection and warrants specialist referral.
TLP-235.src: ACOG Practice Bulletin 151; ECDC/ESCMID toxoplasma in pregnancy guidance; Remington's Infectious Diseases of the Fetus and Newborn
TLP-235.retest: Susceptible pregnant women: repeat each trimester if exposure risk is high. Equivocal: repeat with IgM in 2–3 weeks.

TLP-236.name: Toxoplasma IgM
TLP-236.meas: Detects the early IgM antibody response to Toxoplasma gondii that appears in the first weeks after infection.
TLP-236.sig: IgM is the marker used to look for a recent toxoplasma infection, which matters most in pregnancy because only a fresh infection can affect the baby. IgM can, however, linger for a year or more, so a positive result needs careful interpretation.
TLP-236.ind: A positive IgM raises the possibility of infection within the past few months but is also seen as persistent IgM from old infection or as a false positive; an IgG avidity test resolves this. A negative IgM with negative IgG confirms no recent infection.

fy.n: A negative IgM means there is no sign of a recent toxoplasma infection. Read together with your IgG: if IgG is also negative you are susceptible and should follow food and hygiene precautions in pregnancy; if IgG is positive, the infection is old and you are immune.
fy.bhi: An equivocal IgM is a weak signal that most often turns out to be a non-specific reaction rather than a new infection. The usual approach is to repeat IgM and IgG on a fresh sample in 2–3 weeks; a clear rise points to recent infection, while an unchanged or negative repeat is reassuring.
fy.hi: A positive IgM suggests toxoplasma infection could be recent, but this marker can persist for over a year and false positives are common, so it is not a diagnosis on its own. Your doctor will usually add an IgG avidity test – high avidity means the infection is older than 3–4 months and, in early pregnancy, reassuring.

TLP-236.notes: In pregnancy, a positive IgM before 16 weeks with low IgG avidity indicates possible acute infection and needs specialist referral; IgM positivity with negative IgG should be repeated in 2–3 weeks to check for seroconversion. Rheumatoid factor and other IgM antibodies can cause false positives.
TLP-236.src: ACOG Practice Bulletin 151; CDC toxoplasmosis laboratory guidance; ESCMID
TLP-236.retest: Positive or equivocal: repeat paired IgM/IgG with avidity in 2–3 weeks. Negative: no repeat unless new exposure.

TLP-237.name: Rubella IgM
TLP-237.alias: German measles IgM, Rubella antibody IgM
TLP-237.meas: Detects the short-lived IgM antibody that appears within days of a new rubella infection or recent MMR vaccination.
TLP-237.sig: Rubella IgM is the test for a current or very recent infection, the only situation in which rubella threatens an unborn baby. Because true rubella is now rare in vaccinated populations, a positive IgM is more often a false positive than genuine infection and must be interpreted with care.
TLP-237.ind: A positive IgM may indicate acute rubella (within ~8 weeks), recent MMR vaccination, or a false positive from other viral infections (parvovirus, EBV, CMV), rheumatoid factor or autoimmune disease. Negative IgM excludes recent infection in most cases.

fy.n: A negative rubella IgM means there is no evidence of recent rubella infection – the expected result for almost everyone. Your immunity status is shown by the IgG result: if that is protective, no further action is needed; if not, MMR vaccination before pregnancy is advised.
fy.bhi: An equivocal IgM is usually a weak cross-reaction from another recent viral illness or vaccination rather than rubella. If you are pregnant, or have had a rash or fever, your doctor may repeat IgM with IgG in 2–3 weeks; an unchanged result with stable IgG is reassuring.
fy.hi: A positive IgM raises the question of recent rubella, but most positives in people without a rash or known contact are false alarms from other infections or a recent MMR dose. If you are pregnant this needs prompt review – a repeat sample, IgG avidity and sometimes PCR settle it. Please do not act on this result alone.

TLP-237.notes: Only order in pregnancy when there is a rash illness or contact with a case; unsolicited positive IgM in a woman with high-avidity IgG is almost always a false positive. IgM can persist for several weeks after MMR vaccination.
TLP-237.src: PHE/UKHSA rubella in pregnancy guidance 2019; CDC Manual for Surveillance of Vaccine-Preventable Diseases; WHO rubella lab manual
TLP-237.retest: Positive or equivocal: repeat with IgG and avidity in 2–3 weeks. Negative: no repeat unless a rash illness or exposure occurs.

TLP-238.name: CMV IgG
TLP-238.meas: Detects long-lasting IgG antibodies to cytomegalovirus, a common herpes-family virus that most Indian adults have acquired silently in childhood.
TLP-238.sig: CMV is the commonest infectious cause of hearing loss and developmental problems in newborns, almost always following a first infection in the mother during pregnancy. IgG status shows whether a woman is already immune or still susceptible, and helps interpret a positive IgM.
TLP-238.ind: A positive IgG indicates past infection; the virus stays dormant for life, and reactivation in pregnancy carries a much lower risk than primary infection. A negative IgG indicates susceptibility – hygiene measures around young children's saliva and urine reduce the risk.

fy.n: No CMV antibodies were found, so you have never had this virus and are not immune. Nothing is wrong, but in pregnancy it is worth reducing exposure: wash hands after nappy changes or wiping a toddler's nose, avoid sharing cups or cutlery with young children, and do not kiss them on the lips.
fy.bhi: Your CMV IgG is equivocal – a faint signal that may be early seroconversion or a non-specific reaction. If you are pregnant or planning IVF, the test is usually repeated with IgM in 2–3 weeks; a rise would indicate recent infection, a stable low result usually means old exposure or nothing at all.
fy.hi: A positive IgG shows you have had CMV in the past – true for roughly 9 in 10 Indian adults – and the virus now lies dormant. With a negative IgM this is old exposure and poses little risk to a pregnancy. If IgM is also positive, an avidity test helps decide whether the infection was recent.

TLP-238.notes: Seroprevalence in India exceeds 85–95%, so a positive IgG is expected; CMV IgG is also checked before organ transplant and immunosuppressive therapy to guide monitoring. Index cut-offs are assay-specific.
TLP-238.src: ACOG Practice Bulletin 151; SMFM consult series on CMV 2016; ESCMID
TLP-238.retest: Susceptible women planning pregnancy: repeat only if symptoms or known exposure. Equivocal: repeat with IgM in 2–3 weeks.

TLP-239.name: CMV IgM
TLP-239.meas: Detects the early IgM antibody response to cytomegalovirus, present during and for some months after a new infection or a reactivation.
TLP-239.sig: CMV IgM is used to look for a recent infection, the situation in which the virus can cross the placenta. Because IgM also appears with reactivation and can persist for a year, a positive result needs IgG avidity testing before any conclusion about pregnancy risk.
TLP-239.ind: A positive IgM may reflect primary infection within the past few months, reactivation of old infection, or a false positive from EBV, parvovirus or rheumatoid factor. Negative IgM with positive IgG indicates old, latent infection; negative IgM with negative IgG indicates no infection.

fy.n: A negative IgM means there is no sign of a recent or reactivated CMV infection. Your IgG result tells the rest of the story: positive IgG means old, dormant infection that carries little risk, while negative IgG means you are susceptible and should follow simple hygiene measures around young children.
fy.bhi: An equivocal IgM is a weak signal that is more often a cross-reaction from another recent viral illness than true CMV. If you are pregnant or undergoing fertility treatment, a repeat IgM with IgG and avidity in 2–3 weeks will clarify; an unchanged result with high-avidity IgG is reassuring.
fy.hi: A positive IgM suggests CMV activity possibly recent, but this marker persists for months and also appears with harmless reactivation, so on its own it does not mean a new infection. The next step is an IgG avidity test – high avidity indicates infection older than about 4 months. In pregnancy your doctor may involve a fetal medicine specialist.

TLP-239.notes: In pregnancy, positive IgM with low IgG avidity before 14–16 weeks suggests primary infection and warrants specialist referral; routine CMV screening is not universally recommended, so results are best interpreted alongside symptoms and exposure history.
TLP-239.src: SMFM consult series on CMV 2016; ACOG Practice Bulletin 151; ECCI consensus on congenital CMV 2017
TLP-239.retest: Positive or equivocal: IgG avidity now and repeat paired serology in 2–3 weeks. Negative: no repeat unless new illness.

TLP-240.name: H. pylori IgG Antibody
TLP-240.alias: Helicobacter pylori IgG, H. pylori serology
TLP-240.meas: Detects IgG antibodies to Helicobacter pylori, the stomach bacterium linked to gastritis, ulcers and, over decades, stomach cancer.
TLP-240.sig: H. pylori infects over half of Indian adults and is the main preventable cause of peptic ulcers and gastric cancer. Antibody testing is a convenient first screen, but because antibodies remain for years after the bacterium is gone, it cannot distinguish current from past infection.
TLP-240.ind: A positive IgG indicates current or past H. pylori infection; active infection is confirmed by stool antigen or urea breath test before treatment. A negative result makes infection unlikely in someone never treated. Serology is not used to check cure.

fy.n: No H. pylori antibodies were detected, so infection with this stomach bacterium is unlikely – a good result for long-term gut health. If you have persistent indigestion or upper-abdominal pain despite this, other causes such as acid reflux, medication effects or diet are worth discussing with your doctor.
fy.bhi: Your antibody level is equivocal – neither clearly positive nor negative. This can reflect early infection, a fading response after past clearance or a non-specific reaction. If you have symptoms, a stool antigen test or urea breath test gives a definite answer about active infection and is the sensible next step.
fy.hi: A positive antibody shows you have been infected with H. pylori at some point. Because antibodies persist for years, it does not prove the bacterium is still there. If you have symptoms or a family history of stomach cancer, your doctor will usually confirm active infection with a stool antigen or breath test before prescribing a course of eradication treatment.

TLP-240.notes: Serology remains positive for 1–3 years after successful eradication, so it must not be used to confirm cure; stool antigen and urea breath test require stopping acid-suppressants (PPIs) for 2 weeks and antibiotics for 4 weeks. Indian seroprevalence is high (~60–80%), so a positive result is common.
TLP-240.src: Maastricht VI/Florence consensus 2022; ACG Clinical Guideline on H. pylori 2024; ISG (Indian Society of Gastroenterology) guidelines
TLP-240.retest: Positive: confirm activity with stool antigen or breath test. After treatment: test of cure by breath or stool test at ≥ 4 weeks, not by repeating this antibody.

TLP-241.name: Malaria Rapid Antigen (Pf/Pv)
TLP-241.dn: Malaria rapid antigen test (P. falciparum / P. vivax)
TLP-241.alias: Malaria RDT, Malaria antigen card test, HRP-2 / pLDH test
TLP-241.meas: Detects malaria parasite proteins (HRP-2 for P. falciparum, pLDH for P. vivax) in blood within about 15 minutes, identifying which species is present.
TLP-241.sig: Falciparum malaria can become life-threatening within a day or two, so a rapid answer matters. The antigen test is fast and species-specific, and is read alongside the blood smear, which remains the reference method and quantifies the parasite load.
TLP-241.ind: A positive result indicates current malaria of the species shown. HRP-2 can stay positive for 2–4 weeks after successful treatment, so it is not used to check cure. A negative result in a very low parasite count or in HRP-2-deleted strains can be falsely negative.

rng.n: Negative for Pf and Pv antigens (Negative)
rng.hi: Positive – P. falciparum, P. vivax or mixed (Positive)

fy.n: No malaria antigens were detected, making malaria an unlikely cause of your fever. If fever continues in a malaria season or after travel, a repeat test with a blood smear every 12–24 hours for two or three days is standard, because parasites can be too few to detect on the first day.
fy.hi: A positive result is consistent with active malaria of the species shown. Vivax malaria is usually milder but can relapse from dormant liver forms; falciparum malaria can worsen quickly and needs treatment the same day. Your doctor will confirm with the smear, start the right antimalarial promptly and arrange follow-up blood tests.

TLP-241.notes: HRP-2 antigen may persist 2–4 weeks after cure (a positive test after recent treatment does not mean failure); very high parasite loads can rarely cause a false negative (prozone). Pregnant women and children under 5 with positive results need urgent review.
TLP-241.src: NVBDCP / NCVBDC India National Malaria Treatment Guidelines 2023; WHO Guidelines for Malaria 2024
TLP-241.retest: Negative with ongoing fever: repeat with smear every 12–24 h for 48–72 h. After treatment: smear (not RDT) on day 3, 7 and 28 to confirm clearance.

any.label: Negative
any.text: Negative for Pf and Pv antigens

any.label: Positive
any.text: Positive – P. falciparum, P. vivax or mixed

TLP-242.name: Malaria Parasite Smear (MP)
TLP-242.alias: MP smear, Thick and thin blood film for malaria, Peripheral smear for malaria parasite
TLP-242.meas: Microscopic examination of stained thick and thin blood films to look for malaria parasites inside red cells, identify the species and estimate how many red cells are infected.
TLP-242.sig: The blood smear is the gold-standard malaria test: it confirms infection, names the species, stages the parasite and gives a parasite count that guides how urgently and where you are treated. It is also the only test that reliably tracks clearance after treatment.
TLP-242.ind: Parasites seen indicates active malaria; the species (P. falciparum, P. vivax, mixed) and parasitaemia percentage indicate severity – ≥ 2–5% falciparum parasitaemia, or any gametocytes/schizonts of falciparum, signal higher risk. No parasites seen does not fully exclude malaria at low counts.

rng.n: No malaria parasites seen (No parasites seen)
rng.bhi: Parasites seen, < 2% red cells infected (Low parasitaemia)
rng.hi: Parasites seen, ≥ 2% red cells infected or severe-malaria features (High parasitaemia)

fy.n: No malaria parasites were seen on careful examination of your blood film. A single negative smear does not completely exclude malaria when parasite numbers are low, so if fever with chills persists, your doctor will usually repeat the smear every 12–24 hours for two or three days before ruling it out.
fy.bhi: Malaria parasites were seen at a low level, confirming infection of the species reported. Most people at this parasite count are treated at home with a full course of tablets and feel better within 2–3 days. Take every dose, and if vivax is reported, a follow-on medicine to clear dormant liver forms prevents relapse.
fy.hi: A high parasite count, or features of severe malaria, were seen on your film. This is more serious, particularly with falciparum, and usually needs treatment in hospital with injectable medicine and close monitoring of blood counts, sugar and kidney function. Please see your doctor or go to an emergency department today.

TLP-242.notes: Parasitaemia ≥ 2% in a non-immune person, or ≥ 5% in any patient, is a WHO severe-malaria criterion; other severe features (impaired consciousness, jaundice, low haemoglobin, kidney injury) override the count. Pregnant women and young children are treated as high risk at any count.
TLP-242.src: WHO Guidelines for Malaria 2024; NCVBDC (NVBDCP) India National Treatment Guidelines 2023; WHO Basic Malaria Microscopy
TLP-242.retest: Negative with ongoing fever: repeat every 12–24 h for 48–72 h. After treatment: repeat smear on days 3, 7 and 28 to confirm clearance.

any.label: High parasitaemia
any.text: Parasites seen, ≥ 2% red cells infected or severe-malaria features

TLP-243.name: Dengue NS1 Antigen
TLP-243.alias: Dengue NS1, NS1 antigen ELISA, Dengue early antigen
TLP-243.meas: Detects the non-structural protein 1 released by the dengue virus into blood during the first week of illness, before antibodies appear.
TLP-243.sig: NS1 is the earliest dengue marker – positive from day 1 of fever – allowing a diagnosis days before antibody tests turn positive. Early recognition lets you and your doctor watch platelet counts and warning signs through the critical phase around days 4–7.
TLP-243.ind: A positive NS1 indicates current dengue infection. Sensitivity is highest on days 1–5 and falls after day 5, especially in a second dengue infection, so a negative NS1 late in the illness does not exclude dengue – IgM should then be checked.

fy.n: No dengue NS1 antigen was detected. In the first five days of fever this makes dengue less likely, though not impossible; after day five the antigen naturally fades and a dengue IgM test becomes the better check. If fever continues, keep fluids up and let your doctor know about any bleeding, severe abdominal pain or persistent vomiting.
fy.bhi: Your NS1 result is equivocal – a weak signal that may be very early or fading infection, or a non-specific reaction. The sensible next step is a repeat NS1 with dengue IgM in 2–3 days and a platelet count. Meanwhile drink plenty of fluids, use paracetamol rather than ibuprofen or aspirin for fever, and watch for warning signs.
fy.hi: A positive NS1 is consistent with current dengue infection. Most people recover with rest and plenty of fluids, but platelet counts can fall around days 4–7, so your doctor will usually check a blood count every 1–2 days. Use only paracetamol for fever, avoid aspirin and ibuprofen, and seek care urgently for bleeding, severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting or drowsiness.

TLP-243.notes: Sensitivity ~90% on days 1–3, falling to 60–70% by day 5–7 and lower in secondary infections; NS1 does not distinguish serotypes. Results are interpreted with the day of fever, platelet count and haematocrit per national guidelines.
TLP-243.src: WHO Dengue Guidelines 2009 (rev. 2011); NCVBDC India National Guidelines for Clinical Management of Dengue 2023; CDC dengue laboratory guidance
TLP-243.retest: Negative on day 1–2 with persisting fever: repeat NS1 at day 3–5, then IgM after day 5. Positive: no repeat needed; monitor platelets daily through the critical phase.

TLP-244.name: Widal — S. typhi O
TLP-244.dn: Widal test – S. typhi O antibody
TLP-244.alias: Widal TO titre, Typhoid O antigen titre, Salmonella typhi O agglutinin
TLP-244.meas: Measures antibodies against the O (body) antigen of Salmonella typhi by tube agglutination, reported as the highest dilution that still clumps.
