TLP-244.sig: The O antibody rises about 7–10 days into typhoid fever and falls after recovery, so it is the Widal component that best reflects a recent infection. Because many Indians carry background antibody from past exposure or vaccination, only a high or rising titre is meaningful.
TLP-244.ind: An O titre ≥ 1:160, or a four-fold rise between paired samples 7–10 days apart, suggests active typhoid fever. Lower titres are common in healthy people in endemic areas. A negative titre in the first week of fever does not exclude typhoid – blood culture is the definitive test.

fy.n: Your S. typhi O antibody is below the level considered significant, so this test gives no support for typhoid fever. Widal can be negative in the first week of illness, however, so if fever continues, your doctor may repeat it in 7–10 days or, better, send a blood culture, which detects the bacteria directly.
fy.bhi: An O titre at this level is borderline. In India many healthy people have background antibody at this titre from past exposure or typhoid vaccination, so on its own it does not confirm typhoid. A repeat test after 7–10 days showing a four-fold rise, or a blood culture, is needed before treating.
fy.hi: A high O antibody titre, with a fever lasting more than a few days, is consistent with typhoid fever. It is not proof – recent vaccination, past infection and cross-reacting infections such as malaria or dengue can also raise it – so your doctor may confirm with a blood culture and decide on antibiotics from the whole picture.

TLP-244.notes: Widal is unreliable in the first 5–7 days of fever, after antibiotics, and in vaccinated people; a single titre has limited value in endemic India and paired sera showing a four-fold rise are preferred. Blood culture (or bone marrow culture) remains the reference standard, and Typhi Dot IgM is more useful in week 1.
TLP-244.src: ICMR / IAP guidelines on enteric fever; WHO Background document on typhoid fever 2003; Mackie & McCartney Practical Medical Microbiology
TLP-244.retest: Repeat with a paired sample 7–10 days after the first to look for a four-fold rise; a single titre should not be used to start or stop antibiotics.

TLP-245.name: Widal — S. typhi H
TLP-245.dn: Widal test – S. typhi H antibody
TLP-245.alias: Widal TH titre, Typhoid H antigen titre, Salmonella typhi H agglutinin
TLP-245.meas: Measures antibodies against the H (flagellar) antigen of Salmonella typhi, reported as the highest serum dilution that agglutinates.
TLP-245.sig: H antibodies appear slightly after O antibodies but persist for months to years after infection or vaccination, so they show past exposure more than current illness. A raised H titre is interpreted alongside the O titre – both raised together strengthens suspicion of typhoid.
TLP-245.ind: An H titre ≥ 1:160, especially with a raised O titre or a four-fold rise on paired samples, supports typhoid fever. An isolated raised H titre with a normal O titre most often reflects old infection or vaccination rather than current disease (the 'anamnestic' reaction).

fy.n: Your S. typhi H antibody is not raised, which offers no support for typhoid fever and also suggests no recent vaccination or past typhoid. Because antibodies take a week or more to develop, a persisting fever should still be reviewed by your doctor, who may prefer a blood culture over repeating the Widal.
fy.bhi: An H titre at this level is borderline and, on its own, more likely reflects an old infection, past typhoid vaccination or an unrelated fever nudging antibody up. It becomes meaningful only if the O titre is also raised or a repeat sample in 7–10 days shows a clear rise – your doctor will interpret it with your other results.
fy.hi: A high H antibody titre can occur in typhoid fever, but because H antibodies last for months to years, it can equally reflect a past infection or vaccination. Read together with the O titre and your symptoms, it helps your doctor decide whether typhoid is likely; a blood culture is the most reliable way to confirm before antibiotics.

TLP-245.notes: H titres stay elevated long after recovery or Vi/whole-cell vaccination and rise non-specifically during other fevers (anamnestic response); a raised H with normal O titre rarely indicates current typhoid. Interpretive cut-offs vary by region, and a four-fold rise on paired sera is more reliable than any single value.
TLP-245.src: ICMR / IAP guidelines on enteric fever; WHO Background document on typhoid fever 2003; Mackie & McCartney Practical Medical Microbiology
TLP-245.retest: Repeat with a paired sample 7–10 days later if the diagnosis is still open; a single H titre should not guide antibiotic decisions.

TLP-246.name: Widal — S. paratyphi AH
TLP-246.dn: Widal test – S. paratyphi A (AH) antibody
TLP-246.alias: Widal AH titre, Paratyphoid A H agglutinin
TLP-246.meas: Measures antibodies against the flagellar (H) antigen of Salmonella paratyphi A, the second most common cause of enteric fever in India.
TLP-246.sig: Paratyphoid A causes an illness almost identical to typhoid and is increasingly common in South Asia, yet it is not covered by the standard typhoid vaccine. The AH titre is the Widal component that points to this organism rather than S. typhi.
TLP-246.ind: An AH titre ≥ 1:160, or a four-fold rise on paired sera, suggests paratyphoid A fever. Lower titres are common background findings in endemic regions. Cross-reaction with S. typhi H antibody can produce a modest rise even in true typhoid.

fy.n: Your paratyphi A antibody is not raised, so there is no serological support for paratyphoid A fever. As with the other Widal components, antibodies can lag a week behind symptoms; if fever persists, a blood culture or a repeat Widal in 7–10 days is the sensible next step your doctor may suggest.
fy.bhi: A borderline AH titre is a weak signal that can come from past exposure, cross-reaction with typhoid antibodies or another current infection. It does not by itself confirm paratyphoid fever; a repeat paired sample showing a four-fold rise, or a positive blood culture, would be needed before treatment is based on it.
fy.hi: A high AH titre is consistent with paratyphoid A fever, an illness very similar to typhoid that the usual typhoid vaccine does not prevent. Because Widal results can be raised by past infection or cross-reaction, your doctor may confirm with a blood culture and will choose antibiotics based on your symptoms and local resistance patterns.

TLP-246.notes: Paratyphi A accounts for up to 20–30% of enteric fever in parts of India; there is no O-antigen component for paratyphi A in the standard Widal kit, so AH is the sole marker. Cut-offs are population-dependent and paired sera 7–10 days apart are preferred over a single titre.
TLP-246.src: ICMR / IAP guidelines on enteric fever; WHO Background document on typhoid fever 2003; Mackie & McCartney Practical Medical Microbiology
TLP-246.retest: Repeat with a paired sample 7–10 days later to look for a four-fold rise; blood culture in the first week is more reliable.

TLP-247.name: Widal — S. paratyphi BH
TLP-247.dn: Widal test – S. paratyphi B (BH) antibody
TLP-247.alias: Widal BH titre, Paratyphoid B H agglutinin
TLP-247.meas: Measures antibodies against the flagellar (H) antigen of Salmonella paratyphi B, a less common cause of enteric fever.
TLP-247.sig: Paratyphoid B is uncommon in India but produces the same prolonged fever as typhoid and needs the same treatment. The BH titre completes the Widal panel so that the three main enteric fever organisms are covered.
TLP-247.ind: A BH titre ≥ 1:160, or a four-fold rise on paired sera, suggests paratyphoid B fever. An isolated modest BH rise more often reflects cross-reaction with other Salmonella antibodies or past exposure than current infection.

fy.n: Your paratyphi B antibody is not raised – the expected result, as this organism is an uncommon cause of fever in India. It provides no support for paratyphoid B infection. If your fever continues without a clear cause, your doctor may suggest a blood culture, which looks for the bacteria themselves rather than antibodies.
fy.bhi: A borderline BH titre is most often a cross-reaction from other Salmonella antibodies, past exposure or an unrelated infection rather than paratyphoid B itself. It becomes meaningful only if it rises four-fold on a repeat sample in 7–10 days or is backed by a positive blood culture, so your doctor will read it alongside the rest of the panel.
fy.hi: A high BH titre, with a fever of several days, is consistent with paratyphoid B fever, which behaves and is treated like typhoid. Because this organism is rare and cross-reactions are possible, your doctor may confirm with a blood culture before deciding on antibiotics; the whole Widal panel and your symptoms guide that decision.

TLP-247.notes: Paratyphi B is responsible for a small minority of enteric fever cases in India; isolated BH elevation should prompt consideration of cross-reactivity with non-typhoidal Salmonella. Paired sera and blood culture remain the reference approach.
TLP-247.src: ICMR / IAP guidelines on enteric fever; WHO Background document on typhoid fever 2003; Mackie & McCartney Practical Medical Microbiology
TLP-247.retest: Repeat with a paired sample 7–10 days later if enteric fever is still suspected; do not act on a single borderline titre.

TLP-248.name: Dengue IgM
TLP-248.alias: Dengue IgM ELISA, Dengue MAC-ELISA, Anti-dengue IgM
TLP-248.meas: Detects IgM antibodies against the dengue virus, which appear from about day 4–5 of fever and remain for 2–3 months.
TLP-248.sig: IgM is the dengue test that becomes reliable after the NS1 antigen fades, so together the two cover the whole illness. A positive IgM confirms recent dengue and identifies people who need platelet monitoring through the critical phase.
TLP-248.ind: A positive IgM indicates dengue infection within the past 2–3 months – usually the current illness. It may be negative in the first 3–4 days of fever and can be weak in a secondary infection (where IgG rises faster). Cross-reaction with chikungunya, Zika or other flaviviruses can occur.

fy.n: No dengue IgM was found. If you are within the first four days of fever this does not rule dengue out, because antibodies have not had time to form – the NS1 result covers that window. If fever continues beyond day five with a negative IgM and NS1, dengue becomes unlikely and other causes should be considered.
fy.bhi: An equivocal IgM is a weak signal – possibly the earliest rise of antibodies, or a cross-reaction with a related virus such as chikungunya. A repeat IgM (with IgG) in 3–5 days usually clarifies. In the meantime, keep well hydrated, use paracetamol only, and report bleeding, severe abdominal pain or persistent vomiting promptly.
fy.hi: A positive IgM is consistent with dengue infection, most likely the current illness. Most people recover fully with rest and fluids, but platelet counts can change around days 4–7, so your doctor will usually check a blood count every 1–2 days. Avoid aspirin and ibuprofen, and seek urgent care for bleeding, severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting or drowsiness.

TLP-248.notes: IgM appears day 4–5 and persists 2–3 months, so a positive result after a recent past dengue episode may not reflect current illness; in secondary dengue IgM may be low or absent while IgG is high. Interpretation always uses day of fever, NS1 and platelet trend together.
TLP-248.src: WHO Dengue Guidelines 2009 (rev. 2011); NCVBDC India National Guidelines for Clinical Management of Dengue 2023; CDC dengue laboratory guidance
TLP-248.retest: Negative before day 5 with persisting fever: repeat IgM at day 5–7. Equivocal: repeat with IgG in 3–5 days.

TLP-249.name: Dengue IgG
TLP-249.dn: Dengue IgG antibody (past or secondary dengue)
TLP-249.meas: Detects long-lasting IgG antibodies against dengue virus, which appear late in a first infection and rise very early and high in a second one.
TLP-249.sig: A second dengue infection with a different serotype carries a higher risk of severe disease, and the pattern of IgG is what reveals it: high IgG within the first week of fever points to secondary dengue. Outside an acute illness, IgG simply records past exposure.
TLP-249.ind: IgG positive with IgM positive early in illness suggests secondary dengue (higher risk of plasma leak). IgG positive with IgM negative and no fever indicates past infection. IgG negative with positive NS1 or IgM indicates a primary infection.

fy.n: No dengue IgG was detected, so there is no evidence of a past dengue infection. If NS1 or IgM is positive, this is your first dengue episode, which is usually milder than a repeat one. Mosquito protection remains important, because a future infection with a different dengue type can be more severe.
fy.bhi: An equivocal IgG is a weak signal that may be early antibody in a current infection or faint memory from long-ago exposure. On its own it needs no action. If you currently have fever, a repeat IgG with IgM in 3–5 days shows whether it is rising, helping your doctor judge whether this is a first or repeat infection.
fy.hi: A positive IgG shows you have had dengue before – common for adults in Hyderabad. If you currently have fever and NS1 or IgM is also positive, this suggests a secondary infection with a somewhat higher chance of complications around days 4–7, so your doctor will monitor platelets more closely. Without fever it simply records past exposure.

TLP-249.notes: IgG persists for life after infection and cross-reacts with other flaviviruses (Japanese encephalitis, Zika, yellow fever vaccine); a high IgG within 7 days of fever onset is the serological hallmark of secondary dengue. Dengue vaccine, if received, also produces IgG.
TLP-249.src: WHO Dengue Guidelines 2009 (rev. 2011); NCVBDC India National Guidelines for Clinical Management of Dengue 2023; CDC dengue laboratory guidance
TLP-249.retest: During acute fever: paired IgG/IgM 3–5 days apart to distinguish primary from secondary infection. Otherwise no repeat needed.

TLP-250.name: Chikungunya IgM
TLP-250.alias: Chikungunya IgM ELISA, CHIKV IgM, Anti-chikungunya IgM
TLP-250.meas: Detects IgM antibodies to chikungunya virus, which appear from about day 4–7 of illness and persist for several months.
TLP-250.sig: Chikungunya shares mosquito, season and early symptoms with dengue but is distinguished by severe, often prolonged joint pain. Confirming it explains lingering joint symptoms, avoids unnecessary dengue-style monitoring and guides treatment of the arthritis.
TLP-250.ind: A positive IgM indicates chikungunya infection within the past 3–4 months – usually the current fever-with-joint-pain illness. A negative IgM in the first 4–5 days of fever does not exclude it (PCR is the test then). Occasional cross-reaction with other alphaviruses and dengue occurs.

fy.n: No chikungunya IgM was detected. In the first four to five days of fever this is not conclusive, as antibodies are still forming; if joint pain and fever continue, a repeat IgM after day 7, or a PCR test in the early days, will settle it. A negative result alongside a positive dengue test points to dengue as the cause.
fy.bhi: An equivocal IgM is a weak signal that may be early antibody or a cross-reaction with dengue or another virus. If your fever started within the past week, a repeat IgM in 5–7 days usually gives a clear answer. Rest, fluids and paracetamol are appropriate meanwhile; avoid aspirin until dengue has been ruled out.
fy.hi: A positive IgM is consistent with a recent chikungunya infection. Fever usually settles within a week, but joint pain and stiffness can persist for weeks to months in some people – this is expected and usually improves with time. Your doctor may suggest anti-inflammatory measures once dengue has been excluded, and gentle movement helps stiff joints recover.

TLP-250.notes: IgM appears day 4–7 and may persist 3–6 months, so a positive result can reflect an episode a few months earlier; RT-PCR is preferred in the first 5 days of illness. Co-infection with dengue is possible in the same season – both panels are interpreted together.
TLP-250.src: NCVBDC India Guidelines on Clinical Management of Chikungunya 2016; WHO SEARO chikungunya guidelines; CDC chikungunya laboratory guidance
TLP-250.retest: Negative before day 5–7 with persisting symptoms: repeat IgM after day 7. Positive: no repeat needed.

TLP-251.name: Typhi Dot IgM
TLP-251.alias: Typhidot-M, Typhoid IgM rapid test, S. typhi IgM
TLP-251.meas: Detects IgM antibodies against a specific outer-membrane protein of Salmonella typhi, which appear within the first week of typhoid fever.
TLP-251.sig: Typhi Dot IgM turns positive 2–3 days after fever begins, earlier than the Widal test, and is less affected by past exposure or vaccination. It is a useful early pointer to typhoid while blood culture results are awaited.
TLP-251.ind: A positive IgM suggests current or very recent typhoid fever. False positives occur with other febrile illnesses (dengue, malaria) and IgM can persist for a few months after recovery; a negative result early in illness or after antibiotics does not fully exclude typhoid.

fy.n: No typhoid IgM antibodies were found, which makes typhoid an unlikely cause of your fever, particularly if you have been unwell for more than three or four days. Very early illness or antibiotics taken beforehand can give a negative result, so if fever persists your doctor may send a blood culture or repeat the test in a few days.
fy.hi: A positive IgM is consistent with a current or recent typhoid infection. Typhoid is treated with a full course of antibiotics chosen for local resistance patterns, and fever can take 3–5 days to settle once treatment starts. Your doctor may send a blood culture to confirm and identify the best antibiotic; good hand hygiene protects those around you.

TLP-251.notes: Sensitivity and specificity are moderate (~70–90%) and vary by kit; IgM may remain positive for 2–3 months after infection. It does not detect paratyphoid A or B, and blood culture in the first week remains the reference standard.
TLP-251.src: ICMR / IAP guidelines on enteric fever; WHO Background document on typhoid fever 2003; published Typhidot-M evaluation studies
TLP-251.retest: Negative with persisting fever: repeat after 3–5 days or send blood culture. Positive: no repeat needed; not useful for confirming cure.

TLP-252.name: Leptospira IgM
TLP-252.meas: Detects IgM antibodies against Leptospira bacteria, acquired from water or soil contaminated by animal urine, which appear from about day 5–7 of illness.
TLP-252.sig: Leptospirosis surges in the monsoon and can progress from a flu-like fever to jaundice, kidney failure or lung bleeding if untreated, yet responds well to early antibiotics. IgM testing identifies it among the look-alike fevers of the rainy season.
TLP-252.ind: A positive IgM indicates recent leptospiral infection – usually the current illness. It may be negative in the first 5–7 days, and can persist for months after recovery. Cross-reaction with other infections (dengue, hepatitis, syphilis) can cause false positives.

fy.n: No leptospira IgM was detected. Antibodies take 5–7 days to form, so a negative result very early in a fever that followed wading through flood water or contact with animals is not conclusive – your doctor may repeat the test after a week. If you have been ill for longer, leptospirosis is unlikely and other causes should be sought.
fy.bhi: An equivocal IgM is a weak signal that may be early antibody or a cross-reaction with another infection. Because leptospirosis responds best to prompt antibiotics, your doctor may treat on clinical grounds if you had a clear exposure to contaminated water, and repeat the test in 5–7 days to confirm a rise in antibody.
fy.hi: A positive IgM is consistent with a recent leptospira infection, which typically follows contact with flood water, wet soil or rodent-contaminated surroundings. Most people recover with antibiotics; because a minority develop jaundice, kidney or breathing problems in the second week, your doctor will check liver and kidney tests and ask you to report yellowing, reduced urine or breathlessness.

TLP-252.notes: IgM appears day 5–7 and may persist for months; MAT (microscopic agglutination test) is the reference standard and PCR is preferred in the first week. Seasonal peak in India is July–October; Weil's disease (severe form) needs hospital care.
TLP-252.src: WHO / ILS Human Leptospirosis guidelines 2003; NCDC India Programme for Prevention and Control of Leptospirosis guidelines 2015; CDC
TLP-252.retest: Negative with strong exposure history: repeat after 5–7 days. Equivocal: repeat paired sample in 1 week.

TLP-253.name: Scrub Typhus IgM
TLP-253.alias: Orientia tsutsugamushi IgM, Scrub typhus ELISA, Anti-scrub typhus IgM
TLP-253.meas: Detects IgM antibodies to Orientia tsutsugamushi, the bacterium transmitted by larval mite (chigger) bites that causes scrub typhus.
TLP-253.sig: Scrub typhus is a major and under-recognised cause of monsoon fever across India and can progress to pneumonia, meningitis or multi-organ failure, yet it responds within 48 hours to the right antibiotic. IgM testing brings it into the fever work-up when a bite mark (eschar) is not obvious.
TLP-253.ind: A positive IgM suggests current or recent scrub typhus – usually the present illness, particularly with an eschar, rash, enlarged nodes or raised liver enzymes. It may be negative in the first 5–7 days. Background positivity exists in endemic areas, and false positives occur with other rickettsial and viral infections.

fy.n: No scrub typhus IgM was detected. In the first week of fever this is not fully conclusive, because antibodies are still forming; if you have a persistent fever with a dark scab-like bite mark, rash or body ache after time in grassy or rural areas, your doctor may repeat the test in 5–7 days or treat on clinical suspicion.
fy.bhi: An equivocal IgM is a weak signal that may be early antibody or background exposure in an endemic area. Because scrub typhus improves dramatically with a simple antibiotic, your doctor may start treatment on clinical grounds if the picture fits and repeat the test in a week to confirm a rise in antibody.
fy.hi: A positive IgM is consistent with scrub typhus, an infection from mite bites in grassy or scrub-covered areas. It responds quickly to a specific antibiotic – fever usually settles within 48 hours – and untreated it can affect the lungs, brain or kidneys, so prompt treatment matters. Your doctor may check liver enzymes, platelets and, if needed, a chest X-ray.

TLP-253.notes: IgM appears day 5–7 and persists for months; cut-offs (OD or index) are kit-specific and vary by endemic background – the Indian ICMR consensus uses a higher OD threshold in high-prevalence regions. IFA is the reference standard; PCR of blood or eschar is preferred in week 1.
TLP-253.src: ICMR–DHR Guidelines for Diagnosis and Management of Rickettsial Diseases in India 2015; WHO; Indian Academy of Pediatrics rickettsial guidelines
TLP-253.retest: Negative with typical features: repeat after 5–7 days or add PCR. Positive: no repeat needed; assess response to treatment clinically.

TLP-254.name: Multiplex Fever PCR (dengue, malaria, typhoid, chikungunya, scrub typhus)
TLP-254.alias: Fever pathogen PCR panel, Tropical fever multiplex PCR, Syndromic fever PCR
TLP-254.meas: Detects the genetic material of five common Indian fever pathogens – dengue virus, malaria parasites, Salmonella typhi/paratyphi, chikungunya virus and Orientia tsutsugamushi – directly from blood in a single test.
TLP-254.sig: In the first days of a fever, before antibodies form, PCR is the most sensitive way to identify the cause. Testing five pathogens together shortens the time to a specific diagnosis and the right treatment, and can detect co-infections that antibody tests miss.
TLP-254.ind: A positive result for any target indicates the genetic material of that organism is present, consistent with active infection (rarely, residual DNA after recent treatment). A negative panel makes these five infections unlikely but does not exclude them after the first week, when pathogen load falls and serology becomes the better test.

rng.n: All five targets not detected (Not detected)

fy.n: None of the five fever pathogens' genetic material was found in your blood, making dengue, malaria, typhoid, chikungunya and scrub typhus unlikely as the cause – especially within the first week of illness. If fever continues, your doctor will look at other causes and may add antibody tests, which become more reliable after day five to seven.
fy.hi: Genetic material of one or more of the five pathogens was detected – strong evidence of active infection with the organism named on your report. Each has a specific plan: antibiotics for typhoid and scrub typhus, antimalarials for malaria, and supportive care with platelet checks for dengue. Please share this with your doctor promptly.

TLP-254.notes: Most sensitive in days 1–7 of fever; sensitivity falls once the immune response clears pathogen from blood. Multiplex panels are laboratory-developed or CE-marked assays without a universal reference range – results are reported per target as detected/not detected, and Ct values (if shown) are not standardised for clinical interpretation.
TLP-254.src: ICMR guidelines on syndromic fever diagnosis; NCVBDC dengue and malaria guidelines 2023; manufacturer assay validation
TLP-254.retest: Negative in week 1 with ongoing fever: add serology (NS1/IgM, Widal/Typhi Dot, scrub IgM) after day 5–7. Positive: no repeat needed for diagnosis.

TLP-255.name: HPV High-Risk DNA Panel
TLP-255.alias: hrHPV DNA, HPV genotyping (16/18/other high-risk), HPV PCR
TLP-255.sample: Cervical / anogenital swab in liquid-based cytology medium
TLP-255.meas: Detects the DNA of the 14 high-risk human papillomavirus types that cause cervical and other anogenital cancers, usually reporting HPV 16 and 18 separately from the other types.
TLP-255.sig: Almost all cervical cancers are caused by persistent high-risk HPV infection, which develops silently over 10–20 years and is fully preventable if pre-cancerous change is found in time. HPV DNA testing is now the WHO-preferred primary screening test because it catches risk years before a Pap smear would.
TLP-255.ind: HPV 16 or 18 positive carries the highest risk and warrants colposcopy. Other high-risk types positive warrants cytology triage or repeat in 12 months, since most such infections clear spontaneously within 1–2 years. A negative result gives strong reassurance for 5 years.

rng.n: High-risk HPV DNA not detected (Not detected)
rng.bhi: Positive for high-risk types other than 16/18 (Other high-risk types detected)
rng.hi: Positive for HPV 16 and/or 18 (HPV 16 and/or 18 detected)

fy.n: No high-risk HPV DNA was detected, which means your risk of developing cervical pre-cancer over the next five years is very low – this is the most reassuring screening result available. Routine screening can be repeated in five years (or as your doctor advises), and HPV vaccination is still worthwhile if you are under 45 and have not had it.
fy.bhi: A high-risk HPV type other than 16 or 18 was detected. This is common – most people clear the virus within one to two years without harm – but it means closer follow-up. Your doctor will usually check a Pap test on the same sample or repeat HPV in 12 months; only persistent infection or abnormal cells need further examination.
fy.hi: HPV type 16 and/or 18 was detected. These two types cause about 70% of cervical cancers, so guidelines recommend a colposcopy (a magnified cervical examination) even if your Pap smear is normal. This is not a cancer diagnosis: it identifies people who benefit from a closer look and, if pre-cancerous cells are found, simple treatment that prevents cancer.

TLP-255.notes: Recommended as primary screening every 5–10 years from age 30 (WHO) or every 5 years from age 25–30 (ASCCP); not recommended under 25 because transient infection is very common. In men and for anal/penile swabs there is no established screening algorithm and results guide clinical examination only. Vaccinated women still need screening.
TLP-255.src: WHO cervical cancer screening guideline 2021; ASCCP Risk-Based Management Consensus 2019; FOGSI GCPR on cervical cancer screening
TLP-255.retest: Negative: repeat in 5 years. Other high-risk positive with normal cytology: repeat HPV in 12 months. HPV 16/18 positive: colposcopy, not a repeat test.

any.label: Other high-risk types detected
any.text: Positive for high-risk types other than 16/18

TLP-256.name: Anti-HBs
TLP-256.alias: HBsAb, Hepatitis B immunity antibody, Anti-HBs quantitative
TLP-256.meas: Measures the protective antibody against the hepatitis B surface protein, produced after vaccination or after recovery from natural infection.
TLP-256.sig: Anti-HBs is the marker of immunity to hepatitis B: a level of 10 mIU/mL or more protects against infection. Checking it confirms that a vaccine course worked and identifies who needs a booster before immune-suppressing treatment, healthcare work or other exposure.
TLP-256.ind: Anti-HBs ≥ 10 mIU/mL indicates immunity (from vaccine if anti-HBc is negative, from past infection if anti-HBc is positive). Below 10 mIU/mL indicates no protection – never vaccinated, vaccine non-response, or waning after vaccination long ago. Anti-HBs is absent in active infection (HBsAg positive).

fy.lo: Your antibody level is below the protective threshold, so you are not currently immune to hepatitis B. If you were never vaccinated, a three-dose course is the next step; if you completed a course long ago, a single booster with a recheck 1–2 months later usually restores protection. This matters especially before immune-suppressing treatment.
fy.blo: You have protective antibody, though at a modest level. This is enough to prevent infection – immune memory from vaccination persists even as the measured level drifts down over the years. A booster is generally considered only for people at ongoing high exposure risk, such as healthcare workers, dialysis patients or those starting immune-suppressing therapy; your doctor can advise.
fy.n: Your antibody level shows robust immunity to hepatitis B, whether from vaccination or from a past infection that has fully resolved (your anti-HBc result tells which). No booster is needed and, for most people, this test does not need repeating. This immunity protects you and any future children from a virus that can cause long-term liver damage.

TLP-256.notes: Post-vaccination check (1–2 months after the third dose) is recommended for healthcare workers, dialysis patients, immunocompromised persons and babies born to HBsAg-positive mothers; a level ≥ 10 mIU/mL at that check confers long-term protection even if it later falls. Anti-HBs may be transiently detectable after hepatitis B immunoglobulin. Values above 1000 mIU/mL are reported as > 1000.
TLP-256.src: CDC/ACIP Hepatitis B recommendations 2018; WHO Hepatitis B position paper 2017; AASLD Hepatitis B Guidance 2018
TLP-256.retest: Non-immune: recheck 1–2 months after completing vaccination or a booster. Immune: no routine repeat; recheck only before immunosuppression or after a high-risk exposure.

TLP-257.name: Anti-HBc Total
TLP-257.alias: HBcAb, Anti-HBc IgG+IgM, Hepatitis B core antibody
TLP-257.meas: Detects antibodies to the inner core protein of the hepatitis B virus, which are produced only after natural infection – never after vaccination.
TLP-257.sig: Anti-HBc is the lifelong footprint of hepatitis B exposure and separates vaccine immunity from immunity earned through infection. Before immune-suppressing drugs such as biologics, rituximab or chemotherapy it is essential, because a resolved hepatitis B infection can reactivate when the immune system is suppressed.
TLP-257.ind: Positive with HBsAg negative and anti-HBs positive indicates resolved past infection (reactivation risk under immunosuppression). Positive with HBsAg negative and anti-HBs negative ('isolated anti-HBc') may indicate resolved infection with lost anti-HBs, occult infection or a false positive – HBV DNA clarifies. Positive with HBsAg positive indicates current infection.

fy.n: No core antibody was found, which means you have never been infected with hepatitis B. Any immunity shown on your anti-HBs test comes from vaccination. If anti-HBs is also low, you are neither exposed nor protected, and a vaccine course is worth considering – especially before immune-suppressing treatment or if you are in a higher-exposure setting.
fy.bhi: Your core antibody result is in the grey zone – a weak signal that is more often a non-specific reaction than true past infection, but cannot be dismissed if you are about to start immune-suppressing treatment. Your doctor may repeat the test, check anti-HBs, and if the picture is still unclear, order an HBV DNA test before treatment begins.
fy.hi: A positive core antibody shows you have been infected with hepatitis B at some point. With HBsAg negative, the infection has resolved – but the virus can lie dormant and reactivate if the immune system is strongly suppressed. Before biologics, chemotherapy or high-dose steroids, your doctor may check HBV DNA and prescribe a preventive antiviral.

TLP-257.notes: Isolated anti-HBc (HBsAg and anti-HBs both negative) occurs in 1–4% of Indian blood donors and requires HBV DNA testing before immunosuppression; infants carry maternal anti-HBc for up to 12–18 months. Anti-HBc IgM (a separate test) distinguishes acute from past infection.
TLP-257.src: AASLD Hepatitis B Guidance 2018; EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines on HBV 2025; ASCO/AGA guidance on HBV reactivation prophylaxis; CDC
TLP-257.retest: Grey zone: repeat with anti-HBs and consider HBV DNA before immunosuppression. Positive resolved infection: HBV DNA and liver enzymes before and during immunosuppressive therapy.

TLP-258.name: Chlamydia trachomatis NAAT
TLP-258.alias: Chlamydia PCR, CT NAAT, Chlamydia trachomatis DNA
TLP-258.sample: First-void urine / urogenital, rectal or throat swab
TLP-258.meas: Detects the genetic material of Chlamydia trachomatis, the commonest bacterial sexually transmitted infection, using a nucleic acid amplification test.
TLP-258.sig: Chlamydia is silent in about 70% of women and half of men, yet untreated it can cause pelvic inflammatory disease, tubal infertility, ectopic pregnancy and, in men, epididymitis. NAAT is far more sensitive than culture and a single course of antibiotics cures it.
TLP-258.ind: A positive result indicates current chlamydia infection at the sampled site and requires treatment of the person and all recent partners. A negative result reliably excludes infection at that site if the sample was taken more than 2 weeks after exposure; other sites (rectal, throat) may need separate swabs.

rng.n: Chlamydia trachomatis DNA not detected (Not detected)

fy.n: No chlamydia was detected in the sample tested, so infection at that site is very unlikely – provided the sample was taken at least two weeks after any possible exposure. Because chlamydia often causes no symptoms, regular screening when you have a new partner, and consistent condom use, remain the best protection for fertility and long-term health.
fy.hi: Chlamydia was detected, indicating a current infection that needs treatment even if you feel entirely well. A short course of antibiotics clears it in almost everyone; partners from the past 60 days should be tested and treated too, and avoid sex until a week after everyone has finished treatment. Your doctor will usually also check for gonorrhoea, syphilis and HIV.

TLP-258.notes: Sample-site matters – a negative urine or vaginal swab does not exclude rectal or pharyngeal infection; window period ~2 weeks. Test of cure is only routinely required in pregnancy (3–4 weeks after treatment); residual DNA can give false positives if retested within 3 weeks. Reinfection is common, so retest at 3 months.
TLP-258.src: CDC STI Treatment Guidelines 2021; WHO STI guidelines 2021; NACO STI/RTI guidelines; BASHH chlamydia guideline
TLP-258.retest: Positive: retest for reinfection at 3 months (test of cure at 3–4 weeks only in pregnancy). Negative after a very recent exposure: repeat at 2 weeks.

TLP-259.name: Neisseria gonorrhoeae NAAT
TLP-259.alias: Gonorrhoea PCR, NG NAAT, GC DNA test
TLP-259.sample: First-void urine / urogenital, rectal or throat swab
TLP-259.meas: Detects the genetic material of Neisseria gonorrhoeae, the bacterium causing gonorrhoea, using a nucleic acid amplification test.
TLP-259.sig: Gonorrhoea causes discharge and pain in many men but is often silent in women, where it can lead to pelvic inflammatory disease and infertility. Rising antibiotic resistance makes accurate diagnosis, correct treatment and partner notification particularly important.
TLP-259.ind: A positive result indicates current gonorrhoea at the sampled site. A culture may be added to check antibiotic sensitivity. A negative result excludes infection at that site beyond the ~2-week window period; throat and rectal sites need their own swabs.

rng.n: Neisseria gonorrhoeae DNA not detected (Not detected)

fy.n: No gonorrhoea was detected in the sample tested, making infection at that site very unlikely if the sample was taken two or more weeks after any possible exposure. If you have symptoms such as discharge or pain on passing urine despite this result, other causes – including chlamydia or mycoplasma, tested separately – should be considered with your doctor.
fy.hi: Gonorrhoea was detected, indicating a current infection that needs prompt treatment. Because the bacterium is becoming resistant to older antibiotics, treatment is usually a single injection of a specific antibiotic, sometimes with a sensitivity culture. Partners from the past 60 days need testing and treatment, avoid sex for a week afterwards, and retest at 3 months.

TLP-259.notes: Throat infection is common and often symptomless, and is harder to cure – a test of cure at 2 weeks is recommended for pharyngeal gonorrhoea; residual DNA can persist up to 2 weeks after treatment. Low-prevalence populations have a higher false-positive rate on some assays, and confirmatory testing may be used. Co-infection with chlamydia is frequent.
TLP-259.src: CDC STI Treatment Guidelines 2021; WHO STI guidelines 2021; NACO STI/RTI guidelines; BASHH gonorrhoea guideline 2019
TLP-259.retest: Positive: test of cure at 2 weeks for throat infection or if symptoms persist; retest all sites at 3 months for reinfection. Negative after recent exposure: repeat at 2 weeks.

TLP-260.name: Mycoplasma genitalium NAAT
TLP-260.alias: M. genitalium PCR, MG NAAT, Mgen DNA
TLP-260.meas: Detects the genetic material of Mycoplasma genitalium, a small sexually transmitted bacterium that cannot be grown in routine culture.
TLP-260.sig: M. genitalium is a recognised cause of urethritis in men and cervicitis and pelvic inflammatory disease in women that is frequently missed because it needs a specific NAAT. It is also often resistant to common antibiotics, so a confirmed diagnosis changes which treatment is chosen.
TLP-260.ind: A positive result indicates current infection, most relevant when there are symptoms (discharge, pain, bleeding after sex) or persistent urethritis/cervicitis after standard treatment. A negative result excludes it at the sampled site. Screening of people without symptoms is not recommended.

rng.n: Mycoplasma genitalium DNA not detected (Not detected)

fy.n: No Mycoplasma genitalium was detected, so this organism is not the explanation for any genital symptoms you may have. If discharge, discomfort or bleeding after sex continue, your doctor will look at the other results in this panel and at non-infectious causes; no further action is needed for mycoplasma itself.
fy.hi: Mycoplasma genitalium was detected, consistent with a current infection – a common cause of persistent urethritis or cervicitis. It is treated with a specific two-step antibiotic course rather than the usual STI antibiotics, because resistance is common; where available, a resistance test guides the choice. Current partners should be tested and treated, with a test of cure 3–4 weeks later.

TLP-260.notes: Guidelines recommend testing only symptomatic people and partners of positive cases, not routine screening; macrolide-resistance testing (23S rRNA mutation) is recommended where available because azithromycin resistance exceeds 50% in many populations. Test of cure at 3–4 weeks after treatment (not earlier) is standard.
TLP-260.src: CDC STI Treatment Guidelines 2021; BASHH/European (IUSTI) M. genitalium guideline 2021; WHO STI guidelines 2021
TLP-260.retest: Positive: test of cure 3–4 weeks after completing treatment. Negative: no repeat unless new symptoms.

TLP-261.name: Trichomonas vaginalis NAAT
TLP-261.alias: Trichomoniasis PCR, TV NAAT, Trichomonas vaginalis DNA
TLP-261.sample: Vaginal / urethral swab or first-void urine
TLP-261.meas: Detects the genetic material of Trichomonas vaginalis, a single-celled parasite and the most common curable sexually transmitted infection worldwide.
TLP-261.sig: Trichomoniasis causes discharge, itching and discomfort in women, is usually silent in men, and increases the risk of acquiring HIV and of preterm birth in pregnancy. NAAT detects it three to five times more often than the traditional wet-mount microscopy, so cases are no longer missed.
TLP-261.ind: A positive result indicates current trichomonas infection requiring treatment of the person and all partners. A negative result excludes it at the sampled site; symptoms then point to bacterial vaginosis, candida or other causes.

rng.n: Trichomonas vaginalis DNA not detected (Not detected)

fy.n: No trichomonas was detected, so this parasite is not the cause of any discharge or irritation you may have. Vaginal symptoms are more often due to bacterial vaginosis or thrush, which are not sexually transmitted and are easily treated – worth discussing with your doctor if symptoms persist.
fy.hi: Trichomonas was detected, indicating a current infection. It is cured by a short course of a specific antibiotic; all sexual partners must be treated at the same time, even without symptoms, and avoid sex until everyone has finished treatment. Because reinfection is common, a repeat test about 3 months later is recommended, and your doctor may offer other STI tests.

TLP-261.notes: NAAT is the recommended test (sensitivity > 95% vs 50–60% for wet mount); in men urine or urethral swab is used. Retesting within 3 weeks of treatment can be falsely positive from residual DNA. In pregnancy, treatment is recommended for symptomatic infection; screening is advised for people living with HIV.
TLP-261.src: CDC STI Treatment Guidelines 2021; WHO STI guidelines 2021; NACO STI/RTI guidelines; BASHH trichomonas guideline
TLP-261.retest: Positive: retest at 3 months for reinfection (all sexually active women; men where feasible). Negative: no repeat unless new symptoms or exposure.

TLP-262.name: Colour (Stool)
TLP-262.meas: The visible colour of the stool sample, which reflects bile pigment, transit time, diet, medicines and the presence of blood.
TLP-262.sig: Colour is a quick first clue to how the liver, bile ducts and gut are working. Pale, black or red stool can point to bile obstruction or bleeding that needs proper follow-up.
TLP-262.ind: Black/tarry stool suggests bleeding from the stomach or upper gut (or iron/bismuth intake); red suggests bleeding from the lower gut or haemorrhoids; pale clay-coloured stool suggests reduced bile flow (liver or bile-duct disease); green often reflects rapid transit or diet; yellow greasy stool suggests fat malabsorption.

fy.n: A brown or yellowish-brown stool confirms that bile is flowing normally from your liver and that there is no obvious sign of bleeding. Colour shifts a little with diet, so no action is needed; keep a varied, fibre-rich diet and adequate fluids.
fy.hi: An unusual colour has been recorded. Black or red stool can mean bleeding somewhere in the gut (though iron tablets, beetroot and certain foods mimic this); pale or clay-coloured stool can mean bile is not reaching the gut. Share this with your doctor, mention any medicines or foods, and repeat the test if they advise.

TLP-262.notes: Breast-fed infants normally pass yellow, seedy stool; meconium in newborns is greenish-black.
TLP-262.src: Henry's Clinical Diagnosis and Management by Laboratory Methods, 24th ed.
TLP-262.retest: Repeat on a fresh sample after stopping iron/bismuth or colour-rich foods for 2–3 days if the result was unexpected.

TLP-263.name: Consistency
TLP-263.meas: How formed, soft, loose or watery the stool is, reflecting water content and transit time through the bowel.
TLP-263.sig: Consistency tells you how quickly food is moving through the gut and how well water is being absorbed. Persistently loose or hard stool is often the first sign of infection, malabsorption, or irritable bowel.
TLP-263.ind: Loose or watery stool suggests infection, food intolerance, malabsorption, medicines or inflammatory bowel disease; hard or pellet-like stool suggests constipation, low fibre or fluid intake, hypothyroidism, or slow transit.

fy.n: A formed, soft stool means your bowel is absorbing water normally and food is moving through at a healthy pace. This supports a well-functioning gut; keep it that way with regular fibre, adequate water and daily movement.
fy.hi: Your stool was recorded as loose, watery or unusually hard. Loose stool most often follows a gut infection, a food intolerance or a new medicine; hard stool points to constipation from low fibre or fluids. If this pattern has lasted more than a couple of weeks, or comes with weight loss or blood, discuss it with your doctor.

TLP-263.notes: Infants and young children normally pass softer stool; consistency in toddlers depends heavily on diet.
TLP-263.src: Bristol Stool Form Scale; Henry's Clinical Diagnosis and Management by Laboratory Methods, 24th ed.
TLP-263.retest: Repeat after an acute diarrhoeal illness has settled, or when a new bowel pattern persists beyond 2 weeks.

TLP-264.name: Reaction
TLP-264.meas: Whether the stool is acidic, neutral or alkaline, which reflects fermentation of undigested carbohydrate and the type of bacteria in the gut.
TLP-264.sig: An acidic stool is a classic sign that sugars such as lactose are not being absorbed and are being fermented by gut bacteria. It is a cheap pointer towards carbohydrate malabsorption in children and adults with bloating or diarrhoea.
TLP-264.ind: Acidic stool (pH below about 5.5) suggests carbohydrate malabsorption such as lactose intolerance, or a viral gastroenteritis; strongly alkaline stool suggests protein breakdown, secretory diarrhoea, or bacterial overgrowth.

fy.n: A neutral or mildly alkaline reaction is what a healthy, well-digested stool looks like. It suggests that the sugars and starches you eat are being absorbed properly rather than fermented in the bowel. No action is needed; a balanced diet with fibre keeps gut bacteria happy.
fy.hi: Your stool reaction was outside the usual neutral range. An acidic stool is commonly seen when milk sugar (lactose) or other carbohydrates are not being absorbed, or during a viral tummy infection; a strongly alkaline stool can reflect bacterial imbalance. Your doctor may suggest a short lactose-free trial or a breath test to confirm.

TLP-264.notes: Breast-fed infants normally have a mildly acidic stool (pH 5–6) because of milk-sugar fermentation, so an acidic result is less specific in this age group.
TLP-264.src: Henry's Clinical Diagnosis and Management by Laboratory Methods, 24th ed.; Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
TLP-264.retest: Repeat on a fresh sample tested within 30 minutes of collection if the result was borderline; consider a lactose breath test if acidic.

TLP-265.name: Mucous
TLP-265.meas: Whether visible jelly-like mucus is present in the stool, produced by the lining of the bowel.
TLP-265.sig: A small amount of mucus is normal and invisible, but visible mucus means the bowel lining is irritated or inflamed. Together with pus cells and blood it helps distinguish infective or inflammatory colitis from simple diarrhoea.
TLP-265.ind: Visible mucus suggests bacterial or amoebic dysentery, inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis, Crohn's), irritable bowel syndrome, or, in large amounts with blood, a rectal lesion.

fy.n: No visible mucus was seen, which suggests the lining of your bowel is not irritated or inflamed. This is reassuring alongside a normal pus-cell and blood result. Keep your gut lining healthy with fibre, fluids and good hand and food hygiene.
fy.hi: Mucus was seen in your sample, which means your bowel lining is irritated. Common causes are a gut infection (including amoebic dysentery), irritable bowel syndrome, or inflammatory bowel disease. Look at the pus-cell, blood and parasite results alongside this, and discuss with your doctor, especially if mucus has persisted for more than a week.

TLP-265.src: Henry's Clinical Diagnosis and Management by Laboratory Methods, 24th ed.
TLP-265.retest: Repeat with a fresh sample after treatment of any infection, or if symptoms persist beyond 2 weeks.

TLP-266.name: Blood (Stool)
TLP-266.alias: Gross blood, Frank blood in stool
TLP-266.meas: Whether blood can be seen with the naked eye in the stool sample.
TLP-266.sig: Visible blood means bleeding from somewhere in the gut, most often the lower bowel. It is never ignored because it can reflect infection, piles, inflammatory bowel disease, or a growth that needs early attention.
TLP-266.ind: Bright red blood suggests haemorrhoids, anal fissure, dysentery, colitis or a polyp/tumour of the rectum or colon; dark or mixed-in blood suggests bleeding higher in the bowel.

fy.n: No visible blood was found, which suggests there is no significant bleeding from your bowel. Very small, hidden amounts are checked separately by the occult blood test. A fibre-rich diet and avoiding straining help protect the lower bowel.
fy.hi: Blood was seen in your stool. The most common causes are piles or a small tear at the anus, an infection such as dysentery, or inflammation of the bowel; less often it can signal a polyp or growth. Please see your doctor soon for an examination, and mention any pain, weight loss or change in bowel habit.

TLP-266.notes: Red colouring from beetroot, food dyes or some medicines can be mistaken for blood; the lab confirms with a chemical test where possible.
TLP-266.src: Henry's Clinical Diagnosis and Management by Laboratory Methods, 24th ed.
TLP-266.retest: Any visible blood warrants clinical review rather than a simple retest; your doctor may order a colonoscopy or infection panel.

TLP-267.name: Pus Cells (Stool)
TLP-267.meas: The number of white blood cells seen per microscope field in the stool, a sign that the bowel wall is inflamed.
TLP-267.sig: Pus cells mean the bowel lining is being invaded or inflamed rather than just irritated. They help separate invasive infections (Shigella, Salmonella, amoebae) and colitis from viral or toxin-type diarrhoea that settles on its own.
TLP-267.ind: Raised pus cells suggest bacterial dysentery, amoebic colitis, ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, or antibiotic-associated colitis; absence points towards viral gastroenteritis, toxin-mediated food poisoning, or non-inflammatory causes.

fy.n: Only occasional white cells were seen, which suggests your bowel wall is not inflamed. If you have had loose motions, this favours a mild viral or food-related upset that usually settles with fluids and rest rather than an invasive infection.
fy.bhi: A modest number of white cells was seen, which hints at mild inflammation of the bowel lining. This can happen during or just after a gut infection or with irritable bowel flare-ups. If loose motions, mucus or cramps continue, your doctor may repeat the test or add a stool culture.
fy.hi: Many white cells were seen, which indicates real inflammation of the bowel wall. Common causes are bacterial or amoebic dysentery, and sometimes inflammatory bowel disease. Please see your doctor; a stool culture or parasite test can identify the cause, and fluids are important while you recover.

TLP-267.notes: Counts are method-dependent (wet mount vs stained smear); breast-fed infants may show a few leukocytes normally.
TLP-267.src: Henry's Clinical Diagnosis and Management by Laboratory Methods, 24th ed.; IDSA 2017 infectious diarrhoea guideline
TLP-267.retest: Repeat 1–2 weeks after treatment if symptoms persist, using a fresh sample examined within 1 hour.

TLP-268.name: Epithelial Cells (Stool)
TLP-268.meas: The number of lining cells shed from the bowel wall that are seen in the stool under the microscope.
TLP-268.sig: A few shed lining cells are normal turnover, but large numbers mean the bowel surface is being damaged or irritated. Read together with pus cells and mucus, they add weight to a picture of colitis or dysentery.
TLP-268.ind: Increased epithelial cells suggest bowel irritation or inflammation from infection, inflammatory bowel disease, or harsh laxatives; low or absent cells are of no concern.

fy.n: Only occasional lining cells were seen, which is the normal daily turnover of the bowel surface. It suggests the wall of your gut is intact and not being irritated. Nothing needs to be done; a gentle, fibre-rich diet keeps the lining healthy.
fy.hi: More lining cells than usual were seen, which means the surface of your bowel is being shed faster than normal. This usually goes with irritation from an infection or inflammation, or strong laxative use. On its own it is not serious; interpret it with your pus-cell and mucus results and let your doctor guide any follow-up.

TLP-268.src: Henry's Clinical Diagnosis and Management by Laboratory Methods, 24th ed.
TLP-268.retest: Repeat only if other stool findings are abnormal or symptoms persist.

TLP-269.name: RBC cells
TLP-269.meas: The number of red blood cells seen per microscope field in the stool, indicating bleeding into the bowel even when not visible.
TLP-269.sig: Red cells under the microscope reveal bleeding that is too small to see. Combined with pus cells they point to invasive infections or colitis; without pus cells they raise the question of piles, fissures or polyps.
TLP-269.ind: Red cells suggest amoebic or bacterial dysentery, inflammatory bowel disease, haemorrhoids, anal fissure, polyps or colorectal tumours; none seen is normal.

fy.n: No red blood cells were seen under the microscope, which suggests there is no bleeding into your bowel at this time. This is reassuring, particularly alongside a negative occult blood test. Continue routine bowel-health habits such as fibre and hydration.
fy.bhi: A few red cells were seen, indicating a small amount of bleeding. Common and usually harmless causes are piles, a small anal tear or straining, but a recent gut infection can also do this. Mention it to your doctor and repeat the test after any infection has cleared.
fy.hi: Many red cells were seen, which means there is definite bleeding into your bowel. Together with pus cells this often reflects dysentery or colitis; without them, piles, polyps or other bowel lesions need to be considered. Please see your doctor promptly so the source can be found.

TLP-269.notes: Menstrual contamination can give a false-positive result; collect the sample away from the menstrual period where possible.
TLP-269.src: Henry's Clinical Diagnosis and Management by Laboratory Methods, 24th ed.
TLP-269.retest: Repeat with a clean, fresh sample after treatment of any infection; persistent red cells need clinical evaluation.

TLP-270.name: Macrophages
TLP-270.meas: Whether large immune scavenger cells (macrophages) are seen in the stool, a sign of active tissue inflammation in the bowel wall.
TLP-270.sig: Macrophages appear in stool when the bowel wall is inflamed enough to release tissue immune cells, most typically in bacillary dysentery. They are easily confused with amoebae, so their presence is reported carefully alongside the parasite result.
TLP-270.ind: Presence suggests bacillary (Shigella) dysentery, other invasive bacterial colitis, or inflammatory bowel disease; absence is normal.

fy.n: No macrophages were seen, which suggests there is no active inflammation deep in your bowel wall. This is the expected result in a healthy gut and in mild, self-limiting tummy upsets. No follow-up is needed for this item.
fy.hi: Macrophages, a type of immune cell, were seen in your stool. This usually means the bowel wall is inflamed, most commonly from a bacterial dysentery such as Shigella, and occasionally from inflammatory bowel disease. Your doctor may arrange a stool culture and will guide treatment; keep well hydrated in the meantime.

TLP-270.notes: Macrophages can be mistaken for Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites on wet mount; iodine or trichrome staining is used to distinguish them.
TLP-270.src: Henry's Clinical Diagnosis and Management by Laboratory Methods, 24th ed.
TLP-270.retest: Repeat after treatment if symptoms persist, ideally on a fresh sample examined within 1 hour.

TLP-271.name: Fat globules
TLP-271.meas: Whether droplets of undigested or unabsorbed fat are seen in the stool under the microscope.
TLP-271.sig: Fat should be almost fully absorbed in the small intestine. Fat globules in stool are a simple screen for malabsorption, pointing to pancreatic enzyme shortage, bile problems, or damage to the intestinal lining such as coeliac disease.
TLP-271.ind: Fat globules suggest pancreatic insufficiency, coeliac disease, giardiasis, small-bowel bacterial overgrowth, bile-salt deficiency, or recent use of mineral oil/fat-blocking medicines; absence is normal.

fy.n: No significant fat droplets were seen, which suggests your pancreas, bile flow and small intestine are digesting and absorbing fat normally. This makes fat malabsorption unlikely as a cause of any bloating or loose motions. No action is needed.
fy.hi: Fat droplets were seen in your stool, which suggests fat is not being fully digested or absorbed. Common reasons include a shortage of pancreatic enzymes, coeliac disease, a Giardia infection, or recent fat-blocking medicines or oily laxatives. Your doctor may confirm with a 72-hour faecal fat, faecal elastase or coeliac antibody test.

TLP-271.notes: A high-fat meal, castor oil, mineral oil or orlistat in the 48 hours before collection can give a false-positive result.
TLP-271.src: Henry's Clinical Diagnosis and Management by Laboratory Methods, 24th ed.
TLP-271.retest: Repeat on a normal diet after stopping oily laxatives or fat-blocking drugs for 48–72 hours; consider faecal elastase if persistent.

TLP-272.name: Starch granules
TLP-272.meas: Whether undigested starch grains are seen in the stool on iodine staining, indicating incomplete carbohydrate digestion.
TLP-272.sig: Starch is normally broken down by pancreatic and intestinal enzymes. Its persistence in stool suggests rapid transit or enzyme shortage and often accompanies bloating, gas and acidic stool from bacterial fermentation.
TLP-272.ind: Starch granules suggest pancreatic insufficiency, rapid intestinal transit (diarrhoea), small-bowel disease, or a very high-starch diet with poor chewing; absence is normal.

fy.n: No undigested starch was seen, which suggests the carbohydrates you eat are being broken down and absorbed properly. This is reassuring for pancreatic and small-intestinal function. Chewing well and eating at a relaxed pace helps keep it this way.
fy.hi: Undigested starch grains were seen in your stool. This most often happens when food moves through the gut too quickly (as in diarrhoea) or when pancreatic enzymes are in short supply; a heavy starchy meal eaten hurriedly can also do it. If it persists with bloating or weight loss, your doctor may check pancreatic function.

TLP-272.notes: Common and usually insignificant in infants on newly introduced cereals.
TLP-272.src: Henry's Clinical Diagnosis and Management by Laboratory Methods, 24th ed.
TLP-272.retest: Repeat after an episode of diarrhoea settles; persistent starch with fat globules warrants faecal elastase testing.

TLP-273.name: Undigested food particles
TLP-273.meas: Whether recognisable pieces of food such as vegetable fibres, seeds or meat fibres are seen in the stool.
TLP-273.sig: Some plant fibre is always undigested, but abundant food residue, especially meat fibres, means food is passing through too fast or digestive enzymes are not doing their job. It is a soft but useful sign of maldigestion when read with fat and starch findings.
TLP-273.ind: Excess undigested food suggests rapid transit, pancreatic insufficiency, low stomach acid, poor chewing or dental problems, or small-bowel disease; a small amount of vegetable fibre is normal.

fy.n: Little or no undigested food was seen, which suggests your stomach, pancreas and intestine are breaking down meals properly. Some fibre from vegetables and seeds is always expected and is a sign of a healthy diet. No follow-up is needed.
fy.hi: A noticeable amount of undigested food was seen in your stool. This usually reflects food moving through the gut quickly, eating fast without chewing well, or, less often, a shortage of digestive enzymes. Try slowing down at meals; if it continues with bloating, loose motions or weight loss, discuss it with your doctor.

TLP-273.notes: Corn, seeds and leafy vegetables commonly appear intact in stool and are not by themselves abnormal.
TLP-273.src: Henry's Clinical Diagnosis and Management by Laboratory Methods, 24th ed.
TLP-273.retest: Repeat after correcting chewing/dental issues or once diarrhoea settles; persistent findings may prompt pancreatic testing.

TLP-274.name: Ova eggs
TLP-274.meas: Whether eggs of intestinal worms such as roundworm, hookworm, whipworm or tapeworm are seen in the stool under the microscope.
TLP-274.sig: Worm infections are common in India, especially in children, and silently cause anaemia, poor growth and abdominal symptoms. Finding eggs confirms the infection and identifies the worm so the right deworming medicine can be chosen.
TLP-274.ind: Eggs seen indicate infection with roundworm (Ascaris), hookworm, whipworm (Trichuris), tapeworm (Taenia/Hymenolepis) or liver flukes depending on the egg type; none seen is normal but does not fully exclude light infection.

fy.n: No worm eggs were found in your sample, which makes an intestinal worm infection unlikely. Because eggs are shed intermittently, a single negative test is not absolute; if symptoms such as abdominal pain, anaemia or itching persist, your doctor may ask for a second sample. Hand-washing and well-cooked food keep the risk low.
fy.hi: Worm eggs were found in your stool, which confirms an intestinal worm infection. These are usually picked up from contaminated soil, water or undercooked food and are very treatable with a short course of deworming medicine from your doctor. Family members may need checking too, and a repeat test after treatment confirms clearance.

TLP-274.notes: Sensitivity improves with concentration techniques and three samples on separate days; egg counts (Kato-Katz) are used for intensity where available.
TLP-274.src: WHO Bench Aids for the Diagnosis of Intestinal Parasites; Garcia, Diagnostic Medical Parasitology
TLP-274.retest: Collect 3 samples on alternate days if suspicion is high despite a negative result; repeat 2–4 weeks after treatment to confirm cure.

TLP-275.name: Cysts
TLP-275.meas: Whether the resistant cyst forms of single-celled parasites such as Giardia or Entamoeba are seen in the stool.
TLP-275.sig: Cysts are the infective stage of protozoal parasites and are shed even when symptoms are mild. Identifying them explains chronic bloating, greasy stools or intermittent diarrhoea, and prevents spread to others.
TLP-275.ind: Cysts seen indicate Giardia lamblia, Entamoeba histolytica/dispar, or non-pathogenic commensals such as Entamoeba coli, Endolimax nana or Iodamoeba butschlii (the species is reported); none seen is normal.

fy.n: No parasite cysts were seen, which makes infection with Giardia or amoebae unlikely. Cysts are shed on and off, so if you have ongoing bloating, greasy stools or intermittent diarrhoea your doctor may request a second sample or a stool antigen test. Safe drinking water and hand hygiene are your best protection.
fy.hi: Parasite cysts were seen in your stool. Depending on the species, this may be a true infection such as Giardia or Entamoeba histolytica, which is easily treated, or a harmless commensal amoeba that needs no treatment. Your doctor will interpret the species named on the report and may add an antigen test to decide.

TLP-275.notes: Entamoeba histolytica cannot be distinguished from the harmless E. dispar by microscopy alone; antigen or PCR testing is needed to confirm.
TLP-275.src: WHO Bench Aids for the Diagnosis of Intestinal Parasites; Garcia, Diagnostic Medical Parasitology
TLP-275.retest: Three samples on alternate days raise detection; repeat 2–3 weeks after treatment to confirm clearance.

TLP-276.name: Larva
TLP-276.meas: Whether the mobile larval stage of a worm, most importantly Strongyloides stercoralis, is seen in the stool.
TLP-276.sig: Larvae in stool almost always mean Strongyloides, a worm that can persist for decades and become life-threatening if immunity is lowered by steroids or biologic drugs. Detecting it before such treatment matters greatly.
TLP-276.ind: Larvae seen indicate Strongyloides stercoralis (or hookworm larvae in an old sample); none seen is normal but a single negative sample misses many light infections.

fy.n: No worm larvae were seen in your sample, which is the expected result. Strongyloides larvae are shed irregularly, so if you are about to start steroids or immune-suppressing medicines your doctor may still add a blood antibody test for extra safety. Wearing footwear on soil reduces the risk of picking it up.
fy.hi: Worm larvae were seen in your stool, which most often means a Strongyloides infection. This is acquired through bare skin contact with contaminated soil and is treatable with specific medicine, but it must not be left untreated, especially before any steroid or immune-suppressing therapy. Please see your doctor promptly.

TLP-276.notes: A sample left standing for many hours can contain hatched hookworm larvae that mimic Strongyloides; fresh samples are essential.
TLP-276.src: CDC DPDx; Garcia, Diagnostic Medical Parasitology
TLP-276.retest: If suspicion is high, examine 3 fresh samples or use agar-plate culture; repeat after treatment and add serology in immunosuppressed patients.

TLP-277.name: Adult worms or segments
TLP-277.meas: Whether whole worms or flat tapeworm segments are visible in the stool sample to the naked eye.
TLP-277.sig: Seeing an adult worm or tapeworm segment is direct proof of infection and immediately identifies the type of worm. It guides the choice of deworming medicine and, for tapeworm, prompts a check of family and food sources.
TLP-277.ind: Presence indicates roundworm (Ascaris), pinworm (Enterobius), or tapeworm (Taenia/Hymenolepis) segments; absence is normal.

fy.n: No worms or tapeworm segments were seen, which is the expected result. This rules out a heavy worm burden, though light infections are better picked up by the microscopic egg examination. Good hygiene, clean water and well-cooked meat keep you protected.
fy.hi: A worm or tapeworm segment was found in your stool, confirming an intestinal worm infection. This is common, not dangerous in most cases, and clears with a short course of deworming medicine from your doctor. Tapeworm usually comes from undercooked meat, so household members may need testing and a follow-up stool check confirms clearance.

TLP-277.notes: Pinworms are best detected by an adhesive-tape test of the perianal skin in the early morning rather than stool examination.
TLP-277.src: CDC DPDx; Garcia, Diagnostic Medical Parasitology
TLP-277.retest: Repeat stool examination 2–4 weeks after deworming to confirm cure; for tapeworm confirm that the head (scolex) has been passed.

TLP-278.name: Others
TLP-278.meas: Any additional microscopic finding not covered elsewhere, such as yeast cells, Charcot-Leyden crystals, muscle fibres or unusual crystals.
TLP-278.sig: This line captures incidental findings that can still be informative. Abundant yeast hints at antibiotic-related overgrowth or immune weakness, while Charcot-Leyden crystals point to an allergic or parasitic reaction in the gut.
TLP-278.ind: Budding yeast in large numbers suggests candidal overgrowth after antibiotics, diabetes or immunosuppression; Charcot-Leyden crystals suggest amoebic or worm infection or eosinophilic gut disease; meat fibres suggest maldigestion.

fy.n: Nothing unusual was noted beyond the standard items on your stool report, which is the expected result. Occasional yeast or plant material is a normal part of gut contents. No action is needed on this line; a fibre-rich diet and sensible antibiotic use keep the gut ecosystem balanced.
fy.hi: An additional finding has been noted on your stool report. Most commonly this is an overgrowth of yeast after antibiotics or in diabetes, or crystals that accompany an allergic or parasitic reaction in the gut. These are rarely serious on their own; your doctor will read them with the rest of the report and decide whether any treatment is needed.

TLP-278.notes: Small numbers of yeast are normal gut flora; only budding yeast or pseudohyphae in large numbers are considered significant.
TLP-278.src: Henry's Clinical Diagnosis and Management by Laboratory Methods, 24th ed.
TLP-278.retest: Repeat after completing any antibiotic course or treating an identified parasite if the finding was significant.

TLP-279.name: PAP Smear
TLP-279.sample: Cervical cells (conventional smear or liquid-based cytology)
TLP-279.meas: Cells brushed from the neck of the womb (cervix) examined for early pre-cancerous changes, infection and inflammation.
TLP-279.sig: Cervical cancer is one of the commonest cancers in Indian women yet almost entirely preventable. A PAP smear catches abnormal cells years before they can become cancer, when simple treatment is curative.
TLP-279.ind: Abnormal results are graded by the Bethesda system: ASC-US and LSIL indicate mild changes usually from HPV infection that often resolve; ASC-H, HSIL and AGC indicate higher-grade changes needing colposcopy; infections (Candida, Trichomonas, bacterial vaginosis) and reactive inflammation may also be reported.

rng.n: Negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy (NILM (normal))

fy.n: Your smear shows no abnormal or pre-cancerous cells, which is very reassuring for cervical health. Reactive changes or a minor infection may be mentioned and are treated simply if needed. Keep up routine screening every 3 years (or 5 years with HPV co-testing) and consider HPV vaccination if not already done.
fy.bhi: Your smear shows mild cell changes (ASC-US or LSIL). These are usually caused by the common HPV virus and most clear on their own within 1–2 years. Your doctor may arrange an HPV test or a repeat smear in 6–12 months, and colposcopy if changes persist. This is not cancer, and early follow-up keeps it that way.
fy.hi: Your smear shows higher-grade cell changes that need prompt attention. These are pre-cancerous changes, not a cancer diagnosis, and are very treatable when found at this stage. Your doctor will refer you for colposcopy, a closer look at the cervix with a small biopsy, to decide on treatment. Please do not delay this appointment.

TLP-279.notes: Screening is recommended from age 25–30 (India) or 21 (ACOG); an unsatisfactory or inadequate sample should be repeated in 2–4 months; results in pregnancy are interpreted the same way but treatment is usually deferred.
TLP-279.src: Bethesda System 2014; ASCCP 2019 risk-based management guidelines; ICMR/FOGSI cervical screening recommendations
TLP-279.retest: Normal: repeat in 3 years (5 years with negative HPV co-test). ASC-US/LSIL: HPV test or repeat in 6–12 months. Unsatisfactory: repeat in 2–4 months.

any.label: NILM (normal)
any.text: Negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy

TLP-280.name: Urine Culture
TLP-280.meas: Whether bacteria grow from the urine in significant numbers, which organism it is, and which antibiotics it responds to.
TLP-280.sig: Culture is the definitive test for a urinary tract infection and the only way to choose an antibiotic that will actually work, which matters in India where resistance is common. It also distinguishes true infection from contamination during collection.
TLP-280.ind: Significant growth (typically ≥ 10^5 CFU/mL of a single organism) indicates urinary infection with E. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus, Enterococcus or others; mixed low-count growth suggests contamination; no growth with symptoms may reflect prior antibiotics or non-bacterial causes.

rng.bhi: 10^3 – 10^4 CFU/mL or mixed flora (Low count / mixed)

fy.n: No significant bacteria grew from your urine, which means a bacterial urinary infection is unlikely at this time. If you still have burning or frequency, causes such as vaginal irritation, stones or prior antibiotic use may be responsible; drinking plenty of water and not holding urine helps prevent infections.
fy.bhi: A low bacterial count or a mixture of organisms grew, which most often reflects contamination from skin during collection rather than a true infection. If you have symptoms, your doctor may ask you to repeat the test with a careful midstream clean-catch sample before treating.
fy.hi: A significant number of bacteria grew, confirming a urinary tract infection; the organism and the antibiotics it responds to are listed on your report. Your doctor will choose treatment from the sensitive options, and you should complete the full course and drink plenty of fluids. A repeat culture after treatment confirms clearance, especially in pregnancy or recurrent infections.

TLP-280.notes: In symptomatic women, ≥ 10^2–10^3 CFU/mL of a uropathogen can be significant; in pregnancy any significant growth (even without symptoms) is treated; catheter specimens use ≥ 10^3 CFU/mL.
TLP-280.src: IDSA 2010/2019 UTI guidelines; European Urinalysis Guidelines; Kass criteria
TLP-280.retest: Test of cure 1–2 weeks after treatment in pregnancy, recurrent infection or persisting symptoms; repeat contaminated samples with a fresh midstream collection.

TLP-281.name: Thyroglobulin
TLP-281.meas: A protein made only by thyroid tissue, used as a marker of how much thyroid tissue is present and active.
TLP-281.sig: In people who have had their thyroid removed for cancer, thyroglobulin should fall to near zero, so any measurable level flags residual or recurrent disease. In an intact thyroid it rises with goitre, inflammation or overactivity and is less specific.
TLP-281.ind: High levels suggest goitre, thyroiditis, Graves' disease, thyroid nodules or, after thyroidectomy, residual or recurrent differentiated thyroid cancer; very low levels in an intact thyroid can occur with thyroxine over-replacement or, rarely, congenital thyroglobulin deficiency.

fy.lo: Your thyroglobulin is very low. If you have had your thyroid removed for cancer this is exactly what your doctor hopes to see, suggesting no residual thyroid tissue. If your thyroid is intact it may reflect thyroxine tablets suppressing the gland, and usually needs no action beyond routine thyroid monitoring.
fy.n: Your thyroglobulin is within the range seen in people with a healthy, intact thyroid gland. This suggests no unusual thyroid enlargement or inflammation. If you have had thyroid cancer surgery, any measurable level should be discussed with your doctor because the target after surgery is much lower.
fy.hi: Your thyroglobulin is raised. With an intact thyroid this commonly reflects a goitre, nodules, an overactive gland or thyroiditis and is not by itself a sign of cancer. After thyroid cancer surgery a rising level can signal remaining or returning thyroid tissue, so your doctor may arrange a scan. Thyroglobulin antibodies must be checked alongside, as they can interfere.

TLP-281.notes: Ranges are assay-specific and only valid when anti-thyroglobulin antibodies are negative; post-thyroidectomy targets are < 0.2 ng/mL (suppressed) or < 1 ng/mL (stimulated); results should be trended on the same assay.
TLP-281.src: ATA 2015 Thyroid Nodule and Differentiated Thyroid Cancer Guidelines; manufacturer reference interval (Roche Elecsys)
TLP-281.retest: After thyroid cancer surgery, measure every 6–12 months on the same assay together with anti-Tg antibodies; otherwise repeat only as directed by your doctor.

TLP-282.name: Stool Occult Blood
TLP-282.meas: Tiny amounts of blood in the stool that cannot be seen with the naked eye.
TLP-282.sig: Hidden blood loss is often the only early clue to bowel polyps, colorectal cancer or ulcers, and to iron-deficiency anaemia of unknown cause. As a screening test it lowers colorectal cancer deaths when acted on with colonoscopy.
TLP-282.ind: A positive result suggests bleeding from polyps, colorectal cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, ulcers, haemorrhoids or NSAID/aspirin-related gut irritation; a negative result makes significant bleeding unlikely but does not exclude a lesion that bleeds intermittently.

fy.n: No hidden blood was detected in your stool, which makes a bleeding polyp, ulcer or bowel growth unlikely at present. Because some lesions bleed only now and then, regular screening still matters: from age 45–50, repeat an immunochemical stool test yearly or have a colonoscopy as your doctor advises.
fy.hi: Hidden blood was detected in your stool. The commonest explanations are piles, small tears, gut irritation from painkillers, or a polyp, but a positive result must always be followed up with a colonoscopy to look directly at the bowel. Please arrange this with your doctor; most causes found are benign and treatable.

TLP-282.notes: Guaiac-based tests can be falsely positive after red meat, raw vegetables or iron and falsely negative with vitamin C; immunochemical (FIT) tests need no dietary restriction and detect only lower-gut bleeding.
TLP-282.src: USPSTF 2021 colorectal cancer screening; ACG 2021 guideline
TLP-282.retest: Negative: annual FIT for screening from age 45–50. Positive: colonoscopy rather than repeat stool testing.

TLP-283.name: Stool Calprotectin
TLP-283.meas: A protein released by white blood cells into the stool when the bowel lining is inflamed.
TLP-283.sig: Calprotectin reliably separates inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's, ulcerative colitis) from irritable bowel syndrome without an immediate colonoscopy. It also tracks how well inflammatory bowel disease is controlled on treatment.
TLP-283.ind: Raised levels suggest inflammatory bowel disease, infective colitis, NSAID-related gut damage, diverticulitis or colorectal neoplasia; normal levels make active bowel inflammation unlikely and favour irritable bowel syndrome for functional symptoms.

fy.n: Your calprotectin is in the normal range, which strongly suggests there is no active inflammation in your bowel. If you have bloating, cramps or altered bowel habit, a functional cause such as irritable bowel is much more likely than inflammatory bowel disease. Diet, stress management and regular routine are the mainstays.
fy.bhi: Your calprotectin is mildly raised, a grey zone that can follow a recent gut infection, use of anti-inflammatory painkillers, or low-grade bowel inflammation.
