Your doctor will usually repeat the test in 4–6 weeks after stopping such painkillers; a persistently raised level may prompt a closer look at the bowel.
fy.hi: Your calprotectin is clearly raised, which indicates significant inflammation in your bowel. This is most often seen with inflammatory bowel disease or an infective colitis, and sometimes with painkiller damage or diverticulitis. Your doctor is likely to recommend a colonoscopy to find the cause; if you already have inflammatory bowel disease, it suggests active disease needing treatment review.

TLP-283.notes: Children under 4 years have higher normal values (often up to 100–150 µg/g); levels rise with NSAIDs and proton-pump inhibitors; cut-offs vary by assay.
TLP-283.src: NICE DG11 (2013); ECCO/ESGAR 2019 guidelines; BSG 2019 IBD guideline
TLP-283.retest: Repeat in 4–6 weeks for borderline results; in known IBD, measure every 3–6 months to monitor disease control.

TLP-284.name: Stool Lactoferrin
TLP-284.meas: An iron-binding protein shed by white blood cells into the stool, indicating active inflammation in the bowel.
TLP-284.sig: Lactoferrin, like calprotectin, flags whether the gut is truly inflamed. It is particularly useful for separating inflammatory diarrhoea (infective colitis, inflammatory bowel disease) from irritable bowel or viral upsets, and for monitoring disease activity.
TLP-284.ind: A positive result suggests inflammatory bowel disease, bacterial or amoebic colitis, Clostridioides difficile infection or NSAID damage; a negative result favours non-inflammatory causes such as irritable bowel syndrome or viral gastroenteritis.

fy.n: Your lactoferrin test is negative, which suggests there is no active inflammation in your bowel right now. Symptoms such as loose motions or cramps are more likely to have a non-inflammatory cause, for instance irritable bowel or a passing viral upset. No further inflammation testing is usually needed unless symptoms change.
fy.hi: Your lactoferrin test is positive, meaning white blood cells are entering your bowel and it is inflamed. This is seen with bacterial or amoebic infections, inflammatory bowel disease and some antibiotic-related colitis. Your doctor will read this with your calprotectin, culture and parasite results and may arrange further tests such as colonoscopy.

TLP-284.notes: Breast-fed infants test positive because human milk is rich in lactoferrin; the quantitative cut-off shown is for common ELISA kits and varies by manufacturer.
TLP-284.src: IDSA 2017 infectious diarrhoea guideline; ACG 2018 ulcerative colitis guideline
TLP-284.retest: Repeat after treatment of an identified infection, or as part of periodic monitoring in inflammatory bowel disease.

TLP-285.name: Giardia Antigen (stool)
TLP-285.meas: Proteins from the parasite Giardia lamblia detected directly in the stool, showing current infection.
TLP-285.sig: Giardia is one of the commonest causes of prolonged bloating, greasy stools and weight loss in India, and is easy to miss on microscopy because cysts are shed intermittently. The antigen test picks it up in a single sample with high accuracy.
TLP-285.ind: A positive result indicates current Giardia infection; a negative result makes giardiasis unlikely, though very light infections can occasionally be missed.

fy.n: No Giardia antigen was found, which makes this common parasite an unlikely cause of your symptoms. If chronic bloating, greasy stools or weight loss persist, your doctor may look at other causes such as lactose intolerance or coeliac disease. Safe drinking water and hand-washing keep the risk low.
fy.hi: Giardia antigen was detected, confirming a current infection with this water-borne parasite. It explains symptoms like bloating, foul greasy stools and fatigue, and clears with a short course of medicine from your doctor. Household contacts with symptoms should be tested, and boiling or filtering drinking water prevents re-infection.

TLP-285.notes: Antigen may remain detectable for 1–2 weeks after successful treatment; testing for cure should wait at least 2 weeks.
TLP-285.src: IDSA 2017 infectious diarrhoea guideline; CDC DPDx
TLP-285.retest: Retest 2–4 weeks after treatment if symptoms persist; a single negative in a symptomatic person may be repeated on a second sample.

TLP-286.name: Entamoeba histolytica Antigen (IgG)
TLP-286.alias: Amoebic antigen, Amoebiasis serology, E. histolytica IgG
TLP-286.meas: Either the parasite's own proteins in stool (current gut infection) or IgG antibodies in blood (exposure to invasive amoebiasis), depending on the method used.
TLP-286.sig: Entamoeba histolytica causes amoebic dysentery and liver abscess, yet under the microscope it looks identical to harmless amoebae. Antigen testing confirms the true pathogen in stool, while IgG antibodies support a diagnosis of invasive disease such as liver abscess.
TLP-286.ind: A positive stool antigen indicates current intestinal infection with the pathogenic E. histolytica; a positive IgG indicates present or past invasive amoebiasis (colitis or liver abscess); negative results make invasive amoebiasis unlikely.

fy.n: The test is negative, which makes an infection with the disease-causing amoeba Entamoeba histolytica unlikely. If cysts were seen on your stool microscopy they most probably belong to a harmless look-alike species that needs no treatment. Clean water and washed, cooked food remain your best protection.
fy.bhi: The result is in the equivocal zone, meaning it is neither clearly positive nor negative. This can happen early in an infection, after a past exposure, or from assay cross-reaction. Your doctor may repeat the test in 2–3 weeks or add a stool PCR to clarify, especially if you have diarrhoea with blood or mucus.
fy.hi: The test is positive, which suggests infection with the pathogenic amoeba. A positive stool antigen means current gut infection; a positive blood antibody means current or past invasive disease, and in India antibodies can persist for years. Your doctor will decide on treatment and, if you have fever or right-sided abdominal pain, may arrange a liver ultrasound.

TLP-286.notes: IgG remains positive for years after infection, so in endemic areas a positive antibody does not prove active disease; stool antigen kits vary in their ability to distinguish E. histolytica from E. dispar.
TLP-286.src: WHO/PAHO 1997 amoebiasis consensus; IDSA 2017 infectious diarrhoea guideline
TLP-286.retest: Repeat equivocal serology in 2–3 weeks; stool antigen may be repeated 2–4 weeks after treatment to confirm clearance.

TLP-287.name: Clostridium difficile Toxin (if antibiotic history)
TLP-287.alias: C. diff toxin A/B, CDI test, Clostridioides difficile
TLP-287.meas: Toxins produced by the bacterium Clostridioides difficile in the stool, which cause antibiotic-associated diarrhoea and colitis.
TLP-287.sig: C. difficile overgrows when antibiotics wipe out normal gut bacteria, and its toxins can cause severe, even life-threatening, colitis. Finding the toxin explains diarrhoea that starts during or after antibiotics and directs specific treatment.
TLP-287.ind: A positive toxin test indicates active C. difficile infection; a negative toxin with positive GDH antigen suggests carriage without active toxin production; negative results point to other causes of diarrhoea.

fy.n: No C. difficile toxin was found, so this infection is unlikely to be the reason for your loose motions. Diarrhoea after antibiotics is often a simple imbalance of gut bacteria that settles once the course ends; fluids and, if your doctor agrees, a probiotic can help. Seek review if fever, blood or severe pain develop.
fy.bhi: The screening antigen was positive but toxin was not detected, an indeterminate pattern. It may mean you carry the bacterium without it actively causing disease, or that toxin levels were too low to detect. Your doctor may send a confirmatory PCR test and will decide on treatment based on your symptoms.
fy.hi: C. difficile toxin was detected, which confirms an infection of the bowel usually triggered by a recent antibiotic course. It is treatable with a specific antibiotic, and your doctor may stop the original antibiotic if possible. Keep well hydrated, wash hands with soap and water (alcohol gel does not kill the spores), and report worsening pain, fever or blood promptly.

TLP-287.notes: Testing should only be done on unformed stool in patients with ≥ 3 loose stools in 24 hours; infants under 1 year are frequently colonised and should not be tested routinely.
TLP-287.retest: Do not repeat within 7 days of a negative result or as a test of cure; retest only if symptoms recur after treatment.

TLP-288.name: Lactose Hydrogen Breath Test
TLP-288.alias: Lactose intolerance test, LHBT, Lactose HBT
TLP-288.meas: The rise in hydrogen (and methane) in your breath after drinking a lactose solution, which happens when unabsorbed lactose is fermented by gut bacteria.
TLP-288.sig: Most Indian adults lose some ability to digest milk sugar, and lactose intolerance is a frequent, easily fixed cause of bloating, gas and loose motions. The breath test confirms it objectively rather than relying on guesswork or unnecessary dairy avoidance.
TLP-288.ind: A rise in breath hydrogen of ≥ 20 ppm above baseline indicates lactose malabsorption; a flat curve indicates normal lactose digestion or, rarely, a non-hydrogen-producing gut flora; an early peak within 30–60 minutes suggests small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth.

fy.n: Your breath hydrogen did not rise significantly, which suggests you digest milk sugar normally and lactose is not the cause of your symptoms. There is no need to avoid dairy; if bloating or loose motions continue, your doctor may consider fructose intolerance, bacterial overgrowth or irritable bowel.
fy.hi: Your breath hydrogen rose clearly after the lactose drink, which is consistent with lactose malabsorption, a very common and harmless condition where the enzyme that digests milk sugar is reduced. Symptoms usually improve by limiting milk, choosing curd, hard cheese or lactose-free milk, and taking lactase drops if needed. A dietitian can help you keep calcium intake adequate.

TLP-288.notes: Requires 12-hour fast, no antibiotics for 4 weeks and no laxatives or probiotics for 1 week; methane should be measured alongside hydrogen (rise ≥ 10 ppm is positive) to avoid false negatives; symptoms during the test are recorded to distinguish intolerance from silent malabsorption.
TLP-288.src: North American Consensus on Hydrogen and Methane Breath Testing (Rezaie et al., 2017); ACG 2020 SIBO guideline
TLP-288.retest: Repeat only if the test was done without proper preparation or if symptoms change; a negative test in a strongly suggestive history may be repeated with methane measurement.

TLP-289.name: Fructose Hydrogen Breath Test
TLP-289.meas: The rise in breath hydrogen (and methane) after drinking a fructose solution, showing whether fruit sugar is absorbed or fermented in the bowel.
TLP-289.sig: Fructose from fruit, honey, sweeteners and soft drinks is poorly absorbed in a sizeable proportion of people and drives bloating, gas and diarrhoea that mimic irritable bowel. Confirming it allows a targeted, not blanket, dietary change.
TLP-289.ind: A rise of ≥ 20 ppm above baseline indicates fructose malabsorption; a flat curve indicates normal absorption; an early rise suggests small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth.

fy.n: Your breath hydrogen did not rise after the fructose drink, which suggests you absorb fruit sugar normally and fructose is not driving your symptoms. You can continue to enjoy fruit and honey; if symptoms persist, your doctor may look at lactose, bacterial overgrowth or irritable bowel instead.
fy.hi: Your breath hydrogen rose after the fructose drink, which is consistent with fructose malabsorption. This is not dangerous but explains bloating and loose motions after fruit juice, honey, mango, apples or sweetened drinks. Reducing high-fructose foods, eating fruit with meals and pairing it with glucose-rich foods usually helps; a dietitian can guide a low-FODMAP approach.

TLP-289.notes: Even healthy people malabsorb large fructose loads, so a 25 g dose is used; interpretation depends on symptoms during the test; same preparation rules as the lactose test.
TLP-289.src: North American Consensus on Hydrogen and Methane Breath Testing (Rezaie et al., 2017); Rome IV
TLP-289.retest: Repeat only if preparation was inadequate or symptoms change; retesting after a dietary trial is rarely needed.

TLP-290.name: IGF-1 (Insulin-like Growth Factor)
TLP-290.meas: A hormone made by the liver in response to growth hormone, giving a stable day-long picture of growth hormone activity.
TLP-290.sig: Growth hormone itself is released in short bursts, so a single measurement is unreliable; IGF-1 smooths this out. It is the screening test for both excess growth hormone (acromegaly) and deficiency, and shifts with nutrition, thyroid and liver health.
TLP-290.ind: High levels suggest acromegaly or gigantism (growth hormone excess), puberty or pregnancy, or growth hormone supplementation; low levels suggest growth hormone deficiency, malnutrition, hypothyroidism, poorly controlled diabetes, liver disease or chronic illness.

fy.lo: Your IGF-1 is below the range expected for your age. This can reflect low growth hormone output, but is more often due to under-nutrition, an underactive thyroid, poorly controlled diabetes, liver problems or a long-standing illness. Your doctor may check thyroid and nutritional status first and, if needed, arrange formal growth hormone testing.
fy.n: Your IGF-1 is within the range expected for your age and sex, which suggests your growth hormone axis is working normally. This supports healthy muscle, bone and metabolic function. Regular exercise, adequate protein and good sleep all help maintain normal growth hormone activity.
fy.hi: Your IGF-1 is above the range expected for your age. In adolescents and in pregnancy this is often normal, but in adults a persistently high level can indicate excess growth hormone (acromegaly), particularly with enlarging hands, feet or facial features, headaches or sweating. Your doctor may repeat the test and, if still high, arrange a glucose-suppression test and pituitary imaging.

TLP-290.notes: IGF-1 is strongly age-dependent: it peaks in puberty (up to ~600 ng/mL) and declines steadily with age (adults > 60 y roughly 50–180 ng/mL); the lab's age- and sex-specific reference interval and the reported Z-score should be used; values are assay-specific.
TLP-290.src: Endocrine Society 2014 Acromegaly & 2011 Adult GH Deficiency guidelines; assay-specific age tables (IDS-iSYS / Immulite)
TLP-290.retest: Repeat a borderline result on the same assay in 4–8 weeks; in treated acromegaly or growth hormone therapy, monitor every 3–6 months.

TLP-291.name: Haemoglobin Electrophoresis / HPLC
TLP-291.alias: Hb HPLC, Hb variant analysis, Thalassaemia screen, HbA2 / HbF
TLP-291.meas: The proportions of the different haemoglobin types (HbA, HbA2, HbF) and any abnormal variants such as HbS or HbE in your red cells.
TLP-291.sig: India has a high carrier rate of beta-thalassaemia, HbE and sickle cell traits, and carriers are usually healthy and unaware. Identifying carrier status before marriage or pregnancy lets couples know the risk of a child with a serious blood disorder.
TLP-291.ind: HbA2 ≥ 3.5% indicates beta-thalassaemia trait; raised HbF suggests delta-beta thalassaemia, HPFH or thalassaemia major; variant peaks indicate HbS (sickle), HbE, HbD-Punjab or other haemoglobinopathies; a normal pattern does not exclude alpha-thalassaemia trait.

rng.n: HbA > 95%, HbA2 2.0–3.4%, HbF < 2%, no variant (Normal pattern)
rng.bhi: HbA2 3.5–3.9% (with iron deficiency) or minor variant (Borderline HbA2)
rng.hi: HbA2 ≥ 4.0%, raised HbF, or HbS/HbE/HbD present (Abnormal pattern)

fy.n: Your haemoglobin pattern is normal, which means you are very unlikely to carry beta-thalassaemia, sickle cell or HbE trait. This is reassuring for you and for any future children. The common alpha-thalassaemia trait can hide behind a normal pattern, so if your red cells are small (low MCV) with normal iron, your doctor may suggest a genetic alpha test.
fy.bhi: Your HbA2 sits in a borderline zone, or a minor variant was noted. Borderline HbA2 can be a mild form of beta-thalassaemia trait or can be shifted by iron deficiency, which lowers HbA2. Your doctor will usually correct iron and repeat the test, recommending genetic testing if your partner is also a carrier or you are planning a pregnancy.
fy.hi: Your haemoglobin pattern is abnormal, most often meaning you carry a thalassaemia, sickle or HbE trait. Carriers are generally healthy and need no treatment, but if your partner is also a carrier there is a 1-in-4 chance per pregnancy of a child with a serious blood disorder. Discuss partner screening and genetic counselling with your doctor before planning a family.

TLP-291.notes: Iron deficiency lowers HbA2 and can mask beta-thalassaemia trait; HbF is normally high in infants under 6–12 months; recent transfusion within 3 months invalidates the result; alpha-thalassaemia requires DNA testing.
TLP-291.src: ICMR / Indian National Thalassaemia Guidelines 2016; BSH 2010 guideline for haemoglobinopathy screening; WHO
TLP-291.retest: Repeat after correcting iron deficiency if HbA2 is borderline; test partner if abnormal; no repeat needed for a normal pattern in a non-transfused adult.

any.label: Borderline HbA2
any.text: HbA2 3.5–3.9% (with iron deficiency) or minor variant

any.label: Abnormal pattern
any.text: HbA2 ≥ 4.0%, raised HbF, or HbS/HbE/HbD present

TLP-292.name: Random Blood Sugar (RBS)
TLP-292.alias: RBS, Random plasma glucose, Casual glucose
TLP-292.meas: The glucose level in your blood at any time of day regardless of when you last ate.
TLP-292.sig: A random sugar is a quick snapshot useful during fever, infection or acute illness, when stress and steroids can push glucose up. It cannot replace a fasting test or HbA1c for diagnosis, but a clearly high value with symptoms is itself diagnostic of diabetes.
TLP-292.ind: A value ≥ 200 mg/dL with symptoms (thirst, frequent urination, weight loss) indicates diabetes; 140–199 suggests impaired glucose handling or stress hyperglycaemia during illness; below 70 indicates hypoglycaemia, usually from diabetes medicines, missed meals, alcohol or rarely insulin-producing tumours.

fy.lo: Your random sugar is below the normal range, which can cause shakiness, sweating and confusion. If you take diabetes medicines this suggests the dose or meal timing needs review with your doctor; in someone not on such medicines, prolonged fasting, alcohol or an underlying condition may be responsible and deserves evaluation.
fy.n: Your random sugar is in the healthy range, which suggests your body is handling glucose well even after meals. This is reassuring, particularly during a fever when stress can push sugar up. Keep it there with regular activity, a balanced diet and periodic fasting sugar or HbA1c checks if you have a family history of diabetes.
fy.bhi: Your random sugar is higher than ideal. During infection or on steroids this is often temporary stress hyperglycaemia, but it can also be the first sign of pre-diabetes or diabetes. Your doctor will usually confirm with a fasting glucose and HbA1c once you are well; cutting sugary drinks and staying active is a sensible start.
fy.hi: Your random sugar is in the diabetic range. If you also have thirst, frequent urination or unexplained weight loss this is consistent with diabetes; without symptoms, or during acute illness, your doctor will confirm with a repeat fasting test or HbA1c. Either way, please see your doctor soon, since sustained high sugar during infection slows recovery.

TLP-292.notes: Diagnosis of diabetes on a random value requires classic symptoms or confirmation by a second test; steroids, IV dextrose and acute illness raise random glucose; fluoride tubes must be separated promptly to avoid falsely low values.
TLP-292.retest: Confirm any value ≥ 140 mg/dL with fasting plasma glucose and HbA1c once acute illness has settled, ideally within 2–4 weeks.

TLP-293.name: Blood Culture & Sensitivity
TLP-293.sample: Whole blood in aerobic/anaerobic culture bottles
TLP-293.meas: Whether bacteria or fungi are growing in the bloodstream, which organism it is, and which antibiotics will work against it.
TLP-293.sig: Bacteria in the blood (bacteraemia) can rapidly become sepsis, and typhoid, a common cause of prolonged fever in India, is best diagnosed by blood culture in the first week. It is the single most important test for choosing the right antibiotic in a serious fever.
TLP-293.ind: Growth of a pathogen (Salmonella Typhi, E. coli, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Candida, etc.) indicates bloodstream infection; growth of skin organisms in one of two bottles suggests contamination; no growth makes bacterial sepsis less likely but does not exclude it after antibiotics.

rng.bhi: Skin flora in 1 of 2 sets (Probable contaminant)

fy.n: No bacteria or fungi grew from your blood after 5 days, which makes a bloodstream infection unlikely. If antibiotics were started before the sample was taken the test is less sensitive, so your doctor will still interpret it alongside your symptoms and other fever tests such as malaria, dengue and typhoid serology.
fy.bhi: A skin-type organism grew in only one of the culture bottles, which usually means the sample picked up bacteria from the skin during collection rather than from your blood. Your doctor will judge this against your clinical picture and may repeat cultures from two separate sites before treating.
fy.hi: An organism grew from your blood, confirming a bloodstream infection; the report names it and lists the antibiotics that work against it. Your doctor will start or adjust treatment based on this list, and completing the full course is essential. Repeat cultures may be taken to confirm the infection has cleared, especially for typhoid or staphylococcal infections.

TLP-293.notes: Collect before antibiotics where possible, two sets from separate sites, 8–10 mL per adult bottle (1–3 mL in infants); typhoid yield is highest in week 1 of fever and falls after antibiotics; final negative report requires 5 days of incubation.
TLP-293.src: CLSI M47; IDSA/ASM Guide to Utilization of the Microbiology Laboratory 2018; ICMR Treatment Guidelines for Antimicrobial Use
TLP-293.retest: Repeat 48–72 hours after starting therapy for S. aureus, Candida or persistent fever; repeat with two fresh sets if a contaminant is suspected.

TLP-294.name: G6PD Screen
TLP-294.alias: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, G6PD deficiency test, G6PD qualitative
TLP-294.meas: Whether your red blood cells have enough of the enzyme G6PD, which protects them from damage by certain drugs, infections and foods.
TLP-294.sig: People with G6PD deficiency can develop sudden red-cell breakdown (haemolysis) when given drugs such as primaquine, dapsone, sulpha antibiotics or high-dose antimalarials. Checking before these medicines are prescribed prevents a potentially dangerous reaction.
TLP-294.ind: A deficient result indicates inherited G6PD deficiency, carrying a risk of haemolysis with oxidant drugs, fava beans and infections; an intermediate result is seen in female carriers and may still carry some risk; a normal result means these medicines can be given with usual precautions.

rng.n: M: Normal activity (≥ 60% of normal) | F: Normal activity (≥ 60% of normal)
rng.hi: M: Deficient (< 30% of normal) | F: Deficient (< 30% of normal) (Deficient)

fy.n: Your G6PD activity is normal, which means your red cells are protected against oxidant stress. Medicines such as dapsone, primaquine or hydroxychloroquine can be prescribed with the usual monitoring. Note that a screen done during or just after a haemolytic episode can read falsely normal because young red cells have more enzyme.
fy.bhi: Your G6PD activity is in the intermediate range, a pattern usually seen in women who carry one affected gene. Some of your red cells are vulnerable, so oxidant drugs such as dapsone or primaquine can still trigger mild haemolysis. Your doctor may request a quantitative enzyme assay and will choose medicines and doses with this in mind.
fy.hi: Your screen shows G6PD deficiency, an inherited condition common in India that usually causes no day-to-day problems. The key is avoiding triggers: dapsone, primaquine, sulpha drugs, nitrofurantoin, naphthalene mothballs and fava beans. Tell every doctor and pharmacist about this result, and seek help promptly if you notice dark urine, yellow eyes or sudden weakness after a new medicine or infection.

TLP-294.notes: Qualitative screens (fluorescent spot / methaemoglobin reduction) reliably detect hemizygous males but miss many heterozygous females, who need a quantitative assay; test at least 3 months after a haemolytic episode or transfusion; newborns should be screened before discharge in high-prevalence communities.
TLP-294.src: WHO 2016 G6PD classification (updated 2022); BSH 2020 guideline on laboratory diagnosis of G6PD deficiency
TLP-294.retest: If tested during acute haemolysis, transfusion or reticulocytosis, repeat after 3 months; intermediate results should be confirmed by quantitative assay.

TLP-295.name: Chlamydia trachomatis IgG
TLP-295.alias: Chlamydia serology, C. trachomatis IgG, Chlamydia antibody test (CAT)
TLP-295.meas: Antibodies in the blood showing past or persistent infection with Chlamydia trachomatis, a common sexually transmitted bacterium.
TLP-295.sig: Chlamydia infection is often silent yet scars the fallopian tubes, making it a leading cause of tubal infertility and ectopic pregnancy. A positive IgG in a woman having difficulty conceiving flags a higher chance of tubal damage and guides earlier tubal assessment.
TLP-295.ind: A positive result indicates past or chronic exposure to Chlamydia trachomatis and, in fertility work-up, a raised likelihood of tubal disease; a negative result makes tubal factor from chlamydia less likely; equivocal results usually reflect low-level or cross-reacting antibody.

fy.n: No chlamydia antibodies were found, which suggests you have not had a significant past infection and lowers the chance that scarred fallopian tubes are contributing to difficulty conceiving. Consistent condom use with new partners keeps it that way; if tubal problems are still suspected, your doctor may proceed with a tubal patency test.
fy.bhi: Your result is in the equivocal zone, which may reflect a low level of antibody from an old or minor exposure, or cross-reaction with related bacteria. It does not by itself prove tubal damage. Your doctor may repeat the test in 2–4 weeks or move directly to a tubal assessment if you are being investigated for infertility.
fy.hi: Chlamydia antibodies were detected, which indicates a past infection, often one you never noticed. This does not mean you are currently infected, but it raises the possibility of scarring in the fallopian tubes. Your doctor may recommend a tubal test (HSG or laparoscopy) earlier in your fertility work-up, plus a current-infection PCR for you and your partner.

TLP-295.notes: IgG persists for years and cannot distinguish current from past infection; current infection is diagnosed by NAAT on urine or swab; cross-reaction with Chlamydia pneumoniae can occur with less specific assays.
TLP-295.src: ESHRE 2015 female infertility work-up guidance; NICE CG156; BASHH chlamydia guideline
TLP-295.retest: Repeat equivocal results in 2–4 weeks; a positive IgG does not need repeating but should prompt tubal assessment and NAAT for current infection.

TLP-296.name: Peripheral Blood Karyotype (G-banding, 20 cells)
TLP-296.meas: The number and structure of all 46 chromosomes in your white blood cells, examined under the microscope after banding.
TLP-296.sig: About 3–5% of couples with recurrent pregnancy loss carry a balanced chromosome rearrangement that causes no problems for them but leads to miscarriages or an affected child. Finding it explains the losses and opens the door to embryo testing or donor options.
TLP-296.ind: An abnormal result may show a balanced translocation or inversion (carrier at risk of unbalanced pregnancies), a numerical abnormality such as 47,XXY (Klinefelter) or 45,X mosaicism (Turner), or a marker chromosome; a normal 46,XX or 46,XY result excludes large chromosomal causes but not small deletions or single-gene disorders.

fy.n: Your chromosome analysis is normal, meaning all 46 chromosomes are present with no large rearrangements. This makes a chromosomal cause for recurrent pregnancy loss unlikely on your side. It does not detect very small changes or single-gene conditions, so your doctor will continue with the other parts of the recurrent-loss work-up.
fy.hi: Your chromosome analysis shows an abnormality, most often a balanced rearrangement where pieces of two chromosomes have swapped places. Carriers are usually healthy, but some eggs or sperm carry an unbalanced set, which can cause miscarriage. A genetic counsellor will explain your finding and options such as pre-implantation genetic testing of embryos or prenatal testing in a future pregnancy.

TLP-296.notes: Standard 20-cell analysis detects mosaicism of roughly 10% or more; resolution of G-banding is about 5–10 Mb, so microdeletions require microarray or FISH; low-level mosaicism may need 30–50 cells; results should always be delivered with genetic counselling.
TLP-296.src: ESHRE 2017/2022 Recurrent Pregnancy Loss guideline; ASRM 2012 committee opinion; ISCN 2020 nomenclature
TLP-296.retest: A constitutional karyotype does not change and need not be repeated; if abnormal, test the partner and offer counselling; if mosaicism is suspected, extend to 50 cells or test a second tissue.

TLP-297.name: Products of Conception — Chromosomal Microarray
TLP-297.alias: POC microarray, POC CMA, Miscarriage tissue genetic testing
TLP-297.sample: Products of conception (fresh tissue in saline or transport medium)
TLP-297.meas: A genome-wide scan of the miscarriage tissue for missing or extra chromosomes and smaller copy-number changes that explain why the pregnancy did not continue.
TLP-297.sig: More than half of early miscarriages are due to a random chromosome error in the embryo, not to anything the parents did or carry. Knowing this gives an answer, avoids unnecessary further testing, and helps decide whether parental karyotyping or embryo testing is worthwhile.
TLP-297.ind: An aneuploidy (trisomy, monosomy X, triploidy) indicates a sporadic error with low recurrence risk; an unbalanced structural change may point to a parental balanced translocation; a normal (euploid) result suggests non-chromosomal causes such as uterine, immune, clotting or endocrine factors should be pursued.

fy.n: The miscarriage tissue showed a normal chromosome set, so a random chromosomal error was not the cause of this loss. That makes it more worthwhile to look at other factors such as the shape of the uterus, thyroid and blood-sugar control, clotting or immune conditions, which your doctor will now focus on. These causes are often treatable.
fy.bhi: The test found a small chromosomal change whose significance is uncertain, meaning current knowledge cannot say whether it caused the loss. A genetic counsellor may suggest testing both parents to see if the change is inherited and harmless. Your doctor will still continue the standard recurrent-loss evaluation.
fy.hi: The tissue showed a chromosome abnormality, most commonly an extra or missing chromosome that arose by chance at conception. This is the commonest reason for miscarriage and is not caused by anything you did; recurrence risk is low for most such findings. If the change is a structural imbalance, your doctor will arrange chromosome tests for both partners and counselling.

TLP-297.notes: Maternal cell contamination can give a false 46,XX result and is checked by comparing with a maternal sample; microarray cannot detect balanced rearrangements or triploidy on some platforms; this is the ESHRE-recommended first-line test after a second loss.
TLP-297.src: ESHRE 2022 Recurrent Pregnancy Loss guideline; ACOG Practice Bulletin 200; ACMG technical standards for CMA
TLP-297.retest: Each pregnancy loss is tested separately; a parental karyotype is indicated if an unbalanced structural abnormality is found.

TLP-298.name: Serum ACE
TLP-298.meas: The level of an enzyme produced in large amounts by the immune cell clusters (granulomas) that form in sarcoidosis.
TLP-298.sig: Sarcoidosis can present in the skin and scalp as scarring hair loss, and serum ACE supports the diagnosis and tracks disease activity. It is not specific, so it is read alongside chest imaging, calcium and, where possible, a biopsy.
TLP-298.ind: Raised ACE suggests active sarcoidosis, and is also seen in tuberculosis, leprosy, hyperthyroidism, diabetes, liver disease and silicosis; low or normal ACE does not exclude sarcoidosis, and low levels occur with ACE-inhibitor medicines or steroid treatment.

fy.n: Your ACE level is within the normal range, which makes active, widespread sarcoidosis less likely, although about a third of people with sarcoidosis have a normal ACE. If skin or scalp changes still suggest it, your doctor may rely on a skin biopsy or chest imaging. Blood-pressure medicines of the ACE-inhibitor type can lower the value, so mention them.
fy.bhi: Your ACE level is mildly raised, a zone that overlaps with healthy people and with conditions such as thyroid overactivity, diabetes or liver disease. On its own it is not diagnostic. Your doctor will consider it together with your symptoms, calcium level and chest X-ray, and may repeat the test in a few weeks.
fy.hi: Your ACE level is clearly raised, which in the right clinical setting supports a diagnosis of sarcoidosis, an inflammatory condition that can affect skin, lungs, eyes and lymph nodes. Tuberculosis and a few other conditions can also raise ACE, so your doctor will arrange imaging and usually a biopsy to confirm before treatment. ACE then helps track response to treatment.

TLP-298.notes: Reference intervals are assay-specific (the values shown are for common kinetic assays); children and adolescents have higher normal values (up to ~1.5x adult); ACE-inhibitor drugs and corticosteroids lower the result; ACE genotype (I/D polymorphism) causes wide individual variation.
TLP-298.src: ATS/ERS/WASOG 1999 sarcoidosis statement; ATS 2020 sarcoidosis diagnosis guideline; manufacturer reference intervals
TLP-298.retest: Repeat in 4–8 weeks for borderline values; in confirmed sarcoidosis, monitor every 3–6 months as a marker of activity on the same assay.

TLP-299.name: TPHA / TP-PA (treponemal)
TLP-299.alias: TPHA, TP-PA, Treponemal antibody, Treponema pallidum haemagglutination
TLP-299.meas: Antibodies specifically directed against Treponema pallidum, the bacterium that causes syphilis.
TLP-299.sig: Treponemal tests confirm that a positive screening test (VDRL/RPR) truly reflects syphilis rather than a false-positive from pregnancy, autoimmune disease or other infections. Syphilis can mimic many skin and hair conditions, including patchy 'moth-eaten' hair loss, and is fully curable when identified.
TLP-299.ind: A reactive result indicates current or previously treated syphilis (antibodies persist for life); with a reactive VDRL/RPR it suggests active or recently treated infection; a non-reactive result excludes syphilis except in the first 2–4 weeks after exposure; indeterminate results need repeat or an alternative treponemal test.

fy.n: Your treponemal antibody test is non-reactive, which means there is no evidence of syphilis, past or present. If any earlier screening test was positive, this confirms it was a false alarm. Very recent exposure (within a few weeks) can be missed, so if that applies your doctor may repeat the test after 4–6 weeks.
fy.bhi: Your result is indeterminate, meaning the reaction was too weak to call clearly positive or negative. This can happen very early in infection, after past treated infection, or from non-specific antibody. Your doctor will usually repeat it in 2–4 weeks or run a different treponemal test (such as FTA-ABS or a treponemal EIA) together with a VDRL/RPR to clarify.
fy.hi: Your treponemal antibody test is reactive, confirming a syphilis infection at some point. Because this antibody stays positive for life, your doctor will use the VDRL/RPR titre and your history to tell whether it is an active infection needing treatment or an old, treated one. Syphilis is curable with antibiotics; partners may need testing.

TLP-299.notes: Remains reactive lifelong after infection regardless of treatment, so it cannot be used to monitor cure; may be non-reactive in the first 2–4 weeks of primary syphilis; rare false positives occur with leprosy, Lyme disease and other spirochaetal infections; in pregnancy a reactive result requires prompt treatment to prevent congenital syphilis.
TLP-299.src: CDC STI Treatment Guidelines 2021; WHO 2016 syphilis guidelines; NACO India STI guidelines
TLP-299.retest: Repeat indeterminate results in 2–4 weeks; a reactive result does not need repeating, but VDRL/RPR should be followed at 6 and 12 months after treatment.

TLP-300.name: Direct Coombs Test
TLP-300.meas: Whether antibodies or complement proteins are already stuck to the surface of your red blood cells, marking them for destruction by the immune system.
TLP-300.sig: A positive direct Coombs test is the hallmark of autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, which occurs in up to 10% of people with lupus and can also follow certain drugs or infections. Checking it explains an unexplained anaemia or a raised bilirubin and LDH in an autoimmune patient.
TLP-300.ind: A positive result suggests autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (including lupus-associated), drug-induced haemolysis, a transfusion reaction, haemolytic disease of the newborn, or cold agglutinin disease; a negative result makes immune-mediated haemolysis unlikely.

fy.n: Your direct Coombs test is negative, meaning no antibodies are found coating your red cells. This makes immune-mediated red-cell destruction an unlikely cause of any anaemia, which is reassuring in lupus and related conditions. Other causes such as iron deficiency, chronic inflammation or medicines would be considered instead.
fy.bhi: Your direct Coombs test is weakly positive. Small amounts of antibody on red cells are found in a few healthy people and in those with lupus or on certain medicines, without any actual red-cell destruction. Your doctor will check haemoglobin, reticulocyte count, bilirubin and LDH to see whether haemolysis is really occurring before any action is taken.
fy.hi: Your direct Coombs test is clearly positive, meaning your immune system is coating your red cells with antibody, which can lead to their premature destruction (autoimmune haemolytic anaemia). This can be part of lupus, triggered by a medicine, or follow an infection. Your doctor will confirm with haemoglobin, reticulocyte, bilirubin and LDH results and, if haemolysis is active, discuss treatment.

TLP-300.notes: Positive in 1–15% of hospitalised patients and 0.1% of healthy donors without haemolysis; recent transfusion (within 3 months), IV immunoglobulin, and drugs such as cephalosporins, methyldopa and penicillins can cause a positive result; monospecific IgG/C3d typing indicates warm vs cold antibody type.
TLP-300.src: BSH 2017 guideline on the diagnosis and management of autoimmune haemolytic anaemia; AABB Technical Manual
TLP-300.retest: Repeat with haemolysis markers if weakly positive or clinically unexpected; monitor during treatment of autoimmune haemolytic anaemia as directed.

TLP-301.name: Myositis-Specific Antibody Panel (LIA)
TLP-301.alias: Myositis line immunoassay, MSA/MAA panel, Extended myositis blot
TLP-301.meas: A panel of autoantibodies (such as anti-Mi-2, MDA5, TIF1-γ, NXP2, SAE, Jo-1 and other synthetases, SRP, HMGCR, PM-Scl, Ku) that mark different types of inflammatory muscle and skin disease.
TLP-301.sig: Dermatomyositis is not one disease: each antibody predicts a distinct pattern of skin, muscle, lung and cancer risk. Identifying the antibody guides how hard to look for lung involvement or an underlying cancer and helps predict the course.
TLP-301.ind: Anti-Mi-2 suggests classic skin-and-muscle disease with a good outlook; anti-TIF1-γ and anti-NXP2 in adults raise cancer risk; anti-MDA5 suggests skin-predominant disease with a risk of rapidly progressive lung disease; anti-synthetase antibodies (Jo-1, PL-7, PL-12) suggest antisynthetase syndrome with lung involvement; anti-SRP and anti-HMGCR suggest necrotising myopathy; a negative panel does not exclude myositis.

fy.n: No myositis antibodies were detected. Around 30–40% of people with dermatomyositis have no identifiable antibody, so this does not rule the condition out, but it removes the specific antibody-linked risks such as rapidly progressive lung disease. Your doctor will rely on your skin findings, muscle enzymes, and where needed imaging or biopsy to complete the picture.
fy.bhi: One or more antibody bands were weakly positive. Weak bands on this type of test can be genuine early findings or non-specific background reactivity, so on their own they should not be over-interpreted. Your rheumatologist or dermatologist will weigh them against your symptoms and may repeat the panel or confirm with a different method in 3–6 months.
fy.hi: A myositis antibody was clearly detected, and the antibody named on your report tells your specialist what type of disease to expect and what to watch for. Depending on the antibody, this may mean additional checks of the lungs (breathing tests, CT scan) or age-appropriate cancer screening, and it helps tailor treatment. Review the result with your rheumatologist or dermatologist.

TLP-301.notes: No numeric reference range; results are reported as negative, weak or positive per antibody by line immunoassay and should be confirmed by immunoprecipitation or ELISA where results are unexpected; anti-MDA5 and anti-TIF1-γ have important clinical implications and warrant specialist review; juvenile dermatomyositis has a different antibody profile (NXP2, TIF1-γ predominate) without the adult cancer association.
TLP-301.src: EULAR/ACR 2017 classification criteria for idiopathic inflammatory myopathies; McHugh & Tansley, Nat Rev Rheumatol 2018; BSR 2022 myositis guideline
TLP-301.retest: Repeat weak or borderline results in 3–6 months or confirm by an alternative method; a clearly positive antibody does not need repeating.

TLP-302.name: Serum Bile Acids
TLP-302.meas: The concentration of bile acids in the blood, which rises when the liver cannot clear them properly from the circulation.
TLP-302.sig: Persistent itching without a rash, especially in older adults, can be the first sign of cholestasis (impaired bile flow) even when routine liver enzymes look normal. Bile acids are the most sensitive blood marker of cholestasis and are the standard test for itching in pregnancy.
TLP-302.ind: Raised bile acids suggest cholestatic liver disease (primary biliary cholangitis, drug-induced cholestasis, bile-duct obstruction), intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy, cirrhosis or portal-systemic shunting; low values have no clinical significance.

fy.n: Your bile acid level is normal, which suggests bile is flowing freely from your liver and a liver cause for itching is unlikely. In older adults the commonest reasons for itching are dry skin, medicines, kidney or thyroid changes, which your doctor will now consider. Regular moisturising and reviewing new medicines is a good first step.
fy.bhi: Your bile acids are mildly raised, which can occur after a meal if the sample was not fasting, with some medicines, or as an early sign of impaired bile flow. Your doctor may repeat the test fasting and check liver enzymes (ALP, GGT); if you are pregnant, the value will be followed closely as it guides the timing of delivery.
fy.hi: Your bile acids are clearly raised, which indicates cholestasis, a slowing of bile flow from the liver. This commonly explains generalised itching and can result from medicines, gallstone or bile-duct blockage, autoimmune bile-duct disease or, in pregnancy, intrahepatic cholestasis. Your doctor will arrange liver enzymes, an ultrasound and possibly autoimmune tests; treatments exist that lower bile acids and relieve itching.

TLP-302.notes: Levels rise 2–3-fold after meals, so a fasting sample is preferred; in pregnancy ≥ 10 µmol/L (non-fasting) is diagnostic of intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy and ≥ 100 µmol/L signals high stillbirth risk; reference intervals vary by method (enzymatic vs LC-MS).
TLP-302.src: RCOG Green-top Guideline 43 (2022) on intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy; EASL 2009 cholestatic liver disease guideline; manufacturer reference interval
TLP-302.retest: Repeat fasting if the first sample was post-prandial; in cholestasis of pregnancy, repeat weekly or as directed until delivery.

TLP-303.name: β-hCG (serum, quantitative)
TLP-303.alias: Beta hCG, Quantitative hCG, Serum pregnancy test
TLP-303.meas: The level of human chorionic gonadotropin, a hormone produced by the placenta from a few days after implantation.
TLP-303.sig: Many dermatology medicines, including isotretinoin, methotrexate and several biologics, can seriously harm a developing baby, so pregnancy must be excluded before starting and during treatment. A blood hCG is the most sensitive way to do this and can detect pregnancy before a missed period.
TLP-303.ind: A positive result (≥ 25 mIU/mL) indicates pregnancy, or rarely a molar pregnancy, germ-cell tumour or certain other cancers; a grey-zone result (5–25) may be very early pregnancy, a recent miscarriage, or perimenopausal pituitary hCG; a negative result (< 5) excludes pregnancy beyond about 10 days from conception.

fy.n: Your hCG is negative, which means you are not pregnant at the time of testing (a pregnancy less than about 10 days old could still be too early to show). This clears the way for medicines that must not be taken in pregnancy; reliable contraception during treatment, and repeat testing as your doctor schedules, keep it that way.
fy.bhi: Your hCG is in the grey zone between negative and positive. This may be very early pregnancy, a recent miscarriage, or, around the menopause, a small amount of hCG from the pituitary gland. Your doctor will repeat the test in 48–72 hours: a rising level suggests pregnancy. Hold off starting any pregnancy-unsafe medicine until this is clarified.
fy.hi: Your hCG is positive, which indicates pregnancy. Please contact your doctor before starting or continuing any medicine flagged as unsafe in pregnancy, such as isotretinoin, methotrexate or certain biologics, and arrange an early antenatal visit. Very rarely a high hCG without pregnancy reflects other conditions, which your doctor will consider if an ultrasound does not show a pregnancy.

TLP-303.notes: Doubles roughly every 48 hours in early pregnancy, peaking at 8–10 weeks; in men and non-pregnant women the normal value is < 5 mIU/mL, rising to < 10–14 after the menopause; heterophile antibodies and recent hCG injections (fertility treatment) can cause false positives; for isotretinoin, two negative tests before starting and monthly tests during treatment are required.
TLP-303.src: ACOG Practice Bulletin 193 (early pregnancy loss); iPLEDGE / AAD isotretinoin monitoring recommendations; manufacturer reference interval
TLP-303.retest: Repeat in 48–72 hours for indeterminate results; monthly during isotretinoin or other teratogenic therapy; before each restart of a pregnancy-unsafe medicine.

TLP-304.name: Quantiferon-TB Gold Plus (IGRA)
TLP-304.alias: IGRA, QFT-Plus, Interferon-gamma release assay, Latent TB test
TLP-304.meas: Whether your immune cells release interferon-gamma when exposed to TB-specific proteins, showing that you have been infected with tuberculosis bacteria at some time.
TLP-304.sig: Around a quarter of Indians carry dormant (latent) TB. Biologic and JAK-inhibitor medicines suppress the immune system and can wake it up into active disease, so a TB blood test before starting, and periodically during treatment, allows preventive therapy to be given first.
TLP-304.ind: A positive result indicates TB infection, latent or active, and does not distinguish between them; a negative result makes TB infection unlikely, though sensitivity falls in immunosuppressed people; an indeterminate result means the test could not be read, usually because of immunosuppression or sample handling.

fy.n: Your TB blood test is negative, which means there is no evidence that you carry the TB bacteria. This is reassuring before starting immune-suppressing treatment. Because the test can be less sensitive if your immunity is already lowered, your doctor will still ask about symptoms and may repeat it yearly while you remain on a biologic or JAK inhibitor.
fy.bhi: Your result is either indeterminate (the test could not be read) or lies in a borderline zone just above the cut-off. Indeterminate results are common with steroids, immune-suppressing drugs or delayed sample processing; borderline positives sometimes revert on repeat. Your doctor will usually repeat the test in 4–8 weeks and may add a chest X-ray before deciding on preventive treatment.
fy.hi: Your TB blood test is positive, meaning your immune system has met TB bacteria at some point. Most often this is latent infection with no symptoms and no risk of spreading it. Your doctor will check for active disease with a chest X-ray and, if clear, will usually recommend preventive TB medicine before or alongside your biologic or JAK-inhibitor treatment.

TLP-304.notes: Not affected by prior BCG vaccination, unlike the skin test; sensitivity is reduced in advanced HIV, on high-dose steroids or biologics, and in children under 2 years; borderline results (0.35–0.99 IU/mL) have a higher chance of reverting; blood must reach the lab and be incubated within 16 hours.
TLP-304.src: CDC/NTCA 2020 latent TB testing guidance; WHO 2018 latent TB guidelines; India TB Elimination Programme (NTEP) guidelines; QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus package insert
TLP-304.retest: Repeat indeterminate or borderline results in 4–8 weeks; retest annually during biologic or JAK-inhibitor therapy or after known TB exposure.

TLP-305.name: Strongyloides stercoralis IgG
TLP-305.meas: Antibodies in the blood against Strongyloides stercoralis, a soil-transmitted worm that can live silently in the gut for decades.
TLP-305.sig: Strongyloides is common in India and usually harmless, but steroids, biologics or other immune-suppressing drugs can trigger a life-threatening hyperinfection. A blood antibody test is far more sensitive than a stool examination and is recommended before starting such treatment.
TLP-305.ind: A positive result indicates current or past Strongyloides infection and, because the worm persists indefinitely, is treated as current infection before immunosuppression; an equivocal result may reflect low antibody or cross-reaction with other worms (filaria, hookworm); a negative result makes infection unlikely but sensitivity is reduced in immunosuppressed patients.

fy.n: No Strongyloides antibodies were found, which makes a hidden infection with this worm unlikely and clears one important safety check before immune-suppressing treatment. If your immunity is already lowered the test can occasionally miss infection, so your doctor may add a stool test or, in high-risk situations, treat preventively.
fy.bhi: Your result is equivocal, which can reflect a low antibody level, a past treated infection, or cross-reaction with other worms such as filaria or hookworm. Because the consequences of missing Strongyloides before immune suppression are serious, your doctor may repeat the test, examine stool samples, or simply give a short, safe course of treatment.
fy.hi: Strongyloides antibodies were detected, which indicates infection with this soil-transmitted worm, probably acquired years ago through bare feet. It usually causes no symptoms, but it must be treated before you start steroids, biologics or similar medicines to prevent a serious flare-up. Treatment is a short course of tablets, and a follow-up antibody test in 6–12 months confirms clearance.

TLP-305.notes: Antibody falls slowly after successful treatment (a 40–50% drop in index by 6–12 months suggests cure); cross-reactivity with filariasis and other nematodes occurs; eosinophilia supports the diagnosis but is absent in many infected people on steroids.
TLP-305.src: CDC Strongyloides testing guidance; IDSA/ESCMID recommendations for screening before immunosuppression; Requena-Méndez et al., PLoS NTD 2013
TLP-305.retest: Repeat equivocal results in 4–6 weeks with stool examination; after treatment, recheck antibody at 6–12 months to confirm a falling index.

TLP-306.name: PIIINP (procollagen-III N-peptide)
TLP-306.alias: Procollagen III N-terminal propeptide, P3NP, PIIINP
TLP-306.meas: A fragment released into the blood when new type III collagen is being laid down, reflecting active scar formation (fibrosis) in the liver and other tissues.
TLP-306.sig: Long-term methotrexate can slowly scar the liver without changing routine liver enzymes. Serial PIIINP is the established non-invasive way to pick up this fibrosis early, so that the drug can be adjusted before permanent damage, and has largely replaced routine liver biopsy.
TLP-306.ind: Persistently raised PIIINP suggests progressive liver fibrosis on methotrexate (or other fibrotic liver disease); it is also raised by active arthritis, psoriatic joint inflammation, growth in children, recent fractures, wound healing, heart failure and kidney disease; low values have no clinical significance.

fy.n: Your PIIINP is in the normal range, which suggests methotrexate is not causing active scarring in your liver at present. This is a good sign for continuing treatment safely. Keeping alcohol to a minimum, managing weight and blood sugar, and attending the scheduled repeat tests protect your liver further.
fy.bhi: Your PIIINP is mildly raised. A single value here often reflects active joint inflammation, a recent injury, or normal variation rather than liver scarring, so it is not by itself a reason to stop methotrexate. Your doctor will repeat the test in 3 months; if it stays raised, a liver stiffness scan is the usual next step.
fy.hi: Your PIIINP is clearly raised, which may indicate ongoing scar formation in the liver related to methotrexate, although active arthritis, heart or kidney disease can also push it up. Your doctor will repeat the test, arrange a liver stiffness scan and review whether to reduce or change the medicine. Do not stop methotrexate on your own.

TLP-306.notes: Adult range shown (radioimmunoassay / UniQ); children and adolescents have much higher physiological values due to growth; not interpretable in active psoriatic arthritis, recent surgery or fracture; the BAD protocol flags pre-treatment > 8.0, or at least three values > 4.2 in 12 months, or two consecutive values > 8.0 as triggers for liver assessment.
TLP-306.src: British Association of Dermatologists 2016 methotrexate guideline; Maybury et al., Br J Dermatol 2014; manufacturer reference interval (Orion Diagnostica UniQ)
TLP-306.retest: Measure before starting methotrexate and every 3 months during therapy; a raised value should be repeated within 3 months and persistent elevation prompts transient elastography or hepatology referral.

TLP-307.name: Methaemoglobin (co-oximetry)
TLP-307.sample: Heparinised whole blood (arterial or venous, analysed promptly)
TLP-307.meas: The percentage of your haemoglobin that has been oxidised into a form that cannot carry oxygen.
TLP-307.sig: Dapsone and several other drugs oxidise haemoglobin, and the resulting methaemoglobin causes bluish lips, headache, breathlessness and fatigue while a standard pulse oximeter reads falsely reassuring. Measuring it directly by co-oximetry catches the problem before it becomes dangerous.
TLP-307.ind: Raised levels indicate drug-induced methaemoglobinaemia (dapsone, primaquine, local anaesthetics such as benzocaine/prilocaine, nitrates, sulphonamides), chemical exposure (aniline dyes, nitrites), or rare inherited enzyme deficiency; low or undetectable levels are normal.

fy.n: Your methaemoglobin is within the normal range, which means your blood is carrying oxygen normally and dapsone (or any other oxidising medicine) is not causing a significant problem at present. Continue the scheduled monitoring, and let your doctor know if you notice bluish lips or fingertips, headache or unusual breathlessness.
fy.bhi: Your methaemoglobin is mildly raised, a level often seen on dapsone that may cause mild tiredness, headache or bluish lips. It is not dangerous at this level, but it shows the drug is having an oxidising effect; the dose may be reviewed and the test repeated. Avoid adding other oxidising medicines without checking first.
fy.hi: Your methaemoglobin is significantly raised, which reduces the oxygen your blood can deliver and can cause bluish skin, breathlessness, headache, rapid heartbeat and, at high levels, confusion. This needs prompt medical attention: contact your doctor or the nearest emergency department today, take your medicine list, and do not take the next dose of dapsone until assessed. Effective treatment is available.

TLP-307.notes: Sample must be analysed within 1 hour (kept on ice) as methaemoglobin rises in stored blood; symptoms typically appear above 10–15%, and levels above 30% are dangerous; G6PD-deficient patients cannot be treated with methylene blue, which is why G6PD is checked alongside; infants under 6 months are more susceptible.
TLP-307.src: Cortazzo & Lee, Methemoglobinemia: A Review (2014); BAD guidelines on dapsone monitoring; Tintinalli's Emergency Medicine
TLP-307.retest: On dapsone: check at baseline and 2–4 weeks after starting or increasing dose, then as symptoms dictate; repeat immediately if cyanosis, breathlessness or headache develops.

clusters.name: Blood & Oxygen Delivery
clusters.caption: Whether your blood can carry enough oxygen, fight infection and clot when needed — the first system to show iron, vitamin or marrow trouble.

story.optimal: Your red cells, white cells and platelets are all within range: oxygen delivery and infection defence look sound, and there is no sign of iron or vitamin shortage.
story.borderline: One or two blood indices sit just outside range. This is usually early iron or vitamin shortage, a recent infection, or normal variation — worth watching rather than worrying about.
story.attention: Your blood picture needs attention. The flagged values point to a specific cause (iron, B12/folate, infection, or marrow output) that your doctor can confirm and treat.

clusters.rule: Status = worst flag among member parameters, except that a single borderline member leaves the cluster Optimal (two or more borderline, or any attention flag, colours it). Parameters with a null result are ignored.

clusters.name: Sugar & Insulin
clusters.caption: How efficiently your body moves glucose out of blood and into cells. Rising values here are the earliest chemical sign of type-2 diabetes developing.

story.optimal: Your sugar control is healthy: fasting glucose, the three-month average and insulin output are all in range, and your cells are responding to insulin normally.
story.borderline: Your sugar handling has begun to drift. This is the pre-diabetic window — silent, common in Indian adults, and the stage at which lifestyle change works best.
story.attention: Your sugar markers are in the diabetic or insulin-resistant range. This needs a doctor’s review now; it is manageable, and the earlier it is addressed the more of the damage is avoidable.

clusters.rule: Status = worst flag among member parameters, except that a single borderline member leaves the cluster Optimal (two or more borderline, or any attention flag, colours it). Parameters with a null result are ignored.

clusters.name: Heart & Blood Vessels
clusters.caption: Lipid quality — not just total cholesterol — plus inflammation drives long-term heart and stroke risk. Non-HDL and ApoB are the modern targets.

story.optimal: Your cholesterol fractions, triglycerides and vascular inflammation marker are in the protective range. Keep the habits that got them there.
story.borderline: Your lipid picture is borderline: not yet a treatment decision, but the trend matters. Diet, activity and weight are the levers, and a recheck in 3–6 months shows whether they are working.
story.attention: Your heart-risk markers are above target. Together with your other results, your doctor will estimate your 10-year risk and decide whether lifestyle alone is enough.

clusters.rule: Status = worst flag among member parameters, except that a single borderline member leaves the cluster Optimal (two or more borderline, or any attention flag, colours it). Parameters with a null result are ignored.

clusters.name: Liver & Digestion
clusters.caption: The liver, pancreas and gut process everything you eat and drink. Mild enzyme rises are usually fatty liver; the gut markers separate inflammation, infection and intolerance.

story.optimal: Your liver enzymes, bile pigments and digestive markers are all normal — no sign of fat build-up, inflammation or bile-flow problems.
story.borderline: One or more liver or digestive markers are mildly raised. In non-drinkers with weight or sugar issues this most often means early fatty liver, which reverses with weight loss.
story.attention: Your liver or digestive markers need attention. The pattern of enzymes and bile pigments points your doctor toward the cause — fatty liver, infection, medication, alcohol or bile obstruction.

clusters.rule: Status = worst flag among member parameters, except that a single borderline member leaves the cluster Optimal (two or more borderline, or any attention flag, colours it). Parameters with a null result are ignored.

clusters.name: Kidney & Fluid Balance
clusters.caption: How well your kidneys filter, whether they are leaking protein, and whether your salts and water balance are steady. Kidney damage is silent until late — these tests are the early warning.

story.optimal: Your kidneys are filtering normally, no protein or albumin is leaking into the urine, and your salt balance is steady.
story.borderline: A kidney or urine marker is slightly off. Early albumin leak or a mildly reduced filtration estimate is reversible when the driver — sugar, blood pressure, dehydration, painkillers — is addressed.
story.attention: Your kidney markers need attention: filtration is reduced or protein is leaking. Your doctor will confirm with a repeat test and look for the cause, since early treatment protects kidney function long-term.

clusters.rule: Status = worst flag among member parameters, except that a single borderline member leaves the cluster Optimal (two or more borderline, or any attention flag, colours it). Parameters with a null result are ignored.

clusters.name: Urine & Urinary Tract
clusters.caption: What the urine itself shows — infection, blood, sugar, crystals, concentration. The urinary tract’s own report card, distinct from how well the kidney filters.

story.optimal: Your urine is clear on every count: no infection, blood, protein, sugar or crystals, and normal concentration.
story.borderline: A urine finding is mildly abnormal — often hydration, a contaminated sample, menstruation or a mild infection. A clean-catch repeat usually settles it.
story.attention: Your urine shows a finding that needs follow-up — infection, blood or protein. The culture and kidney tests in this report point to the cause.

clusters.rule: Status = worst flag among member parameters, except that a single borderline member leaves the cluster Optimal (two or more borderline, or any attention flag, colours it). Parameters with a null result are ignored.

clusters.name: Bones, Minerals & Nutrition
clusters.caption: Vitamin D, B12, calcium and the minerals that keep bones, nerves and energy metabolism working. Deficiency is near-universal in urban Indian adults and is the easiest thing on this report to fix.

story.optimal: Your vitamin and mineral levels are adequate — your bones, nerves and energy metabolism have what they need.
story.borderline: One or more vitamins or minerals are in the insufficient zone — very common with indoor lifestyles and vegetarian diets, and readily corrected with diet or supplements.
story.attention: You have a clear deficiency that can affect bones, nerves, mood or energy. Correcting it under medical guidance is straightforward and often the highest-yield action on this report.

clusters.name: Thyroid & Metabolism Control
clusters.caption: The thyroid sets the pace of your metabolism — weight, energy, cholesterol, heart rate and mood all follow it. Antibodies show whether an autoimmune process is behind any change.

story.optimal: Your thyroid is working normally and is not contributing to any weight, energy or cholesterol symptoms.
story.borderline: Your thyroid is mildly under- or over-active (subclinical). Often it settles on its own; your doctor will usually repeat the test in 6–12 weeks before deciding on treatment.
story.attention: Your thyroid is clearly under- or over-active. This is very treatable and explains symptoms such as fatigue, weight change, cold or heat intolerance and raised cholesterol.

clusters.rule: Status = worst flag among member parameters, except that a single borderline member leaves the cluster Optimal (two or more borderline, or any attention flag, colours it). Parameters with a null result are ignored.

clusters.name: Hormones & Reproduction
clusters.caption: The pituitary–ovary/testis–adrenal axis that governs cycles, fertility, libido, energy and stress response. The pattern across hormones matters more than any single value.

story.optimal: Your reproductive and stress hormones are balanced for your age and sex.
story.borderline: One or more hormones sit outside the usual range. Timing in the cycle, stress, sleep and weight all shift these values, so a repeat at the right time is often the first step.
story.attention: Your hormone pattern points to a specific axis that needs attention — the combination of values narrows the cause, and a specialist can confirm it.

clusters.rule: Status = worst flag among member parameters, except that a single borderline member leaves the cluster Optimal (two or more borderline, or any attention flag, colours it). Parameters with a null result are ignored.

clusters.name: Immunity & Inflammation
clusters.caption: Whether your immune system is quiet, over-active against your own tissues (autoimmunity), or reacting to allergens. The antibody pattern names the process.

story.optimal: No sign of active inflammation or autoimmunity; your immune system looks appropriately quiet.
story.borderline: A low-level inflammatory or antibody signal is present. Low-titre results are common in healthy people and only matter alongside symptoms — your doctor will interpret them in context.
story.attention: Your immune markers show an active process. The specific antibodies that are positive point toward a diagnosis and may warrant referral to a specialist.

clusters.name: Infections & Immunity Status
clusters.caption: Which infections are present now, which you have had before, and which you are protected against by vaccination or past exposure.

story.optimal: No current infection was detected, and where immunity was tested you are protected.
story.borderline: An equivocal or low-level result needs a repeat or a confirmatory test before it can be called positive or negative.
story.attention: An infection or a lack of immunity was detected. Your doctor will decide on treatment, vaccination or precautions — and, where relevant, testing of your partner.

clusters.rule: Status = worst flag among member parameters, except that a single borderline member leaves the cluster Optimal (two or more borderline, or any attention flag, colours it). Parameters with a null result are ignored.

clusters.name: Clotting & Bleeding
clusters.caption: Whether your blood clots too slowly (bleeding risk before procedures) or too readily (thrombosis and pregnancy-loss risk).

story.optimal: Your clotting times and factors are normal — no bleeding tendency and no inherited clotting risk detected.
story.borderline: A clotting value is marginally outside range; this is often sample-related or medication-related and is usually repeated before any conclusion.
story.attention: Your clotting results need attention before any procedure or pregnancy planning; your doctor will identify the cause and, if needed, plan protective treatment.

clusters.rule: Status = worst flag among member parameters, except that a single borderline member leaves the cluster Optimal (two or more borderline, or any attention flag, colours it). Parameters with a null result are ignored.

clusters.name: Cancer Screening
clusters.caption: Screening markers raise a flag, they do not make a diagnosis. Most raised values have benign causes and are resolved by a follow-up test or scan.

story.optimal: Your screening markers are within range. Remember that a normal marker does not replace age-appropriate imaging or examination.
story.borderline: A marker is mildly raised. Benign causes (inflammation, infection, benign enlargement) are far more common than cancer at this level; a repeat or a scan usually settles it.
story.attention: A screening marker is clearly raised and needs prompt follow-up with the appropriate specialist and imaging. Raised does not mean cancer — but it does mean do not delay.

clusters.rule: Status = worst flag among member parameters, except that a single borderline member leaves the cluster Optimal (two or more borderline, or any attention flag, colours it). Parameters with a null result are ignored.

clusters.name: Genetics & Inherited Risk
clusters.caption: Conditions written into your DNA — carrier states, chromosome changes and inherited enzyme variants — that matter for you, for a pregnancy, or for your children.

story.optimal: No inherited variant or chromosomal change of concern was found in what was tested.
story.borderline: A carrier or variant result was found that matters only in combination (for example, with your partner’s result). Genetic counselling explains what it means for you.
story.attention: A genetic finding needs specialist counselling to understand its implications for you and any planned pregnancy.

clusters.rule: Status = worst flag among member parameters, except that a single borderline member leaves the cluster Optimal (two or more borderline, or any attention flag, colours it). Parameters with a null result are ignored.

clusters.name: Muscle & Recovery
clusters.caption: Enzymes released from muscle when it is stressed — by training load, injury, medication or inflammation.

story.optimal: Your muscle enzymes are normal — training load is being absorbed and there is no sign of muscle injury or drug effect.
story.borderline: Muscle enzymes are mildly raised, most often from recent hard exercise. A repeat after 48–72 hours of rest usually normalises it.
story.attention: Muscle enzymes are markedly raised — significant muscle breakdown. Stop training, hydrate, and see a doctor promptly, especially if urine is dark.

clusters.rule: Status = worst flag among member parameters, except that a single borderline member leaves the cluster Optimal (two or more borderline, or any attention flag, colours it). Parameters with a null result are ignored.

clusters.name: Medication Safety
clusters.caption: Whether the drug you are on is at the right level, and whether it is affecting the organs it is known to stress.

story.optimal: Your drug level and the organ-safety checks are in range — the medicine can continue as prescribed.
story.borderline: A safety marker or drug level is marginally off. Your prescriber may adjust the dose or shorten the monitoring interval.
story.attention: A safety check is outside the safe range. Do not stop the medicine on your own — contact your prescriber promptly for a dose review.
