rules.lead: Insulin resistance is established.
rules.text: Your pancreas is producing extra insulin to keep glucose looking normal. This "compensated" phase comes years before diabetes and is the point where weight loss, activity and cutting refined carbohydrate work best.
rules.next: Lifestyle programme now; repeat HOMA-IR and HbA1c in 3–6 months.

rules.lead: Pre-diabetes on both the fasting and the three-month test.
rules.text: Two independent measures agree that your sugar handling has drifted. Roughly a third of people in this band develop diabetes within five years without change — and most of that risk is removable.
rules.next: Structured lifestyle change; discuss with your doctor; recheck HbA1c at 3 months.

rules.lead: Your HbA1c is in the diabetic range.
rules.text: A single result in this range needs confirmation, but it should be acted on as if real. Diabetes is a management problem, not a verdict — the target-organ checks in this report tell you where you are starting from.
rules.next: See a physician within two weeks for confirmation and a management plan.

rules.lead: Low HDL with high triglycerides — the metabolic-syndrome lipid pattern.
rules.text: This pairing is the lipid fingerprint of insulin resistance. It produces small, dense LDL particles that are more plaque-forming than the LDL number alone suggests, so heart risk is higher than your cholesterol implies.
rules.next: Treat the insulin resistance (weight, carbohydrate, activity) — the lipids follow.

rules.lead: Your sugar and fat handling are drifting together.
rules.text: Raised HOMA-IR alongside raised triglycerides means the liver is converting excess carbohydrate into fat. One process, two clusters — fixing the insulin resistance improves both.
rules.next: Carbohydrate reduction and resistance exercise; recheck both in 3 months.

rules.pattern: Fatty liver as the metabolic engine
rules.lead: Fatty liver is likely, and it is both cause and consequence of your insulin resistance.
rules.text: A mildly raised ALT in someone with insulin resistance and no heavy alcohol use usually means fat accumulating in the liver (MAFLD). A fatty liver makes the body more insulin-resistant, which deposits more fat — a loop that weight loss of 7–10% breaks.
rules.next: Ultrasound abdomen ± FibroScan; weight-loss plan; repeat ALT in 3 months.

rules.lead: Two liver enzymes are raised together.
rules.text: ALT with GGT strengthens the fatty-liver interpretation and asks a second question — alcohol. Be honest with your doctor about intake; the pattern reverses with abstinence and weight loss.
rules.next: Review alcohol; ultrasound abdomen; repeat in 6–8 weeks.

rules.lead: Raised uric acid reinforces the metabolic-syndrome pattern.
rules.text: Urate rises with fructose and alcohol intake and with insulin resistance; it is also a gout and kidney-stone risk. It usually falls as the metabolic picture improves.
rules.next: Cut sugary drinks and alcohol; hydrate; recheck in 3 months.

rules.lead: Inflammation is multiplying your lipid risk.
rules.text: Raised hsCRP with above-target LDL roughly doubles the vascular risk that either would carry alone. Inflammation is the process that turns cholesterol into unstable plaque.
rules.next: Address weight, sleep, smoking and dental/gum health; repeat hsCRP in 4–6 weeks (must be free of acute illness).

rules.pattern: Vitamin D as a metabolic cofactor
rules.lead: Low vitamin D is worsening your insulin resistance — and is the easiest lever to pull.
rules.text: Vitamin D deficiency is near-universal in urban Indian adults and independently worsens insulin signalling and inflammation. Correcting it is inexpensive, safe under guidance, and often improves how you feel within weeks.
rules.next: Vitamin D replacement under medical guidance; recheck at 3 months.

rules.lead: Your thyroid is not the reason.
rules.text: A normal TSH rules the thyroid out as a driver of weight, cholesterol or sugar changes. The metabolic picture is lifestyle-and-insulin driven, which is good news: those are the levers you control.
rules.next: No thyroid action needed; annual recheck.

rules.lead: Sugar is beginning to affect your kidneys.
rules.text: Albumin leaking into urine is the earliest sign of diabetic kidney damage — and the stage at which blood-pressure and sugar control, and specific kidney-protective drugs, can halt it.
rules.next: Repeat ACR on two further samples over 3 months; doctor review for kidney-protective treatment.

rules.lead: Diabetes plus above-target non-HDL: your heart risk is now the priority.
rules.text: In diabetes, heart and vessel disease — not sugar itself — is what shortens life. Lipid targets are tighter for you than for the general population, and lifestyle alone may not reach them.
rules.next: Physician review of lipid-lowering therapy; LDL/non-HDL targets set for diabetic risk.

rules.lead: More atherogenic particles than your LDL suggests.
rules.text: ApoB counts particles; LDL measures cholesterol inside them. A high ApoB with a modest LDL means many small, dense particles — the kind that slip into artery walls most easily. ApoB is the number to track.
rules.next: Treat to an ApoB target; recheck in 3 months.

rules.lead: Lipoprotein(a) is raised — an inherited risk that lifestyle does not change.
rules.text: Lp(a) is set by your genes and stays roughly constant for life. It adds to heart and aortic-valve risk independently of LDL, so the rest of your lipid profile needs to be kept tighter to compensate. First-degree relatives should be tested once.
rules.next: One-time result — no need to repeat; tighter LDL target; inform family.

rules.lead: Raised homocysteine, most likely from low B12.
rules.text: Homocysteine damages the vessel lining and rises when B12 or folate is short — common on vegetarian diets. Replacing the vitamin usually brings it down within weeks.
rules.next: B12/folate replacement; repeat homocysteine at 3 months.

rules.lead: Your heart is under strain.
rules.text: NT-proBNP rises when the heart muscle is stretched — from high blood pressure, valve disease, weakened pumping or fluid overload. It is an early, sensitive signal and is also raised when the kidneys are not clearing it.
rules.next: Echocardiogram and cardiology review; check blood pressure and kidney function together.

rules.lead: Kidney filtration is down and protein is leaking — the kidney is taking the strain.
rules.text: These two together indicate that blood pressure or sugar has begun to damage the kidney filters. Both are modifiable; caught here, kidney decline can usually be slowed or stopped.
rules.next: Repeat in 3 months to confirm chronicity; blood-pressure and sugar control; nephrology review if persistent.

rules.lead: Iron-deficiency anaemia — small red cells and empty iron stores.
rules.text: Your body has run out of iron to make haemoglobin. In women this is usually menstrual loss or diet; in men and post-menopausal women, the source of loss must be found (usually the gut).
rules.next: Iron replacement; in men/post-menopausal women, gut evaluation for blood loss; recheck Hb at 4–6 weeks.

rules.lead: Iron stores are low even though haemoglobin is still normal.
rules.text: Ferritin falls first; haemoglobin falls last. You are in the window where fatigue, hair fall and poor exercise tolerance appear before anaemia does — and where replacing iron is quick and effective.
rules.next: Dietary iron ± supplement; recheck ferritin at 3 months.

rules.lead: Small red cells with normal iron stores — check for thalassaemia trait.
rules.text: Small red cells with adequate iron point away from iron deficiency and toward an inherited haemoglobin trait, common in India. Trait carriers are healthy but should not be given iron unnecessarily, and partners should be tested before pregnancy.
rules.next: Haemoglobin HPLC if not already done; partner screening if planning a family.

rules.lead: Large red cells with low B12 — a vitamin-driven anaemia.
rules.text: B12 shortage slows red-cell production and, if prolonged, affects nerves and memory. It is common on vegetarian diets and with acid-suppressing drugs or metformin, and responds well to replacement.
rules.next: B12 replacement (injections if absorption is the issue); recheck at 3 months; consider intrinsic-factor antibodies.

rules.lead: Anaemia with raised ferritin and CRP — inflammation is locking iron away.
rules.text: In chronic inflammation the body hides iron from circulation; iron tablets do not help and may harm. The treatment is finding and settling the inflammatory cause.
rules.next: Look for the inflammatory source (infection, autoimmune, gut); avoid oral iron until reviewed.

rules.lead: Your anaemia is linked to reduced kidney function.
rules.text: Kidneys make the hormone that drives red-cell production; as filtration falls, anaemia follows. Treating iron deficiency first and then, if needed, the hormone itself, restores energy.
rules.next: Nephrology review; iron studies; consider erythropoiesis-stimulating treatment.

rules.lead: Ferritin and iron saturation are both high — true iron overload is possible.
rules.text: Unlike the inflammation-driven ferritin rise, a high saturation means iron is actually accumulating and can damage the liver, heart and pancreas. It is treatable by removing blood.
rules.next: Repeat fasting; HFE genotype; liver assessment; haematology review.

rules.lead: Dengue confirmed with a falling platelet count.
rules.text: Platelets fall from day 3–4 of dengue and recover after day 7. The count itself is less important than the trend and the warning signs — abdominal pain, vomiting, bleeding, lethargy, a rising haematocrit.
rules.next: Daily CBC until platelets rise; hydrate; immediate review for any warning sign; no aspirin/ibuprofen.

rules.lead: Rising haematocrit with low platelets is a plasma-leak warning sign.
rules.text: In dengue, a rising haematocrit means fluid is leaking out of the blood vessels — the change that precedes severe dengue. This combination needs same-day medical assessment.
rules.next: Urgent clinical review; consider admission for fluid monitoring.

rules.lead: The white-cell and CRP pattern looks bacterial.
rules.text: High neutrophils with a markedly raised CRP favour a bacterial cause over dengue or a viral illness, which lowers white cells. This shifts the decision toward cultures and antibiotics.
rules.next: Blood/urine culture before antibiotics; physician review.

rules.lead: Low white cells and platelets — a viral pattern.
rules.text: Viral fevers (dengue, chikungunya, many others) suppress white cells and platelets. Antibiotics do not help; rest, fluids and watching the platelet trend do.
rules.next: Repeat CBC in 24–48 h; confirm with the specific viral tests in this report.

rules.pattern: Reduced filtration confirmed by cystatin C
rules.lead: Two independent estimates agree that kidney filtration is reduced.
rules.text: Creatinine can mislead in very muscular or very slim people; cystatin C does not depend on muscle. When both agree, the reduction is real and should be staged and followed.
rules.next: Repeat in 3 months to confirm chronic kidney disease; find and treat the cause; nephrology referral if eGFR < 45.

rules.lead: Reduced kidney function is now affecting bone-mineral hormones.
rules.text: As kidneys fail to activate vitamin D and clear phosphate, parathyroid hormone rises to compensate — at the cost of bone. This is manageable with vitamin D, phosphate control and diet.
rules.next: Nephrology review of phosphate, calcium and vitamin D management.

rules.lead: Your urine shows the signature of a bacterial infection.
rules.text: White cells plus nitrites in urine point to a urinary infection even before symptoms. The culture in this report identifies the organism and the right antibiotic.
rules.next: Await culture; antibiotics only as prescribed; increase fluids.

rules.lead: Blood and protein together in urine point to the kidney filter itself.
rules.text: Either alone can be innocent; together they suggest inflammation of the filtering units (glomerulus), which needs specialist assessment rather than watchful waiting.
rules.next: Repeat urinalysis with microscopy; nephrology referral if persistent.

rules.pattern: Potassium out of range with reduced eGFR
rules.lead: Potassium is rising as kidney function falls.
rules.text: Kidneys clear potassium; when they slow, it accumulates and can affect heart rhythm. Some blood-pressure drugs and salt substitutes push it higher.
rules.next: Same-day review if potassium is in the high band; medication and diet review.

rules.lead: The pattern suggests bile flow is obstructed rather than liver cells injured.
rules.text: Raised ALP with GGT and direct bilirubin points to the bile ducts — gallstones, a stricture or drug effect — rather than hepatitis. Imaging answers this quickly.
rules.next: Ultrasound abdomen; review medicines and supplements; hepatology if persistent.

rules.lead: A mild, isolated rise in indirect bilirubin is usually harmless Gilbert’s syndrome.
rules.text: With normal liver enzymes and normal direct bilirubin, this is most often an inherited, benign variation affecting 5–10% of people. It causes mild yellowing when fasting or unwell and needs no treatment.
rules.next: No action; mention it before anaesthesia or new medicines.

rules.lead: Your fibrosis score suggests the liver may be scarring.
rules.text: FIB-4 combines age, enzymes and platelets to estimate scarring. An intermediate or high score does not diagnose cirrhosis, but it moves you from "watch" to "assess" — a FibroScan gives the answer non-invasively.
rules.next: FibroScan (transient elastography); hepatology referral if high.

rules.pattern: Low albumin with liver enzyme change
rules.lead: Low albumin alongside raised enzymes suggests the liver’s manufacturing capacity is affected.
rules.text: Albumin is made only by the liver; when it falls, either liver function or nutrition is compromised. With raised enzymes, the liver itself is the likely reason.
rules.next: Hepatology review; INR and ultrasound; nutritional assessment.

rules.lead: Coeliac antibodies with iron deficiency — gluten may be damaging your gut lining.
rules.text: Iron that cannot be absorbed through an inflamed small bowel is a classic presentation of coeliac disease. Do not start a gluten-free diet before confirmation, or the biopsy becomes unreliable.
rules.next: Gastroenterology referral for confirmation (endoscopy/biopsy) while still eating gluten.

rules.lead: Your stool calprotectin says the bowel is inflamed.
rules.text: Calprotectin separates inflammatory bowel disease from irritable bowel syndrome. A raised value means the symptoms have an organic cause that colonoscopy can define — and treat.
rules.next: Gastroenterology referral; colonoscopy; repeat if borderline.

rules.lead: Your thyroid is under-active because your immune system is attacking it.
rules.text: Positive TPO antibodies with a raised TSH is Hashimoto’s thyroiditis — the commonest cause of hypothyroidism in Indian women. The antibodies predict that the thyroid will slow further, so treatment is usually started earlier than in antibody-negative cases.
rules.next: Endocrine review; repeat TSH/FT4 in 6 weeks; treat if TSH > 10 or symptoms/pregnancy planning.

rules.lead: An under-active thyroid may be behind your raised cholesterol.
rules.text: Low thyroid hormone slows LDL clearance. Correcting the thyroid often lowers LDL by 10–20% without any lipid drug — so the thyroid is treated first and lipids rechecked.
rules.next: Treat thyroid; repeat lipid profile 3 months after TSH normalises.

rules.lead: Your thyroid is over-active.
rules.text: A suppressed TSH with raised FT4 is overt hyperthyroidism — the cause of weight loss, palpitations, tremor, heat intolerance and anxiety. It is very treatable, and the antibody result points to the cause.
rules.next: Endocrine referral within 1–2 weeks; TRAb/uptake scan to define the cause.

rules.lead: Thyroid autoimmunity matters for conception and pregnancy.
rules.text: TPO antibodies with a TSH above the pregnancy target (2.5) are linked to miscarriage and to reduced fertility; treating to target before conception improves outcomes.
rules.next: Treat to TSH < 2.5 before trying to conceive; monitor each trimester.

rules.lead: Raised androgens with a high AMH — the biochemical pattern of PCOS.
rules.text: High AMH reflects many small follicles; raised free androgen explains acne, hair growth and irregular cycles. Insulin resistance is the usual driver, which is why the sugar cluster matters here.
rules.next: Gynaecology/endocrine review; pelvic ultrasound; insulin-resistance management.

rules.lead: Insulin resistance is driving your androgen excess.
rules.text: High insulin stimulates the ovary to make androgen and lowers SHBG, which frees more of it. Treating the insulin resistance — weight, activity, and sometimes metformin — reduces the androgen effect and restores cycles.
rules.next: Lifestyle programme; discuss insulin-sensitising treatment; recheck in 3–6 months.

rules.lead: Ovarian reserve is reduced — time matters.
rules.text: Low AMH with a raised FSH means fewer eggs remain. It does not mean pregnancy is impossible, but it shortens the window and changes fertility strategy — do not wait a year before seeking help.
rules.next: Fertility specialist review now; discuss egg freezing or treatment timing.

rules.lead: Raised prolactin with a normal thyroid needs its own explanation.
rules.text: Prolactin suppresses ovulation and libido and causes breast discharge. With the thyroid excluded, common causes are stress, medicines (antacids, antipsychotics) and a small benign pituitary growth.
rules.next: Repeat fasting, rested, off offending medicines; MRI pituitary if persistently raised.

rules.lead: Low testosterone with a high LH — the testes are under-producing.
rules.text: The pituitary is signalling hard but the testes are not responding: primary hypogonadism. This has different causes and treatment from the more common obesity-related low testosterone.
rules.next: Endocrine/andrology review; repeat 8 am testosterone; karyotype if indicated.

rules.lead: Low testosterone with low-normal LH and insulin resistance — a functional, reversible pattern.
rules.text: Excess weight and insulin resistance suppress the signal from the brain to the testes. Testosterone replacement is not the first answer; weight loss and sleep restore it in many men.
rules.next: Weight and sleep programme; repeat testosterone (8 am, fasting) in 3–6 months before considering treatment.

rules.lead: Your stress-hormone balance has shifted toward cortisol.
rules.text: A high cortisol-to-DHEA ratio is seen with sustained stress, poor sleep and over-training. It is not a disease, but it is a measurable reason for exhaustion, poor recovery and weight around the middle.
rules.next: Sleep, load and recovery review; repeat in 3 months.

rules.lead: Abnormal semen with a raised FSH points to the testis itself.
rules.text: High FSH means the testes are not responding to the pituitary’s signal — sperm production is impaired at source. Genetic testing may be recommended before assisted reproduction.
rules.next: Andrology review; repeat semen analysis after 3 months; Y-microdeletion and karyotype if severe.

rules.lead: ANA with anti-dsDNA is a lupus-pattern result.
rules.text: Anti-dsDNA is specific for systemic lupus, and with a positive ANA it makes the diagnosis likely. Kidney and blood-count checks in this report show whether organs are involved.
rules.next: Rheumatology referral; urinalysis, complement and CBC review.

rules.lead: RA factor with anti-CCP is the seropositive rheumatoid pattern.
rules.text: Anti-CCP is highly specific for rheumatoid arthritis and predicts joint damage; together with RA factor it warrants early treatment, which prevents deformity.
rules.next: Rheumatology referral within weeks; baseline joint X-rays.

rules.lead: A low-titre ANA on its own is usually not significant.
rules.text: Up to 15% of healthy people have a weak ANA. With negative specific antibodies and no inflammation, it does not indicate autoimmune disease; it matters only if symptoms develop.
rules.next: No action; repeat only if new symptoms.

rules.lead: Antiphospholipid antibodies — a treatable cause of clots and pregnancy loss.
rules.text: These antibodies make blood clot too readily and are one of the few proven, treatable causes of recurrent miscarriage. The result must be confirmed 12 weeks apart before it is called a syndrome.
rules.next: Repeat at 12 weeks; haematology/obstetric review; anticoagulation plan for pregnancy.

rules.lead: High IgE with eosinophils — an allergic or atopic signature.
rules.text: This pattern supports an allergic driver for eczema, asthma, rhinitis or urticaria. Component-resolved testing identifies which allergens, and parasites should be excluded when eosinophils are high.
rules.next: Allergen-specific testing; stool examination for parasites if eosinophils are markedly raised.

rules.lead: An abnormal protein band was found — this needs haematology follow-up.
rules.text: A monoclonal band is most often a benign condition (MGUS) that simply needs monitoring, but it must be characterised and myeloma excluded, especially with anaemia, kidney or bone findings.
rules.next: Haematology referral; free light chains, calcium, kidney function and skeletal survey.

rules.lead: Latent TB detected — this must be treated before any biologic or immunosuppressant.
rules.text: A positive IGRA means dormant TB bacteria are present. Suppressing the immune system without treating them first risks reactivation. This is a safety gate, not an illness.
rules.next: Chest X-ray; preventive TB therapy per physician before starting the planned drug.

rules.lead: Hepatitis B surface antigen is positive — you carry the virus.
rules.text: This may be a chronic infection acquired long ago. It is manageable, and monitoring or treatment protects the liver. Household and sexual contacts should be tested and vaccinated.
rules.next: Hepatology review; HBV DNA, HBeAg, liver assessment; vaccinate contacts.

rules.lead: You are not protected against hepatitis B — vaccination is recommended.
rules.text: No surface antibody and no infection means you have neither had the virus nor responded to a vaccine. Three doses give lifelong protection; healthcare workers and partners of carriers should not delay.
rules.next: Hepatitis B vaccination course; check anti-HBs 1–2 months after the last dose.

rules.lead: You are not immune to rubella — vaccinate before conceiving.
rules.text: Rubella in early pregnancy causes serious birth defects. One MMR dose, followed by a three-month wait before trying to conceive, closes this risk completely.
rules.next: MMR vaccination; avoid pregnancy for 1 month (3 months per Indian practice); recheck IgG.

rules.lead: Both syphilis tests are reactive — treatment and partner testing are needed.
rules.text: A reactive screening test confirmed by a specific treponemal test indicates syphilis, current or past. It is curable with penicillin, and treating it before or during pregnancy prevents transmission to the baby.
rules.next: Treatment per physician; partner notification and testing; repeat RPR titre to confirm cure.

rules.lead: Typhoid antibodies with raised liver enzymes — enteric fever with liver involvement.
rules.text: Typhoid commonly inflames the liver mildly; this settles with treatment. Blood culture, if sent before antibiotics, guides the antibiotic choice as resistance is common.
rules.next: Physician review for antibiotic therapy; blood culture; hydration.

rules.lead: Malaria antigen is positive — treat today.
rules.text: Malaria is a same-day treatment condition; the species (falciparum vs vivax) decides the drug and whether a course to prevent relapse is needed. Low platelets and haemoglobin are expected and recover with treatment.
rules.next: Immediate physician review; species-specific antimalarial; repeat smear to confirm clearance.

rules.lead: Hepatitis C antibody is positive — confirm and, if active, cure.
rules.text: Antibody shows exposure; a viral-load test shows whether infection is active. Active hepatitis C is now cured in over 95% of people with 8–12 weeks of tablets.
rules.next: HCV RNA; hepatology review; fibrosis assessment.

rules.pattern: Vitamin D deficiency with secondary PTH rise
rules.lead: Low vitamin D is now pulling calcium from your bones.
rules.text: When vitamin D is low, parathyroid hormone rises to keep blood calcium normal by drawing on bone. This is the biochemical stage before bone thinning — and it reverses fully with replacement.
rules.next: Vitamin D replacement; repeat vitamin D and PTH at 3 months; bone density if over 50.

rules.lead: High calcium with a non-suppressed PTH points to an over-active parathyroid gland.
rules.text: Calcium should switch PTH off; when it does not, one of the four small parathyroid glands is usually overactive. It causes stones, bone loss, fatigue and low mood, and is curable surgically.
rules.next: Endocrine referral; 24-h urine calcium, bone density, kidney ultrasound.

rules.lead: More than one nutrient is short — this is a dietary or absorption pattern, not a coincidence.
rules.text: Two or more deficiencies together usually mean a restricted diet, poor absorption (gut, acid-suppressing drugs, coeliac) or increased loss. Replacing them all, and asking why, restores energy faster than treating one at a time.
rules.next: Dietitian review; consider coeliac screen and gut evaluation; replace under guidance.

rules.lead: Your B12 deficiency is caused by autoimmune gastritis (pernicious anaemia).
rules.text: Antibodies against the stomach lining stop B12 being absorbed from food, so tablets will not work reliably — injections are needed, lifelong. The stomach should also be checked periodically.
rules.next: B12 injections; gastroenterology review for gastroscopy surveillance.

rules.lead: A clotting or platelet result raises bleeding risk for any planned procedure.
rules.text: A prolonged INR or low platelet count must be explained before a laser, peel, biopsy or surgery. Common causes are liver disease, medicines (aspirin, anticoagulants), vitamin K shortage or a sample artefact.
rules.next: Repeat to exclude artefact; medication review; defer elective procedures until reviewed.

rules.lead: An inherited clotting variant was found.
rules.text: This increases clot risk during pregnancy, on the combined pill, and after surgery or long travel. It does not need daily treatment, but it changes decisions at those moments and matters for first-degree relatives.
rules.next: Haematology counselling; avoid oestrogen-containing contraception; thromboprophylaxis plan for pregnancy/surgery.

rules.lead: Clotting factors are being consumed — a severe-illness warning.
rules.text: High D-dimer with falling platelets and fibrinogen indicates disseminated intravascular coagulation, which accompanies severe sepsis or severe dengue. This requires hospital care.
rules.next: Immediate hospital assessment.

rules.pattern: PSA raised with low free fraction
rules.lead: PSA is raised and the free fraction is low — this pattern needs urology review.
rules.text: A raised total PSA has many benign causes; a low free:total ratio makes a significant cause more likely. This is the combination that justifies MRI and, if needed, biopsy — a shared decision with your urologist.
rules.next: Urology referral; multiparametric MRI prostate.

rules.lead: PSA is raised but the free fraction is reassuring.
rules.text: A high free:total ratio favours benign enlargement or inflammation of the prostate over cancer. A repeat after 6–8 weeks (no cycling, no ejaculation for 48 h, no infection) often settles it.
rules.next: Repeat PSA in 6–8 weeks; urology review if still raised.

rules.lead: Cervical screening has flagged a change that needs a closer look.
rules.text: A high-risk HPV type or cell changes on the smear identify the small group of women who need colposcopy. Changes at this stage are pre-cancerous, not cancer, and are treated simply; this is exactly what screening is for.
rules.next: Colposcopy referral.

rules.lead: A screening tumour marker is raised — this needs follow-up, not alarm.
rules.text: Tumour markers rise with smoking, inflammation, benign cysts, liver disease and menstruation as often as with cancer. The right response is a targeted scan or repeat, guided by which marker is raised.
rules.next: Physician review; repeat in 4–6 weeks and imaging as indicated.

rules.lead: Muscle damage plus a stress-hormone shift — training load is not being absorbed.
rules.text: Raised CK shows muscle breakdown; a high cortisol:DHEA ratio shows the recovery system is behind. Together they are the biochemical picture of over-reaching, which precedes over-training and injury.
rules.next: Reduce load for 1–2 weeks; prioritise sleep and protein; repeat CK and cortisol/DHEA.

rules.lead: Iron stores are low — performance drops before haemoglobin does.
rules.text: Endurance training increases iron loss and demand. Ferritin below 30–50 impairs oxygen delivery and recovery even with a normal haemoglobin; athletes are typically treated at a higher threshold.
rules.next: Iron replacement under guidance; recheck ferritin at 8–12 weeks.

rules.lead: CK is markedly raised — if you take a statin or fibrate, tell your doctor today.
rules.text: A high CK can be from hard exercise, injury or a viral illness, but in anyone on cholesterol-lowering tablets it must be reviewed promptly as a possible drug effect.
rules.next: Repeat after 48–72 h rest; medication review; check kidney function.

rules.lead: A safety marker for your medicine is outside range.
rules.text: Systemic dermatology drugs (isotretinoin, methotrexate, cyclosporine, dapsone) each stress a specific organ. This result is the monitoring doing its job — the dose or the drug may need adjusting.
rules.next: Do not stop the drug yourself; contact your prescriber for a dose review and repeat test.

rules.lead: Cyclosporine level or kidney function is off — dose review needed.
rules.text: Cyclosporine narrows kidney blood vessels; a creatinine rise of 30% from baseline, high potassium or high blood pressure are the signals to reduce the dose.
rules.next: Prescriber review; repeat creatinine, potassium, blood pressure.

rules.lead: Dapsone is affecting your red cells.
rules.text: Dapsone can break down red cells or convert haemoglobin to a form that cannot carry oxygen, especially with G6PD deficiency. Blue-tinged lips, breathlessness or dark urine need same-day review.
rules.next: Prescriber review; check G6PD status; dose reduction or drug change.

rules.lead: Pregnancy test is positive — the planned medicine must not be started.
rules.text: Isotretinoin, methotrexate and several systemic dermatology drugs cause serious birth defects. A positive hCG is an absolute stop for these; discuss safe alternatives with your dermatologist and obstetrician.
rules.next: Do not start/continue the drug; obstetric review.

rules.lead: Everything measured is within range.
rules.text: Every cluster in this package is green. That is a baseline worth keeping — the value of this report is the comparison next year, when a drifting number can be caught while it is still just a number.
rules.next: Repeat the package annually, or sooner if symptoms change.

rules.lead: One value is mildly outside range, with everything else normal.
rules.text: An isolated borderline result in an otherwise normal report is usually biological variation, hydration, a recent meal or exercise, or a minor illness. It rarely indicates disease on its own.
rules.next: Repeat that test in 6–12 weeks; no other action unless symptoms.
